lesson.text: Locks and deadlocks

A **lock** (mutex) lets only one thread enter a critical section at a time. Locks fix races but add costs: they serialize work (hurting throughput) and can cause **deadlock**, where threads wait on each other forever. The classic recipe: thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2, thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1. Defenses: acquire locks in one global order, hold them briefly, never call unknown code or do I/O while holding one, and use timeouts. Related hazards are **livelock** (threads keep reacting without progress) and **starvation** (one thread never gets its turn).
Prefer designs that avoid sharing

items: **Immutability**: data that never changes can be read by any number of threads without locks.
**Share-nothing / message passing**: each worker owns its data; communicate via queues or channels.
**Atomic operations** and database transactions for the few truly shared counters or records; let the database enforce invariants (unique constraints, `UPDATE ... WHERE stock > 0`).
**Idempotent** operations so retries and duplicates do no harm.

lesson.text: Misconceptions

items: "It passed my tests, so it is thread-safe." Races depend on timing; absence of failure proves little. Use race detectors and stress tests.
"async makes code faster." It improves waiting-heavy workloads; it does not speed CPU-bound work.
"More threads means more speed." Contention, context switches and locks can make it slower.

lesson.text: Agents add `async`, threads or a quick `Lock` freely, and often miss check-then-act races, forget to `await`, or hold a lock across a network call. Tell the agent what is shared and what the invariants are ('stock must never go negative'). Ask it to enumerate the interleavings that could break them, prefer immutable data or database-level guarantees, and run tests with a race detector (for example `go test -race`) and repeated stress runs.

patterns.signal: Code reads shared state, checks it (`stock > 0`), then writes; overselling or double-booking shows up rarely
patterns.why: Make check and write one operation: `UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`, compare-and-swap, or a unique constraint. Check-then-act is a race whatever the language.

patterns.signal: Several threads increment a shared counter or flag and the total comes out too low
patterns.why: An atomic increment or CAS is lock-free and cheap for one word. Once an invariant spans several fields, atomics compose badly; switch to a lock around the whole update.

patterns.signal: An invariant spans several fields or objects (balance plus ledger entry) touched by multiple threads
patterns.why: One lock guarding every read and write of the related fields keeps them consistent. Locks serialise work and can deadlock, so keep the critical section short and never call unknown code inside.

patterns.signal: Two threads hang forever, each holding one lock and waiting for the other's (`accounts[1]`, `accounts[2]`)
patterns.why: Always acquire locks in one agreed order, for example by account id, so a wait cycle cannot form. Lock timeouts only detect deadlock; ordering prevents it.

patterns.signal: A lock is held across a network call, disk read or `await`, and throughput collapses under load
patterns.why: Do the slow I/O outside the lock, then lock only to read or apply the result, revalidating if needed. Every millisecond inside the lock serialises all waiting threads.

patterns.signal: One part produces work (requests, log lines, chunks) faster or slower than another part consumes it
patterns.why: A thread-safe queue decouples the two sides and gives each worker data it owns. Bound it so a fast producer blocks or sheds load instead of exhausting memory.

patterns.signal: Read-mostly configuration or lookup data is shared by many threads and someone proposes a lock on every read
patterns.why: Readers use an immutable object with no locks; a writer builds a new copy and publishes it with one atomic reference swap. Costs a full copy per update, so it suits rare writes.

patterns.signal: Independent I/O calls are awaited one after another, so latency is their sum
patterns.why: Start them together and join with `Promise.all` or a task group, so latency becomes the slowest one. Cap concurrency for large fan-outs and decide how one failure cancels the rest.

patterns.signal: One CPU-heavy request (compression, image resize, `gzipSync`) freezes an async server for every user
patterns.use: Offload CPU work to a worker pool
patterns.why: The event loop is one thread, so CPU-bound work blocks all other tasks. Use async APIs or worker threads or processes; async alone speeds up waiting, not computing.

keyPoints: Concurrency is overlapping tasks; parallelism is simultaneous execution; I/O-bound and CPU-bound work need different tools.
Read-modify-write and check-then-act on shared state are race conditions; tests rarely catch them.
Locks protect critical sections but can cause deadlock; use a global lock order and short critical sections.
The safest concurrency avoids sharing: immutable data, message passing, and database-enforced invariants.

quiz.q: Two request handlers each read `stock = 1`, check `stock > 0`, then write `stock = stock - 1`. Both succeed and you oversell. What kind of bug is this and what is the sturdiest fix?
options: A deadlock; add request timeouts so a stuck handler gives up
A visibility bug; mark the stock variable as volatile
A check-then-act race; do one conditional atomic update
An overflow; store the stock count as a 64-bit integer
quiz.explain: Between the check and the write another request can run, so both pass the check. Performing the check and update as one atomic operation (`UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`) removes the window. Volatile makes writes visible but does not make check-then-act atomic.

quiz.q: Thread A locks `accounts[1]` then waits for `accounts[2]`; thread B locks `accounts[2]` then waits for `accounts[1]`. Both hang. What is the standard way to prevent this?
options: Add more worker threads so one of them can finish first
Make every lock re-entrant so a thread can re-acquire it
Swap the locks for async/await so no thread ever blocks
Acquire locks in one global order, such as by account id
quiz.explain: A consistent acquisition order makes a circular wait impossible. Extra threads only add more waiters, re-entrancy only helps when the same thread re-locks, and async code still needs to protect shared state.

quiz.q: An async Node server slows to a crawl for all users whenever one user uploads a large file that is compressed with `zlib.gzipSync` inside the request handler. What is the most likely cause?
options: Async functions cannot read file uploads larger than the heap
The synchronous compression blocks the single event-loop thread
Node caps pending promises at 100, so later requests queue up
gzip is O(n^2), so one large file outweighs all small ones
quiz.explain: Cooperative concurrency relies on tasks yielding at awaits. A synchronous CPU-heavy call never yields, so every other request waits. Use the async zlib API (which runs on a worker pool) or a worker thread.

quiz.q: Which workload gains the most from replacing sequential `await` calls with `Promise.all` on a single thread?
options: Hashing three large buffers with a pure-JavaScript SHA-256
Multiplying three large matrices held in memory
Fetching profile, orders and ads from three remote services
Sorting three large in-memory arrays of numbers
quiz.explain: The three requests spend most of their time waiting on the network, so overlapping them cuts total latency to roughly the slowest one. The other options are CPU-bound JavaScript and would not overlap on one thread.

quiz.q: A team shares a configuration object across threads and wants to avoid locks. Which design removes the need for locking on reads?
options: Make it immutable and publish changes by swapping in a new instance
Guard every read with one global lock held for the program's life
Let threads edit the shared object in place, keeping writes small
Run reader threads at a lower priority than the writer thread
quiz.explain: Immutable data can be read concurrently with no synchronization because nobody mutates it; updates publish a fresh copy by swapping one reference. In-place edits create races, and priorities do not provide safety.

quiz.q: Under load, throughput on `updateCart` collapses. A profile shows most threads waiting on one mutex that is held while the code makes an HTTP call to a price service. What should you reach for?
options: Acquire the locks in one global order across every caller
Replace the mutex with an atomic counter on the cart total value
Wrap the lock acquisition in a retry loop with a short timeout
Do the HTTP call outside the lock, then lock only to apply it
quiz.explain: Slow I/O inside a critical section serialises every waiting thread, so move it out and lock only to apply the result. Lock ordering prevents deadlock, which is not the symptom here.

exam.q: An agent's CSV loader parses values with `parseFloat` and skips missing ones with `if (x === NaN) continue;`. Missing values are never skipped. What is wrong?
options: NaN is not equal to anything, itself included; use Number.isNaN(x)
parseFloat returns the string 'NaN', so === fails on the type check
NaN only comes from division by zero, never from failed parsing
Float equality needs a tolerance, so compare with Math.abs(x - NaN)
exam.explain: NaN compares unequal to every value, including another NaN, so `x === NaN` is always false. `Number.isNaN(x)` is the correct test. parseFloat returns the number NaN for unparsable input, and a tolerance does not help because any arithmetic with NaN is NaN.

exam.q: A log search feature takes a list of 10,000 error codes and checks each of 5 million log lines with `code in error_codes` (a list). It takes minutes. What is the smallest change with the biggest win?
options: Run the loop on a machine with a faster CPU and more RAM
Sort the log lines first so matching lines are adjacent
Convert the error codes to a set once, before the loop
Read the log file in larger chunks to reduce disk I/O
exam.explain: Membership in a list is O(10,000) per line; a set makes it expected O(1), cutting the work by orders of magnitude. The other options do not change the growth rate, and sorting adds work.

exam.q: You ask an agent for a function that returns the k largest items from a stream of 100 million numbers, using little memory. Which approach should you expect or request?
options: Collect every number in a list, sort it descending, and take the first k
Keep a size-k min-heap; replace its minimum when a larger value arrives
Count occurrences in a hash map, then pick the k largest keys
Recursively split the stream in half and merge the top halves
exam.explain: A size-k min-heap uses O(k) memory and O(log k) work per item. Sorting everything needs O(n) memory and O(n log n) time, and a hash map grows with the number of distinct values.

exam.q: A service fits UTF-8 text into a 100-byte SMS field by cutting the byte array at 100. Some messages now end with the replacement character `U+FFFD`. What happened?
options: The SMS gateway rejects every non-ASCII character it receives
UTF-8 needs a terminating null byte, which the cut removed
The text was really UTF-16, so each byte became half a character
The cut split a multibyte UTF-8 character, leaving invalid bytes
exam.explain: A non-ASCII character spans 2 to 4 bytes, so a fixed byte offset can land inside one; the decoder then replaces the partial sequence with U+FFFD. Truncate on a character (ideally grapheme) boundary instead. A gateway that rejected all non-ASCII would break every such message, not just some endings.

exam.q: Your dependency installer is given packages A, B and C, where A needs B, B needs C, and C needs A. The agent's recursive resolver hangs with growing memory. What is the likely defect and fix?
options: Raise the recursion limit so the resolver can finish the chain
Store the graph as an adjacency matrix instead of a list
Track nodes on the current path and report the cycle as an error
Resolve packages in alphabetical order instead of by dependency
exam.explain: Following edges around a cycle without remembering visited nodes recurses forever. Raising limits only delays the crash and changing the representation changes nothing; the cycle must be detected and surfaced as an error.

exam.q: A route planner uses BFS to find the cheapest route between cities, where each road has a different non-negative toll. It returns routes with the fewest roads, not the lowest total toll. What should it use instead?
options: Depth-first search, which explores each route fully before the next
Dijkstra's algorithm, which handles non-negative edge weights
BFS with a stack instead of a queue, to reach cheap roads sooner
Greedy: always take the cheapest road leaving the current city
exam.explain: BFS minimizes the number of edges, which matches cost only when every edge weighs the same. Dijkstra's algorithm is the greedy-correct choice for non-negative weights. Taking the cheapest next road can lead into an expensive dead end, and DFS has no cost guarantee.

exam.q: You must fit the most non-overlapping meetings into one room. An agent picks the shortest meetings first, and your brute-force test finds a counterexample. Which greedy rule is provably optimal?
options: Pick the meeting that starts earliest, then the next compatible one
Pick the shortest meeting, then the next shortest compatible one
Pick the meeting that ends earliest, then the next compatible one
Pick the meeting with the fewest conflicts, then repeat
exam.explain: Choosing the earliest finish time leaves the most room for the rest, and an exchange argument proves it optimal. Earliest start, shortest first and fewest conflicts all have known counterexamples, which is why greedy rules must be proven or tested against brute force.

exam.q: A service function gets a settings dict from its caller, adds default keys to it and returns it. Later, the caller's own dict contains unexpected keys. What principle was violated, and what is the fix?
options: Dicts are unordered, so new keys can appear in any caller's dict
It mutated the caller's object; copy the dict or build a new one
The dict was garbage collected early and rebuilt with defaults
The function should use recursion to merge nested defaults
exam.explain: Passing an object passes a reference to the same data, so in-place edits are visible to the caller. Returning a new dict (for example `{**defaults, **settings}`) avoids the surprise.

exam.q: A teammate says: 'Python is interpreted, so it never compiles anything.' Which statement about CPython is accurate?
options: Correct: CPython executes source text line by line with no compile step
It compiles source to bytecode, then interprets that bytecode
It compiles every module to machine code before running it
It compiles code only when type hints are present in the file
exam.explain: CPython first compiles source to bytecode (cached in `.pyc` files) and then interprets the bytecode. Recent versions add an optional experimental JIT for hot code, but nothing is compiled to machine code ahead of time. 'Compiled versus interpreted' describes an implementation, not a language.

exam.q: A Java microbenchmark shows version B of a parsing function is 3x slower than version A, from one run each of 100 iterations in a fresh JVM. What should you do before believing it?
options: Accept it, since 100 iterations are enough to average out noise
Rerun with a smaller input to see whether the gap shrinks
Compare bytecode sizes, since smaller bytecode runs faster
Rerun with warm-up and many repetitions in a harness such as JMH
exam.explain: JIT warm-up, caching and noise can dominate a single short cold run. A harness with warm-up and repeated measurements produces comparable steady-state numbers.

exam.q: An async endpoint validates a coupon, then in a separate step marks it as used. Under load, the same single-use coupon is accepted twice. Which fix is most robust?
options: Make check-and-mark atomic in the database, e.g. a conditional update
Add a short sleep between validating the coupon and marking it used
Run more server instances so each request completes sooner
Re-check the coupon in application code right after marking it used
exam.explain: The gap between check and act is the race window; sleeping or re-checking in application code still leaves interleavings. Atomicity enforced by the database (a conditional update or a unique constraint on redemption) closes it even across multiple server instances.

exam.q: A signed 32-bit counter of milliseconds since service start is used to compute uptime. After roughly 25 days the service reports negative uptime. What is the cause and the right fix?
options: Float rounding error; store the uptime as a double instead
The garbage collector reset the counter during a full GC
The counter was stored as UTF-16 text and misparsed
Signed 32-bit overflow after 2^31 ms; use a 64-bit integer
exam.explain: 2^31 milliseconds is about 24.8 days, after which the value wraps to the most negative number. A 64-bit counter lasts about 292 million years.

exam.q: A teammate proposes holding a lock while calling a remote payment API 'to be safe', since it guarantees ordered updates to the account record. What is the main risk?
options: Remote calls are forbidden inside critical sections in most languages
The lock lets the API calls run in parallel and reorder updates
Contenders stall for the API's latency, and a hung call blocks them all
The lock may be released before the API's response arrives
exam.explain: Critical sections should be short and free of I/O, because their duration directly becomes waiting time for all contenders, and a slow or hung call can block them indefinitely. Better: make the call outside the lock and reconcile with an atomic update or idempotency key.

exam.q: A Python service (standard build, with the GIL) resizes images in pure-Python code using a pool of 8 threads on an 8-core machine, and sees almost no speedup over one thread. Why, and what helps?
options: The GIL runs one thread's bytecode at a time; use processes
Eight threads are too few; raise the pool size to 64 threads
Resizing is I/O-bound, so switching to async/await will help
Thread pools run tasks one by one by design; use raw threads
exam.explain: The work is CPU-bound, and in the standard build the GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. A process pool (or native code that releases the GIL, or the free-threaded build) gives real parallelism. More threads add contention, and async only helps waiting-heavy work.

exam.q: What does this program print?
exam.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(len(a))
options: It raises a NameError
exam.explain: `b = a` binds a second name to the same list object; it does not copy it. `append` mutates that one list, so `a` sees four items. Use `a.copy()` or `list(a)` when you need an independent list.

exam.q: Order these growth rates from slowest-growing to fastest-growing as n gets large.
steps: `O(1)`: hash table lookup
`O(log n)`: binary search
`O(n)`: linear scan
`O(n log n)`: comparison sort
`O(n^2)`: comparing every pair
`O(2^n)`: trying every subset
exam.explain: Constant beats logarithmic, which beats linear. `n log n` sits just above linear, quadratic grows far faster, and exponential outgrows every polynomial. At n = 1,000, log n is about 10, n^2 is a million and 2^n has over 300 digits.

exam.q: This binary search returns -1 for some targets that are in the sorted list, for example `search([5], 5)`. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: `hi` is inclusive (`len(xs) - 1`), so when `lo == hi` one candidate is still left to check. `while lo < hi` stops before checking it. With inclusive bounds the loop must be `while lo <= hi`.

exam.q: A JVM service starts cold and gets faster under load. Order what happens to a hot method from source code to fast execution.
steps: `javac` compiles the source to bytecode ahead of time
The JVM starts by interpreting that bytecode
The runtime profiles which methods run often and with which types
The JIT compiles the hot methods to machine code using those observed types
Later calls run the compiled machine code: the warm-up is over
exam.explain: Java is compiled twice: to bytecode before shipping, and selectively to machine code at runtime. The JIT can only compile hot code after it has interpreted it long enough to observe it, which is why benchmarks need warm-up before their numbers mean anything.

exam.q: Order the steps of a tracing garbage collection cycle.
steps: Find the roots: stack variables and globals
Mark every object reachable by following references from the roots
Treat every unmarked object as garbage
Reclaim the memory of the unmarked objects for reuse
exam.explain: A tracing collector decides liveness by reachability from the roots, so marking must start from the roots and finish before anything is freed. This is also why GC does not prevent leaks: an ever-growing cache is still reachable, so it is marked and never reclaimed.

exam.q: This function should return the fewest hops from `start` to `goal`. With `graph = {"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["D"], "C": ["E"], "D": [], "E": ["D"]}`, `shortest_hops(graph, "A", "D")` returns 3 instead of 2. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 7 uses `queue.pop()`, which takes from the right end, so the deque acts as a stack and the search runs depth-first. It reaches D through C and E (3 hops) and marks it seen before the 2-hop path via B. BFS needs first-in, first-out order: `queue.popleft()`.

exam.q: This function should keep only the `k` largest numbers from a huge stream in O(k) memory. On 100 million numbers it runs out of memory and returns far more than `k` items. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 9 pushes the larger value without removing the current minimum, so the heap keeps growing past `k` toward the size of the stream. It must replace the minimum: `heapq.heapreplace(heap, x)` (pop the smallest, then push `x`), which keeps the heap at size `k` with O(log k) work per item.

exam.q: In JavaScript, what does this print? (`é` here is the single code point U+00E9.)
exam.code:
const s = "café🚀";
console.log(s.length);
exam.explain: JavaScript `length` counts UTF-16 code units. `c`, `a`, `f` and `é` take one unit each, and the rocket (U+1F680, outside the Basic Multilingual Plane) takes a surrogate pair of two, so 6. 5 is the number of code points, and 9 is the UTF-8 byte count (1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 4).

title: Systems & the Web
tagline: What actually happens between your code, the OS, the network, and the data.
intro: Every program you ship runs as a process on an operating system, talks over a network, stores data in a database, and faces hostile input. AI agents write code that looks right in isolation, but they routinely get these system-level details wrong: leaked file descriptors, unsafe retries, missing indexes, string-built SQL. This section gives you the mental models to spot those mistakes in review.

topics.title: Operating Systems Essentials
topics.summary: Processes, threads, file descriptors, syscalls, signals and environment variables: what your program really runs on.

lesson.text: Your server works on your laptop, then in production it dies with `Too many open files`, or it ignores a deploy because it never shuts down cleanly. These are operating system problems, not logic bugs. The OS is the layer that shares one machine among many programs, and every program you write talks to it constantly, usually without you noticing.
Processes and threads

A **process** is a running program with its own private virtual address space, its own file descriptor table, and its own environment. Processes are isolated: one process cannot read another's memory, so a crash in one does not corrupt another. A **thread** is a unit of execution inside a process. Threads in the same process share memory, which makes communication cheap but also makes data races possible. The kernel schedules threads onto CPU cores, switching between them many times per second (a **context switch**).

items: Process: isolation, own memory, expensive to create, communicate via pipes, sockets, files.
Thread: shared memory, cheap to create, needs locks or message passing to be safe.
Async/event-loop code (Node, asyncio) runs many tasks on one thread by never blocking; it helps with waiting on I/O, not with CPU-heavy work.

lesson.text: Syscalls: the only door to the kernel

User programs cannot touch disks, networks or other processes directly. They ask the kernel through **system calls** such as `open`, `read`, `write`, `fork`, `execve`, `socket`, `mmap`. A syscall crosses from user mode into kernel mode, which is far more expensive than a normal function call. Standard library functions like Python's `open()` or Node's `fs.readFile` are wrappers over syscalls. This is why reading a file one byte at a time is slow: you pay the syscall cost per byte.
File descriptors: everything is a handle

On Unix-like systems, an open file, a pipe, and a network socket are all referenced by a small integer called a **file descriptor** (fd). Each process starts with 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout) and 2 (stderr). The OS caps how many fds a process may hold (`ulimit -n`, often 1024 by default on Linux). If you open sockets or files and never close them, you eventually hit the cap and every new `open` or `accept` fails. This is a **file descriptor leak**.
Signals and graceful shutdown

A **signal** is a small asynchronous notification sent to a process. `SIGTERM` (15) politely asks it to exit and can be handled; `SIGINT` is Ctrl+C; `SIGKILL` (9) cannot be caught or ignored and kills immediately, with no cleanup. When Kubernetes or a process manager stops your service, it sends `SIGTERM`, waits a grace period, then sends `SIGKILL`. A well-behaved server catches `SIGTERM`, stops accepting new requests, finishes in-flight ones, flushes buffers, and exits.

import signal, sys

def shutdown(signum, frame):
    server.stop_accepting()
    server.drain(timeout=20)
    sys.exit(0)

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, shutdown)

lesson.caption: SIGTERM starts the clock: stop accepting, let in-flight requests finish, and exit well inside the grace period, because SIGKILL does no cleanup.

lesson.text: Environment variables

Each process has a set of key-value strings called its **environment**, inherited by child processes at creation. This is the standard way to pass configuration (ports, database URLs, feature flags) into a program without baking it into code. Two rules matter: values are always strings (so `"false"` is truthy in many languages if you forget to parse it), and changes in a child never propagate back to its parent. Running `export FOO=1` in one terminal does not affect another.

Common misconceptions: threads are not always faster (the Python GIL, lock contention and context switching can make more threads slower); `kill` does not necessarily kill, it sends a signal, which defaults to `SIGTERM`; and a zombie process is a finished child whose parent has not yet collected its exit status, not a running one.

Agents write code that passes a single test run, so they rarely think about resource lifetimes. In review, check that every opened file, socket, DB connection and subprocess is closed on all paths (context managers, `try/finally`), that long-running services handle `SIGTERM`, and that secrets come from the environment rather than being hard-coded. When debugging, tell the agent the exact error and ask it to run `lsof -p <pid>` or `ulimit -n` rather than guessing.
Useful first-aid commands: `ps aux` (what is running), `lsof -i :8080` (who owns a port), `strace -c` or `dtruss` (which syscalls a program makes), `env` (what your process inherited).

patterns.signal: Deploys drop in-flight requests, or the orchestrator has to SIGKILL the service after the grace period
patterns.why: Catch SIGTERM, stop accepting work, drain in-flight requests, flush and close, then exit. Keep the drain shorter than the grace period, because SIGKILL cannot be caught.

patterns.signal: A service runs for hours, then fails with `Too many open files` while CPU and memory look normal
patterns.why: Close files, sockets and pipes on every path with `try/finally`, `using` or `with`. Descriptors are a per-process limit; raising `ulimit` only delays a leak.

patterns.signal: One misbehaving worker or plugin must not crash or corrupt the others
patterns.why: Processes get isolated memory, so a crash stays contained and the OS reclaims its resources. You pay in memory and IPC cost, since data must be copied or shared explicitly.

patterns.signal: Tasks need to share a large in-memory data set and hand work to each other cheaply
patterns.why: Threads share the address space, so no copying or IPC. Every shared mutable value now needs synchronization, and one thread's crash takes down the whole process.

patterns.signal: Two threads update a shared counter without a lock and the total is sometimes too low
patterns.why: `count++` is read-modify-write; interleaved threads lose updates. A mutex or atomic increment makes it indivisible. Keep critical sections short to limit contention.

patterns.signal: A profile or `strace` shows millions of tiny `read`/`write` syscalls and the I/O loop is slow
patterns.why: Each syscall crosses into the kernel and costs far more than a function call. A buffer turns many small calls into few large ones. Flush explicitly where durability or latency matters.

patterns.signal: A producer outpaces its consumer and memory grows steadily in an in-process queue
patterns.why: A bounded queue blocks, slows or rejects the producer when full, so overload becomes visible instead of an eventual OOM. You must choose: block, drop or shed with an error.

patterns.signal: Thread-per-connection server runs out of memory with thousands of mostly idle connections
patterns.why: One thread multiplexes many sockets via `epoll`/`kqueue`, so idle connections cost almost nothing. CPU-heavy or blocking calls on the loop stall everyone; offload them to a worker pool.

patterns.signal: URLs, ports and feature flags are hardcoded and differ between staging and production builds
patterns.why: Same artifact, different config per environment. Values are inherited strings read at start, so parse and validate them on boot and fail fast; changes need a restart.

keyPoints: A process owns isolated memory and resources; threads share a process's memory and need synchronization.
Programs reach the kernel only through syscalls, which are costly, so batch and buffer I/O.
Files, pipes and sockets are all file descriptors, a limited resource that must be closed on every code path.
SIGTERM allows graceful shutdown; SIGKILL cannot be caught.
Environment variables are inherited, string-typed configuration.

quiz.q: A service runs fine for hours, then every new connection fails with `Too many open files`. Memory and CPU look normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: Sockets or files are opened but not closed on some code path (an fd leak)
The kernel ran out of physical RAM and is refusing new allocations
Thread context switches are starving the accept loop of CPU time
A client disconnected early and the process received SIGPIPE
quiz.explain: Sockets and files consume file descriptors, which have a per-process cap. Normal memory and CPU with this specific error points to leaked fds, not RAM, scheduling or a single signal.

quiz.q: Why does a container orchestrator send SIGTERM before SIGKILL when stopping your service?
options: SIGTERM is delivered faster, so shutdown finishes before traffic is rerouted
SIGTERM can be caught, letting the process drain in-flight work and clean up
SIGKILL only stops the main thread, so SIGTERM is needed for the workers
SIGTERM makes the kernel close every file descriptor before exit
quiz.explain: SIGTERM is catchable, enabling graceful shutdown. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so it is the last resort after the grace period expires. Both signals end the whole process, and the kernel closes fds on any exit.

quiz.q: Two worker threads in one process increment a shared counter with no lock, and the final value is sometimes too low. Which statement best explains this?
options: Each thread works on a private copy, and only one copy is kept at exit
The OS isolates thread memory, so one thread's writes are invisible
The threads' unsynchronized read-modify-write steps interleave and lose updates
Each increment is a syscall, and the kernel drops concurrent writes
quiz.explain: Threads share an address space, so concurrent read-modify-write sequences can interleave. Processes, not threads, have isolated memory, and a plain increment is not a syscall.

quiz.q: A script reads a 100 MB file by calling `read(1)` on an unbuffered file descriptor, one byte at a time, and is extremely slow. What is the main reason?
options: Each read opens a new file descriptor, which fills the fd table
Each call is a separate syscall, so the kernel-crossing cost is paid per byte
Single-byte reads bypass the kernel page cache and hit the disk
Each single-byte read triggers a SIGPIPE that must be handled
quiz.explain: Every unbuffered read crosses into the kernel. Buffered or chunked reads amortize that cost across many bytes. The page cache still serves the data; the fd is reused; no signal is involved.

quiz.q: You run `export API_URL=staging.example.com` in terminal A. A program started later in terminal B (a separate shell) reads `API_URL`. What does it see?
options: staging.example.com, because export writes to a machine-wide table
Not A's value: the variable lives in A's shell and passes only to its children
staging.example.com, but only if program B is started with sudo
staging.example.com, once terminal B runs `source ~/.bashrc`
quiz.explain: The environment belongs to a process and is copied to its children. Terminal B's shell never inherited A's export, and the export was never written to any startup file.

quiz.q: An ingest service reads from sockets faster than its database writer can store rows. The in-process queue between them grows by about 200 MB per hour until the process is OOM-killed. What should you reach for?
options: Give the process a larger heap so it lasts longer between restarts
Bound the queue so that a full queue blocks or rejects the reader
Run more reader threads so more data reaches the queue sooner
Flush the queue to disk on every insert so memory stays flat
quiz.explain: A bounded queue turns overload into visible backpressure instead of an eventual crash. A bigger heap only delays the failure, and more readers make the producer even faster.

topics.title: Networking
topics.summary: IP, TCP vs UDP, DNS, ports, TLS, and the full journey of a URL from keystroke to rendered page.

lesson.text: A user reports that your site is slow, but only the first load, and only from another continent. To reason about that you need to know what happens before a single byte of your application code runs. Networking is a stack of layers, each solving one problem and hiding its details from the layer above.
IP and ports: addressing

An **IP address** identifies a network interface (IPv4 like `203.0.113.7`, IPv6 like `2001:db8::1`). IP delivers packets on a best-effort basis: they may be dropped, duplicated, reordered or delayed. A **port** (0-65535) identifies which program on that machine should receive the packet. So a connection endpoint is an IP plus a port, and a TCP connection is identified by the four-tuple of source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Well-known ports: 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH, 5432 Postgres.

`localhost` or `127.0.0.1` is the loopback interface: traffic never leaves the machine. Binding a server to `127.0.0.1` makes it unreachable from other hosts; binding to `0.0.0.0` listens on all interfaces, which is what a container usually needs, and also what accidentally exposes a dev database to the world.
TCP vs UDP

items: **TCP**: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte stream. It uses a handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), acknowledgements, retransmission, and congestion control. Costs: setup latency and head-of-line blocking (one lost packet stalls later data). Used by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, databases, SSH.

**UDP**: connectionless datagrams, no delivery or ordering guarantee, minimal overhead. Used for DNS lookups, real-time voice/video, games, and as the base of QUIC (HTTP/3), which rebuilds reliability and encryption on top of UDP to avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking.

lesson.text: Choose by what a late packet means. If an old game position update is worthless, UDP lets you drop it. If a bank transfer message is lost, you need TCP's guarantees.
DNS: names to addresses

Humans use names; IP needs addresses. **DNS** is a distributed, hierarchical database. Your machine asks a **recursive resolver** (usually your ISP or a public one), which walks from the root servers to the `.com` servers to the domain's authoritative server, then caches the answer for the record's **TTL**. Record types: `A`/`AAAA` (name to IPv4/IPv6), `CNAME` (alias), `MX` (mail), `TXT` (verification, SPF). Caching is why DNS changes take time to propagate: resolvers hold the old answer until the TTL expires.
TLS: encryption and identity

**TLS** sits on top of TCP (or inside QUIC) and gives three properties: confidentiality (eavesdroppers see ciphertext), integrity (tampering is detected), and authentication (the server proves it owns the domain via a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority). During the handshake the client and server agree on parameters, the server presents its certificate, and both derive shared session keys using key exchange. TLS 1.3 completes this in one round trip.
What happens when you type a URL

1. Browser parses https://shop.example.com/cart
2. Checks caches (HTTP cache, HSTS list)
3. DNS: shop.example.com -> 203.0.113.7 (resolver, TTL cache)
4. TCP handshake to 203.0.113.7:443 (1 round trip)
5. TLS handshake: certificate check, key exchange (1 round trip in TLS 1.3)
6. HTTP request: GET /cart  Host: shop.example.com
7. Server (often behind CDN / load balancer) returns HTML
8. Browser parses HTML, fetches CSS/JS/images (repeat 3-6 as needed)
9. Render

Back to the slow first load from another continent: DNS lookup plus TCP plus TLS cost several round trips, each one paying the long-distance latency. Repeat visits reuse connections and caches. CDNs and connection reuse exist to cut exactly these costs.

lesson.caption: On a first visit, DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP each cost a round trip before any HTML arrives; from another continent every one pays the full distance.

lesson.text: Common misconceptions: HTTPS does not hide which domain you visit from the network (DNS and the SNI field can leak it unless encrypted DNS or ECH is used); a valid certificate proves the domain identity, not that the site is trustworthy; and a failed `ping` does not prove a host is down, since ICMP is often blocked.

When an agent debugs 'connection refused', 'timeout' and 'certificate' errors, make it distinguish them: refused means nothing is listening (wrong port or bind address), timeout means packets are dropped (firewall, wrong route), a certificate error means TLS identity failed. Ask it to run `curl -v`, `dig`, and `nc -vz host port` to gather evidence first. Watch for agents 'fixing' certificate errors by turning off certificate checking in the client; reject that.

patterns.signal: Each outgoing request opens a new connection and traces show DNS, TCP and TLS handshakes dominating latency
patterns.why: Reusing warm connections skips several round trips per call. Cap the pool size, and set idle timeouts below the server's so you never reuse a socket the peer already closed.

patterns.signal: A client sends hundreds of tiny messages per second, each as its own request or packet
patterns.why: Fixed per-message overhead (headers, round trips, syscalls) is paid once per batch. Flush on size or a short timer so batching never adds unbounded latency.

patterns.signal: Game state is sent 60 times per second and a late update is useless because a newer one follows
patterns.why: TCP would stall fresh data behind a retransmitted stale packet. Over UDP, tag messages with a sequence number and drop older ones; add your own reliability only for events that need it.

patterns.signal: A real-time TCP stream has small writes that arrive in bursts with roughly 40 ms extra delay
patterns.why: Nagle's algorithm holds small segments until the previous one is ACKed, which combines badly with delayed ACKs. Disabling it cuts latency but sends more packets, so batch writes yourself.

patterns.signal: A DNS record was changed but some clients keep reaching the old server for an hour
patterns.why: Resolvers cache records for the TTL, so drop it to minutes a full TTL before the change and keep the old server serving until traffic drains. Low TTLs mean more lookups.

patterns.signal: A client fails with a certificate error and someone proposes `verify=False` to make it work
patterns.use: Fix the trust chain, keep verification
patterns.why: Without verification TLS still encrypts but no longer proves who you talk to, so any man-in-the-middle wins. Install the missing CA or intermediate, or fix the hostname instead.

patterns.signal: A connection fails and you must decide where to look: refused immediately vs hangs until timeout
patterns.why: Refused means the host answered but nothing listens on that port. A hang usually means a firewall drops packets or the host is unreachable. Each points to a different layer.

patterns.signal: A server in a container listens on `127.0.0.1` and port-mapped requests from the host fail
patterns.why: Loopback inside the container is not the host's loopback, so forwarded traffic never reaches it. Bind all interfaces there and restrict exposure with the port mapping or a firewall.

patterns.signal: Users far from the data centre see slow page loads even though server processing time is small
patterns.why: A page load costs several round trips; terminating TCP and TLS at a nearby edge and caching static assets there shortens each one. Dynamic, per-user responses gain less.

keyPoints: IP gets packets to a host, ports select a program; IP itself is unreliable.
TCP gives reliable ordered streams at a latency cost; UDP gives fast, unreliable datagrams; QUIC rebuilds reliability over UDP.
DNS maps names to addresses through cached, hierarchical lookups governed by TTLs.
TLS provides encryption, integrity and server authentication; never disable certificate verification to fix errors.
A page load costs several round trips (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP), so latency and connection reuse matter.

quiz.q: You are building a live multiplayer game where player positions are sent 60 times per second. A position that arrives late is useless because a newer one follows. Which transport suits this best?
options: TCP, since in-order delivery keeps every client's view exact
TCP, since its congestion control gives the lowest latency
UDP, since stale updates can be skipped without retransmission stalls
ICMP, since it skips the transport layer and has less overhead
quiz.explain: TCP would retransmit and delay newer data behind a lost old packet. For stale-tolerant real-time data, UDP's lack of delivery and ordering guarantees is a feature.

quiz.q: A teammate changes a DNS A record to a new server IP. Some new visitors still reach the old server for an hour. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Resolvers cached the old answer and serve it until the record's TTL expires
Root DNS servers publish zone changes only on a fixed hourly schedule
Browsers keep using the old IP until the user clears the site's cookies
The new server's certificate is not yet trusted, so browsers fall back
quiz.explain: DNS answers are cached for the record's TTL. Lowering the TTL before a planned change shortens this window. Root servers do not hold your records, and cookies and certificates do not choose the IP.

quiz.q: `curl` to your service returns 'Connection refused' immediately. Which is the most likely interpretation?
options: A firewall is silently dropping packets before they reach the host
The server's TLS certificate expired, so the handshake was aborted
The hostname has no DNS record, so there was no address to connect to
The host answered, but no process is listening on that port or address
quiz.explain: Refused means the host actively rejected the connection, typically because nothing listens there. A firewall that drops packets usually causes a timeout instead; DNS failure and expired certs give different errors.

quiz.q: Which statement about TLS is accurate?
options: It verifies that the site's owner is a legitimate, honest business
It encrypts traffic and lets the client verify the server's domain certificate
It hides both the destination IP address and domain from the network
It sanitizes request bodies, protecting the server from injection
quiz.explain: TLS provides confidentiality, integrity and domain authentication. It says nothing about whether the site is trustworthy or secure, the destination IP remains visible, and it does nothing about application-level input.

quiz.q: A Docker container runs a web server bound to `127.0.0.1:3000`. The host maps port 3000 to it, but requests from the host browser fail. What is the likely fix?
options: Switch the server to UDP so the mapping forwards datagrams directly
Map port 443 instead, since browsers block plain HTTP to containers
Bind the server to `0.0.0.0` so it accepts traffic on the container's interface
Raise the container's file descriptor limit so it can accept connections
quiz.explain: Inside a container, 127.0.0.1 is the container's own loopback; forwarded traffic arrives on another interface. Binding to 0.0.0.0 accepts it.

quiz.q: Traces for service A calling service B show 90 ms of every 120 ms call spent on DNS, TCP and TLS handshakes, while B's handler takes only 20 ms. A opens a fresh connection per request. What fits best?
options: Lower the DNS TTL on B's record so lookups refresh faster
Disable Nagle's algorithm on the outgoing client sockets
Reuse warm connections through a pool with keep-alive on
Move the calls from TCP to UDP so handshakes are skipped
quiz.explain: Reusing connections skips the repeated DNS, TCP and TLS round trips, which dominate here. TTL and Nagle changes do not remove handshakes, and UDP would drop reliability for no reason.

topics.title: HTTP & APIs
topics.summary: Methods, status codes, headers, idempotency, API styles, pagination and rate limits: designing contracts clients can rely on.

lesson.text: A mobile app sends `POST /payments` and the connection drops before the response arrives. Did the payment happen? Should the app retry? The answer depends on what the HTTP contract promises, and on whether you designed the API to be safe to retry. HTTP is a simple request/response protocol, but the semantics around it are where real systems succeed or break.
Anatomy of a request

POST /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: 7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7

{"sku": "A-100", "qty": 2}

A request has a **method**, a **path**, **headers** (metadata) and an optional **body**. A response has a **status code**, headers, and a body. HTTP is **stateless**: each request must carry everything the server needs (credentials, context), which is what lets you put many identical servers behind a load balancer.
Methods: safe and idempotent

items: `GET`: read. **Safe** (no side effects) and idempotent. Must not change state.
`PUT`: replace a resource at a known URL. Idempotent: doing it twice leaves the same final state.
`DELETE`: remove. Idempotent (second call finds it already gone).
`POST`: create or perform an action. **Not** idempotent by default; two calls may create two orders.
`PATCH`: partial update. May or may not be idempotent depending on the operation (`set name` vs `increment counter`).

lesson.text: **Idempotent** means repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once. This is the property that makes retries safe. For non-idempotent operations such as payments, the standard fix is an **idempotency key**: the client sends a unique key, and the server stores the result per key, returning the saved result on a repeat instead of acting again.

lesson.caption: The retry carries the same key, so the server returns the saved result instead of charging the card a second time.

lesson.text: Status codes: the contract's vocabulary

items: `2xx` success: `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`.
`3xx` redirect: `301` permanent, `302/307` temporary, `304 Not Modified` (cache still valid).

`4xx` client error (the caller should change something): `400` malformed, `401` not authenticated, `403` authenticated but not allowed, `404` not found, `409` conflict, `422` validation failed, `429` too many requests.
`5xx` server error (not the caller's fault): `500`, `502` bad gateway, `503` unavailable, `504` gateway timeout.

lesson.text: The 4xx/5xx split drives client behavior: retrying a `400` is pointless, while a `503` with `Retry-After` is worth retrying. Returning `200` with `{"error": ...}` in the body breaks monitoring, caches and every generic client.
Headers that matter

`Content-Type` and `Accept` negotiate formats. `Authorization` carries credentials. `Cache-Control` and `ETag` control caching and conditional requests. `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-*` (or the IETF `RateLimit` / `RateLimit-Policy` headers, still a draft standard) communicate limits. `Location` points to a newly created resource.
REST vs RPC vs GraphQL

items: **REST**: resources as nouns (`/users/42/orders`), uniform methods, cacheable, widely understood. Weak spot: clients may over-fetch or need many round trips.
**RPC** (gRPC, JSON-RPC): call named procedures (`CreateOrder`) with typed contracts. Efficient and great for internal service-to-service calls; less cache-friendly and less browser-native.
**GraphQL**: one endpoint, the client specifies exactly which fields it wants. Solves over/under-fetching for varied clients; costs complexity (query cost control, caching, N+1 on the server).

lesson.text: There is no universally best style. Public CRUD-like APIs usually pick REST, internal high-throughput services often pick gRPC, and UI-heavy products with many client shapes sometimes pick GraphQL.
Pagination and rate limits

Never return unbounded lists. **Offset pagination** (`?offset=100&limit=20`) is simple but skips or repeats rows when data changes and gets slow deep into the table. **Cursor pagination** (`?after=<opaque token>`) continues from a stable position and stays fast; prefer it for large or changing data. **Rate limiting** protects the server by capping requests per client; exceeding it returns `429` with `Retry-After`, and well-behaved clients back off exponentially with jitter.

Agents often generate endpoints that return 200 for everything, use POST for reads, add no pagination, and retry blindly in client code. Specify the contract up front: allowed status codes, error shape, pagination style, and which operations need idempotency keys. In review, check that retries only wrap idempotent calls, that `429`/`503` honor `Retry-After`, and that list endpoints have a hard maximum page size.

patterns.signal: A client times out on `POST /payments` and retrying might charge the customer twice
patterns.why: The client sends a unique key per logical operation; the server stores the result under it and replays it on retry. Keys need a retention window and must be scoped to the caller.

patterns.signal: An infinite feed paged with `offset` shows duplicates or skips while new rows are inserted
patterns.why: Return an opaque cursor encoding the last sort key and query `WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor`. Stable under inserts and fast on deep pages, but no jumping to page N.

patterns.signal: One client sends thousands of requests per second and degrades the API for everyone else
patterns.why: A per-client token bucket protects shared capacity and `429` tells the client to slow down, unlike a `5xx`. Limits need a fair key (API key, user), not just IP.

patterns.signal: After an outage, every client retries at the same instant and knocks the recovering service over again
patterns.why: Doubling the delay spreads load over time and random jitter breaks synchronized waves. Cap the delay and attempt count, and only retry idempotent work or retryable statuses.

patterns.signal: A response field must be renamed or removed while old mobile app versions stay in the wild for months
patterns.why: Prefer additive changes; when breaking is unavoidable, publish `/v2` or a version header and run both until old clients fade. Every live version is code you must keep maintaining.

patterns.signal: Errors come back as `200 OK` with `{"error": ...}` and clients retry bad requests forever
patterns.why: `4xx` says fix the request, `5xx` says the server failed and a retry may help; `401` vs `403` separates identity from permission. Proxies, caches and retry logic depend on them.

patterns.signal: Clients re-download the same large, rarely changing resource on every request
patterns.why: The server returns an `ETag`; the client sends `If-None-Match` and gets a body-less `304 Not Modified` when nothing changed. Saves bandwidth, but still costs one round trip.

patterns.signal: A report or export request takes minutes and HTTP calls hit gateway timeouts
patterns.why: Accept the job, return a URL to poll or a callback, and run it in the background. Turns a fragile long request into a tracked job, at the cost of extra state and polling.

patterns.signal: A mobile screen makes five sequential calls and discards most of each response
patterns.why: One request shaped to the screen cuts round trips and overfetch. GraphQL loses easy HTTP caching and needs query cost limits; a BFF is simpler but tied to one client.

patterns.signal: Browsers poll an endpoint every second to learn about rare server-side changes
patterns.why: Push over one long-lived connection gives lower latency and far fewer empty responses. SSE is one-way over plain HTTP; WebSocket is two-way. Both need reconnect and resume logic.

keyPoints: HTTP is stateless request/response; the method and status code carry semantics clients depend on.
Idempotency (same effect when repeated) makes retries safe; POST needs an idempotency key to get it.
Use status codes honestly: 4xx means fix the request, 5xx means the server failed and may be worth retrying.
REST, RPC and GraphQL trade off cacheability, efficiency and client flexibility.
Paginate with cursors for changing or large data and enforce rate limits with `429` plus backoff.

quiz.q: A client times out calling `POST /payments`. Which design lets it retry safely without double-charging?
options: Retry immediately with the same body, since POST is idempotent by spec
Resend it as GET with the payment in the query string so retries are safe
Have the server return 200 on failures so the client never needs to retry
Send an Idempotency-Key; the server replays the stored result for a repeat
quiz.explain: POST is not idempotent by default. A server-stored idempotency key turns a repeat into a replay of the first result. Changing the method or hiding errors does not change what the server does.

quiz.q: A user is logged in with a valid token but requests an admin-only resource. Which status code is most accurate?
options: 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
409 Conflict
400 Bad Request
quiz.explain: 403 means the caller is authenticated but not permitted. 401 means credentials are missing or invalid, 409 signals a state conflict, and 400 a malformed request.

quiz.q: An infinite-scroll feed uses `?offset=N&limit=20` on a table where new rows are inserted constantly. Users see duplicate items. What is the best fix?
options: Switch to cursor pagination anchored to a stable sort key
Raise the page size to 1000 so fewer pages are requested
Add `Cache-Control: no-store` so each page is fetched fresh
Sort by a per-session random seed so pages stay distinct
quiz.explain: New inserts shift offsets, so rows move between pages. A cursor continues from the last seen position and is unaffected by inserts before it. Fresher or bigger pages still shift.

quiz.q: Your public API is hit by one client sending thousands of requests per second. What is the appropriate server response and client behavior?
options: Return 500 and let the client retry immediately until it succeeds
Return 404 for that client's requests so it stops calling
Return 429 with Retry-After; the client backs off with jitter
Close the TCP connection silently so the client times out
quiz.explain: 429 explicitly signals rate limiting. Backoff with jitter prevents synchronized retry storms; immediate retries make overload worse, and misleading codes or silent drops break clients.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes PUT from PATCH?
options: PUT is safe and has no side effects, while PATCH modifies server state
PATCH is idempotent by definition, while PUT may duplicate on retry
PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent; PATCH may not be
PUT can only create new resources; PATCH is the only way to update
quiz.explain: PUT sets a full representation, so repeating it yields the same state. PATCH semantics depend on the operation (set a field vs increment a counter), and neither is 'safe' in the HTTP sense.

quiz.q: `GET /reports/annual` builds a PDF in about four minutes. The load balancer cuts requests at 60 seconds, so users see 504 errors even though the job finishes. Which approach fits best?
options: Return `202 Accepted` and a status URL, run the job in background
Raise the gateway timeout to ten minutes for this one report route
Retry the request with exponential backoff and with added jitter
Add an `ETag` so repeat requests get a `304 Not Modified` reply
quiz.explain: Accepting the job and exposing a status resource turns a fragile long request into a tracked one. A longer timeout keeps the connection fragile, and retries would start duplicate four-minute jobs.

topics.title: Databases
topics.summary: Relational modeling, SQL, indexes, transactions, isolation levels, the N+1 trap, and when NoSQL fits.

lesson.text: Your page loads in 40 ms with 100 test orders and 12 seconds with 2 million in production. Nothing in the code changed. Almost every case like this comes from how data is modeled and queried. A database is not just storage; it is an engine that plans how to answer questions, and your job is to give it the structure and information to do that cheaply.
Relational modeling

A relational database stores data in **tables** of rows and columns. A **primary key** uniquely identifies a row; a **foreign key** references another table's key, and the database enforces that the reference is valid. **Normalization** means storing each fact once: customer details live in `customers`, and `orders` reference them by `customer_id`. This prevents update anomalies (changing an address in one place but not another). You denormalize deliberately, later, for read performance, not by default.

Constraints (`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, foreign keys) are the cheapest, strongest correctness tool you have: they hold even when application code has bugs, or when another service writes to the same table.
Indexes

Without an index, filtering `WHERE customer_id = 7` forces a **sequential scan** of every row. An **index** (typically a B-tree) is a sorted side structure that lets the database jump to matching rows in logarithmic time. Indexes speed up reads but cost disk space and slow every write, because each insert or update must maintain them. Index columns you filter, join and sort on. A **composite index** on `(customer_id, created_at)` serves queries filtering on `customer_id`, or `customer_id` plus a date range, but generally not date alone: column order matters. (Some engines, including Postgres 18 and later, can 'skip scan' such an index when the leading column has few distinct values, but do not design around it.) Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to see whether the planner uses an index or scans.

lesson.text: Transactions and ACID

A **transaction** groups statements so they succeed or fail together. ACID: **Atomicity** (all or nothing), **Consistency** (constraints hold before and after), **Isolation** (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work), **Durability** (committed data survives a crash).
Isolation levels and anomalies

Full isolation is expensive, so databases offer levels. **Read committed** (the default in Postgres, SQL Server and Oracle; MySQL's InnoDB defaults to repeatable read) never shows uncommitted data but a re-read within one transaction may change (non-repeatable read). **Repeatable read / snapshot** gives a stable view of the data. **Serializable** behaves as if transactions ran one at a time, preventing anomalies such as **write skew** (two doctors both go off-call because each saw the other still on-call), at the cost of aborts and retries. A classic bug is **read-modify-write** in application code: read a balance, compute in code, write back. Two concurrent requests lose an update. Fix it with an atomic statement (`SET balance = balance - 100`), a row lock (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), or a higher isolation level.
The N+1 query problem

# N+1: 1 query for orders + 1 query per order = 101 queries for 100 orders
orders = db.query('SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 100')
for o in orders:
    o.customer = db.query('SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = %s', o.customer_id)

# Fix: one JOIN, or one batched IN query
rows = db.query('SELECT o.*, c.email FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id LIMIT 100')
ORMs make N+1 easy to write invisibly through lazy-loaded relationships. Each query is fast; the round trips add up.
When NoSQL

NoSQL covers document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores. Reach for one when you have a specific need: massive horizontal write scale, a flexible per-record schema, extreme low-latency key lookups, or graph traversal. You give up joins, flexible ad-hoc queries and often cross-record transactions. Default to a relational database such as Postgres unless a measured requirement says otherwise; it handles JSON columns, full-text search and large scale better than most people assume.

Agents frequently build SQL by string concatenation, forget indexes on new foreign keys and filter columns, write N+1 loops through the ORM, and do read-modify-write across two statements outside a transaction. Ask for the migration plus the indexes it needs, request `EXPLAIN` output for key queries, and demand parameterized queries. Never let an agent run destructive migrations against production data without a reviewed rollback plan.

patterns.signal: `WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` is slow on a large table
patterns.use: Composite index: filter column, then sort
patterns.why: An index on `(customer_id, created_at)` finds the rows and returns them pre-sorted, so the database stops after 20. Column order matters; each index slows writes.

patterns.signal: An index was added but the endpoint is still slow and nobody checked what the database actually does
patterns.why: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows sequential scans, unused indexes, bad row estimates and sorts. Measure on production-sized data; a tiny dev table can make any plan look fine.

patterns.signal: Logs show one list query followed by hundreds of near-identical `SELECT ... WHERE id = ?`
patterns.why: Fetch related rows in one `JOIN` or one `WHERE id IN (...)` batch instead of a query per row. ORMs hide this behind lazy loading; enable eager loading for that access path.

patterns.signal: Code reads a balance, subtracts in the app, writes it back, and concurrent requests lose updates
patterns.why: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 30` does read and write in one step. Check affected rows to detect the failed condition.

patterns.signal: Two users edit the same record over minutes and the later save silently overwrites the earlier one
patterns.use: Optimistic locking with a version column
patterns.why: Write with `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` and bump the version; zero affected rows means conflict, so reload and retry or ask the user. Wins at low contention, thrashes at high.

patterns.signal: Several writes must all happen or none, such as debit one account and credit another
patterns.why: Atomicity rolls back a partial failure. Isolation level decides which anomalies remain, so pick it deliberately. Keep transactions short and never wait on network calls inside one.

patterns.signal: Duplicate emails appear despite a `SELECT` check in application code before insert
patterns.why: A check-then-insert races between requests; only the database can enforce uniqueness atomically. Catch the constraint violation and map it to a clean `409` for the client.

patterns.signal: The same customer address is copied into many rows and updates leave some copies stale
patterns.use: Normalise to one fact, one place
patterns.why: Store it once and reference it by foreign key so updates cannot diverge. Denormalise later only for a measured read hotspot, and own the work of keeping copies in sync.

patterns.signal: The primary's CPU is saturated by reporting and read traffic while writes are a small share
patterns.why: Route heavy reads to followers to offload the primary. Async replicas lag, so a read right after a write can be stale; keep read-after-write paths on the primary.

patterns.signal: A team wants to move a plain relational app to NoSQL 'because it scales' with no measured bottleneck
patterns.use: Stay relational until a measured need
patterns.why: Relational databases scale far with indexes, replicas and caching while keeping joins, constraints and transactions. Choose a document or key-value store for a specific access pattern.

keyPoints: Normalize to store each fact once, and use constraints to make the database enforce correctness.
Indexes speed reads and slow writes; column order in composite indexes matters; verify with EXPLAIN.
Transactions give atomicity; isolation level determines which concurrency anomalies remain.
Read-modify-write in application code loses updates; use atomic SQL, locks, or stronger isolation.
N+1 queries come from per-row lookups in loops; batch with joins or IN queries.

quiz.q: A query `WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` is slow on a large table. Which index most directly helps?
options: An index on `created_at` alone
A composite index on `(customer_id, created_at)`
An index on `(created_at, customer_id)`
A separate index on `total_cents`
quiz.explain: Equality column first, then the sort column, lets the database find the customer's rows already ordered. Reversing the order or indexing unrelated columns does not support that access path.

quiz.q: Two requests each read a balance of 100, subtract 30 in application code, and write back 70. The final balance should be 40. What happened and what fixes it?
options: A durability failure lost one write; enable synchronous commit
A lost update; use an atomic `SET balance = balance - 30` or a row lock
A deadlock between the requests; add an index on the balance column
A dirty read of uncommitted data; add a CHECK constraint on balance
quiz.explain: Both requests based their write on the same stale read, so one update overwrote the other. Moving the arithmetic into the database statement or locking removes the race.

quiz.q: A list endpoint takes 3 seconds and the logs show 301 near-identical `SELECT ... WHERE id = ?` queries for one request. What is the most likely issue and fix?
options: Missing primary key; add one so each lookup uses an index
Pool too small; add connections so the lookups run in parallel
N+1 queries; fetch related rows with a JOIN or one batched query
Isolation too weak; use serializable so the reads are consistent
quiz.explain: One query plus one per row is the N+1 signature. The fix is to reduce round trips, not to tune isolation or connections.

quiz.q: What does adding many indexes to a write-heavy table risk?
options: Slower inserts and updates, since every index must be maintained
Queries returning stale rows when two indexes disagree
The table silently losing its ACID transaction guarantees
Foreign key constraints no longer being checked on insert
quiz.explain: Indexes are redundant structures kept in sync on every write, and they also take storage. They do not change correctness, only cost.

quiz.q: A team wants to move a normal orders-and-customers app from Postgres to a document database 'because it scales'. There is no measured scaling problem. What is the best advice?
options: Migrate now, since document stores always outscale relational ones
Migrate, since Postgres cannot store JSON or handle large tables
Keep Postgres but drop all indexes to see whether writes scale
Stay on Postgres until a measured need justifies losing joins
quiz.explain: Relational databases cover most workloads, and the trade-offs of NoSQL (no joins, often weaker cross-record transactions) are real costs. Choose it for a measured need.

quiz.q: Two support agents open the same ticket and edit it for several minutes each. The second save silently wipes the first agent's changes. Which approach fits best?
options: Lock the ticket row in the database for the whole edit session
Add a unique constraint on the ticket's ID column in the table
Switch the save to `SET field = field + 1` style relative updates
Add a version column, save with `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`
quiz.explain: Optimistic locking detects the conflict at save time, and zero affected rows tells you to reload. A row lock held for minutes would block everyone, and a unique constraint cannot catch lost updates.

topics.title: Distributed Systems
topics.summary: CAP and PACELC, replication, consistency, queues, caching and safe retries when machines and networks fail.

lesson.text: Your checkout service calls the payment service, which calls the bank. The payment call times out. Did it fail, or did it succeed and the reply got lost? In a single process a function call either returns or throws. Across a network, there is a third outcome: you do not know. Distributed systems is the discipline of building correct behavior despite that uncertainty.
Why it is hard

Three facts drive everything: messages can be delayed, dropped or duplicated; nodes can crash and restart at any time; and there is no shared clock or shared memory, so nodes cannot instantly agree on what is true. A slow node is indistinguishable from a dead one. Design as if every remote call can fail in the ambiguous way.
CAP and PACELC

The **CAP theorem** says that when a network **partition** happens (nodes cannot reach each other), a system must choose between **Consistency** (every read sees the latest write, as if one copy existed) and **Availability** (every request gets a non-error response). Partitions are not optional in real networks, so the real choice is C or A *during a partition*. A bank ledger favors consistency and rejects requests it cannot safely serve; a shopping-cart or social feed often favors availability and reconciles later.

**PACELC** extends this: if there is a Partition choose A or C; **Else**, with no partition, choose between **Latency** and **Consistency**. Even on a healthy network, waiting for replicas to confirm a write costs latency. This is the day-to-day trade-off, far more common than partitions.
Replication and consistency models

**Replication** keeps copies of data on multiple nodes for durability and read scale. In leader-follower replication, writes go to the leader and are copied to followers, **synchronously** (safe, slower) or **asynchronously** (fast, but a leader crash can lose recent writes, and followers lag). Consistency models describe what reads may observe:

items: **Strong / linearizable**: behaves like a single copy; a read after a completed write sees it. Costs coordination and latency.
**Eventual**: if writes stop, replicas converge. Reads may be stale in the meantime.
**Read-your-writes**: a user always sees their own updates, even if others see stale data. Commonly implemented by routing a user's reads to the leader shortly after they write.

lesson.text: Queues and asynchronous work

A **message queue** (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) decouples producers from consumers: the checkout service enqueues 'send receipt' and moves on. Queues absorb bursts and let consumers fail and retry independently. Most queues provide **at-least-once** delivery: a message may be delivered more than once, for example when a consumer crashes before acknowledging. True exactly-once is not achievable end to end; you get **effectively-once** by making consumers **idempotent**.
Retries and idempotency keys

Retries fix transient failures but create duplicates, so they need idempotency keys. Use **exponential backoff with jitter** so thousands of clients do not retry in lockstep and overwhelm a recovering service (a **retry storm**). Set timeouts everywhere; a missing timeout turns a slow dependency into exhausted threads. Cap total attempts, and retry at one layer only, because stacked retries multiply load (3 retries at 3 layers is 27 calls).

lesson.caption: Same backoff schedule, same failures: without jitter the clients hit the recovering service together, with jitter their retries spread out.
