items: Never combine a destructive schema change and the code that depends on it in one deploy.
Make each migration backward compatible with the version currently running, so rollback stays possible.
Backfill large tables in batches to avoid long locks, and make migrations safe to re-run.
Drop old columns only after a full release cycle in which nothing used them.

lesson.text: Agents tend to write the one-shot version: a single migration that renames the column plus the code that uses the new name, and a deploy plan of 'just ship it'. Ask explicitly for expand/contract steps as separate PRs, a stated rollback path for each, and a flag around new behaviour. Review any migration that contains `DROP`, `RENAME` or `NOT NULL` with extra care, and never let an agent run migrations against production directly.

patterns.signal: A payments service must switch all traffic at a chosen moment and revert in seconds; double capacity is affordable
patterns.why: Deploy to the idle environment, verify, then flip the router; reverting is flipping back. Costs double capacity and does not help with incompatible database changes.

patterns.signal: A change is risky in ways tests cannot show, and you want real-traffic evidence with a capped blast radius
patterns.why: Send 1-5% of traffic to the new version and compare error rate and latency to the baseline before widening. Needs good metrics and enough traffic for a meaningful comparison.

patterns.signal: A stateless fleet behind a load balancer gets a backward-compatible change
patterns.why: Replace a few instances at a time behind health checks; cheap and needs no spare environment. Old and new versions serve traffic at once, so both must work with the same data and APIs.

patterns.signal: Code must merge and deploy now, but the feature should go live later or to a subset of users
patterns.why: Deploy with the path off, then release by config, by percentage or segment, with an instant kill switch. Every flag is a branch in the code and doubles test paths.

patterns.signal: The codebase has 40 flags and 30 have been at 100% for six months
patterns.why: Give each release flag an owner and removal date, then delete the flag and the dead branch once fully rolled out. Stale flags are tech debt and can be flipped by accident.

patterns.signal: A heavily used column must be renamed with zero downtime and a safe rollback at each step
patterns.why: Add the new column, dual-write, backfill, move reads, then stop writing and drop the old one in later deploys. Each step works with old and new code; the cost is several releases.

patterns.signal: A migration needs to update every row of a 200-million-row table
patterns.why: Update in small batches with pauses, outside the schema-change deploy, so locks stay short and replicas keep up. Make it resumable and idempotent; it may run for hours.

patterns.signal: A rewritten service path must be checked against production traffic without users seeing its results
patterns.why: Mirror real requests to the new path, discard its responses and diff them against the old. Doubles load on dependencies, and side effects like writes or emails must be suppressed.

patterns.signal: Errors spike right after a deploy and no data or schema changed
patterns.why: Redeploy the previous artifact to stop user impact, then investigate. Roll forward instead only when rollback is unsafe, such as after an irreversible migration; decide which before deploying.

keyPoints: Deploying puts code on servers; releasing exposes it to users. Flags and gradual rollouts keep the two separate.
Rolling updates are cheap but run two versions at once; blue/green gives instant switch and revert at the cost of double capacity; canaries test on real traffic with a capped blast radius.
Feature flags give a fast kill switch, but each flag needs an owner and a removal date.
Use expand/contract so every migration step works with both old and new code, and rollback stays possible.

quiz.q: Your payments service must switch all traffic to a new version at a chosen moment and be able to revert within seconds. You can afford temporary double capacity. Which strategy fits best?
options: Rolling update, replacing one instance at a time until all are new
Blue/green, switching traffic between two environments
Recreate, stopping every old instance before starting any new one
Canary at 1%, widening gradually over several days of observation
quiz.explain: Blue/green keeps the old environment running, so both the cutover and the revert are a single routing change. A rolling update reverts slowly and a recreate causes downtime.

quiz.q: A canary is serving 5% of traffic. Which check is the best basis for deciding to promote it to 25%?
options: Confirm the canary instances started and pass their health checks
Wait for the first support ticket before widening any further
Compare only median latency, since errors are rare at 5% exposure
Compare canary error rate and latency to baseline
quiz.explain: A canary is only useful if you compare it with the baseline on user-visible signals. Health checks and a lack of complaints say little, and ignoring errors misses the likeliest failure.

quiz.q: Your codebase has 40 feature flags, and 30 have been at 100% for over six months. What is the right move?
options: Keep them all permanently as extra safety switches
Convert them into permanent environment variables
Remove the flags and their dead code paths
Add tests for every combination of flags, so each is covered
quiz.explain: Fully rolled-out flags are dead weight: extra paths, confusion and untested combinations. Removing them is part of the flag lifecycle, and testing every combination explodes.

quiz.q: You must rename a heavily used column with zero downtime and a safe rollback at each step. Which sequence is right?
options: Add new column, dual-write and backfill, move reads, drop old later
Run `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` in the same deploy that ships the new code
Deploy the new code first, then rename the column during the next maintenance window
Drop the old column and add the new one inside a single transaction before deploying
quiz.explain: Expand/contract keeps each step compatible with the code that is running. A direct rename breaks old instances during the rollout and cannot be rolled back with code alone.

quiz.q: A release included code plus a migration that dropped a column. Errors spike, so the team redeploys the previous code version, but errors continue. Why?
options: Redeploying cannot replace a container that is already running traffic
Feature flags prevent the previous version from starting after a deploy
Old code needs the dropped column; rollback does not restore data
The load balancer keeps caching the new version's responses for an hour
quiz.explain: Code and data roll back independently. Once the column is gone, the old code fails against it, which is why destructive migrations must be deferred to a later contract step.

quiz.q: A migration must set `region` on all 200 million rows of `orders`. A single `UPDATE` locked the table in staging and ballooned the transaction log. Which approach fits best?
options: Put the change behind a feature flag and flip it for all users
Deploy it to a blue environment and switch traffic over at once
Update in small id-ranged batches with pauses, safe to rerun
Roll it out with a canary at 5% of production traffic
quiz.explain: Batching keeps each transaction short and lets the job resume. A canary or blue/green switch controls traffic to code, not the size of a data update.

topics.title: Infrastructure & Environments
topics.summary: Describe where and how your software runs as versioned, repeatable artifacts instead of hand-built servers.

lesson.text: A classic outage story: the app worked on the developer's laptop and in staging, then failed in production because the production server had a different runtime version, a missing environment variable and a firewall rule that someone had once added by hand and never recorded. Nothing was wrong with the code. The problem was that the environment was an unwritten, unrepeatable thing. This topic is about making the environment as explicit and reviewable as the code itself.
Containers

A **container** packages an application with its dependencies and runtime into an **image**, and runs it as an isolated process that shares the host's operating system kernel. Unlike a virtual machine it does not carry a whole guest OS, so it starts in seconds and is light on resources. The key benefit for shipping is that you build the image once and run the identical artifact on a laptop, in CI, in staging and in production.

# Pin the base image: 'latest' would change under you
FROM node:22.11-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
USER node                      # do not run as root
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

Containers should be **immutable** and **stateless**: you never patch a running container, you build a new image and replace it. Anything that must survive a restart (uploads, databases) lives outside, in a managed database or object storage. Tag images with the commit SHA or a version, not just `latest`, so you can tell exactly what is running and roll back to a known image.
Infrastructure as code

**Infrastructure as code (IaC)** means defining servers, networks, databases and permissions in text files that a tool such as Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi or CloudFormation applies. The files live in version control, go through review, and can recreate an entire environment on demand. Most tools are **declarative**: you describe the desired end state, and the tool computes and applies the difference. Running a **plan** first shows exactly what will change before anything is touched.

resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
  identifier          = "orders-${var.env}"
  engine              = "postgres"
  engine_version      = "16.4"
  instance_class      = var.db_instance_class   # small in staging, larger in prod
  allocated_storage   = 50
  deletion_protection = true
  password            = var.db_password         # injected, never hard-coded
}

The failure mode to watch is **drift**: someone edits a resource in the cloud console, and reality no longer matches the code. The next apply may silently undo the manual fix or, worse, destroy something. The discipline is that every change goes through code and review, and the tool's state file is stored remotely and protected.
Config versus secrets

Following the twelve-factor idea, **configuration** that varies between environments (database host, timeouts, log level, feature toggles) is kept out of the code and supplied at runtime, so the same image works everywhere. **Secrets** are the subset that grants access: passwords, API keys, signing keys, tokens. Ordinary config can sit in version control; secrets must not. They belong in a secret manager (such as AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or your platform's encrypted store), are injected when the process starts, and are rotated on a schedule.

lesson.caption: The same image, tagged with its commit SHA, runs everywhere; only the config injected at runtime changes between environments.

lesson.text: A secret committed to git is compromised, even if you delete it in the next commit, because history and clones keep it. The correct response is always to **revoke and rotate** the credential first, then clean up.
Dev, staging and production parity

Environments exist to catch problems before users do, and they only do that to the extent that they resemble production. Aim for **parity**: the same container image, the same database engine and major version, the same infrastructure code with different parameters. Staging can be smaller, but it should not use a different kind of database or skip the load balancer. Every difference is a place where a bug can hide until production.
Cloud basics

Cloud platforms rent you building blocks at different levels of abstraction. **IaaS** gives you virtual machines and networks you manage. **PaaS** and container platforms run your code or images and handle scaling and patching. **Serverless** functions run per request and scale to zero. Moving up the ladder trades control for less operational work. Whatever the level, you share responsibility: the provider secures the data centre, you secure your configuration, identities and data. Most cloud incidents come from misconfiguration, such as a public storage bucket or an over-broad role, not from the provider being hacked.

Cloud costs and permissions are part of the blast radius. An agent or script with broad credentials can create expensive resources or delete production data in one command. Grant least privilege, set budget alerts, and enable deletion protection on stateful resources.

Agents will happily write a Dockerfile with `FROM node:latest`, run as root, bake a `.env` into the image, or fix a failing deploy by pasting a real key into a config file. Ask for pinned image versions, a non-root user and secrets passed by reference. When asking for IaC changes, require the agent to show the plan output and stop for your review, and never give it credentials that can apply changes to production.

patterns.signal: The app passes in staging but crashes in production because the Node.js version differs
patterns.why: Package runtime and dependencies into one image and run that same image in every environment. Removes version drift; base images still need regular rebuilds for security patches.

patterns.signal: An engineer SSHes into a production server to patch a file or install a package
patterns.why: Never patch running instances; change the code or image and replace them. Every server then matches a known build, at the cost of a pipeline fast enough for urgent fixes.

patterns.signal: Servers, networks and permissions were clicked together in a cloud console and nobody can recreate them
patterns.why: Define resources in Terraform, OpenTofu or similar, reviewed in PRs and applied by CI. Environments become reproducible and auditable; state files need locking and protection.

patterns.signal: A teammate fixed an outage by editing a firewall rule in the console, and the IaC code says otherwise
patterns.use: Codify the change and detect drift
patterns.why: Port the fix into code promptly, apply it and run plan-based drift checks on a schedule. Otherwise the next apply silently reverts the fix or destroys something.

patterns.signal: The database host or log level is hardcoded, and each environment needs its own build
patterns.why: Read environment-specific values at runtime so one artifact runs anywhere. Validate config at startup and fail fast on missing values rather than failing mid-request.

patterns.signal: An API key in `.env` was committed and pushed to a shared repo
patterns.use: Revoke and rotate, then use a secret manager
patterns.why: Treat it as leaked: rotate first, then remove it from history, and load secrets at runtime from a vault or cloud secret store. Deleting it in a new commit does not help; history keeps it.

patterns.signal: Staging uses SQLite and one instance while production runs PostgreSQL behind a load balancer
patterns.why: Use the same image, database engine and major version, and similar topology in staging, scaled down. Each difference hides a class of bugs; full parity on size and data is rarely affordable.

patterns.signal: Reviewers cannot try a PR without merging it to a shared staging that others are also using
patterns.why: Spin up an environment per PR from the same IaC and tear it down on merge. Great for review and QA; costs cloud spend and needs seeded data and cleanup automation.

patterns.signal: User uploads stored inside the container disappear whenever it is replaced or rescheduled
patterns.why: Keep containers stateless; put files in object storage and data in managed databases. Instances become disposable and scalable; you pay for an extra network hop and service.

patterns.signal: CI holds long-lived cloud access keys in its settings for deploys
patterns.why: Let the CI provider exchange its identity token for temporary, scoped cloud credentials per job. No static key to leak or rotate; setup needs trust policies scoped to repo and branch.

keyPoints: Containers package the app and its dependencies into an immutable image that you build once and run unchanged everywhere.
Infrastructure as code makes environments reviewable and repeatable; guard against drift by changing infrastructure only through code.
Config varies per environment and is injected at runtime; secrets live in a secret manager, and a leaked secret must be rotated.
Keep staging close to production in image, database engine and topology, since every difference hides potential bugs.

quiz.q: An app passes in staging but crashes in production because production runs a different Node.js version. Which change best removes this class of problem?
options: Document the required Node.js version carefully in the project README file
Ask the ops team to upgrade production to the newest Node.js version
Build one image with a pinned runtime and promote it everywhere
Install the matching Node.js version on production by hand and note it in a ticket
quiz.explain: A single image carries its own runtime, so every environment runs the same thing. Documentation and manual installs depend on people remembering and are exactly what drifts.

quiz.q: An AI agent committed an API key in `.env`, and the commit was already pushed to a shared repo. What is the correct first response?
options: Revoke and rotate the key, then move it to a secret manager
Delete the file in a new commit so it no longer appears
Make the repository private, since the key is then hidden
Rewrite git history and force-push, then continue using the key
quiz.explain: Once pushed, assume the key is exposed, and history and clones retain it. Rotation is the only step that actually removes the risk; cleaning history is secondary.

quiz.q: A teammate fixed an outage by editing a firewall rule in the cloud console. Your infrastructure is managed with Terraform. What is the best follow-up?
options: Leave it as is, since the console change already fixed the outage
Disable the plan step so Terraform no longer reports any differences
Re-run apply immediately and accept whatever changes it proposes
Add the rule to the Terraform code and apply it via review
quiz.explain: Console edits create drift. An unreviewed apply could silently revert the fix, so reconcile the code with the change through the normal review path.

quiz.q: Staging uses SQLite for convenience while production uses Postgres. A query bug shows up only in production. What is the most useful lesson?
options: Add many more unit tests that mock out the database layer entirely
Match staging's database engine and version to production
Skip staging for any database-related change and verify in production instead
Switch production over to SQLite as well so that both environments match
quiz.explain: Environment differences are where bugs hide. Matching the engine and version lets staging reproduce database-specific behaviour. Mocks cannot reproduce it either.

quiz.q: Which of these is acceptable to keep in a plain configuration file committed to the repository?
options: The request timeout, set to 5 seconds
The password for the production database
The live key for the payment provider
The key used to sign login tokens
quiz.explain: A timeout is ordinary configuration with no access value. Passwords, live provider keys and signing keys are secrets and belong in a secret manager.

quiz.q: Users upload avatars to the container's local disk. After every deploy they vanish, and with three replicas only the one that handled the upload can serve the file. What should you do?
options: Store uploads in external object storage and keep containers stateless
Build the container image once and promote that same image across every environment
Move the storage path into an environment variable per stage
Spin up a preview environment for each pull request
quiz.explain: Containers are replaceable, so durable data must live outside them. Config from the environment only changes where the path points; it still writes to a disk that gets discarded.

topics.title: Observability
topics.summary: Use logs, metrics and traces to understand a running system, and alert on user-visible symptoms.

lesson.text: It is 2am. Customers report that checkout is slow. Your service has twelve dependencies, three databases and a queue. Where do you start? **Observability** is the property of a system that lets you answer questions about its internal behaviour from the data it emits, including questions you did not anticipate when you wrote the code. Without it, production is a black box and every incident is guesswork.
The three pillars
Three kinds of telemetry complement each other. Each answers a different question, and none replaces the others.

items: **Logs**: timestamped records of discrete events. Best for detail about what happened in one specific case. Expensive at volume and hard to aggregate unless structured.

**Metrics**: numeric measurements aggregated over time (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, queue depth). Cheap to store and ideal for dashboards, trends and alerting. They tell you that something is wrong, not why.
**Traces**: the path of a single request across services, as a tree of timed spans. They show where time went and which dependency failed.

lesson.text: Structured logs

Write logs as key-value records, not prose, so they can be filtered and counted. Include a request or trace ID so one user's journey can be followed across services. Log at appropriate levels, and never log secrets or personal data.
Metrics and percentiles

Averages hide pain. If 95 requests take 100 ms and 5 take 10 seconds, the mean is about 600 ms, which describes nobody's experience. Use percentiles: p50 is the typical request, p99 is the slow tail that some real users hit constantly. Also beware high-cardinality labels (such as user ID on a metric): they explode storage cost. Put such detail in logs or traces.

lesson.text: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

A **service level indicator (SLI)** is a measurement of user-visible behaviour, such as the proportion of requests that succeed in under 300 ms. A **service level objective (SLO)** is a target for that SLI over a window, for example 99.9% over 30 days. The **error budget** is the allowed failure: 0.1% of requests, which is about 43 minutes of full outage per 30 days. While budget remains, the team can ship and take risks. When it is spent, reliability work takes priority over features. This turns the vague argument about 'how reliable is reliable enough' into a data-driven agreement, and 100% is the wrong target: it is infinitely expensive and users cannot perceive the difference beyond a point.
Alerting on symptoms, not causes

An alert should mean a human must act now. Alert on **symptoms** that users feel (error rate above threshold, latency SLO burning too fast), not on every possible **cause** (CPU at 80%, one pod restarted). Cause-based alerts are noisy, and miss novel failures. Use causes as dashboards for diagnosis. Burn-rate alerts, which fire when the error budget is being consumed much faster than planned, balance sensitivity with noise. Every alert should link to a runbook, and alerts that are routinely ignored should be fixed or deleted, because alert fatigue makes people miss the real one.
The practical diagnosis flow: an alert on a symptom fires, a metrics dashboard shows which endpoint and when, a trace shows which dependency is slow, and logs for that trace ID show the exact error.

Ask the agent to add telemetry as part of the feature: structured logs with a trace ID, a counter for failures and a latency histogram on the new code path. Agents often log too little where failure is likely, or too much sensitive data (full request bodies, tokens). Check that errors are not swallowed after logging, and that logs contain no secrets. When an agent is debugging an incident, give it real logs and trace data rather than letting it guess from the code.

patterns.signal: Mean latency is 150 ms, yet some users complain the endpoint is very slow
patterns.why: Track p50, p95 and p99; averages hide the slow tail. Record latency histograms, since percentiles cannot be averaged across instances after the fact.

patterns.signal: Debugging means grepping prose log lines like `User 42 failed to pay` across many servers
patterns.why: Emit key-value records (`event=payment_failed user_id=42`) with level and request ID so logs can be filtered and counted. Never log secrets or personal data; volume costs money.

patterns.signal: A failing request passes through gateway, order and payment services and you cannot follow it
patterns.why: Propagate trace context (W3C `traceparent`, OpenTelemetry) so spans from every service join into one trace showing where time went. Sample traces to control cost; keep errors and slow ones.

patterns.signal: A request-driven service has no standard dashboard and every team graphs different things
patterns.why: Rate, Errors, Duration per endpoint describe what callers experience and suit alerts. They show that something is wrong, not which resource is the cause.

patterns.signal: You suspect a database, disk, queue or thread pool is the bottleneck
patterns.why: For each resource check Utilization, Saturation (queueing) and Errors. Systematic and quick for finding the constrained resource; it complements RED, which views the service from outside.

patterns.signal: An alert on CPU above 80% pages someone at night and usually needs no action
patterns.why: Page on what users feel, like error rate or latency SLO burning, and keep cause metrics on dashboards for diagnosis. Alerts nobody acts on train people to ignore pages; delete them.

patterns.signal: Product and engineering argue whether to ship features or spend the sprint on reliability
patterns.why: Agree an SLI and target (99.9% over 30 days is about 43 minutes); while budget remains, ship; when it is spent, prioritize reliability. Needs agreed consequences or it is just a chart.

patterns.signal: A threshold alert fires on brief spikes and still misses slow, sustained degradation
patterns.why: Alert when the error budget burns fast over both a short and a long window. Catches real incidents quickly and ignores blips; more complex to set up than a static threshold.

patterns.signal: Metrics cost exploded after someone added `user_id` as a label
patterns.why: Every label combination is a separate time series; use bounded labels like endpoint and status. Put per-user and per-request IDs in logs and traces instead.

patterns.signal: Log volume and cost are dominated by debug-level lines from healthy requests
patterns.why: Log successes at info or sample them, keep all warnings and errors, and enable debug dynamically when investigating. Sampling can drop the one request you later need, so keep errors unsampled.

patterns.signal: A security review finds tokens and email addresses in production logs
patterns.why: Scrub known sensitive fields in the logging pipeline or log only allow-listed fields, and test it. Fixing every call site by hand misses new ones; logs often have broader access than the database.

keyPoints: Logs give detailed events, metrics give cheap aggregates for trends and alerts, and traces show a request's path across services.
Use structured logs with correlation IDs, and percentiles rather than averages for latency.
SLIs measure user experience, SLOs set targets, and the error budget quantifies how much unreliability is acceptable.
Alert on user-visible symptoms; use cause-level signals for diagnosis, and delete alerts nobody acts on.

quiz.q: Mean latency of an endpoint is 150 ms, yet some users complain it is very slow. What is the most likely explanation and next step?
options: The complaints are probably mistaken, since the mean is within target
A slow tail is hidden by the mean; check p95/p99 and trace slow requests
Those users are on slow mobile networks, so nothing can be done on the server side
The average-latency alert threshold is too low and should be raised
quiz.explain: Averages mask a minority of very slow requests. Percentiles expose the tail, and traces show where those requests spend time.

quiz.q: Your service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. Roughly how much downtime does the error budget allow, and how should a nearly exhausted budget affect decisions?
options: About 43 minutes; slow risky releases and prioritise reliability work
About 7 hours; ship faster, because there is still plenty of room in the budget
Zero minutes; any failure is a breach
About 43 minutes; ignore it until the window resets
quiz.explain: 0.1% of 30 days is roughly 43 minutes. A depleted budget signals that reliability should take priority over new features.

quiz.q: Which alert is best aligned with the principle of alerting on symptoms?
options: CPU on any application server stays above 80% for one minute
Any single container restarts unexpectedly
Failed checkouts exceed what the SLO can tolerate
Disk usage on a log server passes 60%
quiz.explain: Failed checkouts are what users experience. CPU, restarts and disk are potential causes that often cause no user impact and should live on dashboards.

quiz.q: You want to follow one failing request as it passes through the API gateway, the order service and the payment service. Which signal is designed for this?
options: A CPU utilisation metric exported by each service
A counter of total requests received per service
A free-text log line written by each service as it handles the request
A distributed trace sharing one trace ID across spans
quiz.explain: Traces connect the timed steps of one request across services. Aggregated metrics and unstructured logs cannot reliably be stitched into one request's path.

quiz.q: A developer adds `user_id` as a label on a request-count metric for a service with millions of users. What is the main problem?
options: Metric systems do not support labels, so the metric will be rejected
Labels add sampling error, so the counts become less accurate
Each user becomes its own time series, exploding storage and query cost
Storing user IDs anywhere in telemetry is prohibited outright by privacy law
quiz.explain: Each distinct label value creates a separate series. Metrics are for aggregates, while high-cardinality detail suits logs and traces.

quiz.q: Twelve services each have a dashboard built by a different engineer, so during an incident on-call cannot compare them or tell which request-serving service is hurting. Which approach fits best?
options: Per-resource utilisation, saturation and error graphs for every host and disk in the fleet
A standard dashboard of request rate, error rate and duration per service
Alert whenever CPU on any host passes 80 percent
Convert all logs to JSON and search them by field
quiz.explain: RED gives every request-driven service the same three signals. The USE method targets resources like disks and queues, which helps find a bottleneck but not compare services.

topics.title: Releases & Versioning
topics.summary: Version changes meaningfully, communicate them, and plan for app stores and deprecation.

lesson.text: Your library has 5,000 downstream users. You rename a function in a 'minor' update and builds across the internet break. Or your mobile app has a crash, you push a fix, and discover the store review takes two days and half your users never update. Releases are where your work meets other people's expectations, and versioning is the contract that sets those expectations.
Semantic versioning

**Semantic Versioning (SemVer)** uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increment MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible new functionality, and PATCH for backwards-compatible bug fixes. A consumer can then read a version bump and judge the risk: `2.3.1` to `2.3.2` should be safe to take, while `2.x` to `3.0.0` needs reading the notes. Versions below `1.0.0` signal that anything may change. Pre-release tags like `1.4.0-rc.1` mark candidates not yet final.

items: SemVer is a promise about a public API. You must define what that API is (functions, endpoints, config, file formats).
Removing a field, tightening validation, or changing a default can be breaking even if no code signature changes.
Applications (not libraries) often use date-based or build-number versions, because they have no API consumers to warn.
Consumers should pin versions with lockfiles and upgrade deliberately; maintainers should not assume that everyone follows the rules.

lesson.text: Changelogs

A **changelog** is a human-written record of notable changes per version, written for users, not a dump of commit messages. Group entries as Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security, and call out breaking changes and migration steps prominently. Conventional commit messages (`feat:`, `fix:`, `feat!:`) let tooling derive the version bump and draft the changelog, but a human should still edit the result for clarity.

## 3.0.0 - 2026-10-28
### Breaking
- `client.fetch()` now returns a Result object instead of throwing.
  Migrate: replace try/catch with `if (!res.ok)`. See guide.
### Added
- `client.fetchAll()` with automatic pagination.
### Deprecated
- `client.legacyQuery()`; will be removed in 4.0.0.
Release cadence and trains

Teams release either continuously (every merge deploys) or on a schedule. A **release train** departs on a fixed schedule (say every two weeks); features that are ready board it, and those that are not wait for the next one without delaying the train. This gives predictability and cheap coordination for products where every release has overhead, such as installed software and mobile apps. Pair it with feature flags so unfinished work can merge safely but stay dark.

lesson.text: Mobile and app-store specifics

Web backends can be rolled back in seconds, but a mobile release cannot. Binaries pass store review (hours to days), users update on their own schedule, and old versions stay in the wild for months. Consequences:

items: Your backend must support several old client versions at once; version your API and avoid breaking changes.
Use staged rollout (release to a percentage, watch crash rates, then widen) and halt it if the numbers look bad.
Put risky behaviour behind remotely controlled flags or config so you can disable it without a new binary.
Keep a force-upgrade mechanism for the rare case of a security or compatibility emergency, and use it sparingly.
Track crash-free sessions per version, since a regression affects users until they update.

lesson.text: Deprecation

Removing something abruptly breaks users. A good deprecation has stages: announce it, offer a replacement and a migration path, emit warnings at runtime or in docs, set a published removal date or version, measure remaining usage, then remove. Removal is a MAJOR change under SemVer. Measuring usage matters: you may find a large customer still depends on the thing you plan to delete.

Agents can draft changelogs and propose version bumps, but they cannot know which behaviours your consumers rely on. Ask the agent to list every public-facing change in the diff and classify it as breaking or not, then verify the classification yourself. Beware of agents that make 'harmless' changes to defaults, error types or response shapes in a patch release, or that regenerate a changelog from commit titles with no migration advice.

patterns.signal: A library's `parse()` returned an empty list for bad input and now throws, with no signature change
patterns.why: Changed behavior that callers rely on is breaking under SemVer, even without a signature change. Calling it a minor release breaks every consumer that auto-updates within a range.

patterns.signal: A change adds a new optional function or field and fixes nothing that callers rely on
patterns.why: Backward-compatible additions are minor and fixes are patch, so consumers can safely accept them within a `^` range. SemVer only means something once you define the public API.

patterns.signal: The changelog is a pasted `git log` full of `wip` and internal ticket numbers
patterns.why: Group entries under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security, with breaking changes and migration steps first. Written for users, not developers; generate drafts, then edit.

patterns.signal: Each release date slips because one unfinished feature holds everything else hostage
patterns.why: Ship on a fixed schedule with whatever is ready; unfinished work stays behind flags and catches the next train. Predictable for everyone, but a feature may wait one full cycle.

patterns.signal: A crash ships in a mobile app and the fix will take days to clear store review
patterns.why: Wrap risky features in remotely controlled flags so you can disable them in minutes without a new binary. Needs a safe default when config cannot be fetched, and it only covers flagged code.

patterns.signal: A new mobile build goes to every user at once and a crash would hit millions before you notice
patterns.why: Release to a small percentage, watch crash-free rate and key metrics, then widen or halt. You cannot recall installed builds, so halting early is the only damage control.

patterns.signal: Old app versions in the wild keep calling the API months after a new release
patterns.why: Keep the backend compatible with several client versions and enforce a minimum supported version for forced updates. Forcing updates annoys users; reserve it for security or broken versions.

patterns.signal: An endpoint some customers still call must be removed
patterns.why: Announce, provide a replacement and migration guide, emit warnings (such as a `Sunset` header), track usage and remove at a published date. Measure who still calls it rather than guessing.

patterns.signal: A breaking API change is unavoidable but existing integrations must keep working
patterns.why: Run old and new versions side by side and migrate clients over time. Every live version is code you maintain and test, so keep few versions and give each a sunset date.

patterns.signal: Production 2.3 needs an urgent fix while `main` already contains unreleased 2.4 features
patterns.why: Fix on `main`, then cherry-pick to the `release/2.3` branch and ship 2.3.1 from it. Avoids shipping half-done work; each maintained branch adds merge and testing cost.

patterns.signal: Version numbers and tags are bumped by hand and sometimes skipped or duplicated
patterns.why: Derive the next version from commit conventions or PR labels and tag in CI, generating changelog drafts too. Only as accurate as the commit discipline behind it.

keyPoints: SemVer's MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH is a promise about a defined public API: breaking, additive, fix.
Write changelogs for users, with breaking changes and migration steps called out.
Release trains give predictable schedules; flags keep unfinished work from boarding.
Mobile releases cannot be rolled back quickly, so use staged rollouts, remote kill switches and server compatibility with old clients; deprecate in stages with a measured removal.

quiz.q: A library's `parse()` function used to return an empty list for invalid input and now throws an exception. Under SemVer, which kind of release is this?
options: Major, because existing callers can break
Minor, because no new function was added
Patch, because it only fixes how invalid input is handled
None, since the function signature is unchanged
quiz.explain: Behaviour that callers depend on is part of the public API. Changing it incompatibly requires a major version even if signatures do not change.

quiz.q: A critical crash ships in your mobile app. The fix is ready. What reality should shape your plan?
options: The store can roll every user back to the previous build instantly
Store review is skipped entirely for fixes marked as urgent
Only new installs matter, since existing users all update within a few hours
Old installs stay broken until updated, so add flag or server mitigations
quiz.explain: Binaries are in users' hands. Mitigation often combines a new release with server-side or flag-based workarounds for people who have not updated.

quiz.q: You will remove an endpoint that some customers still call. Which plan best follows good deprecation practice?
options: Delete it in the next patch release and mention the removal in the changelog
Keep it running forever, since any removal will break someone
Announce a replacement and date, warn, track usage, remove in a major
Email the affected customers on the day the endpoint is removed
quiz.explain: Staged notice, a migration path and usage measurement let consumers adapt. Removing in a patch violates the SemVer contract.

quiz.q: What is the key benefit of a fixed-schedule release train?
options: Every planned feature is guaranteed to ship in the next release
Urgent hotfixes are forbidden between scheduled departures
Releases happen less often, which by definition reduces the risk of each one
Timing is predictable, and late work waits instead of delaying it
quiz.explain: Predictability and not holding the release hostage to one late feature are the point. Hotfixes can still ship outside the train.

quiz.q: What makes a good changelog entry different from a raw commit list?
options: It is more complete, covering every commit in the release
It explains user impact, flags breaking changes and gives migrations
It credits every author who contributed to the release
It lists every file and module that changed, so readers can audit the release
quiz.explain: Changelogs serve consumers deciding whether and how to upgrade. Commit messages record developer-level steps that rarely answer that.

quiz.q: Release tags are bumped by hand. Last week `2.3.1` was tagged twice and `2.4.0` was skipped, and nobody can say which commits each one holds. What should you reach for?
options: Move to a fixed-schedule release train with a code freeze date before each release
Publish a hotfix from a dedicated release branch each time
Group the changelog into user-facing sections by hand
Derive the next version and tag from commit types in the release pipeline
quiz.explain: Computing the version and tag from commits in CI removes the manual step that went wrong. A release train fixes when releases ship, not how version numbers are assigned.

exam.q: You notice that a PR 'fixing' a failing CI job changes a test assertion from `expect(total).toBe(100)` to `expect(total).toBeGreaterThan(0)` alongside a pricing change. What do you do?
options: Approve it, since the pipeline is green again
Ask why it was weakened; the pricing change may be the real bug
Ask the author to add retries so the test stops failing
Merge it now and open a follow-up ticket to tighten the assertion later
exam.explain: A weakened assertion that makes a red build green is a red flag. The test may have caught a genuine regression in the pricing change.

exam.q: Your staged rollout has reached 5% of users. Crash-free sessions and p50 latency match the previous version, but the server-side error rate for the new version is three times higher. What is the right action?
options: Halt the rollout and investigate the user-visible regression
Keep widening, since errors at 5% exposure are not meaningful
Hold at 5% until the median latency also starts to move
Exclude the 5% cohort from dashboards to reduce the noise
exam.explain: A tripled error rate is a clear user-visible symptom. Catching exactly this while exposure is small is the purpose of a staged rollout; widening would spread it, and latency is not the only signal that matters.

exam.q: Which of these deployments is hardest to reverse with a simple rollback?
options: A new CSS colour palette for the website
A feature behind a flag enabled for 10% of users
A change to the wording of an internal log message
A migration that converts and then drops a column
exam.explain: Data transformations and dropped columns cannot be undone by redeploying code. The others can be reverted by redeploying or flipping a flag.

exam.q: Your app depends on `lib@^2.1.0` and has a committed lockfile pinning 2.1.4. Upstream publishes 2.2.0, labeled a minor release, which actually breaks your usage. What happens on your next CI run using `npm ci`?
options: CI installs 2.2.0 because it satisfies the caret range, so the build breaks
CI installs 2.1.4 from the lockfile; 2.2.0 arrives only when you update deliberately
npm ci stops with an out-of-sync error until the lockfile is regenerated against 2.2.0
npm detects that 2.2.0 violates SemVer and skips it automatically
exam.explain: `npm ci` installs exactly what the lockfile records, regardless of newer versions in range. SemVer labels are a maintainer's promise, not a guarantee, which is why consumers pin and upgrade deliberately.

exam.q: A service has a 99.9% SLO and has achieved 99.99% for the past several windows. Product asks for a risky but valuable migration. How does the error budget inform the decision?
options: It is forbidden, because the SLO must be exceeded at all times
The budget governs incident response only and has no bearing on feature decisions
Ample budget remains, so the risk is acceptable if staged and monitored
The SLO must first be raised to 100% to protect users
exam.explain: Unused budget is room for calculated risk. Staging and monitoring keep the risk within what the SLO allows, and 100% is never a sensible target.

exam.q: You are reviewing a PR from an AI agent that adds a new endpoint. Tests pass. Which question is the most valuable to ask first?
options: Did the agent follow my preferred variable naming conventions?
How many lines did the agent write, and is that too many?
Does it check authorization and validate input, and do tests cover that?
Which model generated the code, and was it the newest one available at the time?
exam.explain: Security checks and input handling are classic gaps, and passing tests only prove what was tested. Style questions are better automated.

exam.q: You roll out a new version across ten instances one at a time. The new code writes to a new `NOT NULL` column that the migration added just before the rollout. During the rollout, instances still on the old version start failing inserts. What was the mistake?
options: Ten instances is too few for a rolling deploy to be considered safe
A rolling strategy was the wrong choice; a canary would have avoided it
The migration was incompatible with the old code still running
The health checks should have run more frequently during the rollout
exam.explain: During a rolling deploy both versions run at once, so the schema must work for both. Add the column as nullable first (expand), and tighten it only after the old code is gone.

exam.q: A page fires whenever the 5-minute error rate exceeds 0.1%, the SLO threshold. It pages several times a week for brief blips that recover on their own, while the monthly error budget stays mostly unspent. What is the best change?
options: Delete the alert, since the budget is healthy anyway
Lower the threshold so problems are caught even earlier
Page on error-budget burn rate instead of the raw error rate
Keep it, and ask on-call to acknowledge blips more quickly
exam.explain: A burn-rate alert fires when the budget is being consumed much faster than planned, so short harmless blips stop paging while sustained problems still do. Deleting the alert loses protection entirely.

exam.q: Your Dockerfile starts with `FROM node:latest` and production deploys tag the image `latest`. Last week a deploy changed behaviour with no code change in your repo. What is the root cause and the fix?
options: Floating tags: pin the base version and tag images by commit SHA
Containers are mutable by design, so prefer patching running instances
The registry was out of date, so clear its cache before each deploy
Node.js releases break on every update, so avoid containers entirely
exam.explain: Floating tags mean the same Dockerfile can build different content over time, and `latest` tells you nothing about what is running. Pinned versions and SHA tags make builds reproducible and rollbacks precise.

exam.q: You ship via blue/green. Right after you flip traffic to green, the error rate climbs. The migration that ran was additive and backward compatible. What is the fastest safe mitigation?
options: Redeploy blue from scratch using the previous commit's build
Patch green in place and keep serving until it is fixed
Pause all traffic until the cause has been fully understood
Flip the router back to blue, still on the old version
exam.explain: Blue is still up and compatible with the database, so a routing change restores service in seconds. Investigate afterwards, from a stable position.

exam.q: A library maintainer adds an optional parameter with a default that preserves old behaviour and a new helper function. Which version bump fits under SemVer from 4.2.7?
exam.explain: Backwards-compatible new functionality is a minor bump, which resets the patch number. A major bump is only for breaking changes.

exam.q: A bug appears in an iOS release that is already at 100% rollout, and your backend team wants to change the API response shape to fix it. What is the key risk?
options: iOS apps may not call third-party APIs once they pass review
Clients ignore response shapes, so only the status code matters
Backend APIs are frozen once the matching app version launches
Older app versions still expect the old shape and may break on it
exam.explain: Old clients persist for months. Backends must remain compatible with them, usually by adding fields or versioning the API.

exam.q: A merged change deployed at 2pm and error rates doubled at 2:10pm. You have a flag guarding the new code path. What is the fastest safe first step?
options: Turn the flag off, confirm errors recover, then investigate
Start rewriting the feature so that the next deploy fixes the root cause
Wait an hour to collect more data before acting
Deploy another change on top to see whether it helps
exam.explain: A flag is a kill switch that restores service in seconds. Investigating after mitigation limits user impact.

exam.q: The same container image must run in staging and in production, but the two use different database hosts and credentials. Where should those differences live?
options: In separate long-lived branches of the code, one per environment
In injected runtime config, with secrets from a secret store
In two separate Dockerfiles that bake the values into each image
In constants at the top of the source file, switched by hostname
exam.explain: One artifact plus injected configuration keeps what you tested identical to what you deploy. Baking values into images or branches breaks that, and credentials never belong in code.

exam.q: Put the stages of a CI pipeline in the order that gives the fastest feedback, as in the lesson's example.
steps: Check out the commit
Install exact dependencies with `npm ci`
Run lint and typecheck
Run unit tests
Run integration tests, only if the fast checks passed
exam.explain: Nothing runs without the code, and nothing builds without dependencies from the lockfile. After that, the cheapest checks go first: lint and typecheck fail in seconds, unit tests next, and the slow integration job runs only once the fast stage is green (`needs: fast-checks`).

exam.q: Order the deploys of a zero-downtime rename of `users.name` to `users.full_name` (expand/contract).
steps: Add `full_name` as a nullable column; old code is unaffected
App writes both columns and still reads `name`; backfill old rows in batches
App reads `full_name` while still writing `name`
Drop `name` once nothing reads or writes it
exam.explain: Expand first, contract last. Each step stays compatible with the version running before it, so any deploy can be rolled back. Reading `full_name` before the backfill would return nulls, and dropping `name` before the last reader is gone crashes old instances and makes rollback impossible.

exam.q: Order the steps of a blue/green deployment, with blue serving live traffic at the start.
steps: Deploy the new version to the idle green environment
Test green under production-like conditions
Switch the router so all traffic goes to green
If errors rise, switch the router back to blue
exam.explain: Green is deployed and tested while it takes no traffic, then the router flips all traffic at once. Blue stays intact, so rollback is another near-instant flip rather than a redeploy.

exam.q: This Terraform defines the production orders database. Click the line with the bug.
exam.code:
resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
  identifier          = "orders-${var.env}"
  engine              = "postgres"
  engine_version      = "16.4"
  instance_class      = var.db_instance_class
  allocated_storage   = 50
  deletion_protection = true
  username            = "orders_app"
  password            = "Tr0ub4dor&3"
}
exam.explain: Line 9 hard-codes a secret in a file that lives in version control, so everyone with repo access, and every clone, has the production password. Use `password = var.db_password` injected from a secret store, and since it was committed, revoke and rotate it. A username is not a secret, so line 8 is fine.

exam.q: This handler logs failed logins for later investigation. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 6 writes the password the user typed into the logs, where many people and tools can read it, and a failed attempt is often a typo of the real password. Never log secrets: delete the field. The rest is good structured logging, with an event name, a reason and a trace ID to correlate.

exam.q: This migration runs in the first deploy of renaming `users.name` to `users.full_name`, while the old app version is still serving traffic. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 8 drops `name` in the same deploy that adds its replacement, while the running code still reads it: old instances fail at once and rolling back the code cannot bring the data back. The contract step belongs in a later deploy, after the app reads `full_name` and nothing uses `name`.

exam.q: A service logs these ten request latencies. What does this print?
exam.explain: The sum is 900 + 5000 = 5900, so the mean is 590 ms, a latency no request actually had. The median is `sorted[5]`, 100 ms. One slow request drags the mean six-fold and leaves p50 untouched, which is why you watch percentiles, including the tail (p99), instead of averages.

exam.q: This applies Semantic Versioning bumps to a release history. What does it print?
exam.explain: 2.3.1 → 2.3.2 (fix) → 2.4.0 (feature resets PATCH) → 2.4.1 (fix) → 3.0.0 (breaking resets MINOR and PATCH) → 3.1.0 (feature). A MAJOR bump always zeroes the lower numbers.

title: Maintaining
tagline: Keep software alive, safe, fast and understandable long after the first release.
intro: Most of a system's life is spent after the first version ships, and most of the code you touch will be code someone else wrote. AI agents make it cheap to add code and easy to add a lot of it, so the discipline of keeping a codebase small, healthy, documented and recoverable matters more, not less. This section teaches the habits that stop that growth from turning into an unmaintainable mess.

topics.title: Refactoring & Technical Debt
topics.summary: Change the structure of code without changing what it does, and treat shortcuts as loans you consciously take.

lesson.text: You are asked to add a new discount rule to a 600-line `calculate_total` function. It mixes tax, shipping, coupons and rounding in one tangle of nested ifs. You can bolt the new rule on and pray, or you can first make the function easier to change. The second option is refactoring.
What refactoring is (and is not)

**Refactoring** is changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behaviour. The second half is the whole definition. If behaviour changes, even for the better, you are doing a feature or a bug fix, not a refactor. Mixing the two in one commit makes review hard and makes it impossible to tell which change broke something.

Typical refactorings are small and mechanical: rename a variable, extract a function, inline a pointless wrapper, replace a conditional with polymorphism, move a function to the module that owns its data. Each step is tiny so that, if tests fail, you know exactly which step caused it.
The safety net: tests

Refactoring without tests is just editing and hoping. Before restructuring code that has no tests, write **characterization tests**: tests that record what the code actually does today, right or wrong, by feeding it inputs and asserting on whatever comes out. They do not claim the behaviour is correct, only that it is current. If a refactor changes an output, the test tells you.

# Characterization test: pin down current behaviour before touching it
def test_total_current_behaviour():
    order = make_order(items=[("widget", 10.00, 3)], coupon="SAVE10", country="DE")
    # Value copied from running the legacy code, not from a spec
    assert calculate_total(order) == 31.48

def test_total_rounding_quirk():
    order = make_order(items=[("pen", 0.333, 3)], coupon=None, country="US")
    assert calculate_total(order) == 1.00  # odd, but customers rely on it
Notice the second test: a quirk is pinned, not fixed. Fixing it is a separate, deliberate, behaviour-changing commit.
A safe refactoring loop

items: Get tests green (add characterization tests if coverage is thin).
Make one small structural change.
Run the tests. Green: commit. Red: revert and try a smaller step.
Repeat until the code is easy to change, then make the actual feature change on top.

lesson.caption: Each pass is one small change: green tests mean commit and take the next step, red means revert and try a smaller step.

lesson.text: A well-known phrasing of this is: make the change easy, then make the easy change.
Technical debt as a tradeoff

**Technical debt** is the future cost created by choosing a quicker or simpler solution now. The metaphor is useful because debt can be rational: shipping a prototype with a hard-coded config to hit a launch date is a loan with a known purpose. What makes debt harmful is when it is accidental, undocumented, or never repaid, so that the interest (slower changes, more bugs, harder onboarding) compounds.

items: **Deliberate and prudent**: we know the shortcut, we wrote it down, we scheduled the payoff.
**Accidental**: we did not know a better design existed; we only learn this later.
**Reckless**: we skipped design because we did not care about the consequences.

lesson.text: Debt is only worth paying down where you keep working. Ugly code in a module nobody touches costs nothing. Ugly code in the file changed every week costs a lot. Prioritise by change frequency times pain, not by aesthetic offence.
Common pitfalls

items: The big-bang rewrite disguised as a refactor: weeks without a green build, then an unreviewable diff.
Refactoring and changing behaviour in the same commit.
Refactoring code you have no reason to touch.
Trusting a green test suite that does not actually cover the path you moved.

lesson.text: Agents are fast, confident refactorers and also fast at quietly changing behaviour. Ask for characterization tests first, then refactor in small commits, and tell the agent explicitly that tests must not change. If the diff edits existing assertions to make them pass, that is a red flag: the agent changed the spec, not the code. Also watch for 'while I was here' cleanups that touch unrelated files.

patterns.signal: You must restructure a function that has no tests and nobody can say what it is supposed to return
patterns.why: Record what the code does today, quirks included, so any behaviour change shows up as a red test. They pin current behaviour, not correct behaviour; fix quirks in a separate commit.

patterns.signal: A new rule must go into a tangled 600-line function and bolting it on feels risky
patterns.why: Make the change easy, then make the easy change: restructure first under green tests, then add the feature on top. Only worth it in code you are about to change anyway.

patterns.signal: A refactor step leaves several tests red and you cannot tell which edit caused it
patterns.why: One small structural change per run; green means commit, red means revert and take a smaller step. Feels slow, but you never debug a large broken diff.

patterns.signal: A single commit both restructures code and changes an output, and the reviewer cannot tell which part is the fix
patterns.why: A pure refactor should leave every test untouched, which makes it easy to review and bisect. Mixing them hides the behaviour change inside noise.

patterns.signal: You want to unit test logic that calls the database or the clock directly and cannot be isolated
patterns.why: Create a point where behaviour can be swapped without editing the call site, such as a parameter, interface or injected function. Adds indirection, so add seams only where tests need them.

patterns.signal: A long chain of `if type == ...` branches grows with every new variant and is copied in several places
patterns.why: Each variant owns its behaviour, so adding one means adding a class, not editing every switch. Overkill for two stable cases; a plain conditional is clearer there.

patterns.signal: A team ships a hard-coded shortcut to hit a launch date and someone asks whether that is acceptable
patterns.why: Debt is fine when it is known, written down and has a payoff plan, like a ticket with an owner. Unrecorded debt compounds silently until nobody knows it exists.

patterns.signal: The team has a long list of ugly modules and limited time to clean up
patterns.why: Pay down debt where change frequency times difficulty is highest; version-control history shows churn. Ugly code nobody touches costs nothing, so leave it.

patterns.signal: An agent's refactor diff edits existing test assertions so the suite goes green
patterns.why: Tell the agent tests must not change in a refactor; changed assertions mean the spec moved, not the structure. Review test files first and reject such diffs.

keyPoints: Refactoring preserves observable behaviour; if behaviour changes it is not a refactor.
Characterization tests pin current behaviour (even quirks) so you can restructure safely.
Work in small steps with a green-red-revert loop and keep refactors in separate commits from feature changes.
Technical debt is a tradeoff: deliberate, recorded debt is fine; invisible, unrepaid debt compounds.
Pay down debt where you actually keep changing code.

quiz.q: What most precisely distinguishes a refactoring from other code changes?
options: It reduces the line count while keeping every feature
It changes structure while leaving observable behaviour the same
It is done by someone other than the code's original author
It always makes the code run faster for the same inputs
quiz.explain: Refactoring is defined by behaviour preservation. Fewer lines or better speed may happen, but neither is required, and if behaviour changes you are doing a different kind of change.

quiz.q: You must restructure a legacy function with no tests. What do you do first?
options: Rewrite it cleanly and compare old and new versions by reading them
Fix the obvious bugs you notice while reading through it
Write tests that record its current outputs for representative inputs
Delete the branches that look dead so there is less to restructure
quiz.explain: Characterization tests give you a safety net that detects behaviour change. Fixing bugs or deleting branches first changes behaviour with nothing to catch mistakes.

quiz.q: During a refactor a test fails because the legacy code rounds 0.999 up in a surprising way. What is the best response?
options: Update the test to expect the new, more sensible rounding
Delete the test, since it only pins down a known bug
Abandon the refactor branch entirely and leave the code alone
Restore the old rounding, and log the bug for a separate fix
quiz.explain: A refactor must preserve behaviour, quirks included. Fixing the quirk is a deliberate, separate change that can be reviewed and rolled back on its own.

quiz.q: Which situation is the best example of acceptable technical debt?
options: Skipping design review because the deadline feels stressful and nobody will check
Hard-coding a config value to hit a launch date, with a backlog item and a cleanup date
Copying a function into five places because the author did not know how to extract it
Leaving every shortcut in place indefinitely because the product still appears to work
quiz.explain: Acceptable debt is deliberate, visible and scheduled for repayment. The others are reckless, accidental or unmanaged.

quiz.q: Where should a team prioritise paying down debt?
options: In the modules that change most often and cause the most friction
In the ugliest modules, wherever they sit and however rarely touched
In the oldest files first, since age is the best predictor of cost
In the largest files first, since size is the best predictor of cost
quiz.explain: Debt costs interest only when you work in that code. High change frequency plus high pain gives the best return; age or size alone are weak signals.

quiz.q: You must add a new discount rule to a tangled 600-line `price()` function, and it is unclear where the rule even belongs. Bolting it onto the end feels risky. What should you reach for?
options: Rewrite `price()` from scratch in a new module
First restructure the code to make the change easy, then add the rule
Append the rule as a new `if` block at the bottom of the existing function
Rank all ugly modules by churn and clean the worst first
quiz.explain: Make the change easy, then make the easy change: refactor in small steps first, then add the rule. A full rewrite is a much bigger and riskier step than the task needs.

topics.title: Dependencies & Supply Chain
topics.summary: Every package you install is code you run and trust, so pin it, update it deliberately and scan it.

lesson.text: A typical web app declares 30 direct dependencies and ends up running 1,500 packages written by strangers. On Monday it builds fine; on Tuesday, with no change to your code, CI breaks or, worse, ships something different. Understanding why requires understanding versions, lockfiles and trust.
Semantic versioning and ranges

**Semantic versioning (semver)** labels a release MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. By convention, PATCH is for bug fixes, MINOR adds backwards-compatible features, and MAJOR signals breaking changes. It is a promise made by humans, so it is sometimes broken. A **version range** in your manifest says which versions you will accept.
Lockfiles

A range lets different machines resolve different versions on different days. A **lockfile** (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `Cargo.lock`, `go.sum`) records the exact resolved version of every direct and transitive dependency, plus integrity hashes. Commit it for applications. In CI, install from the lockfile strictly (`npm ci`, `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt`, `uv sync --locked`, `cargo build --locked`) so the build fails rather than silently re-resolving. Libraries publish ranges for their consumers; applications pin through the lockfile.

lesson.text: Updating on purpose

Pinning does not mean never updating. Unpatched dependencies are one of the most common ways systems get compromised. The goal is controlled change: small, frequent updates raised as separate pull requests (Dependabot, Renovate), each running your test suite. Ten small updates are easier to debug than one 'update everything' diff after two years. Read changelogs for majors, and keep an update cadence rather than waiting for a crisis.
Vulnerability scanning

Tools such as `npm audit`, `pip-audit`, `cargo audit`, OSV-Scanner and GitHub's dependency alerts match your resolved versions against known-vulnerability databases (CVEs, advisories). This only finds known problems. It also produces noise: a vulnerability in a function you never call may not be exploitable. Triage by reachability and exposure, but do not ignore alerts by default. A **software bill of materials (SBOM)** lists what is in a build so you can answer 'are we affected?' fast when a new advisory lands.
Supply chain attacks

items: **Typosquatting**: a malicious package named `reqeusts` or `colourama`, waiting for a mistyped install.
**Dependency confusion**: a public package with the same name as your private internal one, with a higher version, gets pulled in by the resolver.
**Account or maintainer takeover**: a legitimate package gets a malicious release, as in several well-known npm incidents.
**Install scripts**: code that runs at install time, before you have read anything.
**Slopsquatting**: attackers register package names that language models tend to hallucinate.

lesson.text: Mitigations: verify the package name, age, maintainers and download history before adding it; prefer fewer dependencies; use scoped/private registries with explicit routing; enable lockfile integrity checks; disable install scripts by default (pnpm already does, and npm supports `--ignore-scripts`); and add a short cooldown (for example, not installing releases less than a few days old, a setting that pnpm, Yarn and Renovate, among others, now offer) so that obviously malicious releases are caught by others first.
Vendoring

**Vendoring** means copying dependency source into your repository (Go's `vendor/`, or checked-in third-party directories). It guarantees reproducible, offline builds and lets you review exactly what you run, and protects you if a package is deleted from the registry. The cost: you own updates and security patches, and diffs get large. Vendor when availability or auditability matters more than convenience.
Pitfalls

items: Adding a package for ten lines of code you could write yourself.
Not committing the lockfile, or deleting it to 'fix' a conflict.
Treating a passing audit as proof of safety.
Letting a dependency stay on a version no longer receiving patches.

lesson.text: Agents add dependencies freely and sometimes invent plausible package names that do not exist or, worse, that an attacker registered. Require the agent to justify every new dependency, check the name on the registry yourself, and review lockfile diffs. Tell it to prefer the standard library and existing dependencies, and never to delete or regenerate the lockfile to get past an error.

patterns.signal: CI broke overnight with no code change, after a dependency published a new patch release
patterns.why: The lockfile records exact transitive versions and hashes; `npm ci` or `uv sync --locked` fails instead of drifting. Applies to applications; libraries usually publish ranges, not locks.

patterns.signal: Dependencies are two years old and a single 'update everything' attempt broke dozens of tests
patterns.why: Bots like Dependabot or Renovate raise one small PR per update, each running the tests, so breakage is easy to attribute. Costs review time; batch low-risk patch bumps to limit noise.

patterns.signal: Builds must work offline or must survive a package being deleted from the public registry
patterns.why: Copying dependency source into the repo gives reproducible, auditable, offline builds. You then own patching and accept large diffs, so vendor only when availability or audit beats convenience.

patterns.signal: Someone wants to add a package to save ten lines of string padding
patterns.why: Every dependency is a trust decision and an update stream for its whole transitive tree. Small, stable helpers are cheaper to own than to import.

patterns.signal: A newly suggested package name looks almost right, is days old and has few downloads
patterns.why: Check name spelling, age, maintainers and download history to catch typosquatting and hallucinated names. A short cooldown on brand-new releases also blunts maintainer-takeover attacks.

patterns.signal: An internal package name like `acme-utils` could also be registered on the public registry
patterns.why: Route internal scopes only to your private registry so a higher public version cannot win resolution (dependency confusion). Requires registry config on every machine and in CI.

patterns.signal: A scanner reports 40 vulnerabilities and the team is tempted to ignore all alerts
patterns.why: Fix exploitable, exposed ones first; record why others are not reachable instead of muting them. A clean audit only means no known issues, not safety.

patterns.signal: Installing a package can run arbitrary code on developer machines and CI runners
patterns.why: Use `--ignore-scripts` or a package manager that blocks lifecycle scripts, and allowlist the few packages that genuinely need a build step. Some native packages then need manual setup.

patterns.signal: Security asks which services ship a given vulnerable library version and nobody can answer quickly
patterns.why: A software bill of materials lists every component and version per build, so exposure questions become a query. Only useful if generated automatically on each build and stored.

keyPoints: Semver is a convention: caret and tilde ranges allow automatic minor/patch drift, so builds can differ over time without a lockfile.
Commit the lockfile for applications and install strictly from it in CI.
Update dependencies frequently in small, tested steps rather than rarely in large ones.
Scanners find only known vulnerabilities; triage them but do not dismiss them by default.
Typosquatting, dependency confusion and maintainer takeover mean every new package is a trust decision.

quiz.q: Your manifest says `^2.4.1`. What range of versions can the resolver choose without a lockfile?
options: Exactly 2.4.1
2.4.1 up to but not including 2.5.0
2.4.1 up to but not including 3.0.0
Any version of 2.x including older ones
quiz.explain: A caret permits changes that do not modify the leftmost non-zero component, so minor and patch updates are allowed. The tilde form is the one limited to patch updates.

quiz.q: An application commits its lockfile and CI installs strictly from it. What does that give you?
options: Every install resolves the same exact dependency versions and hashes
Dependencies load faster at runtime because they are pre-resolved
You no longer need to update dependencies once the file is committed
Every package in the tree is checked and kept free of vulnerabilities
quiz.explain: The lockfile freezes the full transitive tree, which makes builds reproducible. It does nothing about runtime speed, and pinned vulnerable versions stay vulnerable until updated.

quiz.q: A developer mistypes `pip install reqests` and gets a package that exfiltrates environment variables. Which attack is this?
options: Dependency confusion
Maintainer account takeover
A zero-day in the original library
Typosquatting
quiz.explain: Typosquatting relies on lookalike names. Dependency confusion instead exploits resolvers preferring a public package over a private one with the same name.

quiz.q: `npm audit` reports no vulnerabilities. What can you conclude?
options: The dependency tree is free of malicious packages
No known advisory matches your resolved versions right now
You can stop updating dependencies for a year
All transitive dependencies have been reviewed by humans
quiz.explain: Audits match against known advisories only. A fresh malicious release or an undisclosed flaw will not appear, so a clean audit is not proof of safety.

quiz.q: Your CI re-resolves version ranges on every run, and it broke after a dependency published a patch release with a behaviour change. What is the most lasting fix?
options: Delete the lockfile and reinstall so everything resolves fresh
Change the range to `*` so any published version is accepted
Install strictly from the lockfile and take updates as tested PRs
Vendor every dependency and stop taking any updates at all
quiz.explain: A strict lockfile install stops silent drift, and update PRs make changes deliberate and testable. Deleting the lockfile or using wildcards increases drift, and never updating just accumulates vulnerabilities.

quiz.q: A critical CVE lands for `libfoo 1.4.2`. Security asks which of your 60 services ship that exact version, and answering takes two engineers two days of grepping repos. What fits best?
options: Generate an SBOM for every build and query it by package and version
Disable install scripts by default on every developer machine and on all CI runners
Vendor every dependency into each repository
Triage each alert by whether the vulnerable code is reachable
quiz.explain: An SBOM is a queryable inventory of what each build contains. Reachability triage decides how urgent a finding is, but only after you know which services include the library.

topics.title: Incident Response & Postmortems
topics.summary: When production breaks, stop the bleeding first, coordinate clearly, then learn without blame.

lesson.text: It is 02:10 and checkout error rates jumped from 0.1% to 40%. Three engineers join a call, each starts investigating independently, two of them restart different services, and nobody tells customers anything. The system recovers at 03:30, and nobody is sure why. Structured incident response exists to prevent exactly this.
What counts as an incident

An **incident** is an unplanned event that degrades or threatens a service in a way that needs a coordinated response. Teams classify by **severity**, usually based on user impact rather than technical cause. For example: SEV1 means a core function is down or data is at risk for many users; SEV2 means major degradation or a significant subset affected; SEV3 means a minor issue with a workaround. The exact scale matters less than having one, agreed in advance, because severity determines who is paged, how often updates go out, and whether it is all-hands.
Roles

items: **Incident commander (IC)**: coordinates, decides, delegates. Does not debug. Keeps a single thread of control.
**Operations / responders**: investigate and apply changes to the system.
**Communications lead**: updates stakeholders and status page on a regular schedule.
**Scribe**: keeps a timestamped log of what was seen and what was changed.

lesson.text: Small teams double up roles, but someone must be explicitly in charge. Many people with no commander means conflicting changes, and conflicting changes make a diagnosis impossible.
Mitigate before root cause

The goal during an incident is to restore service, not to understand it. **Mitigation** is any action that reduces user impact: roll back the last deploy, disable a feature flag, fail over, scale up, shed load, block a bad client. Finding the root cause can wait until users are no longer hurting; often the logs and evidence are still there afterwards. A rollback that works in five minutes beats an elegant fix in two hours.
