lesson.text: Note how the log records observations, decisions and actions with times. This becomes the raw material for the postmortem.
Blameless postmortems

After the incident, write a **postmortem** (also called a retrospective or incident review): a timeline, impact, contributing factors, what went well, what went badly, where you got lucky, and concrete follow-up actions with owners and dates. **Blameless** does not mean nobody is accountable. It means you assume people acted sensibly given what they knew at the time, and you ask why the system made the mistake easy. If you punish the engineer who ran the bad command, people hide mistakes, and the next incident is slower to detect.
The limits of 5 whys

The **5 whys** technique asks 'why?' repeatedly to move from symptom to cause. It is simple and a good starting prompt. Its weaknesses: it assumes a single linear chain, whereas real failures have several contributing factors; it stops wherever the investigator stops; and it tends to end at a human ('the engineer did not check') which is where blame creeps in. Prefer asking what conditions allowed this, which safeguards were absent, and what would have made detection faster.
Pitfalls

items: Everyone debugging, nobody coordinating or communicating.
Making several changes at once during an incident so you cannot tell what helped.
Skipping the postmortem when the fix was 'just a rollback'.
Action items nobody owns, which never get done.

lesson.text: Agents are useful during incidents for reading logs, summarising a timeline and drafting a postmortem, but be careful about letting them take live actions in production. Give an agent read-only access while you diagnose, require your explicit approval for any change, and insist on mitigation (rollback, flag off) over a clever patch. Verify any root cause an agent states against the evidence in the logs; agents readily produce a confident, plausible story that the data does not support.

patterns.signal: Errors spiked minutes after a deploy and the cause is not yet understood
patterns.why: Restoring service beats understanding it; a five-minute rollback ends user pain while the evidence stays in logs. Not possible for irreversible data changes, so design migrations to be backward compatible.

patterns.signal: Several engineers are on the call, each debugging and restarting services independently
patterns.why: One person coordinates, decides and delegates but does not debug, keeping a single thread of control. Without one, conflicting changes make diagnosis impossible.

patterns.signal: The new code path is clearly the suspect and it is behind a toggle
patterns.why: Turning off a flag is faster and narrower than a full rollback. Only works if risky features ship behind flags and the off path is tested.

patterns.signal: Two responders each applied a fix at once and nobody knows which one helped
patterns.why: Change one thing, observe, then decide the next step, so cause and effect stay readable. Slower per step but avoids masking or compounding failures.

patterns.signal: After the outage nobody can reconstruct what was seen, decided and changed, or when
patterns.why: A scribe logs observations, decisions and actions with times; it becomes the postmortem timeline. Cheap to do live, nearly impossible to rebuild afterwards.

patterns.signal: Customers and support learn about the outage from social media rather than from you
patterns.use: Dedicated comms lead on a cadence
patterns.why: One person updates the status page and stakeholders on a fixed schedule, even with 'no news yet', so responders are not interrupted. Small teams double up, but someone must own it.

patterns.signal: A draft postmortem concludes that the engineer should have been more careful
patterns.why: Assume people acted sensibly with what they knew and ask why the system allowed the error. Blame hides information; system fixes like guardrails and checks prevent the repeat.

patterns.signal: Your 5 whys analysis ended at a single person and a single linear cause
patterns.why: Real failures have several conditions that combined; list them all instead of one chain. 5 whys is a useful prompt but stops wherever the investigator stops.

patterns.signal: The last three postmortems produced action items that were never done
patterns.why: Each action needs one owner, a due date and a verifiable outcome, tracked like other work. 'Be more careful' is not an action item.

keyPoints: Severity is defined by user impact and drives who is paged and how communication works.
A clear incident commander coordinates; responders change the system; someone keeps the log.
Mitigate first (rollback, flag, failover) and investigate root cause once users are safe.
Blameless postmortems ask why the system allowed the error and end in owned action items.
5 whys is a prompt for thinking, not a complete method: real failures have several contributing factors.

quiz.q: Errors began right after a deploy, and the cause is not yet understood. What should the incident commander prioritise?
options: Reproducing the bug in staging to find the root cause
Writing the postmortem while details are fresh
Asking each engineer to propose and test their own fix in production
Rolling back the deploy to restore service, then investigating
quiz.explain: Mitigation precedes diagnosis. A rollback restores users quickly and leaves the failing version available for analysis afterwards.

quiz.q: What is the incident commander's main job?
options: Writing and deploying the fix as quickly as possible
Drafting and posting the customer status page updates
Coordinating responders and decisions, not debugging
Establishing which engineer caused the incident
quiz.explain: The IC keeps one coherent thread of control. If the commander dives into debugging, nobody is coordinating and conflicting changes follow.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a blameless postmortem?
options: It asks how the system made the mistake easy, assuming people acted sensibly
It leaves out specific events and actions so nobody can be identified
It means nobody owns outcomes or is accountable for follow-up actions
It is reserved for incidents caused by third-party vendors and providers
quiz.explain: Blameless focuses on systemic contributing factors rather than individual fault. It does not hide facts or remove accountability for follow-ups.

quiz.q: Why is the 5 whys technique insufficient on its own?
options: It must always go exactly five levels deep, no more and no fewer
It follows one linear chain and often stops at a person, missing other factors
It needs dedicated analysis tooling that most teams do not have
It only works for hardware failures, not for software or process ones
quiz.explain: The number five is arbitrary; the real problem is that complex failures have several interacting causes and the technique encourages a single chain ending at human error.

quiz.q: Which postmortem action item is best?
options: Add a canary stage that halts rollouts on error spikes; owner Sam; due next sprint
Engineers must be more careful with deploys; owner: whole team; due: ongoing
Review the deploy process thoroughly at some point during next quarter
Remind every engineer to run the full test suite before each deploy
quiz.explain: A good action item is specific, owned, dated and changes the system. Vague exhortations to be careful do not prevent recurrence.

quiz.q: Two hours into an outage, support is overwhelmed with angry tickets and customers are learning status from social media, while every responder is heads-down debugging. What should you reach for?
options: Have every responder reply to customers as soon as they know something
Pause the debugging until a full postmortem draft is written
Stop restarting services until the root cause is confirmed
Assign one person to post status updates on a fixed cadence
quiz.explain: A dedicated comms role keeps customers informed on a predictable schedule without pulling responders off the fix. Ad hoc replies from many responders give inconsistent messages and cost debugging time.

topics.title: Performance
topics.summary: Measure before you optimise, find the hot path with a profiler, and distrust benchmarks that flatter you.

lesson.text: A report page takes 8 seconds to load. A teammate is sure the database is slow and wants to add an index and a cache. Two days later the page takes 7.6 seconds. The real cost was a loop that serialised JSON 4,000 times. The lesson: intuition about performance is unreliable, and optimising the wrong thing is pure cost.
Measure first

Donald Knuth's often-quoted line is that premature optimisation is the root of all evil; the full sentence is that you should not waste effort on small efficiencies about 97% of the time, but should not pass up the critical 3%. The practical rule: define a goal (for example, p95 under 500 ms), measure the current state, find the bottleneck, change one thing, measure again. If you did not measure, you do not know whether it helped.

Pay attention to **latency percentiles**, not just averages. An average of 100 ms can hide a p99 of 4 seconds that hurts one request in a hundred, which at scale is a lot of users. Also separate **latency** (time per request) from **throughput** (requests per second); improving one can hurt the other.
Profilers and flame graphs

A **profiler** shows where time or memory goes. A **sampling profiler** periodically records the call stack (for example 100 times per second), so overhead is low and the result approximates where the program spends time. An **instrumenting profiler** records every call precisely but distorts timing. A **flame graph** visualises sampled stacks: each box is a function, the width is the proportion of samples it appears in, and the stack grows upward. Look for wide boxes, especially wide boxes at the top, since those are where the time is actually spent.

lesson.text:
import cProfile, pstats
# Note: cProfile is a deterministic (instrumenting) profiler. For low-overhead
# sampling of a live process, use a sampler such as py-spy.

def build_report(rows):
    out = []
    for r in rows:
        out.append(render_row(r))   # suspicious
    return out

cProfile.run('build_report(load_rows())', 'prof.out')
stats = pstats.Stats('prof.out')
stats.sort_stats('cumulative').print_stats(10)
# Output shows 71% of time in json.dumps called from render_row

Distinguish **CPU-bound** work (time spent computing), **I/O-bound** work (waiting on disk, network, database) and **memory-bound** work (cache misses, garbage collection). The fix differs: algorithmic improvement for CPU, batching or concurrency for I/O, data layout for memory.
Hot paths and the usual wins
A **hot path** is code executed very often or on the critical path of a request. Optimise there and leave the rest readable. The biggest wins are usually not micro-optimisations:

items: Better algorithm or data structure (a list scan to a hash lookup; O(n^2) to O(n log n)).
Fewer round trips: the N+1 query problem, where one list query triggers N follow-up queries.
Doing less: skip unneeded work, paginate, stream instead of loading everything.
Caching expensive, repeatedly-requested results.

lesson.text: Caching and its price

A **cache** stores the result of expensive work to reuse it. It trades memory and complexity for speed, and brings one of the proverbial 'two hard things' in computer science: **invalidation**. A stale cache returns wrong data. Decide what happens when the source changes: time-to-live expiry, explicit invalidation on write, or accepting staleness. Watch for cache stampedes, where many requests recompute a popular expired key at once, and for a low hit rate, which means the cache is only adding overhead.
Benchmarks that lie

items: Cold versus warm: the first run pays for caching, JIT compilation and disk reads; later runs do not.
Unrealistic data: benchmarking on 100 rows when production has 10 million.
Dead-code elimination: the compiler removes work whose result is unused, so you measure nothing.
Noisy environments: a laptop with other processes, thermal throttling, a single run.
Microbenchmarks that ignore the system: a function 3x faster in isolation may not move end-to-end latency at all.
Averages that hide tail latency.

lesson.text: Good practice: repeat runs, report distributions, use realistic inputs, benchmark in an environment similar to production, and confirm that an improvement shows up in an end-to-end metric.

Agents love to 'optimise' by pattern: they add caches, rewrite loops or reach for concurrency without evidence. Give the agent a measurable target and a reproducible benchmark, ask it to profile before proposing changes, and require before and after numbers. Be suspicious of changes that make code more complex for an unmeasured gain, and check that any cache the agent adds has an invalidation story.

patterns.signal: A teammate is sure the database is the bottleneck but nobody has profiled the slow page
patterns.why: Set a target such as p95 under 500 ms, profile, change one thing, re-measure. Intuition about bottlenecks is often wrong, and optimising the wrong thing is pure cost.

patterns.signal: A flame graph shows one wide box near the top of the stack for a single function
patterns.why: Width is share of samples, so wide boxes are where time goes; fix those and keep the rest readable. Micro-tuning code that takes 1% of time cannot help much.

patterns.signal: A list page issues one query for the list and then one more query per row
patterns.use: Fix N+1 with batching / eager load
patterns.why: Fetch related rows in one `IN (...)` query or a join, turning N+1 round trips into 1-2. Over-eager loading of data you do not show can be slower, so batch what is used.

patterns.signal: The same expensive result is recomputed on every request though its inputs rarely change
patterns.why: Trades memory and complexity for speed; decide up front how entries expire (TTL, invalidate on write, or accept staleness). A cache with no invalidation story returns wrong data.

patterns.signal: When a popular cache key expires, many requests hit the slow backend at the same instant
patterns.why: Let one request recompute while others wait or serve stale data, or add jittered expiry. Adds locking or background refresh logic, so use it only for hot keys.

patterns.signal: The average latency looks fine but users still complain the service is sometimes very slow
patterns.why: Averages hide tails; a p99 of 4 s hurts one request in a hundred, which is many users at scale. Percentiles need histograms, not just sums and counts.

patterns.signal: The profiler shows the CPU mostly idle while requests wait on network or disk
patterns.why: I/O-bound work needs batching, concurrency or fewer round trips; CPU-bound needs a better algorithm; memory-bound needs better data layout. The wrong class of fix does nothing.

patterns.signal: A microbenchmark shows a 10x speedup but end-to-end request latency did not change
patterns.why: Confirm gains in a realistic end-to-end metric with warm runs, production-sized data and repeated measurements. The micro win may be off the critical path, or eliminated as dead code.

patterns.signal: A loader reads millions of rows into memory just to show the first page
patterns.why: Skipping unneeded work usually beats making it faster. Pagination adds API complexity and stable ordering requirements, but bounds memory and latency.

keyPoints: Set a target, measure, change one thing, measure again; intuition about bottlenecks is often wrong.
Sampling profilers and flame graphs show where time goes; wide boxes at the top are the hot spots.
Distinguish CPU-bound, I/O-bound and memory-bound work; the right fix differs.
Algorithms, fewer round trips (N+1) and doing less usually beat micro-optimisation; caches add invalidation problems.
Benchmarks mislead through cold starts, tiny data, dead-code elimination, noise and averages that hide tail latency.

quiz.q: A page is slow. What should you do before changing any code?
options: Add a cache in front of the database to cut query time
Profile or measure to find where the time actually goes
Rewrite the slowest-looking function in a faster language
Add more servers so each one handles fewer requests
quiz.explain: Without measurement you may optimise something that is a tiny fraction of the cost. Caches and hardware may mask the problem and add cost without addressing the bottleneck.

quiz.q: In a flame graph, which feature most clearly flags a good optimisation target?
options: A very tall narrow stack
A box at the far left of the graph
A box with a bright colour
A wide box near the top of the stack
quiz.explain: Width is the share of samples, so wide boxes consume time; those at the top are where time is spent rather than just passed through. Height only shows call depth, and colour and left-right order are usually arbitrary.

quiz.q: Why can an average latency of 100 ms be misleading?
options: Averages cannot be computed meaningfully for latency data
The mean of latency is always higher than the median
Rare, very slow requests hide in the tail yet hit many users
Latency should be reported in seconds, not milliseconds
quiz.explain: Percentiles such as p95 and p99 reveal slow tails that the mean smooths over. At high traffic the tail still represents many real users.

quiz.q: A microbenchmark shows your new function is 10 times faster than the old one, but a load test shows no change in request latency. The most likely explanation?
options: The function accounts for only a small share of request time
The microbenchmark measured the new function but not the old one
Load tests are too noisy to ever detect a latency change
Microbenchmarks always overstate speedups by a factor of ten
quiz.explain: If the function is a small fraction of request time, even a large speedup barely shows end to end (Amdahl's law). That is why you confirm gains in an end-to-end metric.

quiz.q: What is the main risk introduced by adding a cache to speed up a read?
options: Every read gets slower, even when the cache hits
The cache always costs more CPU than the original query
Entries can never be removed once they are cached
Serving stale data after the underlying source changes
quiz.explain: Caches trade freshness and simplicity for speed. Without a defined invalidation or expiry strategy, users see outdated values.

quiz.q: Each hour when the cached homepage feed expires, database CPU spikes to 100% for a few seconds because hundreds of requests all recompute the same value at once. Which approach fits best?
options: Add an index to the feed query so that each individual recompute is much cheaper
Fetch the feed in pages instead of all at once
Let one request rebuild the value while the others wait or get the stale copy
Replace the cache with per-request recomputation
quiz.explain: Single-flight or serve-stale stops the herd from hitting the backend together. An index makes each recompute cheaper but hundreds of simultaneous recomputes still pile up.

topics.title: Documentation & Knowledge Sharing
topics.summary: Write down what the code cannot say: how to run it, why it is this way, and what to do when it breaks.

lesson.text: A new engineer joins and spends three days getting the project to run because the setup steps live in one person's head. Six months later, someone proposes replacing the message queue and nobody remembers why it was chosen. At 3 a.m. the on-call engineer does not know how to restart the worker safely. All three are documentation failures, each of a different kind.
Code says what, docs say why and how

Code, if well written, already shows what it does. Documentation earns its keep by recording what code cannot: purpose, context, decisions, constraints, and procedures. Comments that restate the line below are noise. A comment that says why a surprising choice was made is valuable. A useful framework is to separate four needs: tutorials (learning), how-to guides (doing a task), reference (looking up facts), and explanation (understanding why).
The README

The README is the front door. It should answer, quickly: what is this, who is it for, how do I run it, how do I test it, how do I contribute, and where do I go for more. Test it by having someone new follow it literally on a clean machine; every step they get stuck on is a bug in the README.

# Orders Service
Handles order creation and payment capture for the storefront.

## Quick start
  make setup      # installs deps, starts local Postgres
  make test       # runs unit + integration tests
  make run        # serves on http://localhost:8080

## Where things live
  /api        HTTP handlers
  /domain     business rules (no I/O)
  /docs/adr   architecture decision records
  /docs/runbooks  operational procedures

## Ownership
  Team: Payments. Slack: #payments-eng. On-call: see runbooks/oncall.md
Architecture Decision Records

An **ADR** is a short, dated document recording one significant decision: the context and forces, the options considered, the decision, and the consequences. ADRs are immutable history: if a decision is reversed, write a new ADR that supersedes the old one rather than editing it. They answer the question 'why on earth did we do this?' months later, and stop teams from re-litigating settled choices without new information.

ADR-014: Use Postgres advisory locks for job de-duplication
Status: Accepted (2026-03-02)
Context: Two workers sometimes process the same job. Redis is not otherwise required.
Options: Redis SETNX, advisory locks, unique constraint on job table.
Decision: Advisory locks. No new infrastructure; lock scope matches transaction.
Consequences: Tied to Postgres; a lock held past a crash is released by the DB.
Runbooks

A **runbook** is a step-by-step procedure for an operational task or alert: what the alert means, how to confirm, how to mitigate, how to verify, and who to escalate to. It is written for a tired person at 3 a.m., so use exact commands, expected output and clear stop conditions. Link every alert to its runbook.
Docs as code

**Docs as code** keeps documentation in the repository next to the source, written in plain text such as Markdown, reviewed in pull requests, and checked in CI (link checkers, spell checks, executing code samples). The benefit is that a change to behaviour and its documentation ship in the same change. Docs that live in a separate wiki rot because nothing forces them to move with the code.

lesson.text: Pitfalls

items: Documentation that is out of date is worse than none, because it misleads confidently.
Documenting everything equally; prioritise what is hard to infer and costly to get wrong.
Knowledge locked in chat threads and heads (the bus factor).
Writing for yourself today rather than for a stranger in six months.

lesson.text: Agents read your repository docs as instructions. A good README, a short file such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md stating build and test commands, conventions and no-go areas, and ADRs for key decisions all directly improve agent output. Keep them accurate and concise. When an agent drafts documentation, check it for invented commands, wrong paths and plausible-sounding rationale that nobody actually decided; agents will happily write the 'why' for a decision they never saw.

patterns.signal: Someone proposes replacing a core component and nobody remembers why it was chosen
patterns.why: One short dated record per decision: context, options, decision, consequences. Supersede rather than edit, so history stays honest. Reserve ADRs for significant, costly-to-reverse choices.

patterns.signal: The on-call engineer gets an alert at 3 a.m. and does not know how to restart the worker safely
patterns.why: Exact commands, expected output, stop conditions and escalation, written for a tired stranger. Runbooks rot, so test them in drills and update after every incident.

patterns.signal: A new hire needs three days to get the project running because the steps live in one person's head
patterns.use: README tested on a clean machine
patterns.why: The README must say what it is and how to run, test and navigate it; every point where a newcomer gets stuck is a README bug. Keep it short and link out for depth.

patterns.signal: The wiki describes an API that changed six months ago and misleads readers confidently
patterns.why: Keep docs in the repo, reviewed in the same PR as the behaviour change and checked in CI (links, code samples). Wikis rot because nothing forces them to move with the code.

patterns.signal: A comment says `// increment i` while a surprising workaround nearby has no explanation
patterns.use: Comment the why, not the what
patterns.why: Code already shows what it does; comments earn their place by explaining intent, constraints and non-obvious choices. Restating the line is noise that drifts out of date.

patterns.signal: One document mixes a tutorial, a reference table and troubleshooting steps and serves none well
patterns.why: Learners, doers, lookers-up and understanders read differently, so separate the four kinds. More pages to maintain, but each is easier to find and keep correct.

patterns.signal: Only one engineer understands the billing integration and answers every question in chat
patterns.why: Move answers from chat into the repo and pair others on that area. Prioritise documenting what is hard to infer and costly to get wrong, not everything equally.

patterns.signal: An agent keeps guessing the test command and editing directories that are generated
patterns.why: A short repo file with build and test commands, conventions and no-go areas, loaded every session. Keep it accurate and brief; a stale one misleads agents just like stale docs mislead people.

keyPoints: Docs should capture what code cannot: purpose, rationale, constraints and procedures.
A README must let a newcomer run, test and navigate the project; test it on a clean machine.
ADRs record one decision each with context, options and consequences, and are superseded rather than edited.
Runbooks give exact steps for operational tasks and alerts, written for someone stressed and unfamiliar.
Docs as code keeps documentation reviewed and versioned with the source; stale docs are actively harmful.

quiz.q: Which comment adds the most value?
options: Retry 3 times: the vendor drops connections in nightly maintenance
Increment the retry counter by one after each failed attempt
This function returns the user record from the database
Loop over the list of users and process each one in turn
quiz.explain: It records why a non-obvious choice exists. The others merely restate what the code visibly does.

quiz.q: A team decides to move from REST to gRPC internally. What is the best way to capture this decision for the future?
options: Mention it in the team chat thread where it was discussed
Update the README tagline to say the services use gRPC
Write a dated ADR with context, alternatives and consequences
Rely on the code itself, since the gRPC calls are visible there
quiz.explain: An ADR preserves the reasoning and alternatives so later readers can judge whether it still applies. Chat threads are hard to find and code shows what, not why.

quiz.q: What makes a runbook good for an on-call engineer at night?
options: A detailed history of how the system evolved over the years
Exact commands, expected outputs and when to escalate
A link to the repository so the engineer can read the code
General advice to investigate carefully before acting
quiz.explain: Runbooks are for action under stress, so precision and clear decision points matter. History and general advice slow the responder down.

quiz.q: Why do docs-as-code practices reduce documentation rot?
options: They are written in a more precise, formal language than wikis
They guarantee that engineers enjoy writing documentation
They stop the code from changing once it has been documented
Docs change and get reviewed in the same PR as the code
quiz.explain: Keeping docs next to code and reviewing them together creates a natural moment to update them. It does not guarantee accuracy, but it makes drift visible.

quiz.q: An agent drafts an ADR explaining why a team chose a particular database, but you did not give it the reasons. What should you do?
options: Publish it as is, because it reads well and sounds plausible
Ask the agent to add more detail so the rationale is more convincing
Check each claim against what the team decided; cut invented reasons
Drop the ADR format and record the decision in a wiki page instead
quiz.explain: The risk is plausible but fabricated rationale being recorded as history. An ADR is only valuable if it reflects what was truly considered and decided.

quiz.q: The 40-page payments guide mixes a getting-started walkthrough, a table of every error code and an essay on why the ledger works as it does. New hires and on-call both say they cannot find anything. What fits best?
options: Separate it into a tutorial, how-to guides, a reference and an explanation
Add a table of contents and a search box on top of it
Write an ADR for each section of the guide
Move the whole guide into a single runbook that is linked from every alert page
quiz.explain: Readers arrive with different needs, so each kind of doc should serve one of them. A table of contents makes the mixed page easier to navigate but it still serves none of the needs well.

topics.title: Legacy Code & Migrations
topics.summary: Replace old systems gradually, move data safely, and delete code only when you can prove it is unused.

lesson.text: Your company's billing system is twelve years old, written in a framework nobody hires for, and it makes money. Everyone wants to rewrite it. Two years later the rewrite is still 'almost done', the old system has kept gaining features nobody ported, and the team has two systems to maintain. Legacy modernisation is mostly the art of not doing that.
What legacy means

Michael Feathers defined legacy code as code without tests. More broadly it is code that is valuable, hard to change safely, and often poorly understood. Legacy code is not bad code by definition: it is code that survived long enough to matter. It encodes years of edge cases and bug fixes, which is exactly why rewrites underestimate it.
The strangler fig pattern

The **strangler fig** approach (named for a vine that grows around a tree) replaces a system incrementally. You put a routing layer or facade in front of the old system, then build new implementations of one capability at a time and redirect that traffic to them. The old system keeps working throughout and shrinks until it can be switched off. Each step is small, shippable and reversible, so risk stays low and value arrives early.

Before:   client -> legacy monolith

Step 1:   client -> router -> legacy monolith
Step 2:   client -> router -> /invoices -> NEW invoice service
                          -> everything else -> legacy
Step 3:   ... repeat per capability ...
Final:    client -> router -> new services      (legacy switched off)

lesson.caption: The router moves one capability at a time to the new services while legacy keeps serving the rest, until nothing is left and it is switched off.

lesson.text: Feature parity and verification

Parity is harder than it looks because the old system's behaviour is the real specification, including bugs that customers rely on. Techniques that help: characterization tests against the old system; **shadow traffic** or **dark launching**, where requests go to both systems and the new one's response is compared but not returned; and gradual rollout by percentage of users with a quick switch back. Decide explicitly which quirks to preserve and which to drop.
Data migrations
Code can be rolled back; data often cannot. Schema and data changes need extra care. The standard approach for changing a live database is **expand and contract** (parallel change):

items: Expand: add the new column or table, keeping the old one. Deploy code that tolerates both.
Backfill: copy and transform existing data in small batches, idempotently, so it can be re-run.
Switch: move reads to the new structure, after verifying it matches.
Contract: once nothing uses the old structure, remove it.

lesson.text: During the transition you may use **dual writes**: the application writes to both the old and new stores. They are dangerous. Two writes are not atomic, so one can succeed and the other fail, leaving the stores out of sync, and concurrent writers can apply updates in different orders. Mitigate with a single source of truth, reconciliation jobs that compare and repair, or a change-data-capture pipeline that replicates from one store to the other instead of the app writing twice. Always make the old store the authority until the new one is verified.
Deleting code safely

Dead code costs reading time, build time and security surface. Before deleting, show that nothing uses it: search references, check logs or metrics for calls over a full business cycle (month-end jobs exist), add a deprecation warning or counter first, then remove. Because version control keeps history, deletion is reversible; that makes it safe to be bold once evidence is in. Delete in separate, small commits so reverting is trivial. Beware code reached only by reflection, config, scheduled jobs or external callers.
Pitfalls

items: The big-bang rewrite: long, invisible and risky, and it freezes feature work.
Migrating with no rollback path or no verification step.
Dual writes with no reconciliation.
Never finishing: both systems live forever. Plan and track the end state, including the shutdown.

lesson.text: Agents can translate legacy code across languages quickly, which makes big-bang rewrites tempting. Use that speed inside a strangler approach instead: have the agent port one slice at a time and generate comparison tests against the old behaviour. Review for silently dropped edge cases, and never let an agent run a data migration against production data without a dry run, a backup and your sign-off. Be sceptical when an agent claims code is unused after only a text search.

patterns.signal: Leadership wants a full rewrite of a working twelve-year-old system that still makes money
patterns.why: Put a router in front and replace one capability at a time, redirecting its traffic; legacy shrinks until it can be switched off. Each step is shippable and reversible, but the router adds a hop.

patterns.signal: You must swap an internal library used in hundreds of call sites without a long-lived branch
patterns.why: Introduce an abstraction over the old implementation, move callers to it, build the new one behind it, then switch and delete the old. Trunk stays releasable; costs a temporary interface.

patterns.signal: A column must be renamed in a live database while old and new app versions run side by side
patterns.why: Add new structure, backfill, move reads, then remove the old once unused. Every step is backward compatible; it takes several deploys instead of one migration.

patterns.signal: You need confidence that the new service matches the old one on real production inputs
patterns.why: Send requests to both, return only the old response, and log differences. Real coverage without user risk, but side-effecting calls must be stubbed and it doubles load.

patterns.signal: Millions of existing rows must be converted while the system stays online
patterns.why: Process small batches that can be safely re-run after a crash, with progress checkpoints. Slower than one big UPDATE, but avoids long locks and partial, unrecoverable states.

patterns.signal: During a migration the app writes every change to both the old and the new store
patterns.why: Dual writes are not atomic, so stores drift. Keep one store authoritative and run a job that compares and repairs, or use change data capture to feed the other.

patterns.signal: The new implementation is ready and you are unsure it handles the long tail of real users
patterns.why: Route 1%, then 10%, then more, watching error and parity metrics, and keep a one-step switch back. Requires routing by user or request and both systems running for a while.

patterns.signal: A module looks unused but you are not certain nothing calls it
patterns.why: Search references, then add a usage counter or deprecation log and watch a full business cycle, including month-end jobs. Delete in a small separate commit; version control makes it reversible.

patterns.signal: A migration has been 'almost done' for a year and both systems still need patches
patterns.why: Track the end state, including shutting the old system off, as explicit owned work. Without it, the migration never finishes and you maintain two systems forever.

keyPoints: Legacy code encodes years of edge cases; the old system's behaviour is the real specification.
The strangler fig pattern replaces functionality slice by slice behind a facade, keeping every step shippable and reversible.
Verify parity with characterization tests, shadow traffic and gradual rollout.
Migrate data with expand, backfill, switch, contract; dual writes need a source of truth and reconciliation.
Delete code only after evidence that nothing uses it, in small, revertable commits.

quiz.q: Why do full rewrites of working legacy systems so often go badly?
options: The new language or framework is usually slower than the legacy one
They lose encoded edge cases while the old system keeps changing
Nobody can understand legacy code well enough to start rewriting
Most companies have engineering policies that forbid full rewrites
quiz.explain: The old system embodies many undocumented behaviours and continues to evolve, so the rewrite chases a moving target without shipping value. The old language is not the core problem.

quiz.q: What is the defining feature of the strangler fig pattern?
options: Capabilities move to new code one at a time behind a router as the old system runs
The old system is frozen, rewritten offline, then swapped out over one weekend
Both systems are torn down and rebuilt from scratch on the shared database
The new system is produced by translating the old code line by line
quiz.explain: Incremental replacement behind a facade keeps risk small and each step reversible. The other options are big-bang or copy approaches.

quiz.q: You send each production request to both the old and the new service but only return the old service's response, logging differences. What is this technique?
options: Blue-green deployment switch
Dual writing to both stores
Canary release to a small cohort
Shadow traffic comparison
quiz.explain: Shadow traffic tests the new path with real inputs without affecting users. A canary exposes real users to the new version, and dual writing concerns data stores.

quiz.q: During a migration your app writes every change to both the old and new database. What is the main risk?
options: Writes to either database become impossible
The old database runs out of storage straight away
The two writes are not atomic, so stores can diverge
Backfills can no longer be run against the new store
quiz.explain: One write can succeed while the other fails, or concurrent writers can apply changes in different orders, leaving the stores inconsistent. Keep one authority and reconcile.

quiz.q: You want to delete a module that appears unused. What is the strongest first step?
options: Add usage logging and watch real traffic across a full business cycle
Delete it now, since version control means nothing is really lost
Search for the module name and delete it if there are no hits
Ask the agent to confirm that the module looks unused
quiz.explain: Text search misses reflection, config, scheduled jobs and external callers. Observed runtime usage over a full cycle is real evidence; version control makes deletion reversible but does not prove safety.

quiz.q: The billing migration started a year ago. 20% of customers still run on the old service, both systems need patches, and the team does everything twice. What should you reach for?
options: Begin routing shadow traffic to the new service to compare it with the old system
Add dual writes so both stores always hold the same data
Start a full rewrite of the new service to finish faster
Set a dated decommission milestone with an owner and a cutover plan
quiz.explain: Without an end date an incremental migration stalls with two systems to maintain. Shadow traffic builds confidence but does not retire the old system.

exam.q: A teammate opens a pull request titled 'Refactor: simplify pricing' that also changes how discounts round. What is the best review response?
options: Approve it, since the new rounding is more correct than the old
Ask for the rounding change to move into its own commit or PR
Reject it outright, because rounding behaviour must never change
Ask for more code comments explaining the new rounding logic
exam.explain: Mixing a behaviour change into a refactor hides which change caused any regression and defeats the verification idea. Separate them so each can be reviewed and reverted alone.

exam.q: Scenario: an agent finishes a refactor and all tests pass, but the diff shows it edited three existing test assertions. What do you do?
options: Merge it, since the full test suite is green
Ask the agent to add more tests before merging
Treat it as a likely behaviour change and review why
Delete the edited tests, since they were brittle
exam.explain: Edited assertions mean the specification moved to fit the code. Unless there is a deliberate, justified reason, treat it as a behaviour change and revert or review it explicitly.

exam.q: Scenario: your company publishes an internal package `acme-auth` at version 1.4.0 on its private registry. A build machine suddenly installs `acme-auth` 99.0.0 from the public registry. Which mitigation addresses the root cause?
options: Raise the internal package to version 100.0.0 so it wins again
Run `npm audit` on every build to catch the bad version
Route the internal scope or names to the private registry only
Add a cooldown so new releases are installed a few days later
exam.explain: This is dependency confusion: the resolver saw a higher public version with the same name. Scoping internal packages and pinning that scope to the private registry removes the ambiguity. Out-bidding the version only invites the attacker to go higher, an audit only knows published advisories, and a cooldown merely delays the install.

exam.q: An agent proposes adding the package `python-dateutils-helper` to your project. You cannot find it in documentation you know. What is the best next step?
options: Install it, since the agent has seen far more of the ecosystem
Ask the agent to confirm the package is safe and well maintained
Verify it on the registry yourself, or use an existing dependency
Try it in a throwaway container first, then ship it if tests pass
exam.explain: Models can hallucinate package names that attackers then register. Check existence, age, maintainers and downloads on the registry yourself, and prefer an existing dependency or the standard library. The agent's own assurance is not evidence, and passing tests in a container says nothing about what a malicious package does later.

exam.q: Two problems are reported at once: an internal admin export is broken for three staff who have a manual workaround, and 30% of customers cannot log in. Using an impact-based severity scale, how should they be classified?
options: Login as the higher severity, because it affects many customers with no workaround
Both at the same severity, since both are broken features in production
The export as higher, because it was reported first and has a known owner
Whichever has the more complex technical root cause gets the higher severity
exam.explain: Severity follows user impact, not technical cause or report order. A core function down for many users outranks a minor issue with a workaround, and that drives who is paged and how often updates go out.

exam.q: Scenario: a postmortem's conclusion reads 'engineer failed to check the config before deploying'. How would a blameless review improve it?
options: Remove the engineer's name but leave the conclusion unchanged
Ask why the process allowed it and add automated config validation
Add a rule that engineers must double-check configs before deploys
Ask the engineer involved to write the whole report on their own
exam.explain: Blameless review looks for system conditions, such as missing validation or a confusing interface, that let a reasonable person make the error. Removing a name or demanding care changes nothing structurally.

exam.q: Scenario: an orders page runs one query to fetch 50 orders, then one more query per order to load its customer. It is fast in development and slow in production. What is the best fix?
options: Add an index on the orders table's primary key column
Fetch all 50 customers in one batched query or a join
Move the database to a larger, faster server instance
Cache each customer row for an hour after it is loaded
exam.explain: This is the N+1 query problem: round trips grow with the number of rows, and each one pays network latency in production. Batching or joining removes the extra round trips. A primary key is already indexed, a bigger server does not remove round trips, and a cache adds invalidation problems without fixing the access pattern.

exam.q: Scenario: an agent says it sped up an endpoint by adding an in-memory cache. You read the diff. What must you check that the agent has not shown?
options: Whether the cache variable names are clear and descriptive
Whether the new code is shorter than the code it replaced
Measured before/after numbers and how stale data is invalidated
Whether the cache is a dictionary rather than a list or set
exam.explain: A performance change needs evidence of the bottleneck and of improvement, plus a correct invalidation plan. Cosmetic concerns do not address correctness or benefit.

exam.q: A benchmark loop calls `compute(x)` one million times and discards the result. It reports an astonishing speed. What is the most likely problem?
options: The optimiser removed the unused work, so nothing was measured
The result is correct and the function really is that fast
One million iterations is too few for any meaningful benchmark
Loops in benchmarks always distort the measured timing badly
exam.explain: Optimisers can eliminate work with no observable effect (dead-code elimination). Benchmarks should consume the result so the work cannot be removed.

exam.q: Scenario: a new hire cannot run the project and reports the README's setup steps are missing a database step. What is the best fix?
options: Walk the new hire through the missing step on a call
Post the missing step in the team chat for everyone
Fix the README, verify it on a clean machine, then script it
Close the report, since the other engineers have it working
exam.explain: Setup problems are documentation bugs. Fix the source of truth and verify it so the next person does not hit the same gap; automation removes the class of error.

exam.q: Which belongs in an ADR rather than in a runbook?
options: Commands to restart a stuck worker process safely
Steps to rotate an expired database credential
Escalation contacts and paging order for an alert
Why one queue technology was chosen over two others
exam.explain: ADRs capture decisions and their context. Runbooks are operational procedures.

exam.q: Scenario: you must replace a legacy reporting module used by many teams. Which plan is most consistent with sound migration practice?
options: Rewrite it in isolation for six months, then switch everyone at once
Add a facade, replace one report type at a time and shadow-compare
Delete the module and ask the teams to report whatever breaks
Freeze all feature work on reports until a full rewrite is done
exam.explain: Incremental replacement with verification keeps each step reversible and delivers value early. A big-bang switch concentrates all the risk at one moment.

exam.q: You are renaming a database column on a live system with zero downtime. Which sequence is correct?
options: Rename the column in one migration and deploy new code at the same moment
Drop the old column first, then add the new one and backfill it in batches
Add the new column, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one once unused
Copy the table under a new name, then swap the two tables in a single step
exam.explain: Expand, backfill, switch, contract keeps old and new code working throughout and gives a rollback point. A one-shot rename breaks whichever code version is not yet deployed.

exam.q: Scenario: your team builds firmware in an air-gapped facility and must be able to audit every line of third-party code it ships. Which dependency approach fits best?
options: Use wide caret ranges so builds always pick up the latest fixes
Vendor the source into the repository and own its updates yourself
Fetch packages from the public registry at build time over a proxy
Rely on a vulnerability scanner to approve each package automatically
exam.explain: Vendoring gives offline, reproducible builds and lets you review exactly what ships, at the cost of owning updates and security patches. Ranges and live registry fetches need network access and drift over time, and a scanner only knows published advisories.

exam.q: Put the steps of a safe refactoring loop in order.
steps: Get the tests green, adding characterization tests if coverage is thin
Make one small structural change
Run the tests: commit on green, revert on red
Once the code is easy to change, make the actual feature change on top
exam.explain: Tests come first because they are the safety net that proves behaviour is preserved. Each small change is checked and committed (or reverted) on its own, and the feature change comes last, in a separate step, so refactoring and behaviour change never share a commit.

exam.q: Checkout errors spike right after a deploy. Put the incident response in order.
steps: Declare the incident and assign an incident commander
Correlate the error spike with recent changes
Roll back the suspect deploy
Confirm the error rate is back to baseline
Hold a blameless postmortem to find the root cause
exam.explain: Someone must coordinate before the debugging starts. The responders tie the spike to deploy timing, then mitigate first with a rollback and confirm that it worked. Root cause analysis waits for the postmortem, after users stop hurting.

exam.q: Put the steps of a performance improvement in order.
steps: Define a goal, such as p95 under 500 ms
Measure the current state
Find the bottleneck with a profiler
Change one thing
Measure again
exam.explain: A goal tells you when to stop, and a baseline measurement shows the gap. The profiler finds where time really goes, which is often not where intuition says. Changing one thing at a time and measuring again is the only way to know whether each change helped.

exam.q: This exchange-rate cache is meant to expire entries after 60 seconds. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 8 has the comparison backwards: it returns the cached value only once it is older than the TTL, so it serves stale rates and refetches fresh ones. It should be `time.time() - hit[1] < TTL_SECONDS`.

exam.q: This function was rewritten to fix an N+1 query problem, but the problem is still there. Click the line that causes it.
exam.explain: Line 8 still runs one query per order, ignoring the batch that lines 4-5 already loaded, so the page makes 51 round trips. It should look up `customers[o.customer_id]`.

exam.q: This backfill for an expand-and-contract migration is meant to run in batches and be safe to re-run. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 5 does not skip rows that are already done, so it returns the same first 1,000 users forever and the loop never ends. Adding `WHERE full_name IS NULL` makes each batch pick up new work and makes the job safe to re-run.

exam.q: With no lockfile, which version does `npm install` resolve for this dependency?
exam.explain: A tilde range allows patch updates only (>=4.17.21 <4.18.0), and npm picks the highest match, 4.17.23. A caret range would have allowed 4.18.0, and only a wildcard or a new major range would allow 5.0.0.

exam.q: What does this print?
exam.code:
latencies_ms = [100] * 98 + [2000, 4000]
avg = sum(latencies_ms) / len(latencies_ms)
p99 = sorted(latencies_ms)[int(0.99 * len(latencies_ms))]
print(round(avg), p99)
exam.explain: The sum is 9,800 + 6,000 = 15,800 over 100 requests, so the average is 158. The p99 index is 99, the last sorted value, 4000. The average looks healthy while 1 request in 100 takes 4 seconds, which is why you watch percentiles.

title: Building with AI Agents
tagline: Direct, verify and safely ship work done by AI coding agents.
intro: AI coding agents now write a large share of production code, but they are only as good as the engineer steering them. This section teaches how the models actually work, how to give them the right context, how to structure agentic workflows, and how to verify and secure what they produce. The goal is an engineer who gets leverage from agents without giving up correctness or control.

topics.title: How LLMs Work
topics.summary: Tokens, context windows, next-token prediction and why models confidently invent things.

lesson.text: You ask an agent to call a library function and it writes a beautifully formatted call to a method that does not exist. Nothing crashed inside the model; it did exactly what it was built to do. To predict when agents will help and when they will mislead you, you need a working mental model of what a large language model (LLM) is.
Tokens: the unit of everything

An LLM does not read characters or words. Text is split into **tokens**, chunks of roughly three to four English characters on average, produced by a fixed tokenizer. Common words are one token; rare identifiers, long numbers and non-English text split into many. Tokens matter because the model reasons over them, and because you are billed, rate-limited and capped by token counts.
Next-token prediction

At its core, a model takes a sequence of tokens and outputs a probability distribution over the next token. It picks one, appends it, and repeats. This is called **autoregressive generation**. Training on enormous text and code corpora teaches the network to make these predictions well, and later stages (instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from feedback) shape it into an assistant that follows requests and uses tools.

prompt:  'def add(a, b): return a'
next-token probabilities:
  ' +'   0.93
  ' -'   0.02
  ' *'   0.01
  ...
sample one -> ' +' -> append -> predict again

lesson.text: Sampling and temperature

The model does not have to pick the most likely token. **Temperature** rescales the distribution: low values make output nearly deterministic, high values flatten it and increase variety. Other controls such as top-p restrict which tokens are eligible. Even at temperature zero, results can differ between runs because of batching and floating-point effects, so never assume exact reproducibility.
The context window

The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one request: your instructions, the conversation so far, file contents, tool results, and its own output. The model has no memory beyond it. Every turn, the whole relevant history is resent. Long contexts cost more, respond slower, and models tend to use information in the middle of very long inputs less reliably than information near the start or end.

items: Anything not in the window does not exist for the model on this turn.
Large tool outputs (a 5,000-line log) crowd out useful context.
Agents manage this by summarizing, compacting or starting fresh sessions.

lesson.text: Training cutoff

Knowledge is frozen at the **training cutoff**. A model may not know about a library version released after it, a renamed API, or last month's security advisory. It will often still answer fluently from older patterns. Fix this by putting current docs or the actual source in context, or by letting the agent read the installed package.
Why hallucinations happen

A **hallucination** is fluent output that is not grounded in fact. The model is trained to produce plausible continuations, not to verify truth. When it lacks the fact, the most plausible continuation of 'call the function that does X' is a well-named function. It has no built-in alarm for 'I do not know', although training reduces the rate. Hallucinations are most likely for obscure APIs, exact numbers, citations, and anything newer than the cutoff.

Common misconceptions: that the model looks things up in a database of facts (it does not, unless given a retrieval tool), that confident tone signals correctness (it does not), and that the model understands your whole codebase (it sees only what is in context).

# Plausible but wrong: requests has no such argument.
resp = requests.get(url, retries=3)

# Grounded fix: retries live on an adapter.
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
s = requests.Session()
s.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=Retry(total=3)))

Treat every API call, flag, config key and version number an agent writes as a hypothesis until a compiler, test or the real docs confirm it. Tell the agent to read the installed library source or run the command rather than recall it, and give it the current version number. Agents go wrong most often on exact signatures and recent changes.

patterns.signal: An agent writes a confident call to a library method you have never seen
patterns.why: Models generate plausible continuations, not verified facts. Confirm with the compiler, a test or the installed source before trusting any function, flag or config key.

patterns.signal: The agent uses a library API that was renamed in a release after its training data
patterns.why: Knowledge stops at the training cutoff. Put the installed version number and the real docs or source in context, or let the agent read them, instead of relying on recall.

patterns.signal: An agent session that has run for hours starts ignoring an instruction given at the start
patterns.use: Compact or restart with a summary
patterns.why: Long contexts dilute attention and early content can be summarized away. Start fresh with a short summary and the key constraints, or put durable rules in an instruction file.

patterns.signal: A tool returns a 5,000-line log and the agent's next answer gets worse
patterns.use: Trim tool output to the signal
patterns.why: Everything in the window costs tokens, time and attention. Pass the failing assertion or a filtered excerpt; let the agent fetch more if it needs it.

patterns.signal: You run the same prompt twice at temperature 0 and get slightly different code
patterns.why: Even low temperature does not guarantee identical output across runs or backends. Check results with executable verification rather than expecting byte-identical generations.

patterns.signal: A task involves long numeric IDs, exact character counts or unusual identifiers and the model fumbles them
patterns.why: Tokenization splits rare strings unpredictably, so exact counting and copying are weak spots. Let code or a tool compute it, and let the model orchestrate.

patterns.signal: The model's answer sounds certain about a fact it has no way of knowing from context
patterns.why: Fluency is not a correctness signal; models have no built-in 'I do not know' alarm. Ask what observation or document backs the claim, and verify it.

keyPoints: Models predict the next token from a probability distribution; they generate text, they do not retrieve verified facts.
The context window is the model's only working memory and everything in it costs tokens, time and attention.
Training cutoff means recent APIs and versions may be missing or outdated; supply current sources.
Hallucinations are plausible continuations without grounding; verify specifics with tools, not tone.

quiz.q: An agent writes code calling a plausible-looking method that does not exist in your library. What is the best explanation?
options: It produced a likely-sounding continuation that was never grounded in the real API
It looked the method up in its built-in fact index, which held a stale entry
Its temperature was too low, so it repeated a common pattern instead of the real name
The tokenizer split the real method name and reassembled the pieces in the wrong order
quiz.explain: Models generate plausible text; with no grounding they can invent names that fit the pattern. There is no internal fact index to go stale, low temperature does not cause invention, and tokenization is lossless.

quiz.q: You set temperature to 0 and run the same prompt twice. What should you expect?
options: Byte-identical output every time, since sampling is fully deterministic at 0
Output as varied as at high temperature, because 0 disables the setting
A refusal, because temperature 0 leaves no eligible tokens to sample
Very similar output, but identical results are not guaranteed
quiz.explain: Temperature 0 makes sampling near-deterministic, but infrastructure effects like batching and floating-point differences can still change output.

quiz.q: Why does an agent that has been working for hours sometimes forget an early instruction?
options: Models keep a fixed rolling buffer of only the last ten or so messages
The model discards an instruction once it has followed it a single time in the session
It may have been compacted away, or is weakly attended in a very long context
Instructions expire after a fixed time limit enforced by the provider
quiz.explain: Context is finite and long contexts are summarized or attended unevenly. There is no fixed message count or timer, and nothing is deliberately deleted.

quiz.q: Your project uses a library version released after the model's training cutoff. Best way to get correct code?
options: Raise the temperature so the model explores more possible API variants
Give it the current docs or let it read the installed source
Ask it to rate its confidence and accept only high-confidence code
Use a larger model with the same training cutoff, since it memorized more APIs
quiz.explain: Grounding in current sources fixes a knowledge gap. Temperature, self-reported confidence and a bigger model with the same cutoff do not add knowledge of a release the model never saw.

quiz.q: Which statement about tokens is accurate?
options: Rare identifiers and long numbers can split into many tokens, raising cost
One token always corresponds to exactly one word of the input text
Tokens matter only for billing and have no effect on model behavior
Source code always tokenizes more compactly than the equivalent English prose
quiz.explain: Tokenization splits text into subword chunks; unusual strings fragment into many tokens. Tokens are also what the model actually processes, not just a billing unit.

quiz.q: You ask an agent how many of 4,000 log lines contain a specific 36-character request ID. It answers confidently with a count that is off by a few. Which approach fits best?
options: Ask it to count again more carefully and show each of its steps as it goes
Have it run a command like `grep -c` and report the output
Set the temperature to 0 and rerun the same prompt
Paste all 4,000 lines into the prompt again for reference
quiz.explain: Exact counting is better done by a deterministic tool than by token prediction. Temperature 0 reduces variation but does not make the model reliable at counting.

topics.title: Context Engineering & Prompting
topics.summary: Give the agent the right goal, constraints, examples and project knowledge, and nothing extra.

lesson.text: You type 'fix the login bug' and the agent rewrites your auth module. The model did not misbehave; you gave it a goal with no boundaries and no definition of done. Since the model sees only its context window, the quality of its output is largely determined by the quality of what you put there. This discipline is called **context engineering**: deciding what information the model sees, in what form, at what time.
The anatomy of a good task
A strong request states the outcome, the constraints, where to look, and how to know it worked. Compare a vague and a specific request:

Vague:
  Fix the login bug.

Specific:
  Users with a trailing space in their email get 'invalid credentials'.
  Reproduce with tests/auth/test_login.py (add a failing case first).
  Fix in auth/normalize.py only; do not change the public API.
  Done when `pytest tests/auth` passes and no other tests change.

items: **Goal**: the observable behavior you want, not just the code to write.
**Constraints**: files off limits, libraries to use or avoid, style, compatibility.
**Pointers**: the relevant files, the failing test, the error message verbatim.
**Success criteria**: a command the agent can run to check itself.

lesson.text: Examples beat adjectives

Models imitate patterns in context very well. Saying 'write it like our other handlers' is weaker than pointing at `handlers/orders.py` and saying 'follow this structure'. One or two concrete input-output examples often replace a paragraph of description. Show the format you want, including edge cases.
Persistent project context

Things you would repeat in every session belong in a **project instruction file**, such as `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, which the agent loads automatically. Use it for build and test commands, architecture in a few lines, conventions, and traps. Keep it short and accurate; it consumes context in every request, and stale instructions actively mislead.

lesson.caption: A correction typed in chat lasts one session; the same rule in AGENTS.md is loaded into every new session.

lesson.text:
# AGENTS.md
## Commands
- Test: `make test` (unit, ~20s). Lint: `make lint`.
## Architecture
- `api/` HTTP handlers, `core/` business logic, `db/` queries only.
- Handlers never touch the database directly.
## Rules
- Never edit `generated/`; run `make codegen`.
- Prefer small pure functions; add a test with every bug fix.
Specs for bigger work

For anything non-trivial, write a short spec first: problem, non-goals, interface, acceptance criteria, open questions. Agents can help draft it, but you decide it. A spec in a file survives session resets and lets a fresh agent resume the work.
What to leave out

More context is not better context. Irrelevant files, pasted whole logs, contradictory instructions and speculative history dilute attention and raise cost. Include what the task needs, link to the rest, and let the agent fetch more by reading files. Also avoid piling on emphatic rules in capitals; they tend to cause over-application. State the reason behind a rule so the model can generalize.

items: Paste the failing assertion, not the 3,000-line test run.
Remove instructions that no longer match the code.
Do not include secrets or customer data in prompts.

lesson.text: Common pitfalls: asking for several unrelated things in one prompt, omitting the definition of done, assuming the agent remembers earlier sessions, and arguing with a derailed conversation instead of restarting with a better prompt.

Before sending a task, ask: could a smart contractor who has never seen this repo do it from my message alone? If not, add the missing pointer or constraint. When output drifts, update the instruction file or spec so the correction persists, rather than repeating it in chat each time.

patterns.signal: You are about to send 'fix the login bug' with no file, repro or definition of done
patterns.why: State the observable outcome, what is off limits, where to look, and a command that proves success. Takes a minute to write and prevents sprawling, unverifiable changes.

patterns.signal: You describe the desired style in adjectives and the output keeps missing it
patterns.use: Show an example (point at existing code)
patterns.why: Models imitate patterns in context very well; one concrete file or input-output pair beats a paragraph of description. Pick a good example: bad ones get copied just as faithfully.

patterns.signal: You repeat the same build command and conventions in every new session
patterns.why: Put recurring facts in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md so they load automatically. It costs context every turn, so keep it short and remove lines that no longer match the code.

patterns.signal: The agent keeps re-adding a forbidden dependency despite chat reminders across sessions
patterns.use: Fix the instructions, not the chat
patterns.why: Corrections in chat vanish at the next session; update the instruction file or spec so they persist. Add a mechanical check like a lint rule where the rule really matters.

patterns.signal: A feature spans several sessions and a fresh agent keeps losing the thread
patterns.why: Problem, non-goals, interface, acceptance criteria and open questions in the repo survive session resets and let any agent resume. Overhead is not worth it for a one-line fix.

patterns.signal: The prompt has grown to include whole logs, unrelated files and old contradictory rules
patterns.why: Irrelevant tokens dilute attention and raise cost. Include what the task needs, link to the rest, and let the agent read files on demand.

patterns.signal: One prompt asks for a bug fix, a refactor and new docs at once
patterns.why: Unrelated goals compete for attention and produce one tangled diff. Separate tasks are easier to verify and to revert individually.

patterns.signal: A conversation is full of failed attempts and you keep arguing with the agent to change course
patterns.why: Failed attempts stay in context and steer the model back toward them. A fresh session with a sharper prompt and what you learned is usually faster.

keyPoints: Output quality tracks context quality: state goal, constraints, pointers and a runnable success check.
Concrete examples and pointers to existing code beat abstract descriptions.
Put recurring knowledge in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md; keep it short, accurate and current.
Leave out noise: irrelevant files, huge logs, stale or contradictory rules.

quiz.q: Which request is most likely to produce a correct, reviewable result?
options: Make checkout faster; you know the codebase, so use your best judgment
Cut p95 of POST /checkout: profile first, edit only core/pricing.py, keep `make test` green
Optimize the whole order flow for speed, refactoring any module in it that looks slow to you
Be extremely careful and thorough, checkout is critical; make it as fast as possible
quiz.explain: It defines a measurable goal, a scope and a check. The others lack boundaries or criteria, and exhortations add no information.

quiz.q: What belongs in a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md file?
options: Build and test commands, a short architecture summary, and conventions for every task
The full contents of the key source files, so the agent never has to open them itself
Personal API keys and tokens, so the agent can authenticate without asking
A running log of each debugging session, so context carries over between days
quiz.explain: Instruction files hold stable, broadly useful knowledge. Secrets must never go there, whole files and transient logs just consume context on every request.

quiz.q: The agent keeps adding a forbidden dependency despite chat reminders across sessions. What is the best fix?
options: Repeat the reminder in capital letters at the start of every session
Let it add the dependency, then remove it by hand before each commit
Lower the temperature so it sticks more closely to earlier instructions
Add the rule and its reason to the project instruction file
quiz.explain: Persistent rules belong in the file loaded every session, with the reason so the model can generalize. Chat corrections vanish when the session ends, and temperature does not make a model remember.

quiz.q: Why can pasting an entire 4,000-line log into the prompt hurt?
options: Log text contains characters the tokenizer cannot encode
Models reject any input longer than a few hundred lines
It costs tokens and can bury the one line that matters
It pushes the model into deterministic, low-variety output
quiz.explain: Irrelevant bulk competes with signal in a finite window. The fix is to extract the failing lines or let the agent search the log.

quiz.q: You want output in a specific house style. What usually works best?
options: Describe the style in detail with adjectives such as clean, idiomatic and concise
Point to a representative existing file and ask it to follow that structure
Raise the temperature so it tries several styles, then pick the closest one
Ask for a first draft in any style, then explain everything wrong with it
quiz.explain: Models imitate concrete patterns well. Adjectives are ambiguous and leave the model to guess.

quiz.q: One prompt asks the agent to fix a login bug, refactor the session module and update the docs. The result is a single large diff where nothing is clearly finished or checked. What should you reach for?
options: Add a longer list of adjectives describing the desired code style to the prompt
Move the instructions into the project CLAUDE.md file
Send separate prompts, each with one task and its own done check
Restart the session and paste the same prompt again
quiz.explain: One task per prompt gives a reviewable result with a clear check for each. A project instruction file holds standing conventions, not a particular set of three tasks.

topics.title: The Agent Loop & Tools
topics.summary: How agents call tools in a read-act-observe loop, and what MCP, subagents and permissions add.

lesson.text: A chat model can only emit text. Yet a coding agent edits files, runs your tests and reads the failure. The difference is not a smarter model but a loop around it, plus a set of tools. Understanding that loop explains agent behavior, cost, and why permissions matter.
Tool calling

A **tool** is a function the host program exposes to the model, described by a name, a description and a parameter schema. The model does not execute anything. It emits a structured request such as 'call read_file with path=src/app.py'. The host program validates it, runs the function, and sends the result back as new context.
The read-act-observe loop

An agent is a loop: the model reads the context, decides on an action (a tool call), the host executes it, and the observation is appended to context. This repeats until the model decides it is done or hits a limit.
