lesson.text: Perspective projection

A perspective camera is defined by a **vertical field of view** (commonly 60 to 90 degrees in games), an **aspect ratio** (width/height) and **near and far planes**. The projection matrix scales x and y by `1/tan(fov/2)` (and x by `1/aspect`) and, crucially, copies view-space depth into `w`. After the divide, `x_ndc = x_view / depth`: farther objects have larger divisors and shrink toward the centre, which is exactly perspective foreshortening. Hence the importance of `w`: it is not a spare number, it is depth.

lesson.caption: The projection copies depth into w, so dividing by it shrinks an object in proportion to its distance: the same bar at 2.7 times the depth is 1/2.7 as tall on screen.

lesson.text: Two consequences that surprise people. First, **perspective-correct interpolation**: attributes such as UVs cannot be interpolated linearly in screen space, or textures swim on slanted surfaces. The rasteriser interpolates `attribute / w` and `1 / w` linearly in screen space and divides per pixel. It is built in; you only notice it when it is disabled (some retro-styled effects deliberately turn it off for the PS1 look). Second, changing the vertical FOV on a wide screen changes the horizontal FOV through the aspect ratio, so ultrawide players may see far more or far less than intended depending on whether the engine fixes horizontal or vertical FOV.
Orthographic projection

An orthographic camera defines a box instead of a frustum. The projection only rescales and shifts; `w` stays 1 and no divide changes anything, so parallel lines stay parallel and size does not depend on distance. It is the natural choice for 2D games, isometric strategy games, UI, and, in most engines, for directional-light shadow maps (the sun's rays are parallel). Orthographic depth is linear, which has a nice side effect: depth precision is uniform across the range, so z-fighting is far less of a problem than with perspective.
The depth buffer

To draw opaque geometry in any order, the GPU keeps a **depth buffer** (z-buffer): one value per pixel recording the nearest surface so far. Each incoming fragment's depth is compared with the stored value; if it passes the test (usually 'less than' or, with reversed-Z, 'greater than'), the fragment is shaded and written, otherwise it is discarded, sometimes before the pixel shader even runs (early-Z). A 1080p depth buffer at 32 bits is about 8 MB; at 4K about 33 MB, which matters on bandwidth-limited mobile GPUs.

The stored value is the NDC z, and for a perspective camera NDC z is a function of `1/depth`, not of depth. That makes precision highly nonlinear. With near = 0.1 and far = 1000, a conventional 24-bit fixed-point depth buffer spends roughly half its codes on the first 0.2 m or so. Back-of-the-envelope: the depth step in metres at distance z is about `z^2 / (near * 2^24)`. At 10 m that is about 6e-5 m, but at 500 m it is about 0.15 m: surfaces closer together than 15 cm swap places pixel by pixel, which you see as shimmering stripes called **z-fighting**.

Depth resolution (conventional Z, 24-bit, near=0.1, far=1000)
  distance    smallest resolvable gap
  10 m        ~0.00006 m
  100 m       ~0.006 m
  500 m       ~0.15 m
  1000 m      ~0.6 m

Fix 1: raise near from 0.01 to 0.1: precision improves about 10x everywhere.
Fix 2: reversed-Z with a float32 depth buffer.
Fix 3: split the view into two cameras (near and far) rendered in layers.
Reversed-Z

Floating-point numbers have more representable values near zero. Standard depth puts the near plane at 0 and far at 1, so the dense float region sits where the `1/z` mapping already gives plenty of precision, wasting float resolution. **Reversed-Z** swaps the mapping: near maps to 1 and far to 0, depth is cleared to 0, and the depth test becomes 'greater'. The two nonlinearities (hyperbolic `1/z` and float spacing) now roughly cancel, giving near-uniform precision across the whole range even with an infinite far plane. It needs a floating-point depth format; with a fixed-point 24-bit buffer reversal gives nothing. Modern Unity versions use reversed-Z on the platforms that support it (Direct3D, Metal, Vulkan, consoles), which is why shader code uses macros like `UNITY_REVERSED_Z` rather than assuming near is 0.

lesson.text: The cheapest depth-precision win is always the near plane. Many projects leave near at 0.01 for a camera that never gets within 0.3 m of anything. Moving to 0.1 or 0.3 improves precision about 10 to 30 times across the range, with no cost. Reserve extreme near values for close-up first-person weapons, which are often drawn with a separate camera.
Worked example: world to screen

To place a health bar above an enemy, take the world position, multiply by the view-projection matrix to get clip `(x, y, z, w)`; if `w <= 0` the point is behind the camera, so hide it. Otherwise `ndc = clip.xy / clip.w`, and `screen = (ndc * 0.5 + 0.5) * (width, height)`, flipping y if your UI origin is at the top. Every engine provides a helper for this (such as `Camera.WorldToScreenPoint` in Unity), but knowing the steps explains the classic bug: forgetting the behind-the-camera check draws labels mirrored on screen for enemies at your back, because dividing by a negative `w` flips the point through the origin.

When asking an agent for camera or projection code, state the target graphics API conventions: clip z range, reversed-Z on or off, y-flip for render textures, left or right handed. Agents often produce an OpenGL-style projection matrix and a 'less' depth test, which silently breaks a reversed-Z pipeline (everything fails the depth test and the screen is empty). Ask for a unit test that projects a known near and far point and asserts NDC z values (0 and 1, or 1 and 0), and review whether the code checks `w > 0` before dividing.
Pitfalls checklist

items: Near plane set to 0.001 'to be safe' with a 24-bit fixed depth buffer: precision is roughly proportional to near, so distant surfaces z-fight. The far plane matters much less.
Normals or lighting vectors computed in view space against world-space light directions: always keep both operands in one space.
Using `w` after the divide: after the divide it is 1; keep the original if you need depth.
Assuming screen y goes up. Render-texture sampling and UI toolkits differ by API.

patterns.signal: Lighting changes when the object rotates, and the shader mixes an object-space normal with a world-space light direction
patterns.use: Do lighting in one consistent space
patterns.why: Transform every vector (normal, light, view) into the same space, usually world or view, before any dot product. Mixed spaces give plausible but wrong results that are hard to spot.

patterns.signal: Distant surfaces flicker in stripes (z-fighting) and the camera near plane is set to something like 0.01
patterns.why: Depth precision depends mostly on the near/far ratio, so raising near from 0.01 to 0.3 is the cheapest, biggest win. Too far out and nearby geometry clips through the camera.

patterns.signal: A huge view distance still z-fights after tuning near and far planes
patterns.use: Reversed-Z with a float depth buffer
patterns.why: Mapping far to 0 and near to 1 cancels float and 1/z nonlinearity, giving near-uniform precision. Every hand-written depth compare, clear value and depth read must use the reversed convention.

patterns.signal: A projected world-space label or marker shows up mirrored on screen when its target is behind the camera
patterns.use: Reject points with w <= 0 before dividing
patterns.why: A point behind the camera has negative clip w, and the divide mirrors it onto the screen. Check w first, then hide the marker or clamp it to the screen edge.

patterns.signal: A directional light shadow map, a 2D game or a top-down strategy view needs parallel lines and uniform scale
patterns.why: Ortho keeps w at 1, so size does not change with distance and depth is linear. It gives no depth cue, so it is wrong for first-person views.

patterns.signal: A fog or soft-particle effect reads the depth texture and treats the raw value as distance in metres
patterns.use: Linearise depth with near and far
patterns.why: Stored depth is a nonlinear function of 1/z and may be reversed. Convert it to linear eye depth first using the engine's helper, or effects bunch up near the camera.

patterns.signal: A screen-space effect needs the world position of each pixel but there is no position buffer
patterns.why: Combine pixel UV and depth into NDC, then multiply by the inverse view-projection and divide by w. Saves a G-buffer target at the cost of a matrix multiply per pixel.

patterns.signal: A click or tap on the screen must select the 3D object under the cursor
patterns.use: Unproject a ray from the camera
patterns.why: Map the pixel to NDC at near and far depth, transform both by the inverse view-projection, and raycast between them. Avoids per-object screen-space tests.

keyPoints: Vertices travel object, world, view, clip, NDC, screen; the vertex shader outputs clip space and the GPU does the perspective divide.
Perspective projection puts view-space depth in w, so dividing by w shrinks distant objects; orthographic keeps w at 1 and preserves parallel lines.
Depth is stored nonlinearly (a function of 1/z), so conventional depth buffers have far worse precision in the distance; z-fighting is the symptom.
Reversed-Z with a float depth buffer cancels the nonlinearity and gives near-uniform precision; moving the near plane outward is the cheapest fix.
Always check w > 0 before projecting a point to the screen, otherwise objects behind the camera appear mirrored.

quiz.q: A vertex shader outputs a clip-space position. Who performs the perspective divide by w?
options: The vertex shader, which must divide before writing its output
The fragment shader, once per pixel during shading
The GPU's fixed-function stage after the vertex stage, before rasterization
The CPU, when it uploads the view-projection matrix
quiz.explain: The hardware clips against the clip volume and then divides xyz by w automatically, which is why the shader outputs 4D clip coordinates. If the shader divided itself, the hardware would divide again and shrink everything twice.

quiz.q: Far terrain at 600 m flickers in alternating stripes where two road meshes sit 0.5 m apart vertically. The camera uses near 0.01, far 2000, conventional Z, 24-bit depth. What is the most effective first fix?
options: Raise the near plane to 0.1, since precision scales with near
Halve the far plane to 1000 and keep near unchanged
Widen the camera's vertical field of view
Disable the perspective divide for distant geometry
quiz.explain: Depth resolution at distance z is roughly z squared divided by near times the depth range, so a 10x larger near gives about 10x finer resolution. Halving the far plane changes precision very little, because far barely appears in that estimate.

quiz.q: After switching to reversed-Z, a custom effect that gets depth from the depth texture shows inverted results, and objects fail the depth test in a hand-written pass. What should you check?
options: Whether the depth texture is stored as an 8-bit format
Whether the view matrix is stored column-major or not
Whether the camera near plane exceeds its far plane
Whether depth compare and linearize code assume near is 0
quiz.explain: Reversed-Z flips the mapping, so a 'less' test and non-reversed linearization formulas break; engines expose macros for this. The near plane is still smaller than far in the camera settings, only the stored depth is reversed.

quiz.q: A world-space label follows an enemy using manual projection, but when the enemy is directly behind the player a mirrored label appears in front of the screen. Which step is missing?
options: Clamping the NDC values into the range zero to one
Rejecting points whose clip-space w is zero or negative
Multiplying by the inverse of the projection matrix
Converting the position to object space first
quiz.explain: Points behind the camera have negative w, and dividing by it flips the projected point through the screen centre, producing the mirror. Clamping would hide the symptom, not distinguish front from back.

quiz.q: Why does an orthographic camera give shadow maps for a directional light more uniform depth precision than a perspective camera of the same range?
options: Orthographic depth is stored in a smaller number of bits
Orthographic projection stores w as view depth and divides it out
Orthographic depth is a linear function of distance, not 1 over distance
Orthographic cameras ignore the near plane entirely
quiz.explain: Without the perspective divide, depth maps linearly across the near-to-far range so every distance gets equal resolution. Perspective depth depends on 1/z and concentrates precision close to the camera.

quiz.q: A strategy game must let the player click the terrain or a unit under the mouse. Objects are 3D with perspective, and the cursor is a 2D pixel position. Which approach fits best?
options: Unproject the cursor into a world ray and intersect it
Multiply the cursor position by each object's model matrix
Compare the cursor to each object's projected centre point only
Render the scene to a depth buffer and read the raw depth
quiz.explain: Turning the pixel into a ray from the camera and intersecting it with colliders gives exact 3D hits. Reading raw depth alone gives no object identity and is nonlinear, and a model matrix maps local to world, not screen to world.

topics.title: Meshes and Geometry
topics.summary: What a mesh is on the GPU: vertex attributes and layout, index buffers and the vertex cache, why vertices split, winding and culling, normals and tangent space, budgets and dynamic geometry.

lesson.text: An artist hands over a character that is 12,000 vertices in Blender. The Unity Stats window says the same character costs 19,400 vertices per draw, the shadow passes draw it again, and the normal-mapped face shows a hairline seam down the middle. None of this is a bug. A mesh in a modelling tool is a surface; a mesh on the GPU is a set of buffers with a specific layout, and the two differ in ways that decide memory use, vertex shader cost and shading correctness. This topic covers what those buffers contain, why vertices multiply on import, how triangle order and winding affect speed and visibility, what normals and tangents really are, and what it costs to change a mesh at runtime.
What the GPU receives

To the GPU a mesh is a **vertex buffer** (an array of vertices), usually an **index buffer** (an array of integers that pick vertices to form triangles) and a **topology** that says how to read the indices, almost always as a triangle list. A **vertex** is not just a position. It is a bundle of attributes that the vertex shader reads and the rasteriser interpolates across the triangle. The pipeline topic covers what happens after this data is fetched; this one is about the data itself.

items: **Position**: usually 3 floats in object space. The only attribute every mesh has.
**Normal**: the unit vector the surface faces, used by lighting. Per vertex, not per triangle.
**Tangent**: a unit vector along the texture's U direction, plus a sign in `w` that selects the bitangent's direction. It completes the basis that normal maps are expressed in.
**UV0, UV1**: 2D texture coordinates. UV0 is typically the albedo and normal map layout; UV1 often holds a separate non-overlapping layout for lightmaps.
**Colour**: per-vertex tint, commonly 4 bytes, used for baked occlusion, wind masks and blending weights.
**Bone indices and weights**: for skinning, typically 4 bone indices and 4 weights per vertex.
**Custom data**: extra UV channels or colours reused to carry anything a shader needs, such as a pivot or an animation phase.

lesson.text: In Unity the high-level `Mesh` API exposes these as arrays. The example builds a quad: 4 vertices, 2 triangles, with all attributes set. Unity treats triangles whose indices run clockwise as front-facing, which matters for the winding section later.
Layout, stride and precision

The attributes are packed into a **vertex layout**. The distance in bytes from one vertex to the next is the **stride**, and the buffer size is stride times vertex count. **Interleaved** layout stores all attributes of vertex 0, then of vertex 1, and so on in one stream; it is friendly to passes that read everything. **Separate streams** store each attribute (or group) in its own array, so a depth-only or shadow pass can read just the position stream and skip the rest. Unity's lower-level mesh API lets you choose the format, dimension and stream of every attribute, and most engines default to a convenient but generous layout.

Typical layout                    Compact layout
  Position  float32 x3   12 B       Position  float32 x3   12 B
  Normal    float32 x3   12 B       Normal    snorm8  x4    4 B
  Tangent   float32 x4   16 B       Tangent   snorm8  x4    4 B
  UV0       float32 x2    8 B       UV0       unorm16 x2    4 B
  stride                 48 B       stride                 24 B

50,000 vertices:  2.4 MB          1.2 MB
A mesh drawn in the main pass and 3 shadow cascades reads its
vertex buffer 4 times: 9.6 MB vs 4.8 MB of reads per frame.

Precision is the lever. Unit-length normals and tangents lose almost nothing in 8-bit signed normalized values. UVs in the 0 to 1 range fit 16-bit unsigned normalized values with 1/65535 steps, which is finer than a texel of any realistic texture. Positions are the exception: float16 has only about 3 decimal digits, so a vertex 100 m from the mesh origin lands on a grid of roughly 6 cm. Engines that compress positions store 16-bit integers relative to the mesh bounds instead, which keeps a uniform step of bounds size divided by 65,535.

Half-float UVs are a common trap. float16 spacing grows with magnitude, so UVs near 1.0 snap in steps of about 0.0005, which is a full texel of a 2,048 texture, and tiled UVs up to 8 or atlas coordinates get worse. Use unorm16 for 0 to 1 data and test on the largest texture the mesh uses.
Indexing and the vertex cache

Without indices every triangle would carry its own 3 vertices, so a closed surface where each vertex touches about 6 triangles would store each vertex 6 times. Indexing stores each distinct vertex once and lets triangles refer to it by number. For 100,000 triangles at a 32-byte stride, the non-indexed version is 300,000 vertices, 9.6 MB. An indexed smooth mesh has roughly half as many vertices as triangles, so about 50,000 vertices (1.6 MB) plus 300,000 indices at 2 bytes (0.6 MB), 2.2 MB in total. The shared vertices also get shaded once instead of six times, which is the bigger win.

Index width is a trade-off. **16-bit indices** address vertices 0 to 65,535 and cost 2 bytes each, so they cap a mesh at about 65,000 vertices. **32-bit indices** remove the cap and cost 4 bytes each. Unity defaults to 16-bit and takes `mesh.indexFormat = IndexFormat.UInt32` (in `UnityEngine.Rendering`) for bigger meshes, and the model importer has an index format setting too. Set the format before assigning the triangles, because the same array of ints is interpreted according to it.

Sharing only saves shader work if the GPU remembers a vertex it already shaded. Hardware keeps a small **post-transform vertex cache** keyed by index: when a triangle references an index that was recently shaded, the cached output is reused and the vertex shader does not run. Classic models use a FIFO of roughly 16 to 32 entries; newer GPUs batch work differently, but index locality still pays off. The standard metric is **ACMR**, the average cache miss ratio: vertex shader invocations divided by triangle count. A well-ordered smooth mesh approaches 0.5 and a well-optimised one lands around 0.6 to 0.8, while a random order drifts toward the worst case of 3.0, one miss for every index.

lesson.text: Ordering is free to fix because it only permutes the index buffer. Libraries such as **meshoptimizer** provide `meshopt_optimizeVertexCache` to reorder triangles for the cache, `meshopt_optimizeOverdraw` to draw groups of triangles roughly front to back so the depth test rejects more pixels early, and `meshopt_optimizeVertexFetch` to renumber vertices in first-use order so memory reads are sequential. Run them in that order, offline in the import pipeline, because the overdraw pass trades a little cache efficiency for fewer shaded pixels. Many engine importers expose a mesh optimisation toggle that does a version of the same work.
Why vertex counts grow on import

A GPU vertex is the **unique combination of all its attributes**. Two vertices at the same position are different vertices if their normals, UVs, tangents or colours differ, because one slot in the buffer can hold only one value of each. Modelling tools show you positions; the GPU needs every attribute combination stored separately. A cube has 8 positions, but with flat shading each corner needs a different normal for each of its three faces, so the corner is stored three times: 8 x 3 = 24 vertices. A UV seam does the same thing from the texture side: where an island of the unwrap ends, the 3D point sits at two different UV locations and must exist twice.

items: **Hard edges and split normals**: every smoothing-group boundary duplicates the vertices along it. A low-poly prop with all faces flat has about 3 vertices per triangle and gets almost nothing from indexing.
**UV seams**: every seam edge duplicates its vertices; island padding and mirrored islands add more. Fewer, longer islands mean fewer splits.
**Vertex colour or second UV discontinuities**: a lightmap UV layout that cuts where UV0 does not adds splits.
**Material boundaries**: per-material submeshes share the vertex buffer in some engines, but exporters and tools may duplicate vertices at material seams.

lesson.text: So budget and profile in imported vertices, not in the DCC tool's count. A 12,000-vertex character that arrives as 19,400 is normal; the gap is the price of its shading and texturing choices, and you can reduce it by welding vertices whose attributes differ only by noise and by cutting fewer seams.
Topology, winding and culling

A **triangle list** uses 3 indices per triangle and is the default everywhere. A **triangle strip** reuses the previous two vertices, so n indices give n - 2 triangles, but strips join separate pieces with **degenerate triangles** (zero area, from a repeated index or collinear points) or a primitive-restart index. Strips mattered when index bandwidth was scarce; today a cache-optimised list gets the same reuse without the joins, and strips are rarely worth the effort. Degenerate triangles in a list are pure waste: they are fetched, shaded and then discarded, so clean them out.

Which side of a triangle is its front is decided by **winding order**: the order of its three indices as seen on screen, clockwise or counter-clockwise. With back-face culling on, the GPU discards triangles that wind the wrong way after projection, which removes about half of a closed mesh's triangles before rasterisation. The convention is not universal: OpenGL and glTF default to counter-clockwise fronts, Direct3D defaults to clockwise, Vulkan makes you choose, and Unity treats clockwise as front. A mesh imported with the wrong convention looks inside-out, showing the far inner walls.

lesson.caption: As the triangle turns, the order 0, 1, 2 flips from counter-clockwise to clockwise on screen at the edge-on moment, and from that frame the rasteriser receives nothing. Drawn with the OpenGL and glTF convention (front = counter-clockwise); Unity treats clockwise as front, so there the roles swap.

lesson.text: Mirroring also flips winding. A transform with a negative scale on one axis (a left-handed copy of a right-handed prop) reverses every triangle, and engines detect the negative determinant and flip the front-face rule for that draw. Hand-written shaders and custom culling code need to respect the same rule. Finally, a **manifold** mesh is a closed surface where every edge is shared by exactly two triangles. **Non-manifold** geometry has edges shared by three or more triangles, open boundary edges, or vertices pinched between two fans. It usually renders, but it breaks algorithms that assume a watertight solid: mesh simplification for LODs, mesh-to-SDF and volume voxelisation, boolean operations, cloth, and any stencil shadow-volume or inside-test logic.
Normals and tangent space

Normals are just a vertex attribute, so the choice between smooth and flat shading is a mesh data choice. **Smooth shading** gives the shared vertex one averaged normal, so interpolation across the triangle bends the lighting continuously around the edge. **Flat shading** gives each face its own copy of the vertex with the face normal, which is exactly the vertex split in the previous figure. Unity's `RecalculateNormals` averages only triangles that share a vertex index, so it respects splits: it keeps hard edges where vertices are duplicated, and a UV seam on a smooth surface gets a lighting seam, because the two copies are averaged separately. Build or weld vertices deliberately and set normals explicitly when seams matter.

A **normal map** does not store world or object directions; it stores a perturbation in **tangent space**, a basis at each vertex made of the normal `N`, the tangent `T` along increasing U, and the bitangent `B` along increasing V. The bitangent is derived as `B = cross(N, T) * T.w`, so the tangent's `w` of +1 or -1 carries handedness. That sign is what keeps mirrored UV islands correct, because a mirrored island reverses the direction of U relative to the surface. In the fragment shader the sampled normal is multiplied by the `T`, `B`, `N` basis to reach world space.

The basis is only meaningful relative to how the map was baked. If the baking tool and the engine construct tangents differently (different handling of mirrored UVs, per-pixel or per-vertex orthogonalisation, or Y-up versus Y-down green channel), the stored perturbations are applied in the wrong frame. The symptoms are shading seams along UV borders, bumps that look inverted on mirrored islands, and lighting that changes when the mesh is re-triangulated. **MikkTSpace** is the common standard that most baking tools, glTF and Unity's imported tangents use; the practical rule is to bake and render with the same algorithm, import tangents instead of recalculating them if the exporter supplies them, and check the normal map's green channel convention.

A quick test for tangent trouble is a flat-grey normal map or a debug view that shows the tangent as colour. If lighting is smooth with a flat map but breaks with the real map at UV seams, the baked normals and the engine tangents disagree, not the mesh geometry.
Budgets and cost

Triangle count alone is a poor budget. Cost splits across several things: the vertex shader runs per **vertex** (reduced by the cache), memory and fetch bandwidth scale with **vertices times stride**, the rasteriser works per triangle, and the fragment shader runs per **covered pixel**, in 2x2 quads as the earlier raster figure showed. That last point is why tiny triangles hurt. A triangle covering a fraction of a pixel still launches a whole quad of 4 fragment invocations and may produce no visible pixel, so a 20,000-triangle character that occupies 30 x 60 pixels (about 0.09 pixels per triangle) pays for the geometry and for large quad overshading without any visible gain.

items: **LODs**: swap in coarser meshes by screen size, for example 20,000, 8,000 and 2,500 triangles at near, mid and far, with a cross-fade or dithered transition. This addresses vertex cost and micro-triangle overshading together.
**Attribute diet**: drop channels no shader reads (UV1, colour, tangents on non-normal-mapped materials) and quantise the rest, as in the layout above.

**Mesh compression**: importer quantisation reduces the vertex data stored in memory; transmission formats such as Draco or meshopt in glTF shrink downloads but are decoded to a GPU layout before use.

**Bounds**: the engine culls with the mesh's axis-aligned bounds, so they must contain every vertex that can ever be visible. A vertex shader that displaces vertices, or a skinned character whose arms reach outside its rest-pose box, gets culled while still on screen unless the bounds are enlarged; skinned renderers expose their own bounds and an update-when-offscreen option.

lesson.text: Dynamic geometry

Two systems deform a mesh that is otherwise static. **Skinning** moves each vertex by a weighted sum of bone transforms, `v' = sum of w_i * (bone_i * bindpose_i) * v` with the weights adding to 1, usually 4 influences per vertex. The data is the bone indices and weights per vertex, and the cost is vertices times influences, normally on the GPU. **Blend shapes** (morph targets) store per-vertex deltas for a target pose and add them in proportion to a weight, `v' = v + sum of w_k * delta_k`. They suit shapes that skinning cannot express, such as facial expressions, but their memory scales with shape count: a 52-shape face rig where each shape touches 10,000 vertices stores 52 x 10,000 x 36 bytes (position, normal and tangent deltas) for about 19 MB. In Unity a `SkinnedMeshRenderer` drives both, and `SetBlendShapeWeight` takes weights from 0 to 100.

The third option is changing the arrays on the CPU every frame, for example for a procedural flag or a destructible wall. Every change re-uploads the buffer: 20,000 vertices at 32 bytes is 640 KB per frame, about 38 MB per second at 60 fps. That bandwidth is small; the real costs are the CPU writing the data, validation in the engine and the driver's synchronisation with a GPU that may still be reading the old copy. Allocate once, mark the mesh dynamic, reuse arrays, update only what changed, and avoid whole-mesh `RecalculateNormals` on large meshes every frame. When the motion is a function of time, such as waves, move it into the vertex shader instead and keep the mesh static.

Agents write mesh-building code that compiles and still renders wrong, because the failures are conventions rather than syntax. Tell the agent your engine's winding rule, handedness, index format limit and tangent standard, and ask it to include a validation function: every index below the vertex count, no degenerate triangles, vertex count and ACMR logged, winding agreeing with the stored normals (cross product of two edges against the normal), and bounds containing all vertices. Typical agent mistakes are counter-clockwise indices copied from OpenGL tutorials, 16-bit indices on meshes over 65,000 vertices, RecalculateNormals on a split mesh that creates seams, and per-frame array allocations in dynamic meshes. Also ask for the imported vertex count to be compared against the source tool's count when it generates importer code.
Pitfalls checklist

items: Comparing a DCC vertex count to the engine's: only the engine's count, after hard edges and UV seams, is what the GPU shades.
A procedural mesh above 65,000 vertices left on 16-bit indices: the indices wrap or the engine rejects the mesh.
Triangles authored in the wrong winding for the engine: the mesh looks inside-out, or vanishes with back-face culling on.
Baking normal maps in one tool and shading with tangents from another algorithm.
Half-float positions on large or far-from-origin meshes, and half-float UVs on atlases or tiled textures.
Displaced or skinned geometry with static bounds, which gets culled early at the screen edge.
Meshes with thousands of sub-pixel triangles in the distance and no LODs.

patterns.signal: A prop's imported vertex count is three or four times what the DCC tool reports
patterns.use: Split vertices only at hard edges and UV seams
patterns.why: Every unique attribute combination is its own GPU vertex. Soften edges that do not need to be hard and merge UV islands where stretching is acceptable; keep real seams.

patterns.signal: A mesh is stored as a triangle soup where shared corners are duplicated in the vertex buffer
patterns.why: An index buffer shares vertices between triangles, cutting memory and vertex shader runs. Only vertices with fully identical attributes can be shared.

patterns.signal: A GPU capture shows the vertex stage is heavy and the mesh's ACMR is well above 1
patterns.why: Reordering triangles (for example with meshoptimizer) raises post-transform cache hits, so fewer vertex shader runs per triangle. The image is unchanged; it does nothing for fragment cost.

patterns.signal: Vertex buffers dominate mesh memory and every attribute is stored as 32-bit float
patterns.why: Normals and tangents as snorm8 and UVs as unorm16 can halve the stride. Keep positions at full float when far from the origin, since half floats get coarse quickly.

patterns.signal: A procedural mesh with more than 65,535 vertices renders as scrambled spikes
patterns.use: 32-bit index format or split the mesh
patterns.why: 16-bit indices wrap past 65,535. Set the index format (`Mesh.indexFormat` in Unity) before assigning triangles, or chunk the mesh; 32-bit indices double index memory.

patterns.signal: A normal-mapped mesh shows seams along UV borders and inverted bumps on its mirrored half
patterns.use: Match the tangent basis to the baker
patterns.why: Import tangents in the same convention the map was baked with, usually MikkTSpace, including the w sign for mirroring. Recalculating with a different method breaks the bake.

patterns.signal: Distant characters with dense meshes make the frame fragment-bound because triangles are smaller than a pixel
patterns.why: Swap to simpler meshes as screen size shrinks, cutting wasted 2x2 quad shading and vertex work. Costs memory and authoring time, and needs crossfade or hysteresis to hide popping.

patterns.signal: A skinned or vertex-displaced mesh vanishes near the screen edge even though part of it is visible
patterns.why: Culling uses the bounding box, which does not know about shader displacement or animation reach. Enlarge it to cover the full motion; too large wastes culling efficiency.

patterns.signal: Waves, flags or grass sway are animated by rewriting vertex positions on the CPU every frame
patterns.why: A time-driven vertex shader avoids per-frame CPU work and buffer uploads. Bounds must be expanded, and CPU-side physics will not see the deformed shape.

keyPoints: A GPU vertex is the unique combination of all its attributes; hard edges and UV seams duplicate vertices, so a cube is 8 positions but 24 flat-shaded vertices, and imported counts exceed the DCC count.

Vertex memory is stride times vertex count; quantising normals and tangents to snorm8 and UVs to unorm16 can halve the buffer, while positions need care because half-floats are coarse far from the origin.

Indexing shares vertices, and the post-transform cache only helps if triangle order has locality; ACMR measures shader runs per triangle and reordering (for example with meshoptimizer) can lower it without changing the picture.
16-bit indices stop at 65,535; larger meshes need 32-bit indices (Mesh.indexFormat in Unity), and the format must be set before the triangles are assigned.

Winding decides the front face and culling convention differs between APIs and engines; negative scale flips winding, and manifold geometry (every edge shared by two triangles) is required by many algorithms.
Normal maps live in tangent space, so the tangent and its w sign must match how the map was baked (usually MikkTSpace); mismatches show up as seams and inverted bumps on mirrored islands.

Tiny triangles waste 2x2 quad shading, so LODs matter; displaced or skinned meshes need correct bounds, and per-frame CPU mesh edits cost an upload plus CPU work, so prefer vertex-shader or GPU animation.

quiz.q: A crate modelled as a cube with 8 vertices in the DCC tool shows 24 vertices after import, with hard edges and one UV island per face. What is the correct reading?
options: The importer subdivided each face, so the mesh is now higher resolution than authored
The importer added 16 extra degenerate vertices that the GPU skips at no cost
Each corner has a different normal and UV on each face, so it is stored once per face
Unity duplicates every vertex that is shared by more than one triangle on import
quiz.explain: A GPU vertex is the unique combination of position, normal, UV and other attributes. A hard-edged cube corner needs three normals, so it is stored three times, and the vertex shader runs on 24 vertices. Vertices that match in every attribute stay shared, which is why smooth meshes keep their indexing savings.

quiz.q: A procedural terrain chunk is a 300 x 300 vertex grid, so 90,000 vertices. After assigning the triangles the chunk renders as scrambled spikes or fails validation. What fixes it?
options: Set mesh.indexFormat to UInt32 before assigning the triangles
Call RecalculateBounds after assigning the triangles
Switch the topology from a triangle list to a triangle strip
Remove UV1 so each vertex fits into a 16-bit stride
quiz.explain: The default 16-bit indices can only address vertices 0 to 65,535, so indices for a 90,000-vertex mesh do not fit. Use 32-bit indices, or split the terrain into chunks under the limit, which also culls better. Bounds, topology and attribute count do not change the index range.

quiz.q: The same 8,000-triangle mesh, with identical vertices and attributes, is run through a vertex-cache optimiser. Its ACMR drops from 2.1 to 0.7. What do you expect to change in the frame?
options: Nothing, because vertex count and triangle count are unchanged
Lower fragment cost, because the triangles now cover fewer pixels
A smaller mesh in memory, because the indices are now stored in 16 bits
About a third of the vertex shader invocations for this mesh, with the same image
quiz.explain: ACMR is vertex shader runs per triangle, so 2.1 to 0.7 is about three times fewer runs. Reordering only permutes the index buffer: the covered pixels, the image and the buffer sizes are unchanged. The saving matters most for vertex-bound draws such as shadow passes.

quiz.q: A normal-mapped character baked in an external tool looks right in most places, but shows seams along UV borders and inverted bumps on the mirrored half. The engine recalculates tangents on import. What is the most likely fix?
options: Call RecalculateNormals at runtime so the normals match the map
Make the baker and the engine use the same tangent basis, normally MikkTSpace
Save the normal map at a higher bit depth to keep more precision
Reverse the winding order of the mirrored half of the mesh
quiz.explain: A tangent-space normal map is only valid in the basis it was baked in. A different tangent construction, especially for mirrored UVs and the bitangent sign in w, applies the stored perturbation in the wrong frame. Recomputed normals, bit depth and winding do not change that basis.

quiz.q: A GPU capture of a distant crowd is fragment-bound. Each 20,000-triangle character covers about 30 x 60 pixels, so most triangles are far smaller than a pixel. What is the best fix?
options: Switch the index buffers to 32-bit so the fragment work is batched
Store positions as half floats to reduce the cost of each fragment
Add LODs so distant characters use far fewer, larger triangles
Turn off back-face culling, which costs extra for tiny triangles
quiz.explain: Fragments are shaded in 2x2 quads, so a sub-pixel triangle can still launch four invocations for little or nothing visible. Cutting the triangle count with LODs removes that overshading and the vertex work. Index width, position precision and the culling setting do not change how many quads are launched.

quiz.q: A flag, banner and grass field sway by having a script rewrite every vertex position on the CPU each frame and re-upload the mesh. The profiler shows CPU time and upload bandwidth growing with vertex count. What should you reach for?
options: Reorder the index buffer for better vertex cache efficiency
Quantise the vertex attributes down to 16-bit values
Build a LOD chain with simpler meshes for the far grass
Animate vertices in the vertex shader from a time uniform
quiz.explain: A sine or noise offset in the vertex shader runs on the GPU with no per-frame upload. Cache reordering and quantisation shrink GPU work or memory but leave the CPU rewrite and upload in place.

topics.title: The GPU and the Rendering Pipeline
topics.summary: How a draw call becomes pixels, why GPUs run threads in lockstep groups, and how the CPU and GPU overlap and stall each other.

lesson.text: Your game runs at 48 fps on a mid-range console and the target is 60. The profiler says the main thread takes 6 ms and the GPU takes 20 ms. Which side do you optimise, and what does 'GPU takes 20 ms' even consist of? Without a model of what the GPU physically does, tuning is guesswork: people halve their triangle count when the real cost is overdraw, or merge draw calls when the real cost is a shader that spills registers. This topic builds the model: the pipeline stages, the execution style of the hardware, and the producer-consumer relationship between CPU and GPU.
Frame budgets

Everything is measured against the frame budget: 33.3 ms at 30 fps, 16.67 ms at 60 fps, 8.33 ms at 120 fps. CPU and GPU work in a pipeline, so the frame rate is limited by the slower of the two, not their sum. In the example above the GPU's 20 ms dominates, the frame takes about 20 ms (50 fps, with some scheduling loss giving 48), and optimising the CPU from 6 ms to 3 ms changes nothing visible. Always identify the limiter first.
The pipeline stages

items: **Input assembly**: fetches vertices and indices from buffers according to the vertex layout (position, normal, UV, and so on) and forms primitives, mostly triangles.

**Vertex stage**: runs your vertex shader once per vertex (post-transform vertex cache lets shared vertices skip repeats). Output: clip-space position plus attributes to interpolate. Optional tessellation, geometry and mesh-shader stages can sit here, depending on API and hardware.
**Primitive assembly, clipping and culling**: triangles outside the frustum are dropped, back-facing triangles can be culled, partially visible ones are clipped. Fixed-function.

**Rasterization**: determines which pixels each triangle covers and generates **fragments**, interpolating attributes with perspective correction. Fixed-function and extremely fast, but it has a granularity: pixels are processed in 2x2 quads.

**Fragment (pixel) stage**: runs your fragment shader per fragment. Here are texture sampling, lighting math and most of the GPU's ALU time. Depth testing may happen before this stage (early-Z) when the shader does not modify depth or discard.

**Output merger (ROP)**: depth and stencil tests, blending with the existing colour, and writes to render targets. It is fixed-function but bandwidth-heavy: blending a 4K RGBA16F target touches a 66 MB surface per full-screen layer (read plus write, about 132 MB of traffic).

lesson.caption: Only the vertex and fragment stages run your code; everything between them, including clipping, rasterization and the depth test, is fixed-function hardware.

lesson.text: Compute shaders sit outside this fixed flow: they run general-purpose thread groups with no triangles, used for culling, particle simulation, post-processing and skinning. The same hardware cores execute them.
What a draw call is, and what it costs

A **draw call** is a command that says 'render this index range of this mesh with the currently bound shader, textures and state'. The expensive part is usually on the **CPU**: the engine and driver validate state, translate it to hardware commands and write them into a command buffer. A scene with 5,000 draw calls and cheap shaders can be CPU-bound at 8 ms on a phone while the GPU idles. Remedies reduce CPU work per object: **instancing** (one call draws many copies with per-instance data), **batching** (merging meshes or sharing state so the engine can skip rebinding), GPU-driven rendering (the GPU builds its own draw list from a culling compute pass), and simply culling better (the Graphics APIs and GPU performance topic covers batching and instancing in detail). Modern APIs (Vulkan, D3D12, Metal) lower per-call overhead versus older APIs, but state changes such as switching shader or render target are still costly.

A common misconception is that draw calls are expensive on the GPU. The GPU cost of a draw is mostly the shader work it triggers; a million cheap triangles in one call is fine, while 10 calls of overdraw-heavy fullscreen transparent layers can cost 6 ms on a mobile GPU.
How the GPU executes: thousands of threads in lockstep

A CPU core is built to run one thread fast: deep caches, branch prediction, out-of-order execution. A GPU is built for throughput: many simple lanes, with little control logic per lane. The hardware groups threads into fixed-size bundles that share one instruction stream: **warps** of 32 threads on NVIDIA, **wavefronts** of 32 or 64 on AMD (the width depends on architecture and mode), and SIMD-groups of 32 on Apple GPUs. All lanes in the group execute the same instruction on different data (SIMT). A GPU might have thousands of lanes active simultaneously, and tens of thousands of threads resident.

Memory is slow: a texture fetch that misses cache can take hundreds of cycles. The GPU hides it not with caches and prediction but with **occupancy**: when one warp waits on memory, the scheduler switches to another resident warp at no cost, since each warp's registers stay on chip. If your shader needs many registers per thread, fewer warps fit on a core, occupancy drops, latency is exposed, and the shader stalls. This is why a 'simple-looking' shader with many live temporaries can be slower than a longer one.

Because pixels are shaded in 2x2 **quads** (so the hardware can compute screen-space derivatives for texture mip selection by differencing neighbours), a triangle covering a single pixel still launches work for a whole quad, up to four lanes with three doing wasted helper work. Meshes with millions of tiny triangles are therefore wasteful for the fragment stage, which is a major reason for LODs alongside vertex cost. Mobile GPUs are mostly **tile-based**, which changes where the costs sit; the Graphics APIs and GPU performance topic covers that model and its rules.

lesson.text:
Where the 20 ms goes (example 1440p frame, GPU-bound)
  shadow maps (4 cascades)      3.5 ms   vertex/ROP bound
  opaque geometry               6.0 ms   fragment ALU + texture bound
  lighting / SSAO               4.0 ms   bandwidth bound
  transparents + particles      4.0 ms   overdraw, blending
  post-processing (bloom, TAA)  2.5 ms   bandwidth bound
  total                        20.0 ms   -> 50 fps

Check: halve render resolution. Frame time drops a lot => pixel bound.
       Frame time unchanged => vertex, CPU or sync bound.
CPU-GPU synchronisation and latency

The CPU does not wait for the GPU to finish a draw: it records commands into a queue and moves on. The GPU consumes them later, typically **one to three frames behind** (the driver or engine allows a small number of queued frames to keep both busy). That decoupling is why the pipeline reaches the max of CPU and GPU time, but it adds **latency**: your input at the start of frame N appears on screen after the CPU records N, the GPU renders N, and the display scans it out. Typical end-to-end latency is 2 to 4 frames, or 33 to 66 ms at 60 fps, and low-latency modes shorten the queue at some throughput cost.

Synchronisation points break this overlap. The main one: **reading data back from the GPU** to the CPU (reading pixels, occlusion query results, a buffer written by compute) forces the CPU to wait for the GPU to finish the producing work. A blocking readback inserted in the middle of a frame can turn a 14 ms GPU frame and a 6 ms CPU frame into 20 ms, because the two stop overlapping and run serially. The fix is **asynchronous readback** that delivers the data a few frames later, accepting latency. Similarly, updating a buffer the GPU is still reading forces a stall or a hidden copy; use ring buffers, with several frames of buffers rotating.

lesson.text: VSync and frame pacing hide the limiter. With classic double-buffered VSync on a 60 Hz display, a frame that takes 17 ms drops the game to 30 fps (it misses one refresh and waits for the next). Judge performance by CPU and GPU millisecond timings, not by fps alone, and capture GPU timings with the platform's GPU profiler.
Worked diagnosis

Symptom: 52 fps on a laptop, GPU utilisation 98%, CPU main thread 5 ms. Hypothesis: GPU-bound. Test 1: drop the resolution scale to 50%. Frame time falls from 19 ms to 11 ms, so the cost scales with pixel count: fragment-bound or bandwidth-bound. Test 2: disable post-processing; 3 ms recovered. Test 3: a GPU capture shows the transparent particle pass at 4 ms with heavy overdraw. Fix: fewer, smaller particles, tighter quads cropped to the visible alpha, and half-resolution rendering for the smoke layer. Each step used a measured experiment to narrow the stage, not a guess.

Agents optimise by pattern and will confidently 'reduce draw calls' or 'merge meshes' for a GPU-bound scene, making it no faster. Give the agent measurements: CPU ms, GPU ms, which pass dominates, the target platform. Ask it to say which pipeline stage a change targets and how you would confirm it with a capture. Be sceptical of code that calls blocking GPU readbacks in the frame loop, allocates buffers per frame, or relies on 'it ran fast on my machine' numbers. Verify with the profiler on target hardware.
Pitfalls checklist

items: Optimising the wrong side: always compare CPU ms with GPU ms first.
Counting triangles instead of covered pixels and overdraw.
Synchronous readbacks of render textures or compute results mid-frame.
Many tiny meshes or sub-pixel triangles that waste quad work.
Ignoring thermal throttling: a phone that hits 60 fps for 30 seconds may sustain only 40.

patterns.signal: A teammate proposes a shader optimisation, but nobody has compared CPU and GPU frame times yet
patterns.use: Measure both sides, fix the long pole
patterns.why: CPU and GPU run as a pipeline, so the frame takes as long as the slower one. Saving GPU time in a CPU-bound frame changes nothing but power use.

patterns.signal: Code reads a render texture or buffer back to the CPU mid-frame and the frame is longer than CPU plus GPU work alone
patterns.why: A synchronous read makes the CPU wait for the GPU to drain. An async request returns a frame or more later, so the logic must tolerate stale data.

patterns.signal: A capture shows heavy opaque overdraw: the same pixels shaded several times per frame
patterns.use: Sort opaque draws front to back
patterns.why: Near objects fill the depth buffer first, so early-Z rejects hidden fragments before shading. Conflicts with sorting by state, so engines sort by a key that balances both.

patterns.signal: Opaque fragment shaders are expensive and overdraw stays high even after sorting, for example dense foliage
patterns.why: Render depth only first, then shade with an equal depth test so each pixel is shaded once. Doubles vertex work and draw calls, so it pays only when fragment cost dominates.

patterns.signal: An opaque shader uses `discard`/`clip` or writes depth, and overdraw cost jumped
patterns.why: Discard and depth writes force late depth testing, so hidden fragments get shaded. Restrict them to cutout materials, render those after plain opaques, or use a depth prepass.

patterns.signal: Objects far outside the camera view still appear as draw calls in the frame debugger
patterns.why: Test bounding volumes against the view frustum before submission to skip CPU and GPU work. Needs correct bounds; large meshes that span the view are never culled, so split them.

patterns.signal: Indoor or city levels draw many objects that are fully hidden behind walls or buildings
patterns.why: Baked visibility data or a depth-pyramid test skips hidden draws. It costs CPU or GPU time and memory itself, so it pays only in scenes with heavy occlusion.

patterns.signal: A fragment shader that uses many registers runs slower than a longer but leaner shader
patterns.why: Fewer registers per thread lets more warps stay resident to hide texture latency. Shorten live ranges or split passes; verify the occupancy gain in a GPU profiler.

keyPoints: Frame rate is limited by the slower of CPU and GPU, since they run as a pipeline; measure both before optimising either.
The pipeline runs input assembly, vertex, rasterization, fragment and output merger; most cost is fragment shading, texture bandwidth and blending.
Draw-call cost is mostly CPU-side validation and submission; the GPU cost is the shader work it triggers.
GPUs run threads in lockstep groups (warps or wavefronts) and hide memory latency by switching groups, so register pressure and occupancy matter.
Reading GPU results back on the CPU synchronously stalls the pipeline; use async readback and accept a frame or more of latency.

quiz.q: A profiler shows CPU main thread 14 ms and GPU 9 ms per frame, with VSync off. A teammate proposes cutting shader cost to save 3 ms on the GPU. What happens to the frame rate?
options: It rises to about 83 fps because the frame is now GPU-limited at 12 ms
It stays the same, since the CPU at 14 ms is the limiter
It drops, because a faster GPU waits for the CPU more often
It rises to about 100 fps as the GPU saves a third of its time
quiz.explain: With CPU and GPU pipelined, frame time is the maximum of the two, here 14 ms, so GPU savings are invisible until the CPU improves. The first option confuses summing with taking the max.

quiz.q: A 1440p scene is GPU-bound. Rendering at 50% resolution scale drops GPU time from 19 ms to 11 ms. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: The vertex stage is the bottleneck, since vertex work shrinks with resolution
The CPU is submitting too many draw calls
The frame is limited by pixel work such as fragment shading, overdraw or bandwidth
The GPU readback is stalling the CPU
quiz.explain: Resolution changes the number of fragments, not vertices or draw calls, so a large time drop points to pixel-side cost. A vertex or CPU limit would show little change.

quiz.q: A mid-frame call reads a render texture back to the CPU to compute average brightness. CPU time is 6 ms, GPU time is 14 ms, but the frame takes 20 ms. What is the best fix?
options: Use an asynchronous readback and consume the result a few frames later
Reduce the number of draw calls on the CPU thread
Lower the texture resolution of every material in the scene
Increase the number of frames buffered ahead on the display
quiz.explain: The blocking readback forces the CPU to wait for the GPU, so the two stop overlapping and their times add (6 + 14 = 20). An async readback keeps them pipelined at the cost of a few frames of latency.

quiz.q: A fragment shader needs many registers per thread and its texture fetches are slow. Why can it run slower than a longer shader with fewer registers?
options: Each warp must run on its own dedicated core, so extra registers add warps
More registers force the rasterizer to produce smaller quads
Register use increases the draw-call overhead on the CPU
Fewer warps fit per core, so there is less other work to switch to while memory loads wait
quiz.explain: GPUs hide memory latency by switching to other resident warps, and registers limit how many can be resident. Registers do not change quad size or CPU draw-call cost.

quiz.q: A scene is made of 2 million triangles, many smaller than one pixel, and the fragment stage is slow. What explains the waste?
options: Pixels shade in 2x2 quads, so tiny triangles waste discarded lanes
Each triangle forces its own separate draw call on the GPU
Triangles under one pixel skip depth testing and so cause overdraw
The vertex cache cannot hold more than one triangle at a time
quiz.explain: Quad shading means a one-pixel triangle can still run four fragment invocations, so tiny geometry multiplies fragment cost. Triangle count alone does not create draw calls, and depth testing still applies.

quiz.q: After an artist adds `clip(alpha - 0.5)` to the opaque foliage shader, GPU time jumps and a capture shows the same pixels now shaded many times, though draw order is unchanged. Which fix fits best?
options: Sort all of the opaque draws strictly front to back by depth
Add a depth prepass so early-Z rejects hidden pixels
Enable occlusion culling for the foliage and its meshes
Apply frustum culling to the foliage meshes each frame
quiz.explain: `discard` forces the GPU to shade a fragment before it can finalise depth, so early-Z is lost. A depth prepass writes depth once, then the main pass shades only the nearest pixel; sorting alone does not help while early-Z is off.

topics.title: Shaders
topics.summary: Vertex, fragment and compute shaders in HLSL and GLSL, constant data, interpolation, divergence costs and the variant compilation problem.

lesson.text: An artist sends you a toon-shaded character and asks for rim lighting, dissolve, fog, three quality levels and mobile support. A week later the build takes 40 minutes, the shader count is in the tens of thousands, and the first time the player enters the cave the game freezes for 300 ms. Shaders are tiny programs, but they determine your visuals, your frame time and, through compilation, your hitches and build times. This topic covers what they are, how they get their data, what each GPU stage does with them and where the cost hides.
What a shader is

A **shader** is a program that runs on the GPU, written in a C-like language such as **HLSL** (Direct3D, and what Unity uses for authoring) or **GLSL** (OpenGL, Vulkan via SPIR-V), and compiled to hardware-specific machine code, often by the driver at runtime. Shaders are stateless functions: each invocation sees its inputs and produces outputs, and cannot call back into the CPU or read another invocation's local variables. That purity is what lets the GPU run thousands of them in parallel.

items: **Vertex shader**: once per vertex. Transforms object-space position to clip space, computes values to interpolate (world position, normal, UV, vertex colour). Also where skinning and vertex animation (wind, waves) run.

**Fragment (pixel) shader**: once per covered pixel fragment. Samples textures, evaluates lighting and returns a colour (or several, for multiple render targets). Usually the bulk of shading cost, because pixels far outnumber vertices.

**Compute shader**: no pipeline input. You dispatch a grid of thread groups; threads read and write buffers and textures freely. Used for culling, particle simulation, light binning, blur kernels, procedural generation. They can share fast on-chip memory (`groupshared`) within a group.

lesson.text: Getting data in: uniforms and constant buffers

Per-draw and per-frame values reach the shader as **uniforms** in GLSL or **constant buffers** (cbuffers) in HLSL. The same value is seen by every invocation of that draw. Good practice is to group by update frequency: per-frame (camera matrices, time, light data), per-material (colours, parameters), per-object (model matrix). That way, changing an object's matrix does not re-upload the whole material block. Layout rules matter: constant buffers are packed in 16-byte rows (a `float3` followed by a `float` fits in one row, but a `float3` followed by a `float3` does not), and a mismatch between CPU struct and GPU layout yields garbage parameters, one of the most common silent bugs. Larger or random-access data goes in **structured buffers** or textures. Textures are read through samplers that define filtering (point, bilinear, trilinear, anisotropic) and wrapping.
Interpolation

Vertex shader outputs are interpolated across the triangle, using barycentric weights of the three vertices, with perspective correction so that attributes vary evenly in 3D space and not in screen space. A normal interpolated between unit-length vertices is no longer unit length in the middle (it shrinks), so re-normalize in the fragment shader, as in the example above. Integer or flag values must use `nointerpolation` (HLSL) or `flat` (GLSL), or interpolation will mangle them. Another point: interpolators are limited and each costs bandwidth between stages, so pass only what the fragment stage needs and compute cheap or uniform things in the vertex shader (per vertex is far fewer invocations than per pixel when meshes are not tiny).

lesson.text: Branching and divergence

Because lanes in a warp share an instruction stream, an `if` has two possible costs. If every lane in the group takes the same side (a **uniform** or **coherent** branch, such as one depending on a uniform or a smoothly varying material mask), the GPU executes only that side. If lanes disagree (a **divergent** branch), the hardware executes **both** sides with lanes masked off, paying the sum of both paths. A loop whose trip count varies per lane runs until the longest lane finishes. Consequently, branching on a uniform constant to skip an expensive effect is great; branching per pixel on noisy data to save work often saves nothing, and a branch containing a texture sample can break mip selection because screen-space derivatives become undefined for lanes in non-uniform control flow (use an explicit-mip sample such as `SampleLevel`, or sample before the branch).

items: Prefer arithmetic selection (`lerp`, `step`, `saturate`) for cheap choices; both sides of tiny branches cost little.
Hoist work that does not depend on the lane to the vertex shader or the CPU.
Texture fetches dominate: 8 samples for a blur at 4K can cost more than 100 ALU instructions. Reduce taps, use lower mips, or use half resolution.
On mobile GPUs, `half` precision lowers register use and power; on desktop it may be ignored.

lesson.text: Shader variants and compilation stalls

To support options (fog, normal maps, shadow modes, quality levels) the usual technique is **compile-time keywords** (`#pragma multi_compile` and `shader_feature` in Unity, `#define`s elsewhere) that produce a separate compiled shader per combination. Variants multiply: 10 independent on/off keywords create 2^10 = 1,024 variants for a single pass. A handful of shaders with several keyword groups easily produce tens of thousands of compiled programs. Costs: long build and import times, huge memory for the shader binaries, and a **runtime compile hitch** when a variant is first needed and was not compiled or cached ahead of time. Modern APIs (D3D12, Vulkan, Metal) compile your shader plus the complete pipeline state into a **pipeline state object (PSO)** at first use, and building one can take from a few milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds, which shows up as a freeze when new effects first appear on screen.

lesson.text: Mitigations: strip variants your project never uses (`shader_feature` drops unreferenced variants from builds, `multi_compile` keeps all of them, so use it only where runtime switching is necessary); replace rarely used keywords with runtime branches on uniforms when the branch is coherent and cheap; **warm up** shaders and PSOs during loading screens (in Unity, `ShaderVariantCollection.WarmUp`, and in recent Unity 6 releases `GraphicsStateCollection` for recording and prewarming PSOs); ship precompiled caches where the platform allows; and keep a budget for keywords per shader.

Dynamic branch on a uniform versus a keyword: a coherent runtime `if (_UseFog > 0.5)` costs a few cycles per pixel and creates no extra variants; a keyword doubles variants but gives the leanest code. For features toggled rarely and cheap to evaluate, prefer the runtime branch; for heavy features (parallax mapping, many-light loops), prefer keywords.

Agents write plausible HLSL and GLSL but mix them up (using `vec3` and `mix` in HLSL, `float4x4` and `mul` in GLSL), ignore constant buffer packing, and add a keyword for every request, which explodes variant counts. Say which language, graphics API and render pipeline the shader targets, and ask for the keyword count and variant math in the change. Verify by compiling for all target platforms, checking the build's variant count, checking for per-pixel divergent branches around texture samples, and capturing a frame in the GPU profiler. Treat any agent-written post-process that loops 32 or 64 taps per pixel with suspicion.
Worked example: variant budget

A team's character shader has keywords for normal map, emission, rim, dissolve, two fog modes (mutually exclusive), three shadow qualities, and one for each of two platforms' lighting modes. Naively that is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 2 = 288 variants per pass, times 3 passes (forward, shadow, depth) about 864, before any engine-provided keyword sets such as fog or lightmap options multiply it again. Converting rim, emission and dissolve to uniform-driven branches (coherent per material) leaves 2 x 3 x 3 x 2 = 36 per pass: an 8x reduction in compile time and memory with a measured GPU cost under 0.1 ms.
Pitfalls checklist

items: Forgetting to re-normalize interpolated normals and view vectors.
Dividing by zero or taking sqrt, pow or log of negative values: NaN pixels bleed into bloom and TAA over many frames.
Branching on per-pixel data around `Sample` calls.
Per-frame variant explosion from one keyword per feature.
Assuming warmup happened: test the first-use path on a clean cache on real hardware.

patterns.signal: The fragment shader computes a value that varies linearly across the triangle, such as a fog factor or a scaled UV
patterns.use: Move work from fragment to vertex shader
patterns.why: Vertices are far fewer than pixels, and interpolation delivers the result for free. Only for values that are linear across a triangle; per-pixel lighting detail gets lost.

patterns.signal: An `if` on per-pixel data like noise or a texture value saves nothing in profiles
patterns.use: Branch on uniforms, not per-pixel data
patterns.why: A divergent warp runs both paths. Branch on material or per-draw constants, or use branchless `lerp`/`step` for small bodies; coherent per-pixel branches over large areas can still pay off.

patterns.signal: A texture fetch sits inside a per-pixel branch and edge pixels show blocky mip artefacts
patterns.why: Implicit derivatives are undefined when neighbouring pixels in a quad take different paths. Sample before the branch, or pass explicit gradients or a mip level.

patterns.signal: A shader declares many independent `multi_compile` keywords and builds are slow and memory heavy
patterns.use: Variant budget: fewer keywords plus stripping
patterns.why: Variants multiply per keyword. Use `shader_feature` for material-only toggles, strip unused combinations in builds, and move cheap toggles to uniform branches.

patterns.signal: The game freezes once, for a few hundred ms, the first time a new effect or material appears
patterns.why: The driver compiles the variant or pipeline state on first use. Collect the variants actually used and precompile them during loading; costs load time and needs maintaining.

patterns.signal: A fragment shader evaluates an expensive function of one or two inputs every pixel, like a BRDF term or colour curve
patterns.why: Bake the function into a small 1D/2D/3D texture and sample it. Trades ALU for a fetch and memory, and loses precision between texels, so it suits smooth functions.

patterns.signal: The CPU uploads tightly packed floats but the shader reads the second `float3` from the wrong offset
patterns.why: Constant buffers align fields to 16-byte rows. Lay out data as `float4` groups or add explicit padding so CPU and GPU structs match exactly.

patterns.signal: Per-object, per-material and per-frame constants are all uploaded together in one buffer every draw
patterns.why: Separate per-frame, per-material and per-draw buffers so each is uploaded only when it changes, reducing bandwidth and binding cost on the CPU.

patterns.signal: Lighting looks darker in the middle of large triangles even though vertex normals are unit length
patterns.why: Linear interpolation of unit vectors shortens them between vertices. Call `normalize` in the fragment shader; one cheap instruction per pixel.

patterns.signal: An integer material ID or index passed to the fragment stage gets blended into garbage between vertices
patterns.why: Mark the attribute `nointerpolation` so every fragment gets the provoking vertex's value. Requires all vertices of the triangle to carry the same ID.

patterns.signal: Thousands of independent elements (particles, culling, simulation) are updated in a C# loop each frame
patterns.use: Move data-parallel work to a compute shader
patterns.why: The GPU processes elements in parallel and the data stays on the GPU for rendering. Reading results back costs latency; the gain needs many elements and little branching.

keyPoints: Vertex shaders run per vertex and output clip space plus attributes; fragment shaders run per pixel and dominate cost; compute shaders run user-defined thread groups with no pipeline input.
Constant buffers carry per-draw data in 16-byte packed rows; group them by update frequency and match CPU and GPU layouts exactly.
Attributes are interpolated with perspective correction; renormalize vectors in the fragment shader and mark integers as flat or nointerpolation.
Divergent branches run both paths for a warp, and branching around texture sampling can break derivatives; uniform branches are cheap.
Keyword variants multiply exponentially and uncompiled ones cause first-use hitches; strip, reduce and warm them up.

quiz.q: A fragment shader has `if (noise(uv) > 0.5) { expensiveEffect(); }` and noise varies per pixel. Profiling shows no savings versus always running the effect. Why?
options: Constant buffers are re-uploaded each time a branch is taken
Interpolation is disabled inside any conditional code block
The compiler removes the branch and always runs the effect
Lanes in a warp disagree, so the effect runs masked for the group
quiz.explain: When lanes in a warp diverge, the group still executes the expensive path for any lane that needs it, so the saving disappears. A branch that is coherent across neighbouring pixels (such as one on a uniform) would skip the work.

quiz.q: A shader has 12 independent boolean keywords compiled with multi_compile. The build is slow and memory heavy. Which change gives the largest reduction for the least GPU cost?
options: Warm up every variant during the loading screen at startup
Turn keywords for cheap per-material features into uniform branches
Change the keywords from multi_compile to multi_compile_local
Move each keyword's code path into a separate shader pass
quiz.explain: Twelve independent keywords means up to 4,096 variants; making cheap coherent features runtime branches removes factors of two each. Warmup hides runtime hitches but still compiles and stores every variant, local keywords save global keyword slots without reducing combinations, and extra passes add variants rather than removing them.

quiz.q: A player enters a new area and the game freezes for about 200 ms the first time a particle effect appears, never again afterwards. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Constant buffer packing is wrong, so recompile with fewer fields
A shader variant or pipeline state is compiled on first use; warm it up during loading
The effect has too many vertices; reduce the triangle count of the mesh
The vertex shader runs per pixel; move it to the fragment stage
quiz.explain: A one-time hitch at first appearance is the signature of lazy shader or pipeline compilation, solved by precompiling or warming up in a loading screen. Geometry cost would repeat every frame the effect is visible.

quiz.q: A cbuffer declares `float3 _Color;` followed by `float3 _Offset;`. The CPU uploads a tightly packed struct of six floats, yet the shader reads a wrong offset. What is the likely issue?
options: Constant buffers cannot hold more than one float3 field
The GPU applies perspective correction to cbuffer fields
CPU and GPU disagree about 16-byte packing, shifting the offset
Uniform values must be normalized before every upload
quiz.explain: HLSL packs values into 16-byte rows and does not let a float3 straddle a row boundary, so a CPU struct without matching padding shifts later fields. Perspective correction applies to interpolators only, not constants.

quiz.q: A vertex shader passes a unit-length normal to the fragment stage. A lighting artifact shows darker shading in the middle of large triangles. What is the correct fix?
options: Normalize the interpolated normal in the fragment shader
Pass the normal as nointerpolation so it is constant per triangle
Compute the normal from the clip-space position instead
Multiply the dot product by the triangle's area
quiz.explain: Linear interpolation between unit vectors yields shorter vectors in the middle of a triangle, darkening the dot product; renormalizing restores unit length. Making it flat would give faceted shading instead of smooth.

quiz.q: A post-process fragment shader evaluates an expensive filmic colour curve with several `pow` and `exp` calls on a single input value for every pixel, and the pass is ALU-bound. What should you reach for?
options: Move the curve evaluation into the vertex shader for each vertex
Precompute the curve into a small lookup texture and sample it
Branch on a uniform so the curve is skipped sometimes
Mark the input value as a flat, non-interpolated attribute
quiz.explain: A 1D lookup replaces many ALU ops with one texture fetch for any function of one or two inputs. The vertex shader trick only works for values that vary linearly, and a non-linear curve interpolated across a triangle would be wrong.

topics.title: Textures and sampling
topics.summary: How a GPU turns UV coordinates into colours: texels, filtering, mipmaps, compression formats, atlases and colour space.

lesson.text: Your artist delivers a 4096x4096 rock texture. It looks gorgeous in the editor, shimmers like static when the camera slides along the ground, and on a mid-range phone it takes 64 MB of memory and a visible chunk of your frame time. Every one of those symptoms is a texture-sampling problem. Textures are not pictures to the GPU. They are 1D, 2D or 3D arrays of data that shaders read from, and nearly all of the memory and bandwidth in a typical game goes into them.
UVs, texels and the sampler

A **texel** is one element of a texture (a pixel of the texture, as opposed to a pixel on screen). A mesh vertex stores a **UV** coordinate, normally in the range 0 to 1 across the image. The rasteriser interpolates UVs across each triangle, and for every screen pixel the fragment shader calls something like `tex.Sample(sampler, uv)`. The UV is a continuous position, so the hardware has to decide which texels to read and how to combine them. That decision is the **sampler state**: filter mode (point, bilinear, trilinear), wrap mode (repeat, clamp, mirror) and anisotropy level. Sampler state is separate from texture data in modern APIs, which is why one texture can be sampled in several ways.

Two numbers describe the mismatch that makes sampling hard. A texture has a fixed texel size, and a triangle on screen has a variable pixel size. If a 1024-texel-wide texture covers 256 screen pixels, each pixel spans 4 texels (minification). If it covers 4000 pixels, each texel spans about 4 pixels (magnification). The GPU computes UV derivatives between neighbouring pixels in a 2x2 quad (`ddx(uv)`, `ddy(uv)`) to know which situation it is in. This is also why sampling inside divergent branches or after discards can produce wrong mip selection: the quad needs all four lanes to compute derivatives.
Filtering and mipmaps

**Point** filtering returns the nearest texel: blocky when magnified, and noisy when minified because a pixel that should be an average of 16 texels picks one arbitrary texel, which flickers as the camera moves. **Bilinear** filtering blends the four nearest texels and fixes the magnified case. It does not fix minification, because four texels cannot represent the average of sixteen or sixty-four.

lesson.text: **Mipmaps** solve minification. A mip chain stores the texture at half resolution repeatedly down to 1x1: 1024, 512, 256, and so on. The hardware picks the level whose texel size best matches the pixel footprint, computed from the UV derivatives. **Trilinear** filtering blends between two adjacent mip levels so the transition is smooth. The cost is memory: a full chain adds 1/4 + 1/16 + ... which is about 33 percent. The benefit is large: stable images with no shimmering, and better cache behaviour, because neighbouring pixels read neighbouring texels in a small mip level instead of striding across a huge one.

lesson.text: Anisotropic filtering

A floor stretching away from the camera is the classic failure of trilinear filtering. The pixel footprint on the texture is a long thin ellipse, not a square. Trilinear picks the mip from the longer axis to avoid aliasing, so the floor becomes a blurry smear. **Anisotropic filtering** takes several samples along the long axis of the footprint (2x, 4x, 8x or 16x the maximum). It costs more texture-unit work per pixel, but modern GPUs handle 8x or 16x cheaply on desktop. On mobile it still costs bandwidth, so 2x to 4x is a common compromise. It matters most for ground, roads and walls seen at grazing angles, and not at all for a sprite facing the camera.
GPU compression formats

PNG and JPEG are storage formats. The GPU cannot sample them directly, so the engine decodes them to raw RGBA8 in VRAM: 4 bytes per texel. GPU compression formats are decoded by fixed-function hardware at sample time, so the texture stays compressed in memory and in cache. They are lossy and block-based: each block of texels (4x4 for BC and ETC2, 4x4 up to 12x12 for ASTC) encodes into a fixed 64 or 128 bits, so random access is cheap.

items: **BC1/BC3/BC4/BC5/BC7 (DXT family)**: desktop and console. BC1 is 4 bits per texel (8:1 vs RGBA8), BC7 is 8 bits per texel with high quality. BC5 stores two channels and is common for normal maps; BC4 is one channel.
**ETC2**: mandatory in OpenGL ES 3.0 and effectively universal on Android; 4 or 8 bits per texel. Older but universally supported on mobile.

**ASTC**: variable block size from 4x4 (8 bits per texel) up to 12x12 (0.89 bits per texel), so you can trade quality for size per texture. Supported on modern iOS and Android GPUs and the common mobile default.
**Uncompressed**: RGBA8 or RGBA16F for render targets, LUTs or small UI textures where block artefacts are unacceptable.

lesson.text: Compression happens at import or build time and is slow, since encoders search for the best block encoding. The numbers matter: a 2048x2048 RGBA8 texture with mips is about 22 MB. As ASTC 6x6 (about 3.6 bits per texel) it is under 4 MB. For a mobile game with a 1.5 GB memory ceiling, texture format is often the single biggest memory lever.
