lesson.text: Atlases and sRGB versus linear

A **texture atlas** packs many small images into one large texture so that many objects can share one material and one draw call. It is the backbone of sprite and UI rendering. The pitfalls are bleeding and mips: bilinear filtering near a sprite edge reads the neighbouring sprite, so you need padding (extruded border pixels), and mip levels blend neighbours together faster at lower levels, so atlases often need padding proportional to the highest mip you use, or mips disabled for UI. Texture arrays are an alternative for same-size images: each layer is a clean texture, with no bleeding.

**Colour space** is the other classic trap. Monitors and image files encode colour in sRGB, a non-linear curve (roughly gamma 2.2) that spends more precision on dark tones. Lighting maths (adding light, multiplying albedo by irradiance, blending) is only physically meaningful in **linear** space. If you sample an sRGB texture as raw numbers and light it, your mid-tones are wrong and the result looks washed out or too contrasty. The fix is to mark colour textures (albedo, emissive) as sRGB so the hardware converts to linear on sample, filter in linear space, and convert back when writing to an sRGB render target. Data textures (normal maps, roughness, metallic, masks, height) must be linear: they hold numbers, not colours, and applying an sRGB curve corrupts them.

Misconceptions to drop: 'bigger texture means sharper' (only if the texel density on screen justifies it; beyond that you pay memory and get nothing), 'PNG size on disk is the memory cost' (it is the decoded or GPU-compressed size that counts), and 'mipmaps waste memory' (they cost 33 percent and save more than that in bandwidth and shimmer).

When an agent writes import scripts or shaders, specify the colour space and compression per texture type: albedo sRGB with BC7 or ASTC, normal maps linear with BC5 or ASTC, masks linear. Agents often generate texture code that samples everything the same way, forgets to mark data textures as linear, or recommends 'just use RGBA32 for quality'. Verify by checking a texture's format and memory size in the engine's inspector or a memory profiler, and by looking at a grazing-angle surface for blur (anisotropy) and distant surfaces for shimmer (mips).

A practical budget check: pick the target texel density first (for example 512 texels per metre for hero props, 128 for terrain), derive resolutions from object size, then choose the compression. Starting from 'what looks good in the editor on my 4K monitor' is how projects end up 3 GB over budget.

patterns.signal: Distant ground textures shimmer and crawl as the camera moves slowly
patterns.why: Minified textures skip texels and alias; mips prefilter them and improve cache hits. Costs about 33 percent more memory; skip only for textures never minified, like pixel-exact UI.

patterns.signal: A road or floor turns into a blurry smear at grazing angles while surfaces facing the camera look sharp
patterns.why: Takes extra samples along the stretched axis instead of dropping to a blurry mip. Costs bandwidth, so use 4x to 16x on ground textures and leave it off elsewhere.

patterns.signal: Texture memory is over budget and most textures are stored as uncompressed RGBA8
patterns.why: BC on desktop and console, ASTC on modern mobile, ETC2 as a fallback; textures stay compressed in VRAM at 4x to 8x savings. Lossy, so check normal maps and gradients.

patterns.signal: Roughness, metallic and AO are each a separate greyscale texture per material
patterns.why: Store each mask in one channel of a single texture, cutting fetches and memory. All channels share one resolution and compression, and the packed texture must be linear.

patterns.signal: Normal maps or roughness masks look subtly wrong, with flat or overly bright lighting on slopes
patterns.use: sRGB for colour, linear for data
patterns.why: The sRGB flag decodes gamma on sample, which is right for albedo and wrong for normals, masks and LUTs. Set it per texture by what the data means, not by how it looks.

patterns.signal: Hundreds of small UI icons or sprites each use their own texture and break batching
patterns.why: One texture lets many elements share a material and batch. Pad and extrude edges against bleeding at lower mips; atlases cannot use wrap-mode tiling per element.

patterns.signal: Terrain layers or tiling materials need per-layer wrap and mips but you want one material and one binding
patterns.why: Each slice keeps its own wrap, mips and filtering with no bleeding, indexed by a slice number. All slices must share size and format.

patterns.signal: Normal maps show blocky banding after compression with a generic colour format
patterns.why: Store X and Y in a two-channel format (BC5 or ASTC with normal settings) and rebuild Z in the shader. Higher quality per bit, at the cost of a few ALU instructions.

patterns.signal: A large open world cannot keep every texture's full mip chain resident in memory
patterns.why: Load only the mip levels each texture needs at its current screen size, keeping a memory budget. Textures may look blurry briefly while higher mips stream in.

keyPoints: A texel is a texture element; sampler state (filter, wrap, anisotropy) decides how a continuous UV maps to texel data.
Mipmaps fix minification shimmer and improve cache use for about 33 percent extra memory; anisotropic filtering fixes blur at grazing angles.
GPU block compression (BC, ASTC, ETC2) keeps textures compressed in VRAM, cutting memory 4x to 8x or more versus RGBA8.
Atlases save draw calls but need padding against bleeding and care with mips.
Colour textures are sRGB, data textures (normals, roughness, masks) are linear; mixing them up silently corrupts lighting.

quiz.q: A road texture looks crisp near the camera but turns into a blurry smear far down the road, while a distant wall facing the camera looks fine. Trilinear filtering is on. What fixes it?
options: Raise the texture resolution from 2048 to 4096
Enable anisotropic filtering on that sampler or texture
Switch the filter from trilinear to point sampling
Disable mipmaps so the full resolution is always sampled
quiz.explain: The road's pixel footprint is a long thin ellipse at grazing angles, and trilinear picks the mip from the longer axis, so it blurs. Anisotropic filtering takes multiple samples along that axis. A bigger texture does not change which mip is chosen at distance.

quiz.q: Distant cobblestones shimmer and crawl as the camera moves slowly, even though the texture is high resolution. The texture was imported without mipmaps. What is the underlying cause?
options: Bilinear filtering blends too many texels together
The texture is compressed with a lossy block format
The sampler uses the wrong wrap mode at the edges
Each pixel covers many texels but only samples a few
quiz.explain: Without mips, a pixel covering say 16 texels still reads only 1 to 4 of them, and which ones changes frame to frame, so it shimmers. Mips precompute the average. Compression and wrap mode do not cause temporal shimmer.

quiz.q: A normal map imported with the sRGB option ticked gives lighting that looks subtly wrong and flat on slopes. Why?
options: The sRGB decode curve distorts the stored vector values
sRGB textures cannot be sampled with a trilinear filter
Normal maps need more than 8 bits per channel to work
sRGB import disables compression, so detail is lost
quiz.explain: Normal maps hold direction data, and the sRGB decode bends the stored values non-linearly so the unpacked vectors are wrong. sRGB textures can be filtered normally and compression is unaffected.

quiz.q: Your mobile build is over its memory budget. Profiling shows 400 MB of 2048x2048 RGBA8 textures with mips. Quality must stay close. Which change helps most?
options: Remove mipmaps from all textures
Convert the textures to PNG with maximum compression
Import them as ASTC with a 6x6 or 4x4 block size
Lower anisotropic filtering from 16x to 2x
quiz.explain: ASTC stays compressed in VRAM and cuts size by roughly 4x (4x4 blocks) to 9x (6x6 blocks). PNG is only on-disk compression, since it is decoded to RGBA8 for the GPU, and mips and anisotropy do not touch the base memory cost.

quiz.q: UI icons packed in an atlas show thin coloured lines from neighbouring icons at the edges when the UI is scaled down. What is the best fix?
options: Convert the atlas to a point-filtered sampler only
Add padding with extruded edge pixels or limit the mip levels
Increase the atlas to 8192x8192 to space icons apart
Store the icons as separate uncompressed RGBA16F textures
quiz.explain: Bilinear and mip filtering read texels across icon borders, so edges need padding of repeated border pixels, or mips need to be limited. A larger atlas does not change filter footprints unless the spacing also grows.

quiz.q: Each PBR material ships three separate greyscale textures for roughness, metallic and ambient occlusion. Profiling shows extra texture fetches per pixel and wasted memory from three single-channel files. Which approach fits best?
options: Convert each mask into a slice of a texture array
Stream in only the lower mip levels of the three masks
Turn on anisotropic filtering for the three mask textures
Pack the three masks into channels of one texture
quiz.explain: Channel packing stores three single-channel masks in R, G and B of one linear texture, giving one fetch and one allocation. A texture array still needs separate fetches, and streaming or filtering do not cut the sample count.

topics.title: Lighting and materials
topics.summary: From Blinn-Phong to physically based metallic/roughness materials, normal maps, shadow maps and the precomputed tricks that fake global illumination.

lesson.text: Two scenes with the same geometry can look like plastic toys or like believable stone, metal and skin. The difference is a lighting model and a material description. In a game you also need it to run in about 4 ms of a 16.6 ms frame, with dozens of lights and moving characters. This lesson covers the shading models, the maps that fake detail, and the main techniques for shadows and indirect light.
Diffuse and specular

Light arriving at a surface does one of two things. Some enters the material, scatters and leaves in all directions: that is **diffuse**, and it gives the surface its colour. Some reflects off the surface boundary like a mirror, blurred by roughness: that is **specular**, and it gives highlights. The simplest diffuse model is Lambert: brightness is `max(0, dot(N, L))`, where N is the surface normal and L the direction to the light. It depends only on the angle between normal and light, not on the viewer.

lesson.caption: Lambert brightness follows the cosine of the angle between N and L and clamps to zero once the light passes behind the surface.

lesson.text: **Blinn-Phong** adds specular with a half-vector H, halfway between L and the view vector V. Specular intensity is `pow(max(0, dot(N, H)), shininess)`. High shininess gives a tight highlight (polished surface), low gives a wide one. It is cheap and looks acceptable, which is why it dominated for twenty years. Its problems are that parameters are not physically meaningful (shininess has no real-world unit), it does not conserve energy (a surface can reflect more light than it receives), and it looks wrong at grazing angles, where real surfaces become more mirror-like.

lesson.caption: H always sits halfway between L and V, and the highlight peaks when H lines up with N; higher shininess makes the peak narrower.

lesson.text: Physically based rendering

**PBR** replaces ad-hoc parameters with ones that correspond to measurable properties, and uses a BRDF (bidirectional reflectance distribution function) that conserves energy. The common game workflow is **metallic/roughness**, with three main inputs: base colour (albedo), metallic (0 or 1 in practice, intermediate values only for transitions such as dirt on metal) and roughness (0 mirror-smooth to 1 fully rough). Dielectrics (wood, plastic, skin) have coloured diffuse and a fixed dim specular of about 4 percent reflectance; metals have no diffuse and tint their specular with the base colour.

The standard real-time specular BRDF, Cook-Torrance, has three terms: a normal distribution function D (how many microfacets face the half-vector, controlled by roughness), a geometry term G (microfacets shadowing each other) and a Fresnel term F (reflectance rises toward 100 percent at grazing angles, via Schlick's approximation). The point of PBR is not realism for its own sake. It is that a material authored once looks consistent under sunlight, a torch and an overcast sky, so artists stop retuning per scene. Specular/glossiness is an alternative workflow, equivalent in power but easier to author incorrectly.
Normal maps

A **normal map** stores a perturbed normal per texel (as RGB, in tangent space) so a flat 2-triangle wall shades as though it had bricks, grout and scratches. The shader samples it, remaps from 0-1 to -1..1, and transforms it by the TBN matrix (tangent, bitangent, normal) built from the mesh. It changes shading only, not silhouettes or depth: look at the wall edge-on and it is flat. Normal maps are baked from high-poly sculpts onto low-poly game meshes, and they must be linear data textures, usually stored in BC5 or ASTC with the Z component reconstructed. Mismatched tangent-space conventions (OpenGL-style versus DirectX-style green channel) cause bumps that look inverted when lit from above.
Shadow mapping and its artefacts

**Shadow mapping** renders the scene's depth from the light's point of view into a depth texture (the shadow map). When shading a pixel, you transform its position into light space and compare its depth to the stored depth: if the pixel is farther, something is in front of it and it is in shadow. Cost is one extra depth-only pass per light (or per cascade), plus texture reads when shading. A directional sun typically uses 3 to 4 **cascades**: shadow maps covering nested ranges of the view frustum, so shadows near the camera get high texel density.

items: **Shadow acne**: surfaces shadow themselves because depth precision and slope make them fail the comparison. Fixed with a depth bias and normal-offset bias.
**Peter-panning**: too much bias detaches the shadow from the object's base so it floats. Balance bias per light and scene scale.

**Aliasing and blocky edges**: shadow map texels are visible when one texel covers many pixels. Fixed with cascades, higher resolution, PCF (percentage-closer filtering, averaging several comparisons) or soft filters.
**Shimmering (swimming)**: shadow edges shimmer when the camera moves because texels shift; stabilising cascades by snapping to texel increments reduces it.

lesson.caption: Each pixel looks up the depth the light saw and is in shadow when it is farther; too little bias gives acne, too much gives peter-panning.

lesson.text: Global illumination, lightmaps and light probes

Direct lighting is only a fraction of what you see. **Global illumination (GI)** is light bouncing between surfaces: sunlight hitting a red wall tints the white floor beside it. Real-time ray-traced GI exists on high-end hardware and in some engines, but across mobile, console and PC the dominant technique is still to **bake** it offline. A **lightmap** is a texture, mapped with a second UV channel (UV2) unique per static surface, that stores precomputed direct and indirect light. At runtime shading reads it for almost free. Costs are memory (lightmaps are large), bake time, and the fact that dynamic objects and moving lights are not included.

**Light probes** fill the gap for dynamic objects: a grid of sample points in the scene stores the baked lighting at each point as spherical harmonics (a compact low-frequency representation, typically 9 coefficients per colour channel). A moving character interpolates between the nearest probes to pick up the ambient light of where it stands. **Reflection probes** capture a cubemap of the surroundings for shiny surfaces. Probe placement is a real craft: too sparse and characters glow wrongly walking through shadowed doorways, or too dense and you waste memory and bake time.

Budget thinking: a 2048x2048 lightmap in a compressed format is a few MB, but a large level can need dozens. Lightmap resolution is expressed in texels per metre; spend it on surfaces where the player looks and use lower density on hidden or uniform areas.

Agents tend to write 'realistic' shaders from memory: Phong with energy-violating constants, PBR with gamma-space inputs, or a normal map sampled as sRGB. Tell the agent which pipeline and material model you use, and ask it to modify existing shaders instead of generating them from scratch. Verify with a reference scene: a smooth metal sphere, a rough dielectric sphere and a grey ramp under one light and one environment. Check that roughness 0 gives a sharp reflection, that values stay energy-plausible, and that shadows show neither acne nor floating.

Bring it together on a typical mobile level: static geometry uses baked lightmaps (indirect plus most direct light), one realtime directional light with 2 cascades casts shadows from characters, characters take ambient light from probes, and materials use compact metallic/roughness maps packed into one texture's channels. Each piece trades flexibility for cost, and the skill is deciding where flexibility is actually needed.

patterns.signal: Static level geometry needs soft indirect light and the real-time lighting cost is too high
patterns.why: Precompute direct and indirect light into textures, so runtime cost is one fetch. Lights and geometry must stay static; bakes cost iteration time and lightmap memory.

patterns.signal: A moving character stays brightly lit when walking from a sunny courtyard into a baked dark corridor
patterns.why: Probes sample baked indirect light at points in space, and dynamic objects interpolate between them. Place them densely where light changes, especially at doorways and shadow edges.

patterns.signal: Shiny objects reflect the sky indoors, or reflections do not line up with the room's walls
patterns.why: Place probes per area so reflections show the local surroundings; box projection aligns them with room walls. Real-time probe updates are expensive, so bake them where possible.

patterns.signal: Sun shadows are blocky near the camera because one shadow map covers the whole view distance
patterns.why: Split the view frustum into ranges, each with its own shadow map, so near shadows get the resolution. Each cascade adds a shadow render pass; also cap shadow distance.

patterns.signal: Shadows show stripy self-shadowing (acne), or they float detached from the feet (peter-panning)
patterns.why: Acne means too little bias; detached shadows mean too much. Use a small depth bias plus normal-offset bias, and tune per light rather than raising one value.

patterns.signal: Artists retune shininess per scene because materials look right under one lighting setup and wrong under another
patterns.why: An energy-conserving BRDF with measurable parameters keeps materials consistent under any light. Needs reference values and linear-space lighting to pay off.

patterns.signal: A metal surface looks like dull grey plastic even with low roughness
patterns.why: Metals need metallic = 1 with the tint in base colour; dielectrics need metallic = 0. In-between values are only for transitions such as rust or dirt edges.

patterns.signal: Surface detail like bricks or scratches is needed but the triangle budget is already spent
patterns.why: Fakes shading detail at a texture fetch per pixel. Silhouettes and grazing views stay flat, so large forms still need real geometry or parallax techniques.

patterns.signal: Many point and spot lights cast real-time shadows and shadow rendering dominates the GPU frame
patterns.why: Point lights render up to six shadow faces each. Limit shadowed lights to the few that matter, bake the rest, and cull shadow casters by distance.

keyPoints: Diffuse is scattered colour light; specular is boundary reflection. Blinn-Phong is cheap but not energy-conserving or physically meaningful.
PBR metallic/roughness uses measurable parameters and an energy-conserving BRDF, so materials look consistent under any lighting.
Normal maps fake shading detail only: silhouettes and depth stay flat, and the maps must be linear data.
Shadow maps compare depth from the light; tune bias to avoid acne (too little) and peter-panning (too much), and use cascades for sun shadows.
Baked lightmaps carry static GI cheaply; light probes and reflection probes give dynamic objects matching indirect light.

quiz.q: A character's shadow on the ground appears detached, floating a few centimetres away from the feet. Which setting is the most likely culprit?
options: Shadow bias set too low
Shadow bias set too high
Cascade count set too high
Lightmap resolution set too low
quiz.explain: That is peter-panning: excessive bias pushes the depth comparison so far that shadow contact is lost. Too little bias gives acne (speckled self-shadowing) instead. Cascade count and lightmap density do not move shadow contact.

quiz.q: A metallic sphere looks dull grey instead of reflecting the environment, even though roughness is low. The material has metallic = 0 and a grey base colour. What is wrong?
options: Metallic should be near 1 so the surface uses tinted specular and no diffuse
Roughness should be raised so that the highlight spreads out
The base colour should be white for reflections to appear
The normal map should be disabled to allow reflections
quiz.explain: With metallic = 0 the material is a dielectric with a diffuse grey body and only a ~4 percent specular reflection. Setting metallic to 1 gives full coloured reflection. Roughness changes the blur of reflections, not their strength.

quiz.q: A flat wall with a brick normal map looks convincingly bumpy face-on, but at a steep grazing angle its silhouette is a perfectly straight line. Why?
options: The normal map is stored in too low a resolution
The tangent space is flipped for this mesh
Mipmaps flatten the normals at grazing angles
Normal maps change shading only, not geometry or depth
quiz.explain: A normal map perturbs the normal used in the lighting equation. The triangles stay flat, so the edge outline stays straight. Parallax or tessellation or real geometry is needed to change silhouettes.

quiz.q: A moving enemy walks from a sunlit courtyard into a baked, shadowed corridor but stays brightly lit in the corridor. Static walls look correctly dark. What should you fix?
options: Raise the lightmap resolution on the corridor walls
Add or tighten light probes inside the corridor
Increase the sun's shadow cascade count
Switch the walls from baked to realtime lighting
quiz.explain: Lightmaps only light static surfaces. Dynamic objects get indirect light from probes, and sparse probes near the doorway leave the enemy interpolating sunlit values. Lightmap resolution or cascades do not affect dynamic object ambient.

quiz.q: Why does the metallic/roughness PBR workflow usually give more consistent results across lighting conditions than a Blinn-Phong material with hand-tuned shininess?
options: It avoids using normal maps and shadow maps entirely
It computes lighting at lower cost per pixel on all GPUs
Its parameters map to physical properties and its BRDF conserves energy
It always stores materials in a linear 16-bit float format
quiz.explain: PBR's parameters describe the surface (reflectance, roughness), and the BRDF cannot reflect more energy than arrives, so one material behaves plausibly everywhere. It is usually not cheaper, and it still uses normal and shadow maps.

quiz.q: A 4096 sun shadow map is already in use, yet shadows are crude around the player while shadows on hills 600 m away look fine. Raising the resolution further blows the memory budget. What should you reach for?
options: Cascaded shadow maps that split the view range into slices
Raise the depth bias and the normal bias on the sun light a lot
Cap the number of real-time shadow casters in the scene
Bake the sun shadows into static lightmaps for the level
quiz.explain: Cascades give each distance band its own shadow map, so near slices get high texel density cheaply. Bias fixes acne or floating shadows, not blocky resolution, and baking would lose shadows on moving characters.

topics.title: Render paths, transparency and post-processing
topics.summary: How forward, deferred and forward+ organise lighting work, why transparency is hard, and how HDR, tonemapping, bloom, anti-aliasing and upscalers shape the final image.

lesson.text: You add the 40th point light to a night street scene and the frame rate collapses from 60 to 25, even though nothing else changed. A particle-heavy explosion drops the same game to 20 fps on phones while the CPU is idle. Both problems come from how the renderer organises its work: which **render path** it uses and how it deals with transparent surfaces. This lesson covers those structures and the full-screen processing that turns raw lit pixels into the final image.
Forward, deferred and forward+

**Forward rendering** shades each object in one pass: for every mesh, the fragment shader loops over the lights affecting it and outputs a final colour. It is simple, supports transparency, MSAA and many material types, and uses little memory. Its cost scales as objects times lights: a fragment is shaded for every light that touches its object, including fragments that are later overdrawn. Classic forward therefore caps real-time lights at a handful per object (in Unity's built-in pipeline, a few per-pixel lights plus cheap vertex or spherical-harmonic ones).

**Deferred rendering** splits the work. A geometry pass writes surface attributes (albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, depth) into several render targets, the **G-buffer**. A lighting pass then runs once per light over only the screen pixels it affects, reading the G-buffer. Each pixel is lit once regardless of overdraw, so hundreds of lights are affordable. The costs: a fat G-buffer (e.g. four RGBA8 targets is 16 bytes per pixel, about 33 MB at 1080p, and much more bandwidth), no hardware MSAA (so you rely on post-process AA), and transparent objects still need a separate forward pass. On tile-based mobile GPUs deferred is possible but bandwidth-hungry unless the API keeps the G-buffer on-chip.

lesson.text: **Forward+** (tiled or clustered forward) keeps the forward pass but first builds a per-tile or per-cluster list of lights, usually in a compute shader: the screen is divided into tiles (16x16 pixels is typical) (clusters add depth slices), and each tile records which lights intersect it. The fragment shader loops over only its tile's lights. You get many lights, MSAA and transparency in one path, at the cost of extra compute and list management. Modern pipelines (Unity's Forward+ in URP 14 and later, Unreal's clustered options) lean this way because it scales to many lights without a G-buffer.

items: **Forward**: cheap memory, MSAA and transparency work, light count is the limit. Best for mobile and VR with few lights.
**Deferred**: many lights, decoupled from geometry cost, heavy bandwidth, no MSAA. Best for light-dense scenes on desktop and console.
**Forward+**: many lights with forward's flexibility, needs compute or clustering. A strong default when targeting a wide device range.

lesson.text: Transparency, sorting and overdraw

**Alpha blending** computes `out = src.rgb * src.a + dst.rgb * (1 - src.a)`. The operation is not commutative: blending A over B differs from B over A, so transparent triangles must be drawn **back to front**. Opaque geometry avoids this because the depth buffer resolves visibility in any order. Transparent objects are therefore drawn after opaques, sorted by distance, with depth writes usually off (they test against depth but do not write it). Sorting per object fails for large or intersecting objects (a glass window crossing a smoke cloud), which show popping or wrong ordering. Alternatives: alpha testing (cutout, binary and aliased, great for foliage with alpha-to-coverage), dithered transparency, or order-independent techniques (weighted blended OIT) that approximate the order.

**Overdraw** is shading the same pixel multiple times. Opaque overdraw is reduced by sorting front to back and early-Z, but transparent overdraw cannot be skipped: every layer of a smoke particle is blended. A full-screen particle effect with 10 layers means 10 times the fill-rate cost of the screen, which is exactly the phone explosion problem. Mitigations: smaller quads that tightly fit the visible shape, fewer and larger particles with better textures, half-resolution rendering of particles then compositing, and overdraw visualisation views to find hotspots.

lesson.text: HDR, tonemapping and bloom

Real light spans a huge range: a sunlit pixel can be tens of thousands of times brighter than a shadowed one, but an 8-bit display shows 256 levels. Rendering in **HDR** (high dynamic range) uses float render targets (commonly R11G11B10 or RGBA16F) so lighting values above 1.0 survive until the end. **Tonemapping** then compresses scene-referred values into display range. Clamping at 1.0 loses highlights in a flat white blob; a tonemap curve such as ACES or Khronos PBR Neutral rolls highlights off smoothly and keeps colour. Tonemapping is done after lighting and bloom, in linear space, and before the final sRGB conversion. Auto-exposure adapts the scale factor so a dark cave and noon sun both land in a sensible range.

lesson.text: **Bloom** simulates light scattering in a lens: bright areas bleed into their surroundings. It extracts pixels above a threshold, blurs them across a chain of downsampled textures (a mip-style pyramid, cheap and wide), and adds the result back. Bloom depends on HDR: with clamped input, a white shirt and a sun both have value 1.0 and bloom the same, but in HDR the sun is 50 and stands out. Overused bloom makes everything look like a dream sequence.
Anti-aliasing and temporal upscalers

Rasterisation samples a pixel once, so edges become staircases (aliasing), and thin shaded details shimmer. **MSAA** takes multiple coverage samples per pixel (2x, 4x, 8x) but shades once, so it fixes geometry edges only, and costs bandwidth proportional to sample count. It does not work directly with deferred and does nothing for shader aliasing, for example specular shimmer. **FXAA** is a cheap post-process that detects edges in the final image and blurs them: very fast, works everywhere, slightly soft. **TAA** (temporal anti-aliasing) jitters the camera sub-pixel each frame and accumulates history using motion vectors, effectively supersampling over time. It handles geometry and shader aliasing together. Its artefacts are ghosting behind moving objects, blur and flicker on thin features when history is rejected badly.

**Temporal upscalers** build on TAA: render at lower internal resolution (for example 67 percent per axis, which is about 45 percent of the pixels) and reconstruct a full-resolution image from jittered samples, motion vectors and depth. Examples include DLSS, FSR, XeSS and Unity's STP. Some are ML-based, others hand-tuned, but all need correct motion vectors for every moving thing (animated meshes, particles, vertex animation) to avoid smearing, and UI should be composited after upscaling. Upscaling usually saves GPU time, but it adds a fixed cost and does nothing if the frame is CPU-bound.

Post-process order matters. Typical chain: opaque, transparent, TAA or upscale, bloom and exposure, tonemap, colour grading, then UI. Applying tonemapping before bloom, or running bloom on clamped LDR, gives dull, wrong results.

Agents frequently suggest 'enable MSAA' regardless of render path, add a bloom pass that reads an LDR buffer, or write transparency shaders with depth write on. State your render path and target hardware, then check the result: look for transparent sorting pops, verify HDR is enabled in the camera and pipeline asset before judging bloom, and test TAA or upscaling with fast-moving objects and particles for ghosting. When an agent adds a custom full-screen pass, ask where in the chain it runs.

patterns.signal: Dozens of small overlapping point lights tank a classic forward renderer, which is GPU-bound
patterns.use: Deferred or forward+ for many lights
patterns.why: Deferred lights a G-buffer once per light volume; forward+ builds per-tile light lists. Deferred costs bandwidth and complicates MSAA and transparency, so forward+ often suits mid-range.

patterns.signal: A mobile or VR game uses few lights, needs MSAA, and is bandwidth constrained
patterns.why: No G-buffer, so far less bandwidth, and MSAA works directly. Cost scales with objects times lights, so keep per-object light counts low.

patterns.signal: Transparent objects render in the wrong order and pop in front of each other as the camera moves
patterns.why: Alpha blending is order-dependent, so draw far to near after opaques. Per-object sorting fails for intersecting or self-overlapping meshes; split those meshes.

patterns.signal: Interpenetrating transparent surfaces flicker even with per-object sorting
patterns.why: Weighted blended OIT or per-pixel lists remove the sort dependency. Approximate or memory heavy, so use only where sorting cannot be fixed by splitting geometry.

patterns.signal: Foliage or fences use alpha blending, sort badly and cause heavy overdraw
patterns.why: Treat them as opaque with `clip` so they write depth and need no sorting. Loses soft edges and early-Z; alpha-to-coverage smooths edges when MSAA is on.

patterns.signal: Particle effects with large mostly transparent quads make the GPU fill-rate bound when the camera gets close
patterns.why: Use tighter mesh-shaped sprites, cap particle count and size near the camera, or render particles to a lower-resolution buffer. Low-res buffers need careful upsampling at edges.

patterns.signal: Bloom looks weak and a bright sun glows the same as a white shirt
patterns.why: Without HDR all bright values clip at 1.0, so bloom cannot tell them apart. HDR targets cost bandwidth; tonemap once at the end of the chain.

patterns.signal: Thin wires and shiny specular highlights shimmer in a deferred renderer when the camera moves
patterns.why: TAA accumulates jittered samples over frames, fixing both geometry and shader aliasing. Needs correct motion vectors and can ghost or blur; MSAA only fixes geometry edges.

patterns.signal: A GPU-bound frame at high resolution must get faster and dropping native resolution looks too soft
patterns.why: Render fewer pixels and reconstruct with history and motion vectors. Saves GPU fragment time only; it does nothing for a CPU-bound frame and can ghost on bad motion vectors.

patterns.signal: Vignette, colour grading, grain and tonemapping each run as a separate full-screen pass
patterns.use: Merge post effects into an uber pass
patterns.why: One pass reads and writes the frame once instead of several times, saving bandwidth, especially on mobile. Effects that need neighbouring pixels, like blur, still need their own passes.

keyPoints: Forward cost scales with objects times lights; deferred decouples lights from geometry using a G-buffer; forward+ keeps forward flexibility with per-tile light lists.
Alpha blending is order-dependent, so transparents are sorted back to front, and transparent overdraw is a fill-rate hazard.
HDR render targets keep values above 1.0; tonemapping compresses them to display range, and bloom needs that HDR data.
MSAA fixes geometry edges only, FXAA is a cheap blur, TAA accumulates samples over time and can ghost.
Temporal upscalers render fewer pixels and reconstruct, requiring accurate motion vectors and doing nothing for CPU-bound frames.

quiz.q: A night scene has 60 small point lights, mostly overlapping a few buildings. Classic single-pass forward drops to 25 fps, GPU-bound. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Move to forward+ or deferred so pixels only use nearby lights
Enable 8x MSAA to smooth the edges of lit objects
Turn off HDR so the frame uses less render target memory
Sort opaque objects back to front to reduce overdraw
quiz.explain: Forward shades each fragment against every light touching its object, so cost explodes with overlapping lights. Tiled or deferred lighting limits work to relevant lights. MSAA adds cost, and opaque objects should be sorted front to back, not back to front.

quiz.q: A glass window in front of a smoke cloud renders correctly from one angle, but when the camera moves the smoke suddenly pops in front of the glass. Both are transparent and sorted per object. What is the likely cause?
options: The shaders use alpha-to-coverage instead of blending
The depth buffer is too low in precision for transparents
Per-object sort order flips as the camera moves
The tonemapper runs before the transparent pass
quiz.explain: Blending is order-dependent, and sorting whole objects by pivot distance can flip when large or intersecting objects trade places. Fixes include splitting meshes, adjusting sort priority, or using OIT. Depth precision and tonemap order do not cause a flip of draw order.

quiz.q: Bloom in your game looks weak: a bright sun and a white shirt glow identically and barely at all. The camera is set to LDR and the bloom threshold is 1.0. What do you do?
options: Lower the bloom threshold to 0.1 so all pixels glow
Enable HDR so the sun exceeds 1.0 and passes the threshold
Switch from TAA to FXAA to keep highlights sharper
Increase the shadow cascade count for brighter highlights
quiz.explain: In LDR everything is clamped at 1.0, so the sun and the shirt are indistinguishable to a threshold. HDR retains the intensity difference. Lowering the threshold would make the whole image glow, and AA mode is unrelated.

quiz.q: A frame renders at 1440p with a deferred path and takes 22 ms of GPU time, CPU at 6 ms. You enable a temporal upscaler at 67 percent per axis and GPU time falls to about 14 ms. A second profile of a CPU-bound scene at 18 ms of CPU time shows nearly no gain. Why?
options: Upscalers only work with forward rendering paths
Upscaling disables motion vectors used for CPU work
The CPU is too slow to read the upscaled image back
It only reduces GPU pixel work, not CPU-side work
quiz.explain: The upscaler cuts pixel-shading work on the GPU. If the frame is limited by CPU work such as draw submission or scripts, fewer pixels make no difference. Upscalers work with deferred paths and need motion vectors rather than disabling them.

quiz.q: You want to anti-alias a deferred renderer where thin power lines and shiny specular surfaces shimmer when the camera moves. Which option best addresses both geometry and shader aliasing?
options: TAA with correct motion vectors
MSAA 4x on the G-buffer
FXAA applied before tonemapping
Raising texture anisotropy to 16x
quiz.explain: TAA accumulates jittered samples over time, covering thin geometry and shading shimmer, and works with deferred. MSAA is awkward with a G-buffer and does not fix shader aliasing, and FXAA only blurs edges in a single image. Anisotropy concerns texture sampling.

quiz.q: A chain-link fence and bushes are drawn with alpha blending. Their texture alpha is only ever 0 or 1, yet they sort badly against other transparents and fill-rate is high. Which approach fits best?
options: Order-independent transparency for the whole scene view
Sort all transparent objects strictly back to front every frame
Alpha-tested cutout, with alpha-to-coverage if MSAA is on
Merge all of the post effects into one single uber pass
quiz.explain: Binary alpha needs no blending: cutout writes depth, sorts like opaque geometry and avoids the overdraw. Sorting or OIT would keep paying blend costs for a problem that disappears with a test.

topics.title: Graphics APIs and GPU performance
topics.summary: How OpenGL, Direct3D 12, Vulkan and Metal differ, how draw submission works, and how to find the real bottleneck with GPU capture tools.

lesson.text: Your game holds 60 fps in the editor, then runs at 38 fps on a phone. The team guesses: reduce texture sizes, halve the particles, lower the resolution. Each change is a coin flip, and the result is a month of lost work. Performance work that starts with guessing is expensive; the alternative is knowing how a frame travels from your code to the screen, and measuring where it stalls.
What a graphics API actually does

A graphics API is the contract between your program and the GPU driver. Your CPU code records commands: bind a pipeline, bind resources, set a viewport, draw N triangles. The driver translates them into hardware-specific packets, and the GPU executes them asynchronously, a frame or more behind (the CPU-GPU pipelining described in The GPU and the Rendering Pipeline). What differs between APIs is how much of that translation the driver does for you, and at what CPU cost.

items: **OpenGL / OpenGL ES**: a global state machine with implicit synchronisation. Easy to start, but the driver does a lot of hidden work (validation, state tracking, memory management), with high and unpredictable CPU cost, and it is effectively single-threaded. OpenGL ES remains on older Android devices; on Apple platforms it is deprecated.

**Direct3D 12**: Windows and Xbox. Explicit: you create pipeline state objects (PSOs), manage memory and resource states, record command lists on many threads and submit them to queues. Lower driver overhead and better multicore scaling, at the cost of more code and more ways to be wrong.

**Vulkan**: the cross-platform explicit API (Android, Windows, Linux). Similar philosophy to D3D12, with render passes and subpasses that map well to tile-based GPUs, and explicit synchronisation through barriers and semaphores.
**Metal**: Apple's explicit API for iOS, macOS and tvOS. Lower overhead than OpenGL and a tighter hardware fit than Vulkan on Apple GPUs, including direct access to tile memory features.
**Direct3D 11**: an older, implicit API still widely used for compatibility, sitting between OpenGL and D3D12 in driver overhead.

lesson.text: Engines hide these behind a **render hardware interface** (RHI). That is why you rarely write API calls yourself, yet it still matters which one runs: some features, shader compilation behaviour and bugs differ per backend, and your profiling tools depend on it.
Command buffers, batching and instancing

In explicit APIs you record **command buffers** (command lists) ahead of time and submit them to a queue. Recording is cheap and parallelisable, so several worker threads can each build commands for part of the scene, and submission is a single call. Each draw call still has a CPU cost: binding materials, updating constants, validating state. Typical budgets: a few thousand draw calls on mobile, a few thousand to tens of thousands on desktop, depending on API and engine. Exceed that and the CPU render thread, not the GPU, sets your frame time.

Reducing that CPU cost is the point of **batching**. Static batching merges meshes that share a material into one buffer; dynamic batching merges small meshes on the CPU each frame (cost grows with vertex count, so only worth it for tiny meshes). **GPU instancing** draws many copies of one mesh and material in a single call, with per-instance data (transform, colour) read from a buffer: 5000 trees or grass blades in one call. An SRP-batcher-style approach keeps per-material data resident in GPU buffers so changing material costs little, even if meshes differ. The rule: fewer state changes and fewer calls, not necessarily fewer triangles.

lesson.text: CPU-bound versus GPU-bound

The GPU and the Rendering Pipeline topic introduced the rule that frame time is the slower of CPU and GPU, and the half-resolution test. Here is how to apply them. If the GPU finishes in 9 ms and then idles in a 24 ms frame, you are **CPU-bound**: the GPU is starved by draw submission, scripts, culling, animation or physics, and lowering resolution will not help. If the CPU waits at present or on a fence for a GPU that needs 20 ms, you are **GPU-bound**, and the next question is which kind:

items: **Fill-rate / pixel-bound**: too many pixel shader invocations, from overdraw, expensive shaders, high resolution or post-processing. Fix: lower resolution, cheaper shaders, less overdraw, fewer full-screen passes.

**Vertex-bound**: too many vertices or expensive vertex work, for example high-poly characters with skinning or tessellation. Dense meshes also produce tiny triangles that waste fragment quad work. Fix: LODs, mesh simplification, culling.
**Bandwidth-bound**: too much memory traffic from large textures, uncompressed targets or many render target switches. Fix: compression, smaller formats, fewer passes.
**CPU-bound**: draw calls, state changes, scripts. Fix: batching, instancing, culling, jobs and multithreaded rendering.

lesson.caption: Frame time is the longer bar: a CPU-bound frame leaves the GPU idle, and a GPU-bound frame leaves the CPU waiting.

lesson.text: Tile-based mobile GPUs and bandwidth

Desktop GPUs are usually immediate-mode: they rasterise triangles in submission order, writing directly to a framebuffer in VRAM. Mobile GPUs (Apple, Arm Mali, Qualcomm Adreno, PowerVR) are mostly **tile-based**: they first process geometry to bin triangles into small screen tiles (for example 16x16 or 32x32 pixels), then shade one tile at a time in fast on-chip memory, and write the finished tile to system memory once. This slashes framebuffer bandwidth, which matters enormously because mobile memory access costs power and heat. A sustained thermal limit matters as much as peak speed: a device that hits 60 fps for 30 seconds and then throttles to 40 is a typical outcome of bandwidth-heavy rendering.

lesson.caption: Immediate-mode GPUs hit DRAM for every triangle; tile-based GPUs shade each tile on-chip and write it out once.

lesson.text: Consequences for you: avoid switching render targets mid-frame (it forces a tile flush to memory), avoid reading back the framebuffer, clear or discard targets you do not need to load (a 'load' of a full-screen target is a full read), skip unnecessary full-screen post passes (each is a round trip through memory), and keep MSAA resolves on-chip when the API supports it. Opaque-heavy rendering benefits from the hardware's hidden-surface removal on some GPUs, while alpha-tested and blended content defeats it.
GPU capture tools

Guessing ends with a **frame capture**. **RenderDoc** (free, for Direct3D 11/12, Vulkan, OpenGL) records every API call in one frame and lets you step through draws, inspect bound textures, render targets, shader inputs, meshes and pipeline state. It answers 'why is this object black?' and 'why is this pass drawing 3000 times?'. **Xcode's GPU debugger** and Metal frame capture do the same on Apple hardware, adding per-draw timing, bandwidth and shader cost counters. Vendor tools (Arm Streamline, Snapdragon Profiler, NVIDIA Nsight, AMD Radeon GPU Profiler) provide hardware counters that say whether the limit is ALU, texture, bandwidth or memory. Engine-level tools such as Unity's Frame Debugger and the Profiler's timeline show CPU render thread time and draw sequencing.

Measure the right quantity: GPU time per pass (not the whole frame), draw call count, SetPass or state-change count, and overdraw. Profile on the weakest target device in a release-like build; editor numbers are not representative.

Agents love confident optimisation advice without measurement: 'combine meshes', 'lower shadow resolution', 'use async compute'. Give the agent concrete evidence: frame time, whether CPU or GPU is the long pole, capture excerpts, draw call counts. Ask it to state what number should move if its change works, then verify by profiling before and after on the target device. Be sceptical of generated low-level API code (barriers, synchronisation) that cannot be validated without debug layers such as the Vulkan validation layers or D3D12 debug layer.

A worked example: the phone scene at 38 fps shows GPU time 24 ms at 1080p. Rendering at 720p gives 14 ms: strongly resolution-dependent, so fill rate. A capture shows a 4-layer full-screen fog particle effect and three full-screen post-process passes. Removing two passes and shrinking fog quads recovers 10 ms. No texture or mesh change was needed, and nothing was guessed.

patterns.signal: The frame is GPU-bound and you need to know whether pixel work is the cause
patterns.why: Halve the render resolution: a big drop means fragment or fill-rate bound. Almost no change points at vertex work, CPU submission or fixed-cost passes.

patterns.signal: Halving resolution barely helps a GPU-bound frame that is full of dense meshes
patterns.use: Cut vertex work: LODs, culling, simpler skinning
patterns.why: Vertex cost does not scale with resolution. Confirm in a capture that the vertex stage is busy before reducing triangle counts or skinned bone influences.

patterns.signal: Thousands of copies of the same mesh and material are drawn as separate draw calls and the render thread is busy
patterns.why: One draw submits many copies with per-instance data in a buffer, cutting CPU submission cost. Needs the same mesh and material; per-instance variation must go through instance data.

patterns.signal: Many different static meshes share a few materials and the CPU spends its time on draw submission
patterns.use: Batch and sort draws by state
patterns.why: Combine static meshes or sort draws by shader, then material, so state changes are rare. Static batching costs memory and coarsens culling; state changes cost more than triangles.

patterns.signal: The render thread is pegged on one core while other cores sit idle, on an explicit API
patterns.why: D3D12, Vulkan and Metal let several threads record command buffers in parallel. Requires explicit sync and resource-state tracking; the engine usually exposes it as a setting.

patterns.signal: A mobile game starts at 60 fps, drops to 40 after a minute and the device heats up
patterns.use: Profile sustained performance and cap frame rate
patterns.why: Thermal throttling cuts clocks after the device heats. Test over many minutes, budget below peak, and use a lower frame-rate cap or fewer passes to save power.

patterns.signal: A mobile GPU timeline shows many full-screen passes that read and write the same render targets
patterns.use: Keep render passes merged on tile GPUs
patterns.why: Each pass switch flushes tile memory to DRAM and reloads it. Merge passes, use subpasses or framebuffer fetch, and avoid mid-frame target switches; bandwidth is the scarce resource.

patterns.signal: Each render pass on mobile loads the previous target contents and stores depth that is never read again
patterns.why: Loading and storing whole attachments costs bandwidth on tile GPUs. Clear or discard on load, discard depth and MSAA samples on store, using memoryless attachments where possible.

patterns.signal: A character renders black on one device only, and frame timings do not explain it
patterns.use: Frame capture in RenderDoc or Xcode
patterns.why: A capture shows each draw's bound shaders, textures, constants and render state, so you can see the wrong input. It costs capture overhead and shows one frame, not trends.

keyPoints: The CPU records commands and the GPU executes them asynchronously; frame time is set by whichever side is the long pole.
Explicit APIs (D3D12, Vulkan, Metal) cut driver overhead and allow multithreaded command recording at the cost of complexity.
Reduce draw call CPU cost with batching and instancing; fewer state changes matter more than fewer triangles.
Diagnose first: CPU-bound vs GPU-bound, then fill-rate, vertex or bandwidth. Halving the resolution is a quick test for pixel-bound.
Tile-based mobile GPUs make bandwidth the scarce resource, so avoid render target switches and extra full-screen passes; confirm with captures in RenderDoc or Xcode.

quiz.q: Frame time is 25 ms. The profiler shows the main thread and render thread busy for 24 ms while the GPU finishes its work in 8 ms. Which action is most likely to help?
options: Lower the render resolution to 720p
Compress the textures to ASTC
Reduce draw calls through batching or instancing
Switch the post-process chain to half-resolution targets
quiz.explain: The CPU is the long pole, with the GPU idle for much of the frame. Draw submission cost falls with batching and instancing. Resolution, texture compression and post-process size reduce GPU work, which is not the bottleneck.

quiz.q: You halve the render resolution in a GPU-bound scene and frame time barely changes: 21 ms drops to 20 ms. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: Fill rate from expensive pixel shaders
Vertex work or another resolution-independent cost
Anisotropic filtering cost on ground textures
Overdraw from full-screen particle effects
quiz.explain: Pixel-bound problems scale with pixel count, so a 4x pixel reduction would cut time sharply. A flat result points to work independent of resolution, such as vertex cost. Fill rate, particle overdraw and anisotropy are all resolution-dependent.

quiz.q: A mobile game hits 60 fps for a minute, then drops to 40 and the device gets hot. The GPU timeline shows many full-screen passes reading and writing the same render targets. What is the best explanation and fix?
options: Vertex count is too high, so use LODs for the characters
The CPU is throttling, so reduce scripts per frame
The shader compiler is stalling, so prewarm the shaders
Bandwidth drives heat, so merge passes and avoid target switches
quiz.explain: On tile-based GPUs each full-screen pass round-trips through system memory, and bandwidth costs power and heat that eventually trigger throttling. Merging passes keeps work on-chip. The evidence points at bandwidth, not vertices, CPU or shader compilation.

quiz.q: A forest of 8000 identical trees is drawn as 8000 separate draw calls, each with the same mesh and material, and the CPU render thread takes 14 ms. Which change should lower that cost most?
options: Draw them with GPU instancing using per-instance transforms
Halve the vertex count of the tree mesh with a lower LOD
Reduce the shadow map resolution for the sun
Switch the trees' textures to a smaller atlas
quiz.explain: The cost is CPU submission per draw call. Instancing renders all copies in a few calls with identical state. A lower-poly mesh or smaller shadow map reduces GPU work, and an atlas does not change the number of calls.

quiz.q: A frame capture in RenderDoc shows that a character renders black on one device but not another. What does the capture let you do that profiler timing alone cannot?
options: Measure total frame time with more precision than a profiler
Count the scripts running on the main thread each frame
See how long the CPU spent submitting that draw
Inspect the draw's bound textures and shader inputs
quiz.explain: A capture records the API calls and resource state of one frame so you can step to the draw and see what was bound. Timing tools show how long things took, not what data the draw used. Submission timing and script counts are profiler questions, and neither explains wrong output.

quiz.q: A mobile GPU capture shows every render pass starting with a full load of the previous colour target and ending by storing a depth buffer nobody reads again. Bandwidth is the bottleneck. What should you reach for?
options: Run a resolution-scale test to confirm the pixel cost first of all
Switch the repeated meshes over to GPU instancing here
Cap the frame rate to limit sustained heat on the device
Use clear or don't-care load and store actions on those targets
quiz.explain: On tile-based GPUs, an unneeded load or store moves whole targets through main memory. Clear or don't-care actions skip that traffic. Instancing cuts draw calls, not bandwidth, and a frame cap treats heat, not these transfers.

exam.q: Your game drops to 40 fps on a mid-range phone. The profiler shows the main thread at 9 ms and the GPU at 25 ms, and a 70 percent resolution scale brings GPU time down to 14 ms. A teammate proposes merging meshes to cut draw calls. What should you do instead?
options: Merge the meshes anyway, since fewer draw calls also shorten GPU time
Move gameplay scripts to jobs so the main thread finishes sooner
Target pixel cost: overdraw, full-screen passes and shader complexity
Raise anisotropic filtering so fewer mip levels need to be sampled
exam.explain: The GPU is the long pole and its time scales with resolution, so the cost is pixel work. Draw-call merging and job scheduling reduce CPU time, which is not the limiter, and anisotropy adds texture work rather than removing it.

exam.q: To stop a first-person weapon clipping into walls, a programmer sets the camera near plane to 0.001. Windows on distant buildings now z-fight with their walls. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the far plane so the depth range is spread wider
Restore near to about 0.1 and draw the weapon with a separate camera
Switch the main camera to orthographic for the distant buildings
Turn off early-Z so the windows are shaded before the walls
exam.explain: Depth resolution is roughly proportional to the near distance, so a 100x smaller near plane makes distant precision about 100x worse. A separate weapon camera keeps the close-up case without wrecking the main camera's depth. A larger far plane barely affects precision, and early-Z or orthographic tricks do not address it.

exam.q: A RenderDoc capture shows NaN positions for a few vertices of a mesh. The vertex shader normalizes the vector from each vertex to a point light and uses the result in a displacement. What is the likely cause?
options: A vertex sits exactly at the light, so a zero-length vector is normalized
Mobile GPUs cannot run the normalize intrinsic inside vertex shaders
The mesh's UVs exceed 1.0, so the sampler wraps them to NaN values
The light position is uploaded with a row-major constant buffer layout
exam.explain: Normalizing a zero-length vector divides by zero and produces NaN, which then propagates through every later calculation. normalize works in every stage, wrapped UVs do not create NaNs, and a layout mismatch gives wrong values rather than NaNs only at specific vertices.

exam.q: Your VR title uses deferred rendering. Testers complain about jagged edges, and TAA causes ghosting they find uncomfortable. Which change gives clean geometry edges without temporal history?
options: Switch to forward or forward+ and enable 4x MSAA
Raise anisotropic filtering to 16x on all materials
Increase the shadow cascade count from two to four
Render at 67 percent and apply a temporal upscaler
exam.explain: MSAA resolves geometry edges within a single frame and works naturally with forward paths, which is why forward is common in VR. Hardware MSAA does not fit a G-buffer, anisotropy and cascades do not touch edge aliasing, and an upscaler is temporal and can ghost too.

exam.q: On a tile-based mobile GPU, a custom render pass copies the camera colour target to a texture in the middle of the opaque pass, then rendering continues. GPU time rises by 3 ms although almost no shading was added. Why?
options: The copy compiles a new shader variant on every frame
Ending and restarting the pass stores tiles to memory and reloads them
The copy disables early depth testing for the rest of the frame
The copy forces the CPU to wait for the GPU on every frame
exam.explain: Tile-based GPUs keep colour and depth on chip until a pass ends. Breaking the pass forces a full store to system memory and a reload afterwards, which is pure bandwidth cost. A GPU-side copy does not compile variants, disable early-Z or block the CPU.

exam.q: Two points in view space have the same horizontal offset of 4 m, one at depth 20 m and one at depth 40 m. With a perspective camera, how do their horizontal NDC positions compare?
options: They are identical, since x does not depend on depth
The far point lies twice as far from the screen centre
The far point lies a quarter as far from the centre
The far point lies half as far from the screen centre
exam.explain: The projection puts view depth in w, and dividing x by w makes NDC x proportional to x divided by depth. Doubling the depth therefore halves the distance from the centre. That divide is perspective foreshortening.

exam.q: An artist imports a roughness map with the sRGB option on. In game, surfaces with mid-range roughness look glossier than in the authoring tool. What happened?
options: The sRGB decode lowered mid-range values, so roughness reads too low
The sRGB decode raised mid-range values, so roughness reads too high
Block compression removed high-frequency detail from the roughness
Trilinear filtering averaged roughness across adjacent mip levels
exam.explain: Decoding sRGB to linear maps a stored 0.5 to about 0.21, so the shader sees lower roughness and renders sharper highlights. Roughness is data and must be imported as linear. Compression and filtering soften detail but do not shift mid-range values systematically.

exam.q: A temporal upscaler smears a running character's limbs while the static background looks sharp. Which input most likely needs fixing?
options: The per-tile light lists built for forward+ shading
The shadow map resolution of each sun cascade
Per-pixel motion vectors that include skinned motion
The UI layer, which must be drawn before upscaling
exam.explain: Upscalers reproject history using motion vectors, so anything whose motion is missing from them, such as skinned limbs, smears. Light lists and shadow resolution do not feed the upscaler, and UI should be composited after upscaling, not before.

exam.q: A flight model stores an aircraft's orientation as three Euler angles and adds roll, pitch and yaw rates to them every frame. During a vertical climb the controls start fighting each other. What fixes the root cause?
options: Clamp pitch to plus or minus 89 degrees in the flight model
Integrate angular velocity into a quaternion and renormalize it
Convert the angles to radians before integrating the rates
Switch the transform code to a row-vector matrix convention
exam.explain: At 90 degrees of pitch the Euler representation hits gimbal lock and loses a degree of freedom. Storing orientation as a quaternion has no singularity. Clamping hides the symptom and forbids loops, while units and matrix convention do not change the parametrization.

exam.q: Why does deferred shading make hundreds of small point lights affordable where classic forward rendering struggles?
options: It skips the depth buffer and saves one memory write per pixel
It evaluates lighting per vertex instead of per covered pixel
It bakes every point light into lightmaps when the level loads
Each light is evaluated only for the visible pixels it covers
exam.explain: Deferred writes surface attributes once, then each light shades only the screen pixels it touches, with no wasted work on overdrawn fragments. It still uses depth, lights per pixel and works with fully dynamic lights.

exam.q: QA reports that the first time a player enters the boss arena the game hitches for 250 ms. Replaying the level does not hitch, but the hitch returns after the app is reinstalled. Which explanation fits best?
options: Garbage collection of the previous level's managed objects
Texture streaming loading the boss's highest mip level
Pipeline states for new shader variants compiled and cached
The boss mesh exceeding the size of the post-transform cache
exam.explain: A hitch that appears once, disappears while a cache survives and returns when the cache is wiped is the signature of shader or PSO compilation. Garbage collection and streaming would recur regardless of reinstalling, and the vertex cache causes no hitches.

exam.q: Why are transparent surfaces usually drawn with depth testing on but depth writing off?
options: Depth writes cannot be enabled while blending is active
It lets the GPU sort transparent triangles automatically
It keeps the depth buffer valid for shadow map rendering
Opaques still hide them, but they never cull other transparents
exam.explain: Testing against depth lets opaque geometry in front occlude the glass or smoke, while not writing depth stops one transparent layer from rejecting another behind it when sort order is imperfect. Blending and depth writes can coexist, and the GPU never sorts for you.

exam.q: A handheld console build drops to 40 fps during a rainstorm. The GPU profiler shows the rain particle pass at 9 ms; the particles use a soft-particle shader that reads the depth texture, and several layers cover most of the screen. What is the most effective change?
options: Merge all the rain emitters into one instanced draw call
Render the rain at half resolution with fewer, larger layers
Switch the rain textures to an uncompressed RGBA format
Add more shadow cascades so the rain is lit consistently
exam.explain: The cost is transparent overdraw: every layer is shaded and blended over most of the screen. Half resolution cuts shaded pixels by about 4x and fewer layers cut overdraw. Draw-call merging helps the CPU, uncompressed textures add bandwidth, and cascades add work.

exam.q: A 4096x4096 texture is imported as uncompressed RGBA8 with a full mip chain. Roughly how much GPU memory does it use?
options: About 64 MB
About 48 MB
About 128 MB
About 85 MB
exam.explain: Mip 0 is 4096 x 4096 x 4 bytes = 64 MB, and a full chain adds about one third, giving about 85 MB. Block compression such as BC7 or ASTC 4x4 would cut that by 4x.

exam.q: A designer reports that a door now swings around the middle of the level instead of its hinge after a refactor. In this column-vector engine the new code builds the door's matrix as R * T. What is wrong?
options: The rotation matrix has to be transposed before it is used
The door must use quaternions instead of rotation matrices
Translation is applied first, so the rotation orbits the origin
Non-uniform scale on the door skews the rotation axis
exam.explain: Column-vector chains apply right to left, so R * T moves the door away first and then rotates that offset about the world origin. T * R rotates the door in place and then positions it. Transposing or switching to quaternions keeps the wrong order.

exam.q: In a custom renderer with a fixed constant depth bias, the sun's shadow distance is raised from 50 m to 300 m with the same cascade count and resolution. Shadow acne stripes now cover a large flat floor. Why?
options: The main camera's far plane is now closer than the shadows
Larger shadow texels mean the existing bias is now too small
The baked lightmaps were invalidated by the longer distance
The floor's normal map is now sampled as sRGB colour data
exam.explain: Spreading the same shadow map over six times the distance makes each texel cover far more ground, so the depth error across one texel grows beyond the fixed bias and surfaces self-shadow. Scaling bias with texel size, as many engines do, or adding cascades fixes it.

exam.q: A mesh exported from a tool with counter-clockwise front faces is imported into an engine that treats clockwise as front and culls back faces. It looks inside-out. Which fix is correct?
options: Recalculate the normals, since the stored normals decide which side is culled
Swap two indices in every triangle at import, leaving the stored normals as they are
Convert the mesh from a triangle list to triangle strips so the order is consistent
Set every material to double-sided rendering and accept the extra fill cost
exam.explain: Culling depends on the index order, not on the normals. Swapping two indices per triangle reverses the winding and makes the outside the front face, while the normals were already pointing outward. Double-sided materials hide the symptom but cost extra pixels and break lighting on the back faces.

exam.q: A 50,000-vertex prop stores position float32 x3, normal float32 x3, tangent float32 x4 and UV0 float32 x2 (48 bytes). You want to halve its memory with the least visible risk. Which change does that?
options: Store positions and UV0 as float16 and leave everything else as it is
Quantise everything to 8-bit normalized values relative to the origin
Drop the tangent and rebuild it in the fragment shader from the normal alone
Pack normal and tangent as snorm8 and UV0 as unorm16, keeping float32 positions
exam.explain: 12 + 4 + 4 + 4 gives a 24-byte stride, exactly half, and 8-bit unit vectors and 16-bit UVs lose almost nothing visible. Half-float positions and UVs lose precision away from the origin or on tiled textures, and a tangent cannot be rebuilt from the normal alone because it depends on the UV layout.

exam.q: A flat water plane is displaced up to 6 m by a vertex-shader wave function. When the camera looks so the undisplaced plane is just outside the view, wave crests that should be visible vanish and pop back in. What is the cause?
options: Culling uses bounds from the undisplaced vertices, so they must be enlarged to cover the waves
The depth buffer is too coarse in the distance, so the near plane should be raised
The mesh is using 16-bit indices, so far vertices wrap to the wrong positions
The vertex cache is thrashing, so the index buffer should be reordered
exam.explain: Frustum culling uses the mesh bounds, which come from the stored vertex positions rather than the shader's output. Displaced vertices can be on screen while the rest-pose box is not. Widening the bounds fixes it; depth precision, index width and cache order do not cause popping at the screen edge.

exam.q: Put the stages of the GPU rasterisation pipeline in the order a triangle passes through them.
steps: Input assembly: fetch vertices and indices, form primitives
Vertex stage: transform each vertex to clip space
Primitive assembly, clipping and back-face culling
Rasterization: find covered pixels and generate fragments
Fragment stage: sample textures and compute lighting
Output merger: depth/stencil test, blend and write
exam.explain: Vertices are fetched, then shaded to clip space. Only then can triangles be clipped against the frustum and culled by winding, because both need projected positions. The rasteriser turns surviving triangles into fragments, the fragment shader colours them, and the output merger (ROP) depth-tests, blends and writes them.

exam.q: Order the coordinate spaces a vertex position moves through, from the vertex buffer to a pixel on screen.
steps: Object space, as stored in the vertex buffer
World space, after the model matrix
View space, after the view matrix
Clip space, after the projection matrix
NDC, after the perspective divide by `w`
Screen space, after the viewport transform
exam.explain: The model matrix takes object space to world space, the view matrix (the inverse of the camera's world matrix) to view space, and the projection matrix to clip space, which the vertex shader outputs. The hardware divides by `w` to get NDC and the viewport transform maps NDC to pixels.

exam.q: An import pipeline runs meshoptimizer on every mesh. In what order should these passes run?
steps: `meshopt_optimizeVertexCache`: reorder triangles for post-transform cache reuse
`meshopt_optimizeOverdraw`: reorder triangle groups roughly front to back
`meshopt_optimizeVertexFetch`: renumber vertices in first-use order
exam.explain: Cache optimisation sets the triangle order; the overdraw pass then reorders clusters, trading a little cache efficiency for better early-Z rejection; vertex fetch runs last because it renumbers vertices to match the final index order, so memory reads are sequential. Running fetch first would be undone by the later reorders.

exam.q: This fragment shader produces lighting that is too dark in the middle of large triangles. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 3 uses the interpolated normal as is. Interpolating between unit-length vertex normals gives a shorter vector inside the triangle, so `dot(n, l)` is too small there. Fix: `float3 n = normalize(i.nrmW);`.

exam.q: Every object drawn with this vertex shader ignores its position and stays at a fixed offset from the camera, following it like a skybox, though rotation and scale are right. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 4 builds the position with `w = 0`, which marks it as a direction, so the translation column of every matrix it passes through is ignored: the model's and the view's. The object is placed as if it and the camera both sat at the origin, so it moves with the camera. A point needs `w = 1`: `mul(_Model, float4(i.pos, 1.0))`. The clip-space `w` then also comes out wrong, breaking perspective.

exam.q: This procedural terrain never appears: Unity logs an error when the vertices are assigned and the mesh comes out empty. Click the line with the bug.
exam.explain: Line 7 picks 16-bit indices, which address at most 65,535 vertices, but the grid has 90,000. Unity rejects the vertex array with an error, and the triangle assignment after it fails too, leaving an empty mesh. Fix: `mesh.indexFormat = IndexFormat.UInt32;` before assigning the data.

exam.q: What does this log?
exam.explain: `MultiplyPoint` treats the input as a point (`w = 1`), so it picks up the translation: `p.x = 6`. `MultiplyVector` treats it as a direction (`w = 0`) and ignores translation: `d.x = 1`. The sum is 7.

exam.q: How many shader variants does this pass compile, ignoring stripping?
exam.code:
#pragma multi_compile _ FOG_ON
#pragma multi_compile _ NORMALMAP_ON
#pragma multi_compile _ SHADOWS_SOFT
#pragma multi_compile QUALITY_LOW QUALITY_MED QUALITY_HIGH
exam.explain: Each `multi_compile` line is an independent keyword group and the variant count is the product of the group sizes: 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 = 24. Adding the group sizes (9) is the common mistake; this multiplication is why keyword counts explode.

title: Game Engines
tagline: The loop, the data and the systems every engine is built from.
intro: Every engine, from a hand-rolled C++ loop to Unity or Unreal, is built from the same handful of systems: a loop that spends a fixed time budget, data laid out for the cache, spatial structures that skip work, and simulation, animation, AI, audio and networking that run inside that budget. The last two topics follow a real bug hunt and a real frame-rate investigation through a shipped game, using those systems to find and fix what went wrong. Knowing how these systems work is what lets you read a profiler capture, choose the right tool for a problem and judge whether code an agent wrote will hold up at 60 fps on real hardware.

topics.title: The game loop and time
topics.summary: How a game turns input, simulation and rendering into a steady stream of frames, and why time handling decides whether it feels smooth.

lesson.text: A shipped mobile racing game plays perfectly on the developer's laptop at 240 fps. On a mid-range phone locked to 60 Hz, cars drive through walls, jump physics feels floaty, and a replay recorded on one device desyncs on another. Nothing is wrong with the track or the car. The bug is in how the game measures and spends time. The **game loop** is the small piece of code at the heart of every engine that decides when to read input, when to advance the simulation, and when to draw.
The minimal loop and the frame budget

Strip away the engine and every game is this: repeat forever { read input; update the world; render; present }. One pass is a **frame**. Unlike a web page or a business app, a game does not wait for events. It keeps producing frames whether or not anything happened, because the world (animation, AI, particles) is always moving.

The key number is the **frame budget**: the time one frame may take. At 60 fps it is 1000 / 60 = 16.6 ms. At 30 fps it is 33.3 ms, at 120 fps it is 8.3 ms, and a 144 Hz monitor leaves 6.9 ms. Everything must fit: input, gameplay scripts, animation, physics, culling, command building for the GPU, audio mixing and engine overhead on the CPU, plus the GPU's own work, which runs in parallel but also has to finish inside the budget. Miss it by one millisecond and a frame is shown twice, which the player perceives as a hitch. Budgets are always spoken about in milliseconds, never in fps, because milliseconds add up and fps do not: going from 60 to 55 fps costs 1.5 ms, while going from 30 to 25 fps costs 6.7 ms.

lesson.text: Update and render are separate concerns

A common beginner design ties them together: one function moves the player by a fixed amount, then draws. This makes game speed depend on frame rate. Two corrections exist. The first is to multiply movement by **delta time** (`dt`, the seconds since the previous frame): `position += velocity * dt`. This is the **variable timestep**. It is simple, and fine for animation, camera, UI and most gameplay motion.

Variable timestep has real problems for simulation. Integration error grows with `dt`, so the same jump reaches a different height at 30 fps and at 144 fps. Stacked physics becomes unstable when a big `dt` arrives after a hitch. A one-second stall (debugger break, app resumed from background) produces one `dt` of 1.0 s and every fast object teleports. And nothing is reproducible, because the sequence of `dt` values differs on every run.
Fixed timestep and the accumulator

The fix is to simulate in constant steps, for example 1/50 s or 1/60 s, and decouple that from how often you render. The standard implementation is the **accumulator pattern** (popularised by Glenn Fiedler's article 'Fix Your Timestep'). Real elapsed time is added to a bucket; the simulation drains the bucket in fixed chunks; whatever is left over is the fraction of a step the renderer should interpolate.

Three details matter. First, the **clamp** on `frameTime` (0.25 s here) prevents the **spiral of death**: if a simulation step costs more than its step length, each frame owes more steps than it can pay and the game never catches up. Capping the debt means the game slows down instead of freezing. Second, **interpolation**: rendering is almost never aligned with a simulation tick, so drawing the latest state makes motion judder (a 60 Hz sim shown on a 144 Hz display repeats positions unevenly). Blending the previous and current states by `alpha` makes motion smooth at the cost of showing the world one tick in the past. Third, **extrapolation** (predicting forward instead) avoids the delay but overshoots when things change direction, so most engines interpolate.

items: Run in fixed steps: physics, character controllers that need stability, networked or replayed gameplay, deterministic AI ticks.
Run per rendered frame with variable dt: camera, animation sampling, UI, audio fades, visual-only effects.
Read input once per frame, but apply it inside the fixed step; otherwise two ticks in one frame may both consume the same press, or a press between ticks may be lost.
Never store gameplay-critical timers as frame counts unless the step is fixed.

lesson.text: Vsync, swap chains and frame pacing

Displays refresh at fixed intervals. If you present a frame while the display is mid-scan you get **tearing**, so with **vsync** the GPU waits for the next refresh. The swap chain holds a small queue of buffers (double or triple buffering). With vsync on a 60 Hz display, a frame that takes 17 ms instead of 16.6 ms misses its slot and is shown for two refreshes, so effective output drops to 30 fps for that frame. Average fps hides this: a game at 'average 58 fps' can feel terrible if every few frames one takes 33 ms instead of 16 ms.
