lesson.text: **Frame pacing** is about the evenness of frame delivery, not the average. Stutter is judged by the 1% low or by the frame-time graph, not by fps. Variable refresh rate (G-Sync, FreeSync, ProMotion) lets the display wait for the frame, which tolerates fluctuation. Mobile platforms add their own pacing libraries (Android Frame Pacing, Apple's CADisplayLink) so the engine can target a consistent 30 or 60 instead of oscillating. Capping to 30 deliberately on mobile for thermal reasons is often better than an uncapped 45 that bounces.
CPU-bound, GPU-bound and the pipeline

The CPU prepares frame N+1 while the GPU draws frame N, so the frame rate is set by the slower of the two stages, plus latency from queued frames. If the CPU takes 14 ms and the GPU 9 ms, you are CPU-bound at about 14 ms and lowering resolution does nothing. If the GPU takes 20 ms, you are GPU-bound and cutting scripts does nothing. Always find out which side is the bottleneck before optimising, using a profiler rather than guessing.

Do not 'fix' a frame spike by lowering the fixed step length. A smaller step means more simulation steps per frame, which raises CPU cost and can start the spiral of death. Change the step only for accuracy reasons, and measure steps-per-frame.

items: Misconception: delta time makes a game frame-rate independent. It makes motion roughly independent, but not collisions, jump heights, or determinism.
Misconception: uncapped fps is always better. It burns battery, heats mobile devices and can expose bugs that only appear at extreme dt values.
Pitfall: `Time.deltaTime` style values are often smoothed or clamped by the engine; do not assume they equal the raw measured interval.
Pitfall: loading a level inside a frame produces a single dt of several seconds; clamp or reset the clock after a load.

lesson.text: AI agents love to write `transform.position += direction * speed` with no time term, or to apply forces in the per-frame update because that is where tutorials put it. Tell the agent which code path runs at which rate (fixed vs per-frame) and ask it to state the units of every time value. Verify by running the game at 30, 60 and 144 fps (or with a forced frame cap) and checking that jump height, travel distance and timers match. Agents also rarely add the clamp that prevents the spiral of death.

The loop is where every later topic plugs in: physics runs in the fixed part, rendering and culling in the variable part, and entity architecture decides how cheaply you can iterate thousands of objects inside the 16.6 ms you have.

patterns.signal: Physics or jump height changes with frame rate; a replay recorded at 144 fps desyncs when played at 60 fps
patterns.why: Simulation advances in constant `dt` steps drained from accumulated frame time, so results stop depending on fps. Costs several steps on slow frames and needs render interpolation to look smooth.

patterns.signal: Motion judders on a 144 Hz display although the 60 Hz simulation itself is smooth
patterns.why: Draw `lerp(previous, current, accumulator / dt)` so rendering samples a continuous path. Adds up to one step of visual latency; extrapolation avoids that but mispredicts on sudden turns.

patterns.signal: After a stall or app resume the game freezes for seconds while it runs hundreds of catch-up steps
patterns.why: Cap the time fed to the accumulator (for example 0.25 s) and drop the rest. The game briefly runs slower than real time instead of locking up; lockstep games must handle the dropped time explicitly.

patterns.signal: Average fps looks fine but players report stutter; the frame-time graph shows 33.3 ms spikes among 16.6 ms frames
patterns.why: With vsync a frame that misses its slot costs a whole refresh, so evenness matters more than the mean. Budget in ms, find the spike's cause, or lock to a lower rate that you can always hit.

patterns.signal: A frame is slow and someone wants to optimise shaders, but nobody knows which processor is the bottleneck
patterns.why: Frame time is set by the slower of CPU and GPU, which run in parallel. Halving GPU cost on a CPU-bound frame gains nothing; check main-thread time against GPU time in the profiler first.

patterns.signal: Thousands of objects each need a little behaviour every frame and the profiler shows a huge count of tiny Update calls
patterns.use: Update Method via one manager loop
patterns.why: Giving each object an `Update(dt)` is the Update Method pattern; driving them from one manager over an array removes per-call engine overhead and fixes the order. Lose the convenience of per-object callbacks.

patterns.signal: Objects updated earlier in a frame see neighbours' new state while later ones see old state, so results depend on order
patterns.why: Read from the current state and write to a next buffer, then swap once all updates finish. Every object sees a consistent snapshot. Doubles memory for that state and adds one step of latency.

patterns.signal: Gameplay code calls audio or VFX directly and a burst of events causes spikes or reentrancy bugs mid-update
patterns.why: Push events into a queue and process them at a fixed point in the frame, decoupling sender and receiver in time and allowing merging or throttling. Receivers may act on stale state; guard against feedback loops.

patterns.signal: A pause menu sets the time scale to 0 and its own animations and timers freeze as well
patterns.why: Gameplay reads scaled time (pause, slow motion, hit-stop); UI, audio fades and network timeouts read real time. Mixing them breaks pause and makes timeouts fire wrongly during slow motion.

keyPoints: Frame budget is 1000 / fps in ms: 16.6 at 60, 8.3 at 120. Think and measure in milliseconds, not fps.
Variable dt is fine for visuals; simulation wants a fixed step driven by an accumulator, with the leftover fraction used to interpolate rendering.
Clamp the frame time fed to the accumulator, or one hitch causes a spiral of death.
Smoothness is frame pacing (evenness, 1% lows), not average fps; a missed vsync slot costs a whole refresh.
The slower of CPU and GPU sets frame time; identify the bound side before optimising.

quiz.q: A game targets 120 Hz. Profiling shows 7.9 ms of CPU work and 9.4 ms of GPU work per frame. What happens, and what is the right first move?
options: It holds 120 fps because the CPU fits; reduce nothing.
It is GPU-bound and misses 8.3 ms; reduce GPU work such as resolution or shading cost.
It is CPU-bound; move gameplay code onto worker threads to recover time.
It runs at 120 fps because CPU and GPU times add up to under 17 ms.
quiz.explain: The CPU and GPU overlap, so the slower stage (9.4 ms) sets frame time, exceeding the 8.3 ms budget. Optimising the CPU, which already fits, would not change the result.

quiz.q: Why does an accumulator-based fixed timestep interpolate between the previous and current simulation states when rendering?
options: Because the physics solver needs interpolated states in order to remain stable across steps.
Because render frames land between ticks, so drawing the latest tick alone makes motion judder.
Because interpolation allows the simulation itself to run fewer steps per second overall.
Because the GPU cannot read any state that the CPU wrote during the current tick.
quiz.explain: Render and simulation rates do not align, so the leftover accumulator fraction is the position between ticks. Interpolation only affects what is drawn, never the simulation itself.

quiz.q: After a 3-second stall (the app was backgrounded), a game with a fixed 1/60 s step and no clamp becomes unresponsive for several seconds. Which change fixes it?
options: Shorten the fixed step so each iteration is cheaper.
Switch the whole game to a variable timestep.
Cap the frame time added to the accumulator, for example at 0.25 s.
Enable vsync so the stall is absorbed by the swap chain.
quiz.explain: Without a cap the loop owes 180 steps and if each costs more than its step length it never catches up. A smaller step makes the debt larger, and vsync does not affect simulation catch-up.

quiz.q: A 60 Hz game with vsync averages 55 fps but players report stutter. The frame-time graph shows mostly 16.6 ms frames with frequent 33.3 ms spikes. What explains this?
options: Some frames miss a vsync slot and stay on screen for two refreshes, which makes pacing uneven.
The average fps is below the refresh rate, which stops vsync from functioning correctly.
The fixed timestep is running too many simulation steps on every rendered frame.
Tearing appears because vsync switches itself off at random whenever the load rises.
quiz.explain: A frame finishing just after a refresh waits for the next one, doubling its on-screen time. The average hides the unevenness, which is why frame-time graphs and 1% lows matter.

quiz.q: A character jumps 2.1 m high at 60 fps but 2.4 m at 144 fps. The jump is integrated each rendered frame with `velocity += gravity * dt`. What is the best fix?
options: Multiply gravity by a tuned constant for high refresh rates.
Cap the game at 60 fps on all devices.
Interpolate the character's rendered position more aggressively.
Integrate the jump in a fixed-step update so the same dt is used every tick.
quiz.explain: Explicit integration error depends on dt, so different frame rates give different trajectories. Fixed steps remove that dependency; capping fps or tuning constants hides the symptom on only some devices.

quiz.q: A bullet-hell scene has 20,000 bullets, each a script with its own `Update`. The profiler shows the frame dominated by tiny per-object calls, not by the work inside them. Which approach fits best?
options: A fixed timestep driven by a time accumulator
One manager that loops over an array of bullet data
A double buffer holding the bullet states per frame
An event queue handling the bullet spawn requests
quiz.explain: A single update loop over contiguous data removes per-object call overhead and engine dispatch. A fixed timestep fixes frame-rate dependence and double buffering fixes update-order bias, neither of which reduces call count.

topics.title: Entity architecture: components to ECS
topics.summary: How engines organise game objects, from inheritance trees to components to data-oriented ECS, and what memory layout has to do with it.

lesson.text: A designer asks for a flying explosive barrel that can be picked up, shot, and ridden. In a classic object-oriented design the programmer looks at the class tree: Barrel derives from Prop, Enemy from Character, Vehicle from Actor. A flying barrel that is also rideable needs behaviour from three branches. Developers hit this wall in every engine generation, which is why the industry moved from inheritance to composition and, for high object counts, to data-oriented design.
Deep inheritance and its limits

Early engines modelled the world as a class hierarchy: `Entity > Actor > Character > Enemy > FlyingEnemy > BossFlyingEnemy`. The appeal is obvious, shared code lives in base classes. The failures are structural. Behaviour can only be shared along one axis, so cross-cutting features (can be damaged, can burn, can be carried) get hoisted into ever-bigger base classes until `Entity` is a thousand-line god object. Changing a base class risks every descendant. Designers cannot make new combinations without a programmer. The diamond problem pushes people toward multiple inheritance, which most languages in games avoid.
Component-based design

The mainstream answer is **composition**: an entity is little more than an identity, and its behaviour comes from attached **components**, each of which does one thing (`Health`, `Rigidbody`, `Pickup`, `FlightController`). A flying rideable barrel becomes a barrel mesh plus those components. Unity's GameObject/MonoBehaviour model and Unreal's Actor/ActorComponent model both follow this pattern. The wins: designers combine behaviours in the editor, code is reused without hierarchy, and new features are added as new components instead of edits to base classes.

lesson.caption: A class tree shares behaviour along one axis, so the flying rideable barrel needs three parents; composition just attaches the components it needs to one entity.

lesson.text: But classic component systems, including Unity's MonoBehaviour model, are still object-oriented underneath. Each component is a separately allocated heap object with its own `Update` method, invoked individually by the engine (in Unity, one native-to-managed call per object per callback), and a typical gameplay component touches other components through pointers. Scaling that to tens of thousands of objects runs into the hardware, not the design.
Why memory layout dominates

A modern CPU runs at several GHz, but reading from main memory takes on the order of 100 ns, hundreds of cycles. To hide that, the CPU loads memory in **cache lines** of 64 bytes (128 on some Apple designs) and keeps recently used lines in L1, L2 and L3 caches. L1 is a few cycles away, L2 about ten, L3 tens, RAM hundreds. So the speed of a loop is determined less by instruction count than by how many cache lines it touches and whether the hardware prefetcher can predict the next ones. Linear, contiguous reads are the fastest possible access pattern. Chasing pointers to scattered heap objects is the slowest, because each hop is a potential cache miss.

lesson.text: Data-oriented design and ECS

**Data-oriented design** starts from the question 'what data does this transformation read and write, and in what quantity?' rather than 'what object is this?'. **ECS** (Entity Component System) is its common game architecture: **entities** are just IDs; **components** are plain data with no behaviour (`Position`, `Velocity`); **systems** are functions that run over all entities having a particular set of components. A `MovementSystem` iterates every entity with Position and Velocity in one tight loop.

Many production ECS implementations (Unity Entities, Bevy, flecs) store data in **archetypes**; others, such as EnTT, use per-component sparse sets instead, which make adding and removing components cheaper but iteration over several components less linear. In the archetype model there is one archetype per unique combination of component types. All entities with exactly {Position, Velocity, Health} live in one archetype table, split into fixed-size **chunks** (Unity Entities uses 16 KB chunks) in which each component type is a contiguous array. A query for Position and Velocity visits only matching archetypes and walks each chunk linearly. Adding or removing a component changes the entity's archetype, which means copying its data to another table: a **structural change** that costs far more than writing a value and is deferred through command buffers to stay thread-safe.

items: Pros of ECS: cache-friendly iteration, trivially parallel systems when read/write sets do not overlap, batch-friendly for SIMD and job systems, and easier serialisation of pure data.

Cons: more boilerplate for one-off behaviours, harder debugging of 'who changed this', awkward for rare unique objects such as a single boss, and entity-to-entity references are IDs that can go stale.
Hybrid is normal: GameObjects for authoring and unique objects, ECS for bulk simulation like crowds, bullets, particles-with-logic.
The ECS win is proportional to entity count. At 200 objects, the architecture hardly matters; at 200,000 it is the project.

lesson.text: Worked estimate

Say you move 100,000 agents each frame. With scattered heap objects at roughly one cache miss per agent at about 100 ns, you spend 10 ms on memory stalls alone, over half of a 16.6 ms frame. With SoA/archetype layout, positions and velocities are 12 bytes each, so 100,000 agents is 2.4 MB read linearly, a few hundred microseconds at memory bandwidth, and the loop can be vectorised and split across cores. The same logical operation can differ by 20x depending only on layout.

Before rewriting anything as ECS, profile. If the cost is in rendering, physics or a single slow algorithm, architecture will not help. ECS pays when you have many similar entities doing the same cheap work every frame.

items: Misconception: components alone equal ECS. MonoBehaviour components hold data and behaviour together and live as scattered objects; ECS separates them and packs the data.
Misconception: ECS is always faster. Random access by entity ID, frequent structural changes and tiny entity counts can make it slower or no better.
Pitfall: putting large or rarely used data in a hot component bloats every chunk; keep hot components small and split cold data out.

lesson.text: Agents default to object-oriented patterns: a `List<Enemy>` with per-object `Update()`, `GetComponent` calls inside loops, LINQ in hot paths. If you need scale, tell the agent the entity count target, the framework (GameObjects vs Entities), and ask for the memory layout reasoning explicitly. Verify claims of speedup with a profiler capture, since agents tend to assert 'ECS is faster' without measurement, and check generated ECS code for structural changes inside iteration.

patterns.signal: A new feature needs behaviour from two branches of the class tree, or the base class is a thousand-line god object
patterns.why: Entities become containers of small single-purpose components that designers combine freely. Costs indirection and cross-component lookups; inter-component dependencies must be explicit.

patterns.signal: Tens of thousands of similar entities are updated each frame and the profiler shows the loop is memory-bound
patterns.why: Separating identity, data and systems lets each system stream over packed component arrays and parallelise. Overkill for a few hundred unique authored objects, and debugging is less direct.

patterns.signal: A hot loop touches only position and velocity but walks 128-byte objects or pointers scattered across the heap
patterns.why: Store each field contiguously so every 64-byte cache line is full of data the loop needs and the prefetcher can run ahead. Can give an order of magnitude; makes per-object access and insertion more awkward.

patterns.signal: A struct mixes fields read every frame with large fields read rarely, like names, debug info or spawn data
patterns.why: Move rarely used fields into a separate array or side table so hot iteration loads fewer cache lines. Adds an index or lookup when the cold data is needed.

patterns.signal: A system adds or removes components on thousands of entities while it is iterating them
patterns.why: Record add, remove and destroy operations and play them back at a sync point, so archetype moves do not invalidate iteration or happen one by one. Changes are not visible until playback.

patterns.signal: A game mixes 300 unique hand-authored props with a 150,000-bullet boss pattern
patterns.use: Hybrid: GameObjects plus ECS for hot spots
patterns.why: Keep authored, one-off objects in the familiar component model and move only the massive, uniform populations to ECS. Needs a clear boundary and sync between the two worlds.

patterns.signal: Every new enemy kind is a new subclass that only changes numbers like health, speed and loot
patterns.why: Make the kind a data asset (for example a ScriptableObject or table row) that instances reference, so designers add kinds without code. Behaviour that differs in logic still needs code or a scripting layer.

patterns.signal: Designers want to spawn many configured copies of an authored object, with per-level variants
patterns.why: Clone a fully configured template instead of building objects in code; variants inherit from a base and override fields. Deep variant chains become hard to reason about, so keep them shallow.

patterns.signal: Dozens of ability subclasses each call engine systems in their own way and coupling to physics, audio and VFX keeps spreading
patterns.why: A base class exposes a small protected set of operations (play sound, spawn effect, move) and subclasses implement one `Activate` using only those. Coupling is concentrated in the base, which can grow large.

patterns.signal: Several systems must react when an entity dies, and the health code should not reference UI, audio or quests
patterns.why: The source raises an event and listeners subscribe, so new reactions need no change to the source. Order and flow get harder to trace, and listeners that outlive their targets leak unless they unsubscribe.

patterns.signal: Gameplay code calls `AudioManager.Instance` everywhere and tests cannot swap the real service out
patterns.why: Code asks a registry for an interface, so you can provide a null, logging or test implementation. Still a global dependency in disguise; constructor injection is clearer where you control creation.

patterns.signal: Designers keep asking programmers for small rule changes to abilities or quests, each needing a rebuild
patterns.why: Express behaviour as data (graphs, tables, a small instruction set or a scripting language) interpreted at runtime, so content changes ship without code changes. Interpreters are slower and need tooling and validation.

keyPoints: Deep inheritance trees fail on cross-cutting behaviour; composition of components is the mainstream fix.
Cache lines (64 bytes) and prefetching mean contiguous, tightly packed data beats pointer chasing, often by an order of magnitude.
ECS separates identity (entity), data (components) and logic (systems); archetypes store each component type contiguously in chunks.
Structural changes (adding or removing components) move data between archetypes and are expensive.
Use ECS for large counts of similar entities; keep hybrid designs for unique, authored objects.

quiz.q: A team has an inheritance tree Character > Enemy > FlyingEnemy, and now needs a flying ally that can also be carried. Which problem is this showing?
options: Virtual function overhead makes any deep class tree too slow to use for entities.
Cache lines are too large to hold the data of a big Character base class.
Sharing runs along one axis, so cross-cutting features push logic into base classes.
Inheritance makes it impossible for objects to be allocated in contiguous memory.
quiz.explain: Features that cut across branches cannot be shared cleanly in a single-inheritance tree, and composition solves exactly that. The performance concerns are real but are not what this scenario shows.

quiz.q: A loop updates `pos += vel * dt` over 50,000 structs of 128 bytes each, and it is memory-bound. Which change most likely gives the biggest speedup?
options: Make the update function virtual so that each enemy type can override it freely.
Store positions and velocities in separate contiguous arrays so only needed data is read.
Add more fields to each struct so that all related data sits together in one place.
Call the loop from several threads and put a lock around every individual struct.
quiz.explain: The loop uses 24 of 128 bytes per element, so most of each cache line is wasted. Splitting hot data into contiguous arrays reads only what is needed; locks and virtual calls add cost.

quiz.q: In an archetype-based ECS, a gameplay system adds a `Burning` component to 5,000 entities in the middle of iterating them. What is the main concern?
options: The query will hand back the matching entities in a random and unstable order each time.
Adding data to components makes each entity larger than a single 64-byte cache line.
Systems are never allowed to read components that they did not write themselves in a frame.
Each add is a structural change moving the entity to another archetype, so defer it via a command buffer.
quiz.explain: Changing an entity's component set relocates its data and invalidates the chunks being iterated. Command buffers batch these changes safely after the iteration.

quiz.q: A game has 300 unique, hand-authored interactive props and a 150,000-bullet pattern in a boss fight. How should you apply ECS?
options: Convert everything to ECS for consistency, including the props.
Avoid ECS entirely because the prop count is low.
Use ECS only for the 300 props since they carry the most gameplay logic.
Keep props as authored GameObjects and simulate the bullets as ECS entities.
quiz.explain: ECS benefits scale with the number of similar entities, which is the bullets. The few unique props gain little from conversion and are easier to author as objects.

quiz.q: Why is 'we use components, so we already have ECS' a misconception?
options: Object components bundle data with behaviour on the heap, while ECS separates data and packs it by archetype.
ECS components cannot hold any real data and are used only as marker flags on entities.
Object-based components can never be attached to an entity once the game is running.
ECS has no systems at all and consists only of components that run themselves.
quiz.explain: Composition is shared by both, but the memory layout and the separation of data from logic are what give ECS its cache and parallelism advantages. The other options misstate how ECS works.

quiz.q: Designers add a new enemy kind every week. Each is a new C# subclass whose only difference is its health, speed and loot table, and there are already 40 such classes. What should you reach for?
options: An Entity-Component-System with archetype chunk storage
A Subclass Sandbox with protected helper methods
A data-defined enemy type object that one class reads
An observer event bus between the enemy classes
quiz.explain: Type Object moves the differences into data, so designers add kinds without code or rebuilds. ECS addresses throughput, not subclass proliferation, and a sandbox helps subclasses that differ in behaviour, not in numbers.

topics.title: Scenes, spatial partitioning and culling
topics.summary: How engines organise a world as transform trees and spatial structures so they can skip everything the player cannot see or touch.

lesson.text: An open-world level holds 80,000 renderable objects and 20,000 physics colliders. The camera sees perhaps 1,500 of them. If the engine submits all 80,000 to the GPU, the CPU spends its entire frame issuing draw calls for geometry that ends up off-screen. The first rule of engine performance is: the fastest work is work you never start. **Spatial data structures** and **culling** are how engines decide what to skip, and they underlie rendering, physics queries, AI perception and audio.
The scene graph and transform hierarchy

A **scene** is the collection of entities in a level. Most are arranged in a **transform hierarchy**: a tree where each node has a local transform (position, rotation, scale relative to its parent) and a world transform (the product of all ancestors). A sword is a child of a hand, which is a child of an arm. Moving the arm moves the sword automatically. Each transform is a 4x4 matrix (64 bytes) or an equivalent position/quaternion/scale triple; the world matrix is `parentWorld * local`.

Maintaining that is not free. When a parent moves, all descendants' world matrices go dirty. Engines mark them with **dirty flags** and recompute lazily or in a batch pass, ideally parents before children and in a cache-friendly order (Unity stores transform hierarchies in contiguous arrays and updates them with jobs). Deep hierarchies and very large numbers of independently moving children are a known cost, and a flat structure is cheaper. Non-uniform scale in a parent with rotated children causes shear, which a TRS triple cannot represent.

lesson.text: Why hierarchy is not enough

A transform tree represents **ownership and relative placement**, not **where things are**. Two objects spatially next to each other may be in unrelated branches. Questions like 'what is within 10 m of this explosion?' or 'which objects touch the camera frustum?' would require testing every object, an O(n) scan, and for pairwise questions (collision) O(n^2). With 20,000 colliders, all pairs is 200 million tests. Spatial structures reduce this to roughly O(log n) per query by grouping nearby objects.
Spatial partitioning structures

items: **Uniform grid**: divide the world into equal cells; each object is registered in the cells it overlaps. Lookup is O(1) and simple, ideal for evenly spread, similarly sized objects (bullets, crowd agents, tile maps). It wastes memory on sparse worlds and struggles when sizes vary wildly. Use a hash of the cell coordinates to store only occupied cells.

**Quadtree (2D) and octree (3D)**: recursively split space into four or eight children, subdividing only where objects are dense. Adapts to uneven distributions, such as a city with an empty field next to it. Objects that straddle a boundary either sit in the parent or are stored in several leaves.

**BVH (bounding volume hierarchy)**: a tree where each node holds a bounding box enclosing its children, and the partitioning follows the objects rather than fixed space. Queries descend only into boxes that overlap the query. BVHs handle objects of mixed sizes well, support cheap refit when objects move (grow or shrink boxes up the tree), and are the dominant structure in physics broad phases and ray tracing.
**BSP trees and portals/PVS**: older but still relevant for indoor levels, where precomputed visibility sets say which rooms can possibly be seen from where.

lesson.text: Choosing among them is a trade between build cost, update cost and query cost. Static geometry can use an expensive, high-quality build (a surface-area-heuristic BVH) once. Dynamic objects need structures that update cheaply, a loose grid or refit BVH, or are re-inserted every frame. Rebuilding an octree for 10,000 moving objects each frame is a classic mistake.
Frustum culling

The camera's view volume is a truncated pyramid, the **frustum**, defined by six planes. **Frustum culling** tests each object's bounding volume (sphere or axis-aligned box, wrapping the real mesh) against these planes and discards anything fully outside. Testing the proxy volume is far cheaper than the mesh: an AABB-versus-plane test needs a few multiplies and compares. Done hierarchically, a whole BVH node outside the frustum rejects all its children at once, turning 80,000 tests into a few hundred.
Occlusion culling

Frustum culling only removes what is off-screen. Objects inside the frustum may be hidden behind a wall. **Occlusion culling** removes them. Approaches differ: **precomputed** visibility divides the level into cells and stores, offline, which objects are potentially visible from each cell (Unity's built-in Occlusion Culling works this way and is tied to baked static data); **software rasterisation** draws large occluders into a small depth buffer on the CPU and tests bounding boxes against it; **GPU-driven** methods reuse the previous frame's depth buffer, often organised as a depth pyramid (Hi-Z), and test objects in compute shaders. Unity 6 adds a GPU occlusion culling option in URP and HDRP, which works with the GPU Resident Drawer. Occlusion culling costs time to evaluate, so it pays off in dense occluded scenes (cities, interiors) and may lose in open terrain.

lesson.text: Level of detail

Once an object is known to be visible, it should still cost proportional to its on-screen size. **LOD** swaps in cheaper representations with distance or screen coverage: a 50,000-triangle hero mesh at 5 m becomes 5,000 at 30 m and a 300-triangle impostor or billboard at 200 m. Selection is usually by projected screen-space size rather than raw distance, so a zoomed camera behaves correctly. Cross-fading or dithered transitions hide the pop. LOD also applies to animation update rate, shadow casting, physics and AI tick rate, not only meshes. The extreme version is virtualised geometry (Unreal's Nanite) where clustering and selection happen on the GPU per cluster.

Bounding volumes must be correct. An animated or vertex-displaced mesh whose AABB stays at its bind pose gets culled while still visible, a bug that shows as objects popping out at screen edges. Check bounds for skinned meshes, shader-driven vertex motion and procedural geometry.

items: Misconception: culling makes the GPU faster. It mostly saves CPU submission time and vertex work; fill-rate cost is governed by overdraw and resolution.
Misconception: more partitioning is always better. Every structure has a maintenance cost, and with a few hundred objects a linear scan can win.
Pitfall: culling and LOD thresholds tuned on a dev PC fail on low-end hardware; tune per quality tier.

lesson.text: When an agent builds a spatial system it often picks an octree by reflex, rebuilds it every frame, or loops over all objects for 'nearby' queries inside Update. Tell it the object count, how many move per frame, and whether queries are range, nearest-neighbour or raycast. Ask it to justify the structure against those numbers. Verify with a profiler and a stress scene, and test edge cases: objects on cell boundaries, objects larger than a cell, and objects moving fast enough to skip cells.

patterns.signal: Many same-size objects spread evenly over a level all move every frame and each needs its nearby neighbours
patterns.why: Bucket objects by cell and check only the surrounding cells; insert and remove are O(1), so rebuilding each frame is cheap. Wastes memory on empty space and degrades when objects vary greatly in size.

patterns.signal: Object density is very uneven: dense towns, sparse wilderness, and queries should skip empty regions
patterns.why: Space subdivides only where objects cluster, so queries descend just into occupied nodes. Objects straddling boundaries complicate placement, and moving many objects means frequent node updates.

patterns.signal: Colliders or renderers range from pebbles to buildings, many move, and queries are mostly box or ray overlaps
patterns.why: Boxes follow the objects, handle mixed sizes well and refit cheaply when objects move. Refits degrade tree quality over time, so rebuild periodically; dominant in physics broad phases and ray tracing.

patterns.signal: A hand-written spatial structure for 100 objects made frame time worse than the plain loop
patterns.why: Below a few hundred items a contiguous array scan beats tree traversal thanks to cache locality and no maintenance cost. Measure before adding a structure; partition when counts or query rates grow.

patterns.signal: Moving a parent recomputes every descendant's world matrix immediately, even if nothing reads them this frame
patterns.why: Mark derived data stale when inputs change and recompute lazily or in one batch pass, parents before children. Saves repeated work; the risk is forgetting to set or check the flag and reading stale data.

patterns.signal: The CPU issues draw calls for thousands of objects that end up off-screen
patterns.why: Test cheap bounding volumes against the six frustum planes and reject whole nodes of a spatial tree at once. Bounds must be conservative or visible objects pop out.

patterns.signal: Inside a dense city most in-frustum objects sit behind buildings, yet they are still drawn
patterns.why: Precomputed visibility or a depth-based test removes hidden objects. It has its own CPU or GPU cost and bake time, so it pays off mainly in dense, enclosed scenes, not open fields.

patterns.signal: Distant objects cost as many triangles and draw calls as nearby ones but cover only a few pixels
patterns.why: Swap to simpler meshes, materials or impostors by screen size so cost scales with what is seen. Costs authoring and memory, and visible popping without cross-fades or hysteresis.

patterns.signal: A tall or animated mesh disappears near screen edges although part of it should still be visible
patterns.why: Culling trusts the bounding volume, so bounds must cover animation, vertex displacement and skinning. Enlarge or update bounds; overly large bounds just cull less.

patterns.signal: A deep transform hierarchy with hundreds of independently moving children shows high transform update cost
patterns.why: Parent only when objects truly move together; independent movers at the root avoid cascading dirty propagation and allow parallel updates. Loses automatic relative placement.

keyPoints: A transform hierarchy encodes parenting and relative placement, not spatial proximity; spatial questions need separate structures.
Grids suit uniform dense objects, octrees suit uneven density, and BVHs suit mixed sizes and cheap refits of dynamic objects.
Frustum culling tests simple bounding volumes against six planes, and hierarchical tests reject whole subtrees at once.
Occlusion culling removes objects hidden behind others, at an evaluation cost that pays off mainly in dense scenes.
LOD scales cost with screen size; bounding volumes must remain correct for animated or displaced geometry.

quiz.q: A crowd sim has 20,000 same-size agents spread evenly over a flat arena, all moving every frame, and each needs nearby neighbours. Which structure is the best fit?
options: A hash grid, rebuilt cheaply each frame by cell coordinates.
A deep octree rebuilt each frame with a surface-area heuristic.
A BSP tree precomputed offline for the arena.
The transform hierarchy, since agents are children of one crowd node.
quiz.explain: Uniform, evenly spread, same-size, fast-moving objects are the grid's best case, with O(1) insert. The transform tree gives no spatial proximity, and expensive rebuilds suit static data.

quiz.q: A tall tower mesh occasionally vanishes when its base is near a screen edge, though part of it should be visible. Which cause is most likely?
options: The occlusion depth pyramid was built at too low a resolution for the tower.
The LOD selection switched to a flat impostor much too early for this distance.
Its bounding volume is too small or misplaced, so frustum culling rejects it while visible.
The depth buffer lacks enough precision to represent tall objects near the edges.
quiz.explain: Culling tests the proxy volume, so an incorrect bound rejects a mesh whose real geometry is still in view. Edge-dependent disappearance points at frustum tests rather than occlusion or LOD.

quiz.q: A scene has 100 objects. A developer replaces a linear scan for 'objects in range' with a hand-written octree and finds frame time rose. What is the most plausible reason?
options: Octrees are unable to answer range queries correctly for objects of any kind.
At such small counts, build and maintenance overhead exceeds the tests the structure saves.
Octrees need a GPU in order to run efficiently, and this code ran on the CPU.
Range queries are always faster with a linear scan, whatever the object count is.
quiz.explain: Acceleration structures trade maintenance for fewer tests, which only pays when n is large enough. The claim that linear scans always win is false at scale.

quiz.q: In a dense city, frustum culling leaves 12,000 visible-in-frustum objects, but the player is in a street and sees only 800. Which technique addresses the remaining waste?
options: Add more LOD levels to the far meshes so that each costs less to draw.
Increase the number of frustum planes so the view volume fits more tightly.
Rebuild the octree every single frame so that its results are always accurate.
Use occlusion culling, with baked visibility data or a depth-based visibility test.
quiz.explain: Those objects are inside the frustum but hidden behind buildings, which is the case occlusion culling targets. More LODs lower cost per object but still submit all of them.

quiz.q: A character's sword is parented to its hand. The artist moves the root of the character, and 300 such children across the level update their world matrices. What does the hierarchy guarantee, and what does it not?
options: It guarantees fast spatial queries for finding nearby objects across the whole level.
It guarantees children are always culled together with their parents by the camera.
Children's world transforms follow the parent, but it says nothing about which objects are close.
It guarantees that non-uniform scale can never introduce shear into rotated children.
quiz.explain: A transform tree propagates placement from parent to child. Proximity needs a separate spatial structure, and non-uniform parent scale with rotated children can in fact cause shear.

quiz.q: A street scene draws lamp posts and cars 5 km away with their full 8,000-triangle meshes. They are inside the frustum, not occluded, and each covers only a few pixels, yet they cost as much as near ones. Which approach fits best?
options: A level-of-detail chain with a distance cut-off
Occlusion culling against the nearby buildings in view
Hierarchical frustum culling over a BVH of objects
A dirty flag on each object's cached world matrix
quiz.explain: LOD cuts triangle and draw cost where detail is invisible. Frustum and occlusion culling remove only objects outside the view or hidden, and these are visible, so they would still be drawn at full cost.

topics.title: Physics and collision
topics.summary: How engines simulate rigid bodies, find collisions in two phases, avoid tunnelling, and why all of it runs at a fixed rate.

lesson.text: A player fires a rocket launcher at 120 m/s. On the developer's machine the rocket explodes against walls. On a slow device the rocket flies straight through a thin fence and detonates on the far side. This is **tunnelling**, and it is one of the failures a physics engine is built to prevent. Physics engines are the part of the game that has to be right under the worst conditions, because every other system relies on its output.
Rigid bodies and integration

Most game physics is **rigid body dynamics**: objects have mass, position, orientation, linear and angular velocity, and never deform. Each step the engine applies forces (gravity, thrust, contacts), updates velocities, then positions. The update rule is the **integrator**. The simplest, **explicit Euler**, does `v += a*dt; x += v*dt`. **Semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler** updates velocity first and then uses the new velocity for position, which is nearly as cheap and conserves energy far better, so it is the default in most game engines. **Verlet** and **RK4** are used in cloth, particles or specialised simulations. Explicit Euler with a big `dt` gains energy and explodes, while semi-implicit remains stable for typical game steps.

lesson.caption: Same spring, same dt of 0.05 s: semi-implicit Euler tracks the exact curve, while explicit Euler gains energy every cycle until it leaves the chart.

lesson.text: After integration comes **collision handling**. Contacts are resolved either by impulses (sequential impulse or projected Gauss-Seidel solvers, the basis of Box2D, PhysX, Havok and Bullet) or by position-based methods (XPBD), which have become popular for stable stacking and soft effects. Solvers iterate several times per step over all contacts and **joints**, and the quality of stacking depends on iteration counts. Defaults are small single-digit counts and differ by engine (Box2D v2 recommends 8 velocity and 3 position iterations; Unity's PhysX integration defaults to 6 solver iterations and 1 velocity iteration), and raising them is the usual first knob for wobbly stacks or stretchy joints.
Collider shapes

A physics body does not collide using its render mesh. It uses simplified **colliders**. Primitives (sphere, box, capsule) are the cheapest and have analytic tests. **Convex hulls** are more general but cost grows with vertex count. **Mesh colliders** (arbitrary triangle soup) are legal only for static geometry in most engines because concave meshes lack the volume info needed for stable dynamic response. For complex dynamic shapes, authors approximate with **compound** colliders: several convex pieces on one body. Characters usually use a capsule, since a rounded bottom climbs steps and slides along walls. Sensors or **triggers** report overlap without producing a physical response.
Broad phase and narrow phase

Testing every pair of 5,000 bodies is about 12.5 million pair tests per step. Engines split detection into two stages. The **broad phase** uses cheap bounding volumes (AABBs) and a spatial structure to produce a short list of **candidate pairs** that might touch: sweep and prune along an axis, a dynamic BVH (as in Box2D's dynamic tree or Bullet's DBVT), or a grid. It is conservative, accepting false positives but never false negatives. The **narrow phase** runs exact tests on each candidate pair, using algorithms such as **SAT** (separating axis theorem) for boxes and **GJK** with **EPA** for general convex shapes, and produces a **contact manifold**: contact points, normal and penetration depth. The solver consumes that manifold.

lesson.caption: The broad phase cuts 21 pairs to 3 by AABB overlap; the narrow phase rejects two false positives and returns one contact with a normal and depth.

items: Broad phase cost scales with body count and movement, and narrow phase with candidate pairs times shape complexity.
Collision layers and masks prune pairs before the narrow phase, so decide early which categories ever interact.
Sleeping bodies at rest are excluded until something wakes them, which makes large piles of static debris almost free.

lesson.text: Tunnelling and continuous collision detection

Discrete collision tests positions only at step boundaries. A bullet at 120 m/s with a 1/60 s step moves 2 m per step. A fence 0.1 m thick is simply stepped over: at step n the bullet is before it, at n+1 after, and no overlap is ever observed. Fixes: **continuous collision detection (CCD)**, which sweeps the shape along its motion path and finds the **time of impact**, then stops or resolves there; **speculative contacts**, which create contacts for near-future overlaps and let the solver limit velocity so objects cannot pass; thicker colliders; or, for projectiles, a **raycast** along the movement segment each step, which is the cheapest and most common solution. CCD costs extra, so engines apply it selectively to fast bodies only.

lesson.text: Raycasts and queries

Besides simulation, physics provides **scene queries**: a **raycast** (first hit along a ray), **shape casts** or sweeps (a sphere or capsule swept along a path, ideal for character ground checks and melee), and **overlap tests** (what is inside this volume). These reuse the broad-phase structure and are the backbone of hit-scan weapons, line of sight, ground detection and AI perception. Their cost depends on layer masks and ray length, so a cast against everything out to 1,000 m every frame for 500 agents adds up. Queries run against the state at the last simulation step, so call them from the same stage that owns that data.
Why physics runs at a fixed rate, and determinism

The accumulator loop itself is covered in 'The game loop and time'; here is why physics in particular insists on it. Integrators and solvers are tuned for a specific step size. Stacks stable at 1/60 s may jitter or explode at 1/20 s, and warm-starting contact impulses across frames assumes similar steps. A fixed step (Unity defaults to 0.02 s, i.e. 50 Hz; Box2D docs recommend 1/60 s) gives bounded cost per step and an easy knob for accuracy against CPU load. It is also required for **determinism**: the same inputs producing the same results, needed for replays, lockstep multiplayer and reproducible bugs. True determinism is harder than a fixed step: floating-point results can differ across CPUs, compilers and instruction sets (fused multiply-add, SIMD), body and contact ordering must be stable, and threading must not reorder solver work. Engines advertise cross-platform determinism only in specific modes, so verify rather than assume.

Never move a physics body by setting its transform directly every frame. This teleports it and bypasses collision, so it tunnels and breaks contacts. Drive bodies with velocities or forces, or use kinematic movement that the engine sweeps properly.

Agents routinely mix transform writes with rigidbody physics, apply forces in per-frame update, and raycast in loops with no layer masks. Tell the agent which code runs at the physics rate, which collision layers exist, and the top speed of the fastest object. Verify with a test that fires the fastest projectile at the thinnest wall at several frame rates, and check for tunnelling and jitter. Treat any claim of 'deterministic physics' with suspicion until you have replayed the same inputs on two machines.

patterns.signal: A rocket or ball passes through thin walls on slow devices or at high speed
patterns.why: Swept tests or speculative contacts catch collisions between discrete steps. Costs more per body, so enable it only on fast objects; thickening colliders or smaller steps are partial fixes.

patterns.signal: Bullets are simulated as tiny rigidbodies and sometimes miss targets they visibly crossed
patterns.why: Each step, cast a ray or shape from the previous to the new position and resolve the first hit. Exact and cheap for fast projectiles; you lose free physical bouncing unless you add it yourself.

patterns.signal: Raycasts hit the shooter's own collider, and debris, bullets and ragdolls test against each other needlessly
patterns.why: Assign layers and disable pairs in the collision matrix, and pass masks to queries. Fewer pairs in the broad phase and fewer false hits; the matrix becomes shared config that must be documented.

patterns.signal: Code needs to know when the player enters a zone or pickup, without anything being pushed
patterns.why: Trigger colliders report overlaps but produce no contact response. Most engines need a body on at least one side to raise events, and fast movers can skip a thin trigger between steps.

patterns.signal: Physics cost stays high in a scene where hundreds of crates have stopped moving
patterns.why: Bodies below a velocity threshold for a while are skipped until something wakes them. Applying tiny forces each frame keeps them awake; teleporting a body without waking neighbours leaves things floating.

patterns.signal: A dynamic object uses a detailed concave mesh collider and collisions are slow or unreliable
patterns.why: Approximate the shape with boxes, spheres, capsules or convex hulls; these are fast and robust for dynamic bodies. Keep arbitrary concave meshes for static level geometry.

patterns.signal: Forces or velocity changes are applied in the per-frame update, so acceleration differs between 30 and 144 fps
patterns.use: Apply forces in the fixed physics step
patterns.why: Run force and velocity code where the physics step runs, and read input per frame into state the step consumes. Keeps physics rate-independent; one-shot impulses need care not to apply twice or be missed.

patterns.signal: A custom spring or orbit integrated with `v += a*dt; x += v*dt` in the wrong order gains energy and explodes
patterns.why: Update velocity first, then position with the new velocity; nearly free and far more stable at game step sizes. For stiff springs use smaller substeps; Verlet or RK4 fit cloth or high-precision cases.

patterns.signal: The player capsule is a dynamic rigidbody and jitters on slopes, bounces off steps and gets shoved by props
patterns.why: Move the character yourself with sweeps and resolve slopes and steps explicitly, keeping full control of feel. You must implement pushing and being pushed, so physics interaction is less automatic.

patterns.signal: A ledge-grab or ground check with one thin ray misses edges that the capsule clearly overlaps
patterns.why: Sweep or overlap the actual capsule or sphere so the query matches the body's volume. More expensive than a ray; filter with layer masks and keep the cast distance short.

patterns.signal: The profiler shows garbage allocations from physics queries called every frame
patterns.why: Use the query variants that write hits into a preallocated array and reuse it. Removes GC spikes; size the buffer for the worst case or detect when it fills.

keyPoints: Semi-implicit Euler is the cheap, stable default integrator; explicit Euler gains energy at larger steps.
Collision runs in two phases: a conservative broad phase finds candidate pairs, and a narrow phase produces exact contact manifolds.
Dynamic bodies use primitive, convex or compound colliders; arbitrary concave meshes are for static geometry.
Tunnelling comes from discrete tests on fast or thin objects; use CCD, speculative contacts or swept raycasts.
Fixed-rate physics gives stability, bounded cost and the prerequisite for determinism, which also needs stable ordering and consistent floating-point behaviour.

quiz.q: A 0.05 m thick glass pane is passed through by a ball moving at 30 m/s with a 0.02 s physics step. Which fix targets the root cause?
options: Increase solver iterations so contacts resolve more accurately.
Switch the ball's collider from a sphere to a mesh collider.
Enable continuous collision detection for the ball so its motion is swept.
Lower the gravity so the ball moves more slowly.
quiz.explain: The ball moves 0.6 m per step, far more than the pane thickness, so no overlap is ever observed. Sweeping detects the time of impact; more solver iterations only act on contacts that exist.

quiz.q: What does the broad phase guarantee?
options: Every pair that it reports is guaranteed to be actually in contact right now.
It never misses a pair that could touch, though it may report pairs that do not.
It computes the exact penetration depth and contact normal for every reported pair.
It removes the need for a narrow phase whenever the shapes involved are convex.
quiz.explain: The broad phase is conservative: false positives are filtered by the narrow phase, but false negatives would mean missed collisions. Exact contact data comes from the narrow phase.

quiz.q: A stack of crates is stable in the editor at 60 fps but jitters and collapses on a slow device when physics runs once per variable-length frame. What is the best fix?
options: Run physics at a fixed step with an accumulator, and cap the steps allowed per frame.
Increase the mass of every crate so that they resist being moved by contacts.
Switch the crates to concave mesh colliders in order to gain accuracy at contacts.
Run physics on a separate thread but keep passing it the variable frame time.
quiz.explain: Solver stability and warm-starting depend on a consistent step, which variable frame times break. A thread alone still passes in inconsistent dt, and mass or collider tweaks do not address the cause.

quiz.q: A dev wants a ledge-grab check that works for a capsule character. Which query is most appropriate?
options: A single raycast fired from the centre of the character toward the ledge.
A mesh collider overlap test run against the entire level geometry each frame.
A trigger volume placed by hand on every single ledge in the level.
A capsule or sphere cast, which accounts for the width of the character body.
quiz.explain: A zero-width ray can slip through gaps that the character's body cannot, so a shape cast matches the real volume. Level-wide mesh overlaps and per-ledge triggers are heavier and more error-prone.

quiz.q: A lockstep multiplayer game uses a fixed physics step, yet two players' simulations drift apart after a few minutes. Which factor could still cause it?
options: The fixed step is too small to keep both machines in agreement over time.
Different floating-point behaviour or contact ordering on each machine could do it.
The broad phase uses AABBs, which are not exact enough for lockstep play.
The integrator is semi-implicit rather than explicit, so results differ per player.
quiz.explain: A fixed step is necessary but not sufficient: differing instruction sets, compilers or processing order change results bit-for-bit, and errors compound. The choice of integrator is not what breaks cross-machine agreement.

quiz.q: A hitscan raycast keeps hitting the shooter's own collider, and shell casings, debris and ragdoll limbs all test against each other, wasting physics time. What should you reach for?
options: Collision layers with layer masks on queries and bodies
Continuous collision detection on every single rigidbody
Trigger volumes placed around the shooter's body
Letting every resting body fall asleep after a delay
quiz.explain: Layers and masks decide which pairs and queries are tested at all, removing self-hits and debris-on-debris work. CCD fixes tunnelling and sleeping helps only motionless bodies, so neither changes which colliders are considered.

topics.title: Animation
topics.summary: How engines turn keyframes into skinned, blended, IK-corrected characters at 60 fps, and how animation data is compressed.

lesson.text: A hero character has 70 bones, 40 animation clips (idle, walk, run, jump, a dozen attacks) and must transition smoothly between them in response to a controller that gives no warning. Meanwhile 30 enemies on screen do the same. Animation is a runtime system that samples data, blends it, corrects it, and hands a pose to the renderer, all inside a budget of maybe 1-3 ms of CPU per frame for the whole scene. Understanding the pipeline is what lets you diagnose foot sliding, popping transitions and memory bloat.
Keyframes and curves

An animation clip is a set of **curves**, one per animated channel (for example `bone_17.position.x`, or a quaternion component). Artists author sparse **keyframes**; the runtime interpolates between them. Linear interpolation is cheap but gives visible corners; Bezier or Hermite tangents give smooth motion at the cost of storing tangents. Rotations are stored as unit quaternions and interpolated with nlerp (normalized linear) or slerp, never as independently interpolated Euler angles, which cause gimbal artifacts and non-uniform speed. Sampling a clip at time `t` means: find the surrounding keys for each curve (binary search or a cached cursor), interpolate, write the result into a pose.

lesson.text: Skeletons and skinning

A **skeleton** is a hierarchy of bones. Each bone stores a local transform relative to its parent. A **pose** is the array of local transforms for all bones. To render, the engine walks the hierarchy once, multiplying each local transform by its parent's world transform to get a model-space matrix per bone. Because a mesh is authored in a bind pose, each bone also has an **inverse bind matrix**; the skinning matrix is `world_bone * inverse_bind`.

**Linear blend skinning** gives each vertex up to 4 (sometimes 8) bone indices and weights summing to 1. The vertex shader computes the weighted sum of the bone matrices applied to the bind-pose position. Cost is per vertex, so a 50k-vertex character with 4 influences does 200k matrix-vector products per frame, which is trivial on GPU and expensive on CPU. Modern engines skin on the GPU (vertex shader or compute) and upload a palette of bone matrices (for 70 bones, about 70 x 48 bytes = 3.4 KB per character instance). The known artifact of linear blending is the candy-wrapper collapse at twisting joints; fixes are dual-quaternion skinning, corrective blend shapes, or extra twist bones.

lesson.text: Blending and blend trees

Transitions and locomotion variety come from **blending**: producing a pose as the weighted mix of several poses, per bone (lerp translation, nlerp rotation, with the shortest-arc check on the quaternion dot product). A **blend tree** is a graph of blend nodes driven by parameters. The classic example is locomotion: a 1D blend on `speed` between idle, walk and run, or a 2D blend on `(velocity.x, velocity.z)` among strafing clips. Clips in a blend must be **phase aligned** (foot-down at the same normalized time) or the blend creates sliding and floating; engines sync by normalizing clip length and matching foot-phase markers. **Additive animation** stores a difference from a reference pose (a lean, a breathing cycle, a hit reaction) and adds it on top; **layered** or masked blending applies an upper-body clip over lower-body locomotion using a per-bone mask.

lesson.text: Animation state machines

Blend trees handle continuous variation. **Animation state machines** handle discrete modes: Grounded, Jumping, Falling, Landing, Attacking. Each state holds a clip or a blend tree; transitions have conditions (parameter thresholds, triggers, 'exit time') and a **cross-fade duration**, during which both states are evaluated and blended. During a cross-fade you are paying for two (or more) full evaluations, so long fades with many interruptions are a performance trap. State machines are also a classic source of bugs: transition explosion (every state connects to every other), missing interruption rules, and race conditions between gameplay code setting triggers and the machine consuming them.
Inverse kinematics

Forward kinematics computes the end of a chain from joint angles. **Inverse kinematics (IK)** solves the reverse: given a target (a ledge, a foot placement point, a weapon aim direction), find joint rotations. For two-bone chains (arm, leg) an analytic solver with the law of cosines is exact, fast and stable, and needs a **pole vector** to choose the knee or elbow direction. For longer chains, iterative solvers (CCD, FABRIK) converge in a few iterations. IK runs after the animation pose is evaluated and before skinning, typically blended by a weight so it can fade in. Common uses are foot planting on uneven terrain (raycast, move the foot, lower the pelvis), look-at for head and eyes, and hand attachment to props.
Root motion

In a walk clip the character's root bone advances through space. Either the clip stays in place and gameplay code moves the capsule at a chosen speed (**in-place**), or the root's motion is extracted from the clip and applied to the character (**root motion**). In-place is responsive and predictable, which suits action games with instant direction changes, but feet slide if code speed and clip speed disagree. Root motion matches the feet exactly and suits melee attacks, vaults and climbs, but gives up some control: the character moves only as far as the artist authored, and in networked games the extracted motion must be applied deterministically or be reconciled. Many shipped games use a hybrid: root motion for attacks and traversal, in-place with speed-scaled playback for locomotion.

Foot sliding is a measurable bug: compare the planted foot's world velocity to zero. If it slides, the movement speed and clip speed are out of sync. Fix by scaling playback rate by `actualSpeed / authoredSpeed`, using stride warping, or switching that state to root motion.
Animation compression and cost

Uncompressed, 70 bones x 10 floats (position 3, rotation 4, scale 3) x 30 fps x 2 seconds x 4 bytes is about 168 KB per clip. Forty clips is 6.7 MB for one character; multiply by a roster and memory is a problem, and streaming that data costs bandwidth. Compression strategies: **keyframe reduction** (drop keys that a linear or curve fit reproduces within an error tolerance), **quantization** (quaternions stored as 3 components in 16 bits each, using the fact that unit length determines the fourth; positions in fixed-point ranges per clip), constant-track elimination (channels that never change collapse to one value; scale is usually constant 1), and sample-rate reduction. Typical lossy compression achieves 5-10x with errors below a visible threshold, but the error tolerance must be tighter on bones that magnify error: errors at the hip propagate to every child, so tolerances are applied in an error-at-the-end-effector sense. Over-aggressive compression shows up as foot jitter and finger twitching.

Runtime cost is dominated by the number of animated bones times the number of evaluated clips. Levers: **animation LOD** (distant characters update at lower rates, skip IK and fingers, or use a lower bone count), **culling** (skip evaluation when off-screen, balancing against needing root motion), multithreaded or job-based evaluation, and GPU skinning. Visible budgets: 100 characters at 70 bones with 3 blended clips is about 21,000 bone-evaluations per frame, fine on a modern core, but 10x the count at 120 bones on mobile is not.
Common misconceptions

items: 'Blending two animations averages their positions.' It blends per-bone local transforms; rotations need quaternion handling, and mismatched phase produces sliding regardless of math.
'More keyframes means smoother motion.' Smoothness comes from curve quality and interpolation; dense keys mostly cost memory.
'IK replaces animation.' IK corrects a pose that animation provides; with no good base pose, the result looks robotic.
'Root motion is always better.' It trades control for fidelity and complicates networking and physics interaction.

lesson.text: When an AI agent writes animation code or sets up animator graphs, tell it the specifics: bone count, target platform, whether locomotion is in-place or root-motion, and the networking model. Verify that it does not interpolate Euler angles, does not allocate per frame in the animation update, handles quaternion double-cover (flip when dot < 0), and does not create fully connected state machines. Agents tend to add a transition per request and never prune; ask for a diagram of the state graph and review transition conditions for conflicts and missing exits. Always check the result in motion, not just in code.

The whole pipeline per character per frame is: update state machine and parameters, evaluate active clips and blend trees into a local pose, apply layers and additive offsets, run IK, compute model-space matrices, extract root motion for the gameplay side, then skin on the GPU. Knowing the order tells you where to intervene when something is wrong.

patterns.signal: A character has discrete modes like grounded, jumping, attacking, and switching between them pops
patterns.why: States hold clips or blend trees and transitions blend over a duration. During a cross-fade both states are evaluated; fully connected graphs become unmaintainable, so group states and use sub-machines.

patterns.signal: Locomotion must cover a continuous range of speeds and directions without separate states for each
patterns.why: Blend phase-aligned clips by parameters like speed and direction (1D or 2D). Smooth coverage with few clips; clips must share phase and timing or feet slide and float.

patterns.signal: The character must reload or wave while legs keep running independently
patterns.why: A layer with a bone mask overrides or blends only upper-body bones on top of the base locomotion. Each layer costs evaluation, and mismatched poses at the mask seam can look broken.

patterns.signal: Breathing, leaning or hit reactions need to apply on top of any base animation without authoring every combination
patterns.why: Store a clip as a difference from a reference pose and add it to whatever is playing. Cuts the clip count; additives authored against the wrong reference pose produce distorted results.

patterns.signal: Feet float or clip on slopes and stairs, or hands miss a weapon grip or ledge
patterns.why: Run foot, hand or look-at IK on the blended pose to hit real targets. Corrects contact cheaply; needs reliable targets from raycasts and weighting to avoid knee pops and jitter.

patterns.signal: An attack lunge or vault must move the character exactly as authored with feet locked to the floor
patterns.why: Extract the root bone's motion from the clip and apply it to the character. Exact contact and timing, at the cost of gameplay control; blend with code-driven movement where responsiveness matters.

patterns.signal: Feet slide during in-place locomotion because gameplay moves the capsule faster than the clip was authored
patterns.why: Scale the clip's playback rate by `actualSpeed / authoredSpeed`, or blend between walk and run, so stride matches ground speed. Extreme rates look unnatural; add clips for distant speed ranges.

patterns.signal: Animation CPU cost is dominated by distant characters that cover a few pixels
patterns.use: Animation LOD and reduced update rate
patterns.why: Update far characters at lower rates, skip IK and layers, or use fewer bones by distance; off-screen ones can stop evaluating. Large savings with little visible loss; watch for root motion and events that still need updating.

patterns.signal: Blending two rotations makes a limb spin the long way round
patterns.why: `q` and `-q` are the same rotation; if `dot(a, b) < 0` negate one before nlerp or slerp so blending takes the shortest arc. Missing it is a classic artefact of hand-written blending code.

patterns.signal: Blending walk and run makes the legs scissor because the clips have different lengths
patterns.why: Normalize clip time and align on foot-contact markers so blended clips are at the same phase of the cycle. Requires marked-up clips; clips without matching cycles cannot be synced cleanly.

patterns.signal: Damage or footstep sounds are timed with gameplay timers that drift from the animation
patterns.why: Fire gameplay hooks from markers in the clip so timing follows the animation. Events can be skipped or doubled during cross-fades and reduced update rates, so make handlers idempotent and robust.

patterns.signal: Feet jitter visibly after animation compression was raised to save memory
patterns.use: Compression error measured at end effectors
patterns.why: Key reduction and quantization errors accumulate down the bone chain, so measure error at feet and hands, not per joint. Tighten tolerance on long chains; costs some memory back.

keyPoints: A pose is an array of local bone transforms; skinning multiplies world bone matrices by inverse bind matrices and weights up to 4 influences per vertex.
Blending works per bone with quaternion shortest-arc handling, and only looks right if the clips are phase aligned.
State machines manage discrete modes with cross-fades; blend trees manage continuous parameters like speed and direction.
IK corrects a base pose (feet, aim, hands) after evaluation; root motion trades control for exact foot contact.
Compression uses key reduction, quantized quaternions and constant-track removal, with error measured where it is visible.

quiz.q: A character's feet slide on the ground while running even though the run clip looks fine in the preview. Movement is in-place and gameplay moves the capsule at 7 m/s, while the clip was authored at 5 m/s. What is the most direct fix?
options: Scale the clip playback rate by 7/5 or warp the stride
Enable stronger animation compression on the legs
Increase the number of bone influences per vertex
Switch the pose blend from slerp to plain lerp
quiz.explain: Sliding means the ground speed and the clip's authored speed disagree, so matching playback rate or stride to actual speed fixes it. Compression, skinning weights and interpolation type do not change ground contact speed.

quiz.q: Blending a clip with a second clip that has a quaternion on the opposite hemisphere makes a limb spin the long way round. Which step is missing?
options: Converting quaternions to Euler angles before blending
Flipping one quaternion's sign when the dot product is negative
Normalizing the bone's translation vector
Raising the animation sampling rate to 60 fps
quiz.explain: q and -q represent the same rotation, so interpolation must take the shortest arc by negating when the dot is negative. Euler blending introduces its own artifacts and does not solve this.

quiz.q: A boss has 25 attack animations that must move the character exactly as authored, including lunges and vaults over obstacles, with feet locked to the floor. Which approach fits best?
options: In-place clips with a constant capsule speed set by code
Root motion extracted from clips and applied to the character
Pure IK solving every limb with no authored clips
Dual-quaternion skinning applied on the mesh
quiz.explain: Root motion applies the authored displacement so feet stay planted through lunges and vaults. In-place plus constant speed re-introduces sliding, and skinning type is unrelated to locomotion.

quiz.q: A crowd of 200 characters costs 4 ms of CPU in animation evaluation, mostly for characters far from the camera. Which change gives the largest saving with the least visible loss?
options: Convert all clips to uncompressed data for speed
Add more transitions so that states can exit sooner
Add animation LOD: lower rate, skip IK and fingers far away
Move every crowd character over to root motion
quiz.explain: Cost scales with bones times evaluated clips, and distant characters do not need full fidelity. Uncompressed data and extra transitions do not reduce evaluation work; root motion changes control, not cost.

quiz.q: An animation looks perfect except for visible foot jitter after compression was raised to save memory. What explains this most plausibly?
options: Constant tracks were removed, which breaks foot contact
Hip error was tolerated and propagated down to the foot
The inverse bind matrices were quantized to 4 bone influences
The state machine's cross-fade duration was set too short
quiz.explain: Error in parent bones accumulates down the chain and is magnified at the foot, so tolerances should be measured at end effectors. Constant-track removal is lossless, and cross-fade length does not cause per-frame jitter in a steady clip.

quiz.q: On stairs and slopes, the character's feet clip into steps or hover above them, and its hands miss ledge grips, even though the clips look correct on flat ground. Which approach fits best?
options: Root motion extracted from the authored locomotion clips
Stride-matched playback rate for the run clip
An IK pass after pose evaluation to place feet and hands
Additive layers for lean and hit reactions on top
quiz.explain: The authored clips know nothing about the surface, so IK corrects end effectors against ground or grip targets after the pose is computed. Root motion and playback rate affect travel speed, not where feet land.

topics.title: Game math and game feel
topics.summary: The small pieces of math behind smooth motion, curves, randomness and juice, and why every one of them must be tuned against frame time rather than frames.

lesson.text: A platformer feels tight on the developer's 144 Hz monitor. On a Switch-class device locked to 30 fps the camera lags far behind the player, the screen shake looks like a different effect, and a level generated from seed 1234 on a tester's machine does not match the bug report. None of these are rendering or physics bugs. They come from a handful of small formulas that run every frame: smoothing, curves, springs, random numbers and the "juice" layered on top. Each one either respects frame time or quietly depends on frame rate.
Interpolation and the lerp trap

`Lerp(a, b, t) = a + (b - a) * t` is the most used function in gameplay code. Used with `t = elapsed / duration` it is exact and frame-rate independent: the result depends only on elapsed time. The trap is the smoothing idiom `x = Lerp(x, target, k)` called once per frame with a constant `k`. Each call removes a fraction `k` of the remaining distance, so after one second the remaining fraction is `(1 - k)^fps`. With `k = 0.1` that is 0.9^30 = 4% left at 30 fps but 0.9^144 = 0.00025% left at 144 fps: the same code is a lazy camera on one device and a rigid one on another. Multiplying by `Time.deltaTime` (`k = 6 * dt`) is closer but only a first-order approximation, and once `6 * dt` exceeds 1 during a hitch `Vector3.Lerp` clamps and snaps straight onto the target (an unclamped lerp overshoots).

lesson.text: The correct form is **exponential decay**: choose a rate in 1/s (or a half-life) and derive the per-frame fraction from the frame time, `k = 1 - exp(-rate * dt)`. Two half frames now compose into exactly one full frame, so the curve is identical at any frame rate, and `k` stays in [0, 1) no matter how long a hitch is. To port a value tuned at a known frame rate, `rate = -ln(1 - k) * fps`; `k = 0.1` tuned at 60 fps becomes a rate of about 6.3/s. The same idea applies to rotations with `Quaternion.Slerp` and to colours or volumes.
Easing and tweening

An **easing function** maps normalized time `u` in [0, 1] to progress, usually also in [0, 1]. Ease-out (fast start, gentle stop, for example `1 - (1 - u)^3`) suits things arriving, such as a panel sliding in; ease-in suits things leaving; ease-in-out suits camera moves between two framings. "Back" curves overshoot past 1 and return, and elastic curves oscillate, which reads as springy and playful. A **tween** is just from, to, duration and an easing function evaluated on elapsed time, so it is frame-rate independent by construction. The practical bugs are elsewhere: two tweens fighting over the same property, tweens running on scaled time while the game is paused, and tweens that keep a destroyed object alive. Unity's `AnimationCurve` lets designers draw an easing curve in the Inspector and code calls `curve.Evaluate(u)`; third-party tween libraries add sequencing and ownership rules, and their APIs differ, so check their docs rather than assuming.
Splines and constant speed

Camera rails, racing lines, patrol paths and projectile arcs are **splines**: piecewise cubic curves. A cubic **Bezier** segment has two endpoints and two handles that the curve does not pass through, which gives artists precise tangent control. A **Catmull-Rom** spline passes through every control point and derives tangents from the neighbours, so designers just drop points along a path. The standard (uniform) Catmull-Rom can overshoot or form small loops when points are unevenly spaced; the **centripetal** variant (parameter spacing by the square root of the chord length) avoids cusps and self-intersections and is the safer default for paths.

The spline parameter `t` is not distance. Each segment spans the same range of `t` whatever its length, so moving `t` at a constant rate makes an object rush through long segments and crawl through short ones. For constant speed, **reparameterise by arc length**: sample the curve densely once, store cumulative length in a table, and at runtime convert a distance travelled into `t` by binary search and linear interpolation in the table. Then advance distance by `speed * dt`. Unity's Splines package ships evaluation and length utilities, but the exact API depends on the package version, so read its documentation for the version you use.
