lesson.text: Springs and SmoothDamp

A damped spring pulls a value toward a target with acceleration `-stiffness * (x - target) - damping * velocity`. The **damping ratio** decides the character: below 1 (under-damped) it overshoots and wobbles, which suits UI pops and bouncy pickups; exactly 1 (**critically damped**) reaches the target as fast as possible without overshoot, which suits cameras and aim assist; above 1 it creeps. Unlike exponential decay, a spring has velocity, so a moving target is followed without the visible "snap" in speed when it starts or stops. Integrating a stiff spring with explicit Euler blows up when `dt` is large; use semi-implicit Euler with a capped step, or a closed-form solution. Unity's `Mathf.SmoothDamp` and `Vector3.SmoothDamp` are a critically damped spring with a stable approximation: you pass the velocity by `ref` and keep it between frames, and `smoothTime` is roughly the time to reach the target.
Seeds, determinism and noise

A **pseudo-random number generator** is a deterministic function of its state: the same seed gives the same sequence. That is what makes replays, daily challenges, procedural levels and bug reports reproducible, and it breaks the moment two systems share one generator. `UnityEngine.Random` is a single global stream, so if a particle effect draws three extra numbers, every later "random" choice in level generation shifts. Give each consumer its own generator (`System.Random(seed)`, a small xorshift or PCG struct, or `Unity.Mathematics.Random`, which must not be seeded with 0), derive sub-seeds from a master seed (`hash(worldSeed, chunkX, chunkY)`), and prefer **stateless hashing** for content addressed by position so chunk (12, -3) is identical no matter which chunks generated first. Integer arithmetic is reproducible everywhere; floating point results can differ across compilers, CPUs and platforms, so lockstep multiplayer usually needs fixed-point or tightly controlled floats.

Random values are uncorrelated: neighbouring samples jump arbitrarily, which looks like TV static. **Noise** gives smooth, controllable randomness. **Value noise** assigns random values to lattice points and interpolates them, which shows blocky grid artefacts. **Gradient noise** (Perlin) assigns random gradients instead, giving smoother features; **simplex** noise uses a triangular lattice, is cheaper in higher dimensions and has fewer axis-aligned artefacts. Layering octaves at doubling frequency and halving amplitude (**fBm**) produces terrain-like detail. `Mathf.PerlinNoise(x, y)` returns roughly 0 to 1 (it can slightly exceed the range), and gradient noise is the same value at every integer lattice point, so sampling at whole-number coordinates returns a constant; scale and offset the inputs, and use a seed-derived offset to get different worlds.
Game feel: camera, shake and timing

"Game feel" or **juice** is the layer of small responses that make input feel physical. The camera is the biggest one. A **dead zone** lets the player move inside a box without the camera moving, which removes jitter from small corrections; **look-ahead** shifts the framing in the movement or aim direction so the player sees where they are going; platformers often lock vertical follow to the last grounded height so jumps do not bob the screen. Smoothing on top of that uses the dt-correct decay or SmoothDamp from above, with separate settings per axis.

Good **screen shake** is driven by **trauma**, a value in [0, 1] that hits add to (clamped) and that decays linearly over time. The shake amount is `trauma²` (or cubed), so small hits barely register and big ones dominate, and the fall-off feels natural. The offset and a small roll angle come from **smooth noise** sampled at time times a frequency, not from `Random.insideUnitCircle` each frame: per-frame random jitter changes character with frame rate (more frames, more jumps) and reads as noise rather than impact. Apply the shake to a child offset of the camera so it never disturbs the follow logic, and offer a setting to reduce or disable it for players sensitive to motion.

lesson.text: Three more tools complete the kit. **Hit-stop** freezes the action for 40-120 ms on a heavy hit so the impact registers; setting `Time.timeScale = 0` freezes everything driven by scaled time (and stops `FixedUpdate`), so the timer that ends the freeze, UI and shake must use unscaled time, and a hit-stop during another hit-stop must not restore the wrong scale. **Squash and stretch** scales a sprite or mesh along the motion axis while preserving volume: stretch y by s and scale x by 1/s in 2D, or x and z by 1/sqrt(s) in 3D, then spring back. **Input buffering** and **coyote time**, covered with input handling, forgive presses that arrive slightly early or late. Every one of these is a duration or a rate in seconds. "Freeze for 4 frames" is 133 ms at 30 fps and 28 ms at 144 fps, which is the difference between a crunchy hit and an invisible one.

Test feel at two frame rates on purpose. Set `Application.targetFrameRate = 30` (and disable vSync) in a debug build, play the same moment, then repeat at your maximum. If the camera, shake or hit-stop feels different, some value is counted in frames. Keep tunables in seconds or 1/s in one ScriptableObject so designers can tweak them live in Play Mode.
Common misconceptions

items: 'Multiplying the lerp factor by Time.deltaTime makes it frame-rate independent.' It is only a first-order approximation; use 1 - exp(-rate * dt).
'Spline t is a percentage of the distance.' It is a parameter; constant speed needs an arc-length table.
'A seed makes my generation deterministic.' Only if nothing else draws from that stream and the math is reproducible on every target.
'Shake is random offsets each frame.' Good shake is smooth noise scaled by trauma squared, decaying over seconds.
'Juice is polish for the end of the project.' Camera, hit-stop and input forgiveness define how controls feel and should be in the first playable.

lesson.text: Agents reach for `Vector3.Lerp(current, target, speed * Time.deltaTime)` in Update by default, so state the rule up front: every smoothing, timer and effect duration is expressed in seconds or 1/s and is frame-rate independent. Then make it testable: ask for an EditMode test that runs the smoothing or spring for one simulated second at dt = 1/30 and dt = 1/144 and asserts the results match within a small epsilon, and a test that the same seed produces the same level hash twice in a row. Ask the agent to grep the project for `UnityEngine.Random` in generation code and for frame counters used as timers. For feel itself, have the agent expose every tunable in a ScriptableObject and draw debug gizmos (dead zone box, look-ahead point, trauma value) so you can tune in Play Mode; whether it feels right is your call, not the agent's.

The common thread is that the simulation should describe motion as a function of time, and the frame loop only samples it. Smoothing with decay rates, tweens on elapsed time, arc-length splines, springs with persisted velocity, seeded streams and trauma-driven shake all follow that rule, which is why they look the same on a 30 fps handheld and a 144 Hz monitor.

patterns.signal: `pos = Lerp(pos, target, 0.15f)` runs each frame and the camera lags at 30 fps but feels rigid at 144 fps
patterns.why: Using `k = 1 - exp(-rate * dt)` (or a half-life) removes the same fraction per second at any frame rate and never overshoots on hitches. Still lags a moving target; use a spring when you need to track velocity.

patterns.signal: A UI element or door must move from A to B over a fixed duration with a chosen feel
patterns.why: Compute `t = elapsed / duration`, apply an easing curve and `Lerp(a, b, ease(t))`. Exact and frame-rate independent by construction; restarting mid-tween needs care to avoid jumps.

patterns.signal: A camera or follower must chase a moving target smoothly, without overshoot or sudden velocity changes
patterns.why: Tracks target and velocity together, settling fastest without oscillation. Keep the velocity variable between frames; resetting it every frame or sharing it between objects breaks the motion.

patterns.signal: An object moving along a spline by increasing `t` at a fixed rate speeds up on long segments and slows in tight clusters
patterns.why: Precompute a table from distance to `t` and move by distance, giving constant speed. Costs a lookup table per spline that must be rebuilt when points change.

patterns.signal: A Catmull-Rom path through unevenly spaced points loops or overshoots at sharp corners
patterns.why: Using alpha 0.5 knot spacing avoids cusps and self-intersections while still passing through every point. Slightly more math than uniform; use Bezier when artists need direct tangent control.

patterns.signal: A seeded level differs between runs because particles or other systems draw from the same global random stream
patterns.why: Give each consumer its own generator instance seeded from the master seed, so unrelated code cannot shift its sequence. Seeds must be derived deterministically and generators kept out of shared global state.

patterns.signal: Content must be random but identical whenever the same tile or chunk is revisited, in any order
patterns.why: Hash `(seed, x, y)` into a value instead of advancing a stream, so results do not depend on visit order. Hash quality matters: weak hashes show patterns.

patterns.signal: Screen shake uses a new random offset every frame, looks like jitter and gets stronger at higher fps
patterns.why: Sample smooth noise over time scaled by `trauma^2`, and decay trauma per second. Frame-rate independent and readable; offer a reduced-shake accessibility option.

patterns.signal: A hit-stop counts frames, so it lasts 133 ms on a 30 fps handheld but 28 ms on a 144 Hz monitor
patterns.why: Express hit-stop, flashes and windows as real time so feel is the same on every device. Use unscaled time for the hit-stop timer itself, or a frozen time scale will never end it.

patterns.signal: The camera jerks with every small player motion and the player cannot see what is ahead
patterns.why: Ignore movement inside a dead zone and offset the camera toward the velocity or aim direction with smoothing. Tune per genre; too much look-ahead feels detached.

patterns.signal: Jumps and landings feel stiff and weightless even though the physics is correct
patterns.why: Briefly scale the sprite or mesh along motion on takeoff and impact, preserving volume, and ease back over a fraction of a second. Purely visual; keep colliders unchanged.

keyPoints: Per-frame Lerp(x, target, k) with constant k depends on frame rate; use k = 1 - exp(-rate * dt) or a half-life instead.
Easing maps normalized time to progress, and tweens driven by elapsed time are frame-rate independent by construction.
Spline t is not distance; constant speed needs an arc-length table, and centripetal Catmull-Rom avoids loops on uneven points.
Critically damped springs such as SmoothDamp follow moving targets without overshoot; keep their velocity between frames.
Give each system its own seeded generator or position hash, and use smooth noise, not per-frame random values, for shake and terrain.
Dead zones, look-ahead, trauma-squared shake, hit-stop and squash and stretch are all tuned in seconds, never in frames.

quiz.q: A camera uses `pos = Vector3.Lerp(pos, target, 0.15f)` in Update. Testers on 30 fps devices say it lags; on 144 Hz monitors it feels rigid. What is the right fix?
options: Move the code into FixedUpdate so it runs at a constant rate
Multiply 0.15 by Time.deltaTime and keep the rest unchanged
Use k = 1 - exp(-rate * Time.deltaTime) with a rate in 1/s
Clamp the frame rate to 60 fps on every platform we ship
quiz.explain: Exponential decay derived from dt gives the same curve at any frame rate. FixedUpdate makes the smoothing stutter against rendering, dt-scaling is only approximate and snaps on hitches, and a frame cap hides the bug.

quiz.q: A rail-shooter camera moves along a Catmull-Rom path by increasing t at a fixed rate. It speeds up on long straights and slows in tight clusters of points. What should change?
options: Convert distance travelled to t through an arc-length table
Add more control points so that every segment has more of them
Switch the path to a Bezier spline with the same points
Ease the t value with an ease-in-out curve across the path
quiz.explain: Each segment spans the same range of t regardless of length, so constant speed needs reparameterisation by arc length. More points or a different spline type still has t unrelated to distance, and easing only adds more speed variation.

quiz.q: A daily-challenge dungeon uses `Random.InitState(dailySeed)` and `UnityEngine.Random` for layout. Players report different layouts for the same day. What is the most likely cause?
options: Perlin noise returns different values on each platform
Other systems also draw from the global stream mid-generation
Random.InitState only accepts seeds below 65,536
The seed must be re-applied before every single draw
quiz.explain: UnityEngine.Random is one shared stream, so any extra draw (particles, AI, a coroutine finishing earlier) shifts later values. A dedicated generator or position hashing per system fixes it. The other options are not how the API behaves.

quiz.q: Your screen shake uses `Random.insideUnitCircle * strength` every frame. It looks like jitter, and stronger at 144 fps. Which redesign fixes both problems?
options: Run the shake from FixedUpdate at the physics rate
Divide strength by the frame rate to normalize it
Lerp toward a new random offset with a constant k each frame
Scale smooth noise sampled over time by trauma squared
quiz.explain: Noise sampled from time is smooth and independent of how often you sample it, and trauma squared shapes the decay. Fixed-rate random offsets still jitter, scaling by frame rate does not create smoothness, and constant-k lerp reintroduces frame-rate dependence.

quiz.q: A heavy attack triggers a "4-frame hit-stop" by setting timeScale to 0 and counting frames. Players on handhelds call it crunchy; PC players at 144 fps barely notice it. What is the best change?
options: Raise the hit-stop to 10 frames on every platform
Freeze for a duration in seconds, timed with unscaled time
Run the hit-stop counter inside FixedUpdate instead
Slow time to 0.5 instead of freezing it fully
quiz.explain: Four frames is 133 ms at 30 fps and 28 ms at 144 fps. A duration in seconds measured on unscaled time behaves the same everywhere; FixedUpdate does not even run while timeScale is 0.

quiz.q: A third-person camera is already smoothed, but it twitches with every small strafe, and players cannot see enough of the path ahead when sprinting. What should you reach for?
options: Exponential smoothing with `1 - exp(-rate * dt)` on position
A camera dead zone combined with look-ahead on velocity
Trauma-based noise shake applied to the camera
Squash and stretch applied to the character mesh
quiz.explain: A dead zone ignores small movements and look-ahead shifts framing toward where the player is heading. More smoothing would add lag without showing the path ahead, and shake or squash do not affect framing.

topics.title: Assets, memory and streaming
topics.summary: How source art becomes platform-ready data, how references survive renames, and how budgets, streaming and pooling keep memory and frame time stable.

lesson.text: A mobile game ships with 1.5 GB of uncompressed source art and must run in roughly 1-1.5 GB of RAM shared with the OS, with the process killed silently if it goes over. A console title may have 8-13 GB usable and a 100 GB open world. The work of an engine's asset system is to move data from authoring formats into compact, fast-loading, platform-specific forms, to keep references stable, and to get exactly the right data into memory at the right time without hitches.
Import and cooking pipelines

Source assets (PSD, FBX, WAV, authored files) are optimized for editing, not for loading. An **import** step converts them into engine-internal representations: a texture becomes mip chains with a chosen compression format, a mesh becomes vertex and index buffers with an optimized vertex cache order, audio is encoded. **Cooking** (or building) is the platform-specific pass: ASTC on mobile, BCn (DXT) on desktop and consoles, endianness conversion where needed, packing into archives, and dependency resolution. The output is designed so that loading is mostly a memcpy and pointer fix-up rather than parsing.

Two properties matter. **Determinism**: the same inputs and settings produce the same outputs, so build caches work. **Incrementality**: a change to one texture reimports only that texture and its dependents, using content hashes plus settings hashes. Teams with 100k assets live or die by a shared cache server that avoids reimporting on every machine.
References, GUIDs and dependencies

A prefab references a material, which references textures and a shader. If references were file paths, renaming a folder would break the project. Engines instead give each asset a persistent **GUID** (stored in a sidecar such as a `.meta` file in Unity, or in the asset header) and serialize references as GUIDs. Paths are a lookup index; identity is the GUID. This has consequences. Moving files inside the editor keeps references; moving them outside the editor (a script, a git operation that drops sidecar files) orphans them. Duplicating a sidecar causes GUID collisions. References form a **dependency graph**, and building a bundle must include everything reachable, which is where accidental bloat comes from: one reference from a menu to a high-resolution cinematic pulls the cinematic into the menu's bundle.

items: Hard references load their targets together with the referrer; they are simple and cause loading chains.
Soft or lazy references store only the ID; you request the load explicitly and receive an async handle.
Reference counting on handles lets the system unload an asset when the last user releases it; leaks happen when someone forgets to release.

lesson.text: Memory budgets per platform

Memory is a design constraint, set early and per platform. A plausible mobile budget on a mid-tier phone: 700 MB total app, with textures 250-350 MB, meshes 50 MB, audio 40 MB, animation 30 MB, scripts and managed heap 100 MB, and the remainder for rendering targets and engine. A texture's GPU size is `width x height x bytes-per-pixel x 1.33` (the mip chain adds one third). A 2048 x 2048 RGBA32 texture is 16 MB, plus mips about 21 MB. With ASTC 6x6 (about 3.56 bits per pixel) the same texture is about 1.9 MB base, 2.5 MB with mips, close to an 8x saving. That is why compression format choice is the cheapest memory win in a project.

lesson.text: Loading and streaming

Synchronous loading blocks the main thread: loading a 40 MB bundle from flash at 150 MB/s is about 270 ms, which is 16 dropped frames at 60 fps. Load asynchronously, with decompression and deserialization on worker threads and only the final object instantiation or GPU upload on the main thread, ideally time-sliced to a per-frame budget (for example 2 ms). **Streaming** extends this to the world: divide levels into cells or sublevels, load those near the player based on distance and predicted movement, and unload those behind. **Texture streaming** keeps only the mip levels needed for the current screen size: a texture covering 100 pixels does not need its 2048 level. The system tracks a memory budget and lowers mips when over it, which is why a texture can look blurry for a moment after a camera cut.

lesson.text: Streaming problems rarely show up on a developer machine with an NVMe drive. Test on the slowest target storage (a phone with a full flash, a console on its hard-drive install mode) and with a cold cache. Hitches that appear only when turning quickly are usually missed prefetch, not slow code.
Object pooling

Instantiating a bullet, a particle burst or an enemy costs allocation, component setup and later garbage collection. A **pool** preallocates N instances, hands them out on `Get()` by activating and resetting them, and takes them back on `Release()`. It makes cost predictable: no allocation during gameplay and no garbage. Key rules: pooled objects must be fully reset (velocity, timers, event subscriptions, particle state), pool size needs a cap with a defined policy on exhaustion (grow, recycle the oldest, or refuse), and the pool should be warmed up during a loading screen rather than on first use. Unity ships a ready-made generic pool, `UnityEngine.Pool.ObjectPool<T>`, so a hand-written one like the sketch below is mainly for understanding or for engine-agnostic code.
Fragmentation

Free memory is not always usable memory. Allocating blocks of mixed sizes and freeing them in a different order leaves holes: 200 MB free total but no contiguous 32 MB block, so an allocation fails or the heap grows. Symptoms: memory climbs over a long session though live data is stable, and out-of-memory crashes appear after hours. Mitigations are to allocate by lifetime (per-frame linear arenas reset every frame, per-level arenas freed together, long-lived pools), to use fixed-size block allocators, to keep large buffers resident rather than repeatedly freed and reallocated, and to avoid growing managed collections without bound. In a garbage-collected runtime, the GC heap can fragment too, and large-object allocations may be handled differently, so reuse big arrays.

lesson.text: Misconceptions

items: 'Unloading the scene frees its memory.' Only if nothing still references the assets; a static field or a cached handle keeps them alive.
'Texture size on disk is its memory size.' PNG or JPG sizes are irrelevant; GPU memory depends on dimensions and the GPU format.
'Pooling is always a win.' A small pool of rarely used objects wastes memory; pooling pays off for frequent, short-lived, uniform objects.

lesson.text: Agents love `Instantiate`, `Destroy`, `Resources.Load` and string-path lookups because they are short and work in a demo. Tell the agent the memory budget, the target platform and that assets are loaded by async handle or GUID reference. Verify there are no per-frame allocations (LINQ, string concatenation, new lists in Update), that every load has a matching release, and that hard references do not drag large assets into small bundles. Ask the agent to produce a memory-report check, such as a profiler capture comparison before and after a level transition, rather than claiming it is fine.

patterns.signal: Projectiles or effects are created and destroyed hundreds of times per second and GC or allocation spikes appear
patterns.why: Preallocate instances and reuse them, resetting state on spawn. Allocation becomes predictable; costs resident memory, and stale state from an incompletely reset object causes subtle bugs.

patterns.signal: Thousands of trees or rocks each hold their own copy of the same mesh, material and settings
patterns.why: Share the intrinsic data and keep only per-instance state (transform, colour), which also lets the GPU draw instances in one call. Changing shared data changes every instance, so per-instance edits must stay separate.

patterns.signal: Systems hold raw pointers or object references to entities that may be destroyed and their slots reused
patterns.why: Store an index plus generation number; a lookup detects a stale handle instead of touching freed or reused memory. Adds one indirection per access and a central table to manage.

patterns.signal: A level transition drops frames while the profiler shows file reads and deserialization on the main thread
patterns.why: Read and decode on worker threads, then integrate on the main thread a few objects per frame within a ms budget. Removes hitches; content appears over several frames, so plan loading screens or placeholders.

patterns.signal: An open world does not fit in memory, but the player only needs what is near them
patterns.why: Load cells, LODs and texture mips by distance and priority within a fixed memory budget, evicting what is far. Needs prediction for fast travel and fallbacks for data that arrives late.

patterns.signal: A menu bundle is unexpectedly huge because one reference pulls in a cinematic and its textures
patterns.use: Soft references for rarely used assets
patterns.why: Store only the asset ID and load explicitly when needed, cutting the dependency chain. You must handle load latency and release, and missing references fail at runtime instead of build time.

patterns.signal: Textures dominate memory and are stored as RGBA32 on a memory-tight mobile target
patterns.why: GPU-compressed formats cut texture memory by roughly 4-8x and stay compressed in memory. Quality loss is visible on gradients and normal maps, so choose block sizes per texture type.

patterns.signal: Memory grows across level loads because loaded assets are never released
patterns.why: Pair every load with a release and unload when the count reaches zero. Leaks become traceable; an extra release unloads assets still in use, so tie handles to owner lifetime.

patterns.signal: Each frame makes many short-lived temporary allocations for lists, strings and scratch data
patterns.why: Bump-allocate from a block and reset it at frame end, so allocation is a pointer add with no fragmentation. Nothing may keep pointers into it past the frame.

patterns.signal: The game crashes on allocation after hours of play although free memory looks sufficient
patterns.why: Fragmentation leaves no contiguous block large enough. Group allocations by lifetime (level, frame, permanent) and reuse large buffers instead of reallocating.

keyPoints: Cooking converts editor formats into platform-specific, load-ready data; deterministic, incremental builds depend on hashing inputs and settings.
GUID references make identity independent of path, but they form a dependency graph that can silently bloat bundles.
Texture compression format dominates memory: the same 2048x2048 texture can be 21 MB or about 2.5 MB depending on format.
Load asynchronously and time-slice main-thread work; stream by distance and mip level against a fixed budget.
Pools make allocation predictable, and lifetime-based allocators plus reuse of large buffers fight fragmentation.

quiz.q: A designer reorganizes folders using the OS file manager and the sidecar metadata files are left behind. Prefabs now show missing references. What is the underlying cause?
options: Cooking changed the endianness of the cooked assets
Texture compression invalidated the whole dependency graph
GUIDs carrying identity were lost when assets moved without sidecars
Async loading raced with the move on disk
quiz.explain: References are serialized as GUIDs held in sidecar data; moving the file without it creates new identities. Cooking, compression and async loading are not involved at author time.

quiz.q: A mobile game is at 900 MB with a 700 MB budget, and textures are 520 MB in RGBA32. Which single change is most likely to bring it under budget with the least content work?
options: Switch to ASTC with an appropriate block size
Convert PNG sources to JPG
Pool the textures at runtime
Load textures synchronously to avoid duplicates
quiz.explain: GPU memory is set by the in-memory format; ASTC cuts the size several times over RGBA32. Source file format does not change runtime size, and pooling or synchronous loading do not reduce texture bytes.

quiz.q: After 3 hours of play the game crashes on allocation although a memory capture shows 250 MB free and live data steady. Which diagnosis fits?
options: A mip streaming budget that was set far too high
A GUID collision between two different prefabs
Garbage collection running far too frequently
Fragmentation: free memory exists but in blocks too small
quiz.explain: Enough total free memory but failed allocation with stable live data points to holes in the heap. GC frequency and GUID collisions produce different symptoms, and a streaming budget would degrade quality rather than crash.

quiz.q: A bullet-hell game spawns 300 projectiles per second, each living about 2 seconds, and shows periodic frame spikes with garbage collection in the profiler. What is the best fix?
options: Use `Instantiate` with a lower spawn rate
Preallocate a pool of about 700 projectiles and reset them on reuse
Load the bullet prefab synchronously each time
Destroy bullets on the next frame instead of after 2 seconds
quiz.explain: Peak concurrency is about 600, so a warmed pool with a margin removes allocation and GC entirely. Lowering the spawn rate changes gameplay, and the other options keep the allocations.

quiz.q: A level transition drops 16 frames. The profiler shows a 40 MB bundle read and deserialization on the main thread. What change addresses the cause?
options: Increase the target frame rate to 120 fps
Switch all of the audio over to a lossy format
Add a hard reference from the main menu to the level scene
Load async with worker decode, time-sliced instantiation
quiz.explain: The stall is blocking work on the main thread, so moving it to async loading with a per-frame budget removes the hitch. A hard reference makes loading even more coupled, and the other changes are unrelated.

quiz.q: Homing missiles store references to enemies by array slot. Enemies die and new ones reuse the freed slot, so a missile sometimes retargets a brand-new enemy it was never aimed at. Which approach fits best?
options: An object pool that recycles the enemy instances
Reference counting with explicit load and release calls
Distance-based streaming of enemy data against a budget
Generational handles that fail when the slot is reused
quiz.explain: A handle stores slot plus generation, so a stale handle is detected when the slot is recycled. An object pool is what recycles the slots here and would not fix stale references, and the other two manage asset lifetime.

topics.title: Game AI and navigation
topics.summary: How enemies decide (state machines, behaviour trees, utility AI) and move (A*, navigation meshes, steering) within a frame budget.

lesson.text: Thirty enemies must decide what to do, find a route through a level, and move without bumping into each other, all within perhaps 1-2 ms of CPU per frame. Game AI is not machine learning for most shipped titles; it is a collection of cheap, authorable, debuggable techniques whose goal is believable behaviour that designers can tune. Three layers recur: **decision making** (what do I want), **pathfinding** (how do I get there) and **steering** (how do I move this frame).
Finite state machines

A **finite state machine (FSM)** has a set of states (Patrol, Chase, Attack, Flee), one active at a time, and transitions triggered by conditions (player seen, health below 20%). It is simple, fast and easy to visualize, and it is the right tool for small behaviours. The problem is scale: with N states, transitions grow toward N squared, and adding 'investigate a noise' means touching every state that should be interruptible. Hierarchical FSMs (a Combat super-state containing Attack and Take Cover) reduce this but the structure remains rigid.
Note the `1.2f` hysteresis. Without it, an agent standing exactly on the boundary flips between Chase and Attack every frame. Hysteresis and minimum state durations are the standard cure for flicker.
Behaviour trees

A **behaviour tree (BT)** is a tree of nodes ticked from the root each update (or event-driven). Each node returns Success, Failure or Running. Composite nodes control flow: a **Selector** tries children in order until one succeeds (fallback), a **Sequence** runs children in order until one fails (all conditions and actions must pass). Decorators modify a child (invert, repeat, cooldown, condition gate), and leaves are conditions or actions. Compared to FSMs, BTs make priorities explicit (left-to-right order), are modular (subtrees are reusable), and avoid transition spaghetti. The costs: reactive behaviour requires re-evaluating conditions from the top, which wastes cycles unless you use event-driven invalidation, and the 'Running' state needs careful handling so that a higher-priority branch can abort a lower one cleanly.

Selector
  Sequence [Flee]     : IsHealthLow -> HasCoverNearby -> MoveToCover
  Sequence [Attack]   : CanSeeTarget -> InRange -> Fire
  Sequence [Chase]    : HasTargetLastKnown -> MoveTo(lastKnown)
  Patrol

lesson.text: Utility AI

When many options are plausible and the best depends on a mix of factors, **utility AI** scores each candidate action with a function of the world and picks the highest. A score is typically the product (or weighted combination) of **considerations**, each mapping an input (distance, health, ammo) through a response curve to 0-1. 'Heal' might score high when health is low and no enemy is close; 'Attack' when ammo is plentiful and the target is near. Utility gives smooth, context-sensitive behaviour and avoids hard thresholds, which is why life-simulation and strategy games use it heavily. Its weakness is tuning: curves interact, and a designer cannot easily answer 'why did it do that' without a debugger that shows the scores. Always build a visualization of the considered scores.

items: FSM: few states, clear modes, tiny cost, brittle as it grows.
Behaviour tree: prioritized, modular, designer-friendly, good default for action game enemies.
Utility AI: many competing options, graded responses, needs tooling and tuning.
Combine them: a BT whose selector uses utility scores, or an FSM per high-level mode with BTs inside.

lesson.text: A* pathfinding

**A-star (A*)** finds a least-cost path on a graph. It keeps an open set ordered by `f(n) = g(n) + h(n)`, where `g` is the cost from the start and `h` is a heuristic estimate of the cost to the goal. If `h` never overestimates (is **admissible**), A* returns an optimal path, and the closer `h` is to the true cost, the fewer nodes are expanded. On a 4-connected grid, use Manhattan distance; on an 8-connected grid, octile distance; in continuous space, Euclidean. With `h = 0` it degrades to Dijkstra; an overweighted `h` is faster but gives suboptimal paths, an acceptable trade in games. Real costs: a naive search over a 256 x 256 grid might expand thousands of nodes; an open-set binary heap makes each push and pop O(log n), and a per-node generation stamp avoids clearing arrays between searches.

lesson.text: Games rarely run A* on a raw grid for large worlds. Techniques to stay in budget: hierarchical pathfinding (plan across regions first, then refine), time-sliced searches spread over frames, path caching and sharing between agents going to the same target, and requesting a path only when the target moved far enough to matter.
Navigation meshes

A **navigation mesh (navmesh)** represents the walkable surface as convex polygons (often triangles merged into convex polys) with adjacency across shared edges. It is generated from level geometry by voxelizing the world at the agent's radius, height, step height and maximum slope, finding walkable spans, and building contours and polygons (the approach popularized by Recast). The graph for A* is then polygon centres or edge midpoints, which is far smaller than a grid: a large level might have 5,000 polys instead of 500,000 cells. The path through polygons is converted to a smooth route with the **funnel algorithm**, which finds the shortest line through the sequence of shared edges. Navmeshes are baked per agent type (a large monster needs a different mesh from a human), and dynamic obstacles are handled either by runtime carving or by local avoidance rather than a rebake.

lesson.text: Steering and avoidance

The path is a list of waypoints; **steering behaviours** turn it into per-frame velocity. Core primitives from Reynolds: seek, arrive (decelerate to a stop), pursue (aim at the predicted position), separation, alignment and cohesion for flocks. Each produces a desired velocity or force; you combine them with weights and clamp by max speed and turn rate, so motion respects the character's physical limits. For crowds, **local avoidance** such as RVO or ORCA treats nearby agents as moving obstacles and picks a velocity that avoids collision for the next couple of seconds. This is why 50 agents can cross a plaza without a global replan. Typical failure modes: agents jittering at corners (path corners too tight, no arrival radius), deadlock in doorways (no priority or yielding rules), and agents stuck because the navmesh and physics collider disagree.

Separate what the AI decides from how often it decides. Decisions can run at 5-10 Hz and be staggered across agents, while steering runs every frame. This single change often cuts AI cost by 5-10x with no visible loss.
Budgets and misconceptions

Spend budget where the player notices: agents on screen or near the player get full logic, distant ones get a coarse tick or a simplified simulation (an 'AI LOD'). Perception is the hidden cost: line-of-sight raycasts per agent per target per frame add up (50 agents x 10 targets x 60 Hz is 30,000 raycasts a second), so stagger and cache them. A common misconception is that smarter AI is better; players read intent, so telegraphed, fair, readable behaviour (an enemy that announces its attack) beats clever hidden behaviour.

When asking an AI agent for enemy AI, specify the technique (BT, FSM or utility), the tick rate, the navigation system in use and the agent's physical size. Verify that it does not run A* every frame, does not allocate paths per query (reuse buffers), has hysteresis or cooldowns on state changes, and exposes debug visualization (current state, scores, path). Agents often write an FSM as a giant switch with duplicated conditions or call pathfinding from Update unconditionally; request a repath-only-on-change rule and test with 100 agents to see the cost.

patterns.signal: An enemy at exactly attack range flips between Chase and Attack every frame
patterns.why: Use different enter and exit thresholds (for example exit at 1.2x the range) and minimum state durations. Cures flicker cheaply; FSM transitions still grow toward N squared as states are added.

patterns.signal: An FSM has many states that all need the same 'flee when hurt' or 'stunned' transition
patterns.why: Group states under super-states (Combat contains Attack and Cover) so shared transitions live once at the parent. Reduces duplication; the structure is still rigid when priorities change often.

patterns.signal: After an interruption such as a cutscene or stun the agent should resume exactly what it was doing
patterns.why: Push the interrupting state and pop back to the previous one, so the FSM remembers history. Watch for stacks that grow unboundedly when interruptions nest.

patterns.signal: Designers need explicit priorities like flee over attack over patrol and want to reuse branches across enemy types
patterns.why: Selectors give left-to-right priority and subtrees are reusable modules. Re-evaluating from the root costs cycles unless conditions use event-driven aborts; long Running actions need clean interruption.

patterns.signal: An agent has many options whose desirability depends on graded factors like health, ammo, distance and threat
patterns.why: Score each option with response curves and pick the best, giving nuanced behaviour without transition spaghetti. Hard to tune and explain, so build debug views showing every score.

patterns.signal: Agents must chain actions toward a goal (get key, open door, reach target) in combinations designers cannot script
patterns.why: Actions declare preconditions and effects and a planner searches for a sequence reaching the goal. Emergent and flexible; planning is costly and behaviour is harder to direct, so replan sparingly.

patterns.signal: Agents need the shortest route through a level graph quickly and with optimal results
patterns.why: A heuristic that never overestimates keeps A* optimal, and a tighter one expands fewer nodes. Weighting the heuristic trades optimality for speed; time-slice long searches across frames.

patterns.signal: Grid pathfinding over 500,000 cells is slow and paths zigzag between cell centres
patterns.why: Convex polygons cover walkable space with far fewer nodes, and the funnel algorithm straightens the corridor into a taut path. Baked per agent radius; dynamic obstacles need carving or rebakes.

patterns.signal: Hundreds of units must reach the same destination, such as the player base in an RTS
patterns.why: Compute one integration field from the goal and let every unit follow its local gradient, so cost no longer scales with unit count. Expensive for many distinct goals and needs local avoidance for crowding.

patterns.signal: Agents follow their paths correctly but bump into each other and pile up in doorways
patterns.why: Steering turns waypoints into limited acceleration, and velocity-obstacle avoidance resolves local collisions without global replanning. Dense crowds can still deadlock; add priorities or yielding.

patterns.signal: AI decision logic and line-of-sight checks take most of the frame for 80 agents while steering is cheap
patterns.why: Run decisions and perception at 5-10 Hz spread across frames, while steering runs every frame. Huge savings with slight reaction delay; raise the rate for agents near the player.

patterns.signal: Several behaviours read and write the same facts about targets, last-known positions and alerts
patterns.why: A shared key-value store per agent or squad decouples who senses a fact from who uses it. Easy to overuse; untyped keys and stale entries need naming rules and timestamps.

keyPoints: FSMs suit few modes, behaviour trees give explicit priority and modularity, utility AI handles many graded options but needs debug tooling.
A* with an admissible heuristic is optimal; games often accept a weighted heuristic and time-slicing for speed.
Navmeshes represent walkable space as convex polygons baked per agent size, searched with A* and smoothed by the funnel algorithm.
Steering turns waypoints into physically limited motion, and local avoidance like RVO or ORCA resolves crowds without global replanning.
Decisions can run at low rate and staggered while steering runs each frame; hysteresis prevents state flicker.

quiz.q: An enemy standing exactly at attack range flips between Chase and Attack every frame, producing stutter. Which fix addresses the cause?
options: Add hysteresis: use a larger exit range than entry range
Replace the FSM with A* pathfinding for the enemy
Run the state machine at a much higher tick rate
Increase the navmesh agent radius for this enemy
quiz.explain: The conditions flip across a single threshold, so separate enter and exit thresholds stop oscillation. A higher tick rate makes flicker worse, and pathfinding and agent radius are unrelated.

quiz.q: A designer wants guard AI where 'flee when low health' always outranks 'attack', which outranks 'patrol', and wants to reuse the attack branch for other enemy types. Which structure fits best?
options: A flat FSM with a transition from every state to every other
A behaviour tree whose selector orders the branches by priority
A grid-based A* search over the actions
A steering behaviour blend with equal weights
quiz.explain: A selector tries children in priority order, and subtrees are reusable modules. A flat FSM makes priorities implicit across many transitions, and A* and steering solve different problems.

quiz.q: A* on a 4-connected grid uses Euclidean distance as its heuristic. Compared to Manhattan distance, what is the result?
options: It returns non-optimal paths because it overestimates
It becomes Dijkstra and expands everything
It stays optimal but expands more nodes because it is less informed
It cannot handle obstacles
quiz.explain: Euclidean never overestimates on a 4-connected grid, so it is admissible and optimal, but it underestimates more than Manhattan and so searches more nodes. It is not h = 0, so it does not degenerate to Dijkstra.

quiz.q: A large level has 500,000 walkable grid cells and pathfinding takes 12 ms per query. Which change most directly reduces search size while keeping accurate routes?
options: Switch to a convex-polygon navmesh with funnel smoothing
Lower the steering max speed of every agent
Use Dijkstra instead of A* for each query
Increase the number of agents sharing one search
quiz.explain: A navmesh collapses open areas into a few thousand polygons, so the graph being searched is orders of magnitude smaller. Dijkstra expands more nodes, and speed and agent count do not shrink the graph.

quiz.q: Profiling 80 agents shows AI at 6 ms per frame, with most time in decision logic and line-of-sight checks, while steering is cheap. What change should come first?
options: Remove local avoidance from all of the agents
Switch from a navmesh over to a uniform grid
Stagger decisions and sight checks to about 8 Hz, caching results
Replace behaviour trees with one larger switch statement
quiz.explain: Decisions and sight checks do not need 60 Hz; staggering them cuts cost several-fold while steering stays smooth every frame. Avoidance and the navigation representation are not where the time goes.

quiz.q: In an RTS, a player orders 400 units to move to the same base. Running a separate A* query per unit causes frame spikes. What should you reach for?
options: A* with an admissible heuristic run for each unit
A navmesh with funnel smoothing run for each unit
A flow field computed once from the destination
Staggered low-rate decision ticks for the units
quiz.explain: One flow field gives every cell a direction toward the shared goal, so each unit just reads its cell. Per-unit A*, even optimal or smoothed, repeats the same search 400 times, and staggering only spreads the cost.

topics.title: Input, audio and multiplayer networking
topics.summary: How engines abstract and buffer input, mix audio within a voice budget, and keep multiplayer responsive using authority, prediction, rollback and lag compensation.

lesson.text: A player presses jump 40 ms before landing and expects the jump to happen. A gunshot plays with a hundred other sounds and still has to cut through the mix. Two players 80 ms apart each see themselves react instantly, and neither can cheat. These three systems share a theme: they hide the gap between what the player did and what the machine can show, on a strict clock.
Input abstraction and buffering

Hardcoding `if (key == Space)` breaks on gamepads, remapping and touch. Engines add a layer: raw devices produce **actions** ('Jump', 'Move', 'Fire') through **bindings**, with processing such as dead zones, sensitivity curves and composite bindings (WASD to a 2D vector). Gameplay reads actions, never devices; rebinding, context switching (menu vs. gameplay) and multiple players on one machine then come for free. Analog sticks need a radial dead zone (for example 0.15-0.25) because worn sticks never rest at exactly zero, and rescaling the remainder so output still reaches 1.

Input is sampled at some rate and consumed on a different one. If you poll in a fixed 50 Hz physics step but events arrive at 60 Hz, a short press can fall between ticks and be lost, so capture presses as edge events with timestamps and consume them in the step. **Input buffering** extends this for feel: store a press for a short window (typically 80-150 ms) and consume it when the action becomes legal, such as a queued jump just before landing or combo input during the end of an attack animation. **Coyote time** is the mirror: allow a jump for about 100 ms after leaving a ledge. Both are tuned to match what players believe they did.

lesson.text: Audio mixing and voices

Audio runs on its own real-time thread, producing buffers (commonly 512 or 1024 samples at 48 kHz, roughly 10-21 ms) that must be filled every time or the player hears a crackle. Sources feed **voices**: each playing sound occupies a voice, and each voice costs decoding, resampling, spatialization and effects. Platforms have voice limits (tens to a few hundred), and engines enforce a **voice budget** by priority: when 64 footsteps and explosions compete, the system culls the quietest or lowest-priority instance. Short, frequent sounds are decompressed into memory; long music streams from disk to save RAM; mid-length sounds use compressed-in-memory formats, trading CPU for memory.

A **mixer** organizes sounds into a tree of buses (Master, Music, SFX, Dialogue, UI). Each bus carries its own volume and effects (EQ, compression, reverb sends). Two techniques make a mix legible: **ducking** (sidechain compression lowers music when dialogue plays) and **dynamic range management** so quiet footsteps and loud explosions are both audible at the player's volume. Volume sliders must map perceptually: a linear slider from 0 to 1 sounds wrong because loudness is logarithmic, so convert with `dB = 20 * log10(v)` and clamp at about -80 dB for silence. 3D audio adds distance attenuation, panning or HRTF binaural rendering, Doppler and occlusion.

Hitches in audio usually mean the mixer thread missed its deadline, from long main-thread stalls, cold-loading a compressed clip, or too many voices with heavy effects. Preload and pool common sounds, and move reverbs to shared sends instead of per-voice instances.
Networking: client-server authority

In a networked game, someone decides what is true. In the usual **client-server** model, the server is **authoritative**: clients send inputs, the server simulates and broadcasts state, so a modified client cannot declare 'I have 999 health'. Peer-to-peer without authority is fast to build but invites cheating and needs NAT traversal or relays to connect players. A dedicated or host server sets the rule: **clients propose, the server disposes**. The core difficulty is latency. At 60 ms round trip, naive waiting makes your own character respond 60 ms late, which feels bad.
Lockstep

**Deterministic lockstep** sends only inputs; every machine runs the identical simulation and advances turn N once it has everyone's inputs for N. Bandwidth is tiny (a few bytes per player per tick, which is why RTS games with thousands of units use it), but it requires bit-exact determinism (fixed-point or carefully controlled floating point, deterministic iteration order, seeded random numbers) and the game runs at the speed of the slowest player; typically input is applied a few ticks in the future to hide latency.
Client-side prediction and reconciliation

In action games the client does not wait. **Client-side prediction** applies your own input locally at once. The input, tagged with a sequence number, goes to the server; the server simulates it and returns the authoritative state with the last input sequence it processed. **Reconciliation**: the client compares that state with its predicted state at that sequence; if they differ, it rewinds to the server state and **replays** all inputs not yet acknowledged. Usually the difference is zero and the player notices nothing; after a collision with something unpredicted, the correction is smoothed visually rather than snapped. Other players are not predicted but **interpolated**: remote entities are displayed about 100 ms in the past between two received snapshots so motion is smooth despite packet jitter.

client: tick 100 input#57 -> apply locally, send to server, store in pending[]
server: processes #57 -> sends state {pos, lastProcessed=57}
client: on state: drop pending <= 57, set state=server, replay pending (#58,#59,#60)
        if |predicted - corrected| small: smooth; else snap

lesson.text: Rollback netcode

Fighting games need frame-exact responsiveness. **Rollback** predicts the remote player's input (assume it repeats), simulates immediately, and when the real input arrives and differs, **rolls back** to the last confirmed frame, applies the correct input and **re-simulates** forward to the present within a single frame. This needs a deterministic, fast, snapshot-able simulation: restoring and resimulating 6-8 frames in 16.6 ms leaves little room for anything else. Delay-based netcode in contrast waits and adds fixed input delay, which feels worse above about 3 frames.
Lag compensation

You aim at an enemy you see 100 ms in the past (interpolation) with another 50 ms of travel to the server, so the server sees them elsewhere. **Lag compensation** lets the server rewind: it stores a short history of hitbox positions, and when a shot arrives, it rewinds target positions to the time the shooter saw them (client timestamp minus interpolation delay) and then resolves the hit. The price is that victims sometimes get hit 'behind cover', which designers limit by capping how far the server will rewind (a few hundred milliseconds is common).

lesson.caption: The server keeps a short hitbox history and rewinds the target 150 ms, 100 ms of interpolation plus 50 ms of travel, to test the shot where the shooter saw it.

lesson.text: Bandwidth and tick rate

Tick rate is how often the server simulates and sends snapshots: 20-30 Hz in many shooters, 60-128 Hz in competitive ones, 10 Hz or less in slower games. Bandwidth is roughly `players x entities_state_bytes x rate`: 64 players x 40 bytes x 30 Hz is about 77 KB/s per client downstream before compression. Reduce it with **delta compression** against the last acknowledged snapshot, quantization (a position in 16 bits per axis within bounds), **interest management** (send only what is relevant to this player), and prioritization of nearby entities. Mobile players on cellular budgets want under 10-20 KB/s; packet loss means that you must design for it using UDP-based protocols with selective reliability rather than reliable ordering of everything.

Lockstep and rollback inherit every determinism hazard described in 'Physics and collision' (floating-point differences, unstable ordering), and they fail silently as desyncs. Detect them by hashing the game state each frame and comparing across peers.

AI agents tend to write networking that trusts the client: 'client sends its position' or 'client reports damage'. Tell the agent the authority model (server-authoritative), the tick rate, the latency target and cheat model, and require that every client message be validated as an input or intent. Verify sequence numbers on inputs, that the replay uses the same code path as the simulation, that remote entities are interpolated, not teleported, and that you test with simulated latency (100-200 ms), jitter and 5% packet loss; code that works on localhost proves nothing.

patterns.signal: Input handling is wired straight to actions and now you need rebinding, replays, undo or sending input over the network
patterns.why: Turn each input into a command object or struct with its tick; you can queue, record, replay, undo or transmit it. Adds a layer of indirection and requires commands to be deterministic to replay.

patterns.signal: Code checks `key == Space` and breaks on gamepads, remapping and touch
patterns.why: Gameplay reads named actions like Jump and Move fed by bindings with processing such as radial dead zones. Rebinding, context switching and local multiplayer come for free; more setup up front.

patterns.signal: Players say a jump pressed just before landing was ignored, or presses in a fixed step get lost
patterns.why: Record presses as timestamped edge events and honour them for a short window (80-150 ms) when the action becomes legal. Too long a window causes unintended actions.

patterns.signal: Players fall off ledges while pressing jump and swear they were still on the ground
patterns.why: Allow a jump for about 100 ms after leaving the ground, then clear it so it cannot double-jump. Matches perceived intent; too generous a window feels floaty.

patterns.signal: Important sounds like gunshots disappear when a hundred effects play at once
patterns.why: Limit voices per category, steal the least important, and duck music or ambience buses when key sounds play. Keeps the mix readable; mis-set priorities silence the wrong sounds.

patterns.signal: A volume slider is nearly silent over half its travel and then jumps loud near the top
patterns.why: Hearing is logarithmic, so map slider position to decibels (for example -80 to 0 dB) instead of linear gain. Clamp the bottom to true silence.

patterns.signal: A multiplayer game trusts positions and hits reported by clients, and cheaters teleport or one-shot others
patterns.why: Clients send inputs, the server simulates and owns truth, and only results go out. Prevents most cheats; needs prediction to hide latency and costs server CPU and bandwidth.

patterns.signal: In a server-authoritative game, your own movement feels sluggish because it waits for server confirmation
patterns.why: Apply your input locally at once, keep unacknowledged inputs, and on each server state rewind and replay them. Feels instant; mispredictions cause corrections that must be smoothed.

patterns.signal: Remote players move in jerky steps because snapshots arrive irregularly over the network
patterns.why: Render remote entities about 100 ms in the past between two buffered snapshots, so jitter and loss are hidden. Adds visible latency for others, which lag compensation must account for.

patterns.signal: An RTS has thousands of units and syncing their state would exceed the bandwidth budget
patterns.why: Send only inputs and have every peer run the same deterministic simulation. Tiny bandwidth; any float or ordering difference desyncs, and the slowest connection sets input delay.

patterns.signal: A fighting game needs instant local response despite remote input arriving several frames late
patterns.why: Predict remote input, simulate, and on mismatch restore a saved state and re-simulate to the present. Needs a fast, deterministic, snapshot-able sim; long rollbacks cause visible teleports.

patterns.signal: Shots that clearly hit on the shooter's screen do not register on the server, especially for high-ping players
patterns.why: The server keeps hitbox history and rewinds targets to what the shooter saw (latency plus interpolation delay). Fair for shooters; victims get hit behind cover, so cap the rewind window.

keyPoints: Map devices to named actions with dead zones, and add input buffering and coyote time to match player intent.
Audio is a real-time thread with a voice budget; buses, ducking and perceptual volume mapping keep the mix readable.
Server authority prevents cheating; clients predict their own input and reconcile by replaying unacknowledged inputs.
Lockstep sends only inputs but needs determinism; rollback predicts remote input and re-simulates on mismatch.
Lag compensation rewinds target positions on the server; bandwidth is tuned with tick rate, delta compression and interest management.

quiz.q: Players complain that jumping right before landing is ignored, though the code only checks for a press on the frame the character is grounded. Which fix matches player intent?
options: Raise the character's jump height by some margin
Lower the physics tick rate to save time
Add a radial dead zone to the jump button
Store the press for about 100 ms, consume it on landing
quiz.explain: An input buffer remembers a slightly early press and applies it when the action becomes legal. Jump height, physics rate and dead zones do not address the timing window.

quiz.q: A volume slider sounds almost silent over the lower half of its travel and then jumps loud near the top. The slider writes a linear 0-1 value straight to the mixer gain. What is the right correction?
options: Map the value to decibels with a logarithmic curve
Add a reverb send to each of the buses
Increase the audio buffer size to 4096 samples
Lower the voice limit on every platform
quiz.explain: Perceived loudness is logarithmic, so a linear gain-to-slider mapping feels wrong; converting to dB spreads the change evenly. Reverb, buffer size and voices do not change the slider curve.

quiz.q: In a server-authoritative shooter with 80 ms latency, your own movement feels sluggish because it waits for server confirmation. What should change?
options: Let the client decide its own position without server checks
Apply input locally with prediction, then reconcile against server state
Increase the tick rate to 240 Hz
Switch to deterministic lockstep with a 200 ms input delay
quiz.explain: Prediction gives immediate local response while the server stays authoritative, and reconciliation corrects mismatches. Trusting the client allows cheating, and the other options keep or add delay.

quiz.q: A fighting game uses rollback. The remote player's input arrives 4 frames late and differs from the prediction. What happens?
options: The game pauses until all peers agree on input
The server resolves the conflict and sends a fresh state
The game restores the last confirmed state and re-simulates 4 frames
Local prediction is kept and the late remote input is ignored
quiz.explain: Rollback rewinds to the last confirmed frame and replays forward within a frame, which requires a fast deterministic simulation. Pausing is delay-based netcode, and there is no authoritative server step in peer-to-peer rollback.

quiz.q: Players report that shots that clearly hit on their screen do not register on the server, especially from 150 ms ping players. Which server-side mechanism addresses this?
options: Lag compensation: rewind target hitboxes to the shooter's view time
Lower the snapshot delta compression ratio on the server
Increase the audio voice budget on the server
Reduce the interpolation delay to zero on all clients
quiz.explain: The shooter aimed at where the target appeared in the past, so the server must test against historical positions, within a capped rewind. Compression and audio are unrelated, and zero interpolation delay causes jitter without fixing the time mismatch.

quiz.q: Remote players in a server-authoritative game look jerky because snapshots arrive about 20 times per second at irregular intervals, and the client draws the newest one as soon as it lands. Which approach fits best?
options: Snapshot interpolation, rendering remote players slightly in the past
Client-side prediction with server reconciliation on inputs
Lag compensation that rewinds the server world state for every shot
Deterministic lockstep for every player in the match
quiz.explain: Buffering snapshots and interpolating between two of them turns irregular arrivals into smooth motion. Prediction is for your own inputs, lag compensation is a hit-detection fix, and lockstep would change the whole netcode model.

topics.title: Debugging a game
topics.summary: One investigation from a once-in-three-hours "fell through the floor" report to a fix: replayable runs, debug tools, logs and invariants, tunneling, desync bisection, release crashes, frame capture and soak tests.

lesson.text: A tester writes: 'Fell through the floor in the cargo bay. About three hours into a session, right after a jump pad. Could not do it again.' Over 400 hours of playtests, three people saw it. There is no video and no save file. The player was alive, standing on solid ground one moment, and 40 m below the map the next. This lesson follows that report from symptom to fix, then a shorter online desync and a release-build crash. The code is C#-flavoured pseudocode and nothing depends on an engine. The real subject is the set of decisions that make a game possible to debug at all.
Why games resist debugging

items: **Real time.** A breakpoint stops the clock, so the bug that depends on timing moves or vanishes. Networked peers time out while you stare at one frame.
**Nondeterminism.** Frame time, thread scheduling, input timing, random numbers and iteration order differ on every run. The same build does not do the same thing twice.
**Huge state.** A level holds thousands of entities and gigabytes of memory. Most of the state is irrelevant, and you do not know which part is.
**Seen once.** The bug happens on a tester's machine, in a build you no longer have open, and it comes back as one sentence.

lesson.text: Components

items: **Replay recorder** stores the inputs, the seed and the frame times so a run can be played back exactly.
**Bug-report button** bundles the replay, log tail, screenshot, build id and seed into one file.
**Debug draw** shows invisible things in the world: colliders, rays, nav paths and AI state.
**Developer console** teleports, spawns, sets the time of day and changes the time scale.
**Logger** writes categorised, frame-stamped lines into a ring buffer that is dumped on failure.
**Assertions** check invariants every frame in development builds.
**Crash reporter** collects minidumps from release builds and groups them by callstack.
**Automation** runs replays and bot players on a build server and reports pass or fail.

lesson.text: Stage 1: the report

The one-line report is useless alone. What the team wants is a bug-report button (or a hotkey) that works in every development and playtest build. One press freezes the game for a moment and writes a small bundle. The tester types a sentence and keeps playing. Without the button the team gets prose. With it, the team gets a run.

{
  "build": "0.9.4+8123 (dev)",
  "seed": "0x5EED1F42",
  "platform": "PC, 16 GB, GPU driver 551.23",
  "level": "cargo_bay", "tick": 41872,
  "replay": "cargo_bay.rpl",
  "log_tail": "ring.log",
  "screenshot": "f41872.png",
  "note": "fell through floor after jump pad"
}
Stage 2: determinism, make a run replayable

A replay does not record video. It records the inputs and replays them through the simulation. That works only if the simulation is a pure function of its previous state, its inputs and a seed. Each leak in that purity breaks the replay: reading the wall clock, drawing random numbers from one global generator that rendering also uses, iterating a hash set keyed by pointer, letting a worker thread finish in a different order, or reading anything from the render side. The fixes are mechanical. Run gameplay at a fixed 60 Hz. Give each system its own seeded RNG stream. Iterate in a stable order, such as entity id. Make input the only thing that enters from outside. The recorder starts a new file at each level load, beginning with a state snapshot, and keeps at most the last 15 minutes. The report's tick 41,872 counts from the cargo bay load.

lesson.text: Size is small. At 8 bytes per tick, 15 minutes is 54,000 ticks and about 430 KB raw. Storing only the ticks where an input changes brings that well under 100 KB. Add a full state snapshot every 30 s (1,800 ticks) and seeking is cheap: load the nearest snapshot, then re-simulate at most 1,800 ticks headless, which takes well under a second. The build that produced the report was not fully fixed-step: its physics world took the whole frame time, clamped at 0.1 s. That was the bug, and a variable step is replayable only if you also record the frame time of every frame. The replay did, so the bug came back exactly. The replay from the report was loaded in the editor and run to tick 41,872. The player fell on the first try, and again on the second and the hundredth. Reproduction went from 0 in 300 manual attempts to 100 percent, which changes the work completely: the bug is now a deterministic test, and every experiment (add a log, change a value, rerun) is a rerun of the same 11 minutes and 38 seconds.
Stage 3: look. Debug draw, console and time control

**Debug draw** puts invisible data into the world: collider shapes, raycasts, contact points and normals, navigation paths, AI state labels, velocity vectors. Calls take a duration in ticks, so a ray drawn on tick 100 stays visible on tick 101. Draw calls are compiled out of shipping builds or cost nothing when off. The **console** gives designers and testers direct control: teleport to a place, spawn an actor, set the time of day, set a seed, switch a system's debug view. A tester who can type `tp cargo_bay_lift` reaches a bug in seconds.

**Time control** is the debugger for real-time systems. Slow motion (time scale 0.1) stretches a one-tick glitch over ten rendered frames. Pause plus single-step moves the sim one tick per key press. Freeze-frame stops the simulation but keeps the free camera and debug draw alive, so you can fly around a frozen scene and inspect it from any angle. In the replay, the team paused at tick 41,860 and stepped forward. The capsule collider hung above the floor slab, then in the next drawn frame the capsule was 2.2 m lower, already under the slab, with no contact point drawn.
Stage 4: logs and assertions

Logging every frame to a file is slow and unreadable. The structure that works: **categories** (physics, ai, net, audio) with levels, so you can turn one system up; a **frame number and time stamp** on every line, so lines from different systems line up; and a **ring buffer** in memory (for example the last 8,192 lines, about 1 MB) written without allocation or file I/O. The buffer is dumped when an assertion fires, when the player presses the report button, or when the process crashes. Verbose detail is free until the moment it matters.

An **invariant** is something that must always be true. Checked every frame in development builds, invariants turn a symptom seen three minutes later into a failure on the exact tick it starts. Here the assertion fired at tick 41,870, and the log tail above it already told the story: a physics step with `dt=0.100` just before. A frame of 118 ms is a normal streaming hitch. The engine clamped the physics step to 0.1 s and ran one big step.
Root cause: tunneling

At the moment of the fall the player was descending at 22 m/s after a jump pad. In one normal tick that is 22 / 60 = 0.37 m. In the single 0.1 s step it was 2.2 m. The cargo bay floor is a 0.1 m thick box, and the player's capsule is 1.8 m tall. A discrete test asks only 'do the shapes overlap at the end of the step?' Falling straight down, the capsule overlaps the slab only during 0.1 + 1.8 = 1.9 m of its travel. A 0.37 m step cannot jump over a 1.9 m window. A 2.2 m step can, whenever its start lies in the last 0.3 m before the window, so the end position overlapped nothing and the capsule kept falling.

lesson.text: Why only once in a few hours? Three conditions had to line up, and then only about one try in seven (0.3 m of a 2.2 m step) skips the window. The hitch (about one every few minutes), a fast fall (only jump pads reach 22 m/s), and a thin floor (every other floor in the level was a slab 1 m thick, where deep penetration is pushed out upward). Each is common. All three together happen rarely, and testers could never combine them on demand. There is a second effect inside this class of bug. If a step ends partly inside a thin collider, **penetration resolution** pushes the shape out along the shortest way. Past the middle of the slab the shortest way is down, so the capsule is ejected through the bottom. The same thing happens at the seam of two boxes, where the edge contacts point sideways instead of up.

**Continuous collision detection** is the engine-side name for the sweep, and most engines can turn it on per body. It costs more per body, so it is used for fast and important shapes: the player, projectiles and vehicles. Further layers in the fix: a level validator that rejects colliders thinner than 0.25 m and finds gaps between touching boxes (it found 14 thin floors and the 1 mm seam in the cargo bay), and the dev-build invariant above. A safety net that teleports a fallen player back to the last good position is a good idea for the shipped game, as long as it also logs loudly. The replay becomes the regression test. The build server loads the recorded file, runs it headless at 20x speed, and asserts that the player stands on the cargo bay floor at tick 41,872 and is above `level.minY` at the end of the file. The fix changes the step, so the file no longer replays bit for bit; that is why the test checks an invariant and not a state hash. A second, scripted test forces a 118 ms hitch during a jump-pad fall onto the thin floor. Both fail on the old build and pass on the fixed one. It will fail if someone later removes the sweep, even if nobody remembers why it is there. A bug report turned into a test is how a game stops reintroducing its own old bugs.
Threads and jobs

Moving work onto a job system or worker threads adds a class of bugs that logs make worse. A **data race** is two threads touching the same memory with at least one writing and no ordering between them. The symptoms are state that is corrupted rarely, results that differ between runs, a bug that appears only in release builds, and one that vanishes when you add a log line, because the log changes the timing. The tools are ThreadSanitizer (compiler instrumentation that reports the two conflicting accesses and their stacks), and the engine's own job safety checks in development builds, which throw when two jobs declare conflicting access to the same array. The design rules prevent most of it: one writer per piece of data per phase, read-only inputs to parallel jobs, and double-buffered results. Floating-point sums are also not associative, so reduce parallel results in a fixed order or the replay will drift.
Second investigation: an online desync

Four players in a lockstep match report that after about two minutes their scores differ and units stand in different places. In lockstep each client simulates the whole world from the same inputs, so the clients must stay bit-identical. The tool is a **state checksum**: every tick, hash the simulation state (entity ids, quantised positions, health, RNG state) and compare across clients. Production builds exchange it once per second. Development builds compute it every tick and every system separately. Once hashes differ, they stay different, so the first bad frame can be found by bisection.
