lesson.text: Overrides are sticky and silent. A value that was overridden by accident, even to the same number, stays overridden forever. Periodically audit instances with the Overrides dropdown, and prefer variants over scene-instance overrides for intentional differences, because variants are reviewable assets.
Play Mode

Pressing Play runs the game inside the Editor using the currently loaded scenes. By default changes you make in the Inspector during Play Mode are discarded when you exit, because the Editor restores the scene from its saved state. Changes to **assets** (materials, ScriptableObjects) made during Play Mode are not reverted, since they are edits to files, not to the scene. Play Mode is also not a build: Editor-only code paths, asset loading from the AssetDatabase and missing platform stripping mean that "works in Play Mode" is a weak claim until it runs in a player build.

When an agent changes prefabs, have it do so through the Editor (Editor scripts, the Unity CLI or MCP running C# in the Editor) rather than by editing YAML; the version-control lesson explains why. Then verify the result the way this lesson suggests: open the scene, check the Console for Missing references and check each touched instance's Overrides dropdown for entries nobody intended.

Use variants for families of things (enemy tiers, weapon skins) and nested prefabs for shared parts (wheels, UI widgets). Keep scene overrides for genuinely per-placement data such as a spawn point's patrol route.

patterns.signal: You need `EnemyArmored` that differs from `Enemy` in a few values and should still pick up future fixes to `Enemy`
patterns.why: The variant stores only its differences from the base, so base fixes propagate. Keep chains shallow: deep variant-of-variant stacks make it hard to see where a value comes from.

patterns.signal: The same sub-assembly (a wheel, a door, a light rig) is copy-pasted inside many different prefabs
patterns.why: Each nested instance keeps its own link to its asset, so one edit updates every parent. Costs an extra level of overrides to reason about when a parent tweaks the child.

patterns.signal: A 2,000-line `Player` MonoBehaviour handles movement, health, audio and UI, and every change touches it
patterns.why: Split into `Mover`, `Health`, `PlayerAudio` and so on, each with one job, reused on other objects. Costs more wiring between components; do not split pieces that always change together.

patterns.signal: A component silently fails because a sibling `Rigidbody` or `Collider` it depends on was never added
patterns.why: Unity adds the dependency automatically and blocks removing it, turning a runtime null into an editor guarantee. Only use it for true hard dependencies, or it fights designers.

patterns.signal: Scripts locate collaborators with `GameObject.Find("Player")` or by tag, and break when an object is renamed
patterns.why: A `[SerializeField]` reference is resolved by file ID, survives renames and costs nothing at runtime. For objects spawned at runtime, pass references at spawn time instead.

patterns.signal: A fix made on the prefab asset reaches every instance except one, which still shows the old value
patterns.why: Overrides always win over the asset. Check the Overrides dropdown, revert stale ones, and apply deliberate ones to the asset so instances do not drift.

patterns.signal: Profiler shows high transform change dispatch; thousands of movers share one deep parent
patterns.why: A transform change dirties the whole hierarchy it belongs to, so many movers under one root serialise work. Keep frequently moving objects at the root or in small groups; folders are not free.

patterns.signal: You want a script to stop running but keep the object visible and colliding
patterns.use: Disable the component, not the GameObject
patterns.why: `enabled = false` stops that component's Update and similar callbacks only. `SetActive(false)` deactivates the whole object and its children, hiding renderers and colliders too.

patterns.signal: References to an asset break after files were moved or renamed outside Unity, or a commit lacks `.meta` files
patterns.use: Move assets in the Editor, commit `.meta`
patterns.why: References are by GUID stored in `.meta`; a new `.meta` means a new GUID and every reference breaks. Always move inside Unity and treat `.meta` as source code.

keyPoints: A GameObject is a container; behaviour and data live in Components, and every object has exactly one Transform that defines the hierarchy.
Assets are referenced by GUID in `.meta` files plus local file IDs; losing a `.meta` breaks every reference to that asset.
Prefab instances store only property modifications against the asset, so overrides always win over later changes to the asset.
Variants inherit from a base prefab and nested prefabs keep their own link, which makes shared fixes propagate automatically.
Inspector changes in Play Mode are discarded on exit, but changes to assets made during Play Mode persist.

quiz.q: You fix a collider size on the `Mechanic` prefab asset. Every track updates except track 12. What is the most likely cause?
options: Track 12 has an override on that collider property
Track 12 needs a full asset reimport to refresh
The prefab asset was not saved in Prefab Mode
Track 12 loads the scene additively at runtime
quiz.explain: Instances store property modifications, and an existing override for the collider size takes precedence over the asset's new default. An unsaved asset would fail on every track, not just one.

quiz.q: A child object's `activeSelf` is true, yet it is not rendered and its `Update` never runs. What explains this?
options: Its MeshRenderer component has been disabled
A parent GameObject is inactive in the hierarchy
Its Transform has a scale of zero on every axis
It was instantiated from an unpacked prefab
quiz.explain: Deactivating a parent makes `activeInHierarchy` false for every child while their own `activeSelf` stays true, which stops both rendering and Update. A disabled renderer or zero scale would hide it but Update would still run.

quiz.q: You need `EnemyArmored` that is identical to `Enemy` except for health and a shield mesh, and should pick up future changes to `Enemy`. What do you create?
options: A copy of the `Enemy` prefab asset
An unpacked instance saved as a new prefab
A prefab variant based on `Enemy`
A scene instance of `Enemy` with overrides
quiz.explain: A variant inherits from its base and stores only differences as a reviewable asset. A copy or unpacked prefab loses the link, and scene overrides only apply to that one placement.

quiz.q: A profiler capture shows high cost in transform change dispatch. 3,000 projectiles move every frame, all parented under one `Projectiles` root. What change most likely helps?
options: Set each projectile's position twice per frame
Move the root deeper into a manager object
Disable the projectiles' MeshRenderer components
Spawn projectiles as separate root objects
quiz.explain: Each root hierarchy is a unit for transform updates and change dispatch, so one giant root serialises work; splitting into roots allows parallel processing. Moving the root deeper makes the hierarchy worse, not better.

quiz.q: During Play Mode you tune a light in the scene and a value on a `DifficultySettings` ScriptableObject asset. You exit Play Mode. What remains?
options: The ScriptableObject change, not the light change
The light change, not the ScriptableObject change
Both changes remain until the Editor restarts
Neither change remains after exiting Play Mode
quiz.explain: Scene state is restored on exit, but the ScriptableObject is an asset file and edits to it persist. That asymmetry regularly surprises people who tweak data assets while testing.

quiz.q: A designer renames the `Player` object to `Hero` and the camera rig starts throwing NullReferenceException. Its script grabs the target with `GameObject.Find("Player")` in `Start`. What should you reach for?
options: A `[SerializeField]` field set in the Inspector
Switch the lookup to `FindWithTag("Player")` instead
Move the camera under the Hero in the hierarchy
Add `[RequireComponent]` to the camera script
quiz.explain: A serialized reference is stored by file ID, so it survives renames and costs nothing at runtime. `FindWithTag` only swaps one string for another and breaks the same way when the tag changes.

topics.title: MonoBehaviour Lifecycle, Coroutines, Async and ScriptableObjects
topics.summary: The exact order Unity calls your scripts in, how to sequence systems, when to use coroutines versus Awaitable, and how ScriptableObjects carry data and events.

lesson.text: A bug report: "Sometimes the HUD shows 0 health on level start." It reproduces one time in five, only in builds. The `HUD` reads `player.Health` in its `Start`, and `Player` sets `Health` in its own `Start`. Unity does not promise which `Start` runs first between two objects, and the order can change between Editor and build. Lifecycle bugs are ordering bugs, and you fix them by knowing exactly what Unity guarantees and what it does not.
The lifecycle, in order

items: **Awake**: once, when the object is loaded or instantiated, if its GameObject is active. Runs even if the component itself is disabled. Use it for self-initialisation: caching own components, setting own fields.
**OnEnable**: right after Awake (per object), and again every time the component or GameObject is re-enabled. Subscribe to events here.

**Start**: once, before the component's first Update, and only if the component is enabled. Every Awake and OnEnable of objects in the same loaded scene has run by then, so Start is where you may talk to other objects.
**FixedUpdate**: on the fixed physics timestep (default 0.02 s, 50 Hz). It runs zero, one or several times per rendered frame depending on how much time has accumulated.
**Update**: once per rendered frame. Gameplay logic and input.
**LateUpdate**: once per frame after every Update and after animation evaluation. Cameras that follow animated targets belong here.
**OnDisable**: when the component or GameObject is disabled, and before OnDestroy. Unsubscribe here.
**OnDestroy**: when the object is destroyed or its scene unloads, only if it was previously active (Awake ran).

lesson.text: Between FixedUpdate and Update sit the physics simulation and trigger/collision callbacks; between Update and LateUpdate sits the Animator update for normally updated animators; after LateUpdate come rendering and `WaitForEndOfFrame` coroutines. The frame loop itself is a `PlayerLoop` you can inspect and extend via `UnityEngine.LowLevel.PlayerLoop`.

lesson.text: Fixed timestep arithmetic

At 60 fps a frame is 16.7 ms and the fixed step is 20 ms, so FixedUpdate runs on roughly five of every six frames. At 30 fps (33.3 ms) it runs once or twice per frame. If a frame hitches to 200 ms, Unity would owe 10 fixed steps; the **Maximum Allowed Timestep** setting (default one third of a second) caps the catch-up so a slow frame does not trigger a spiral of ever-more physics work. The consequences for input handling and smooth motion (latching input, Rigidbody interpolation) are covered in the physics lesson.

lesson.text: Controlling execution order

Across different scripts, Unity's default order for the same callback is undefined. You have three tools: the Script Execution Order list in Project Settings, the `[DefaultExecutionOrder(n)]` attribute on a class (lower runs earlier), and, best of all, explicit initialisation where one bootstrapper calls `Init()` on systems in a known order. Fix the HUD bug by having the Player set `Health` in Awake (self-init) and the HUD read it in Start (cross-object), or by having the HUD subscribe to a health-changed event so order stops mattering.
Coroutines

A coroutine is an `IEnumerator` method driven by the engine: `StartCoroutine(Fade())` runs it until the first `yield`, then resumes it at a point in the player loop determined by what was yielded (`null` for next frame after Update, `WaitForFixedUpdate`, `WaitForSeconds`, `WaitForEndOfFrame`). It is a state machine generated by the C# compiler, scheduled by the MonoBehaviour that started it. Coroutines stop when that GameObject is deactivated or destroyed, but **not** when the component is merely disabled. They cannot return values, exceptions inside them are logged rather than propagated, and every `StartCoroutine` plus `new WaitForSeconds` allocates, which matters if you start thousands.

lesson.text: async/await and Awaitable

Since Unity 2023.1 (and so in Unity 6), `UnityEngine.Awaitable` gives you engine-aware async: `await Awaitable.NextFrameAsync()`, `WaitForSecondsAsync`, `FixedUpdateAsync`, `EndOfFrameAsync`, plus `BackgroundThreadAsync()` and `MainThreadAsync()` to hop threads. Awaitables are pooled to avoid allocations, which is why you must await each instance only once. Unlike coroutines, async methods are not tied to any object: if the object is destroyed mid-await, the method resumes anyway and touches a dead object. Pass `destroyCancellationToken` (available on MonoBehaviour) and handle `OperationCanceledException`.

`System.Threading.Tasks.Task` also works because Unity installs a `SynchronizationContext` that resumes continuations on the main thread, but Task allocates more and has no frame-aware waits. Avoid `async void` except for event handlers: exceptions escape to the context and are hard to trace. Rule of thumb: coroutines for simple object-scoped sequences, Awaitable for anything returning a value, composing calls or needing cancellation.
ScriptableObjects as data and events

A **ScriptableObject** is a serializable object that lives as an asset rather than on a GameObject. Fifty enemies referencing one `EnemyStats` asset share one copy of the data instead of fifty serialized copies, and designers tune it without touching scenes. ScriptableObjects also work as decoupled **event channels**: a `GameEvent` asset holds a list of listeners; the player raises it, the HUD and audio listen, and neither references the other, which also solves the cross-scene reference problem.

Runtime writes to a ScriptableObject in the Editor change the asset and persist after Play Mode; in a build they reset on next launch. Never use an SO as save-game storage, and treat runtime state on SOs (like the listener list above) as something to clear explicitly, especially with domain reload disabled.

When an agent writes MonoBehaviours, check three things: cross-object access is not in Awake, every `+=` in OnEnable has a matching `-=` in OnDisable, and every async method awaiting across frames takes `destroyCancellationToken`. Agents also tend to invent Awaitable members from Task habits; ask them to stick to documented `Awaitable` static methods and to compile in the Editor before claiming done.

patterns.signal: `GetComponent<Rigidbody>()` is called inside `Update` on every frame
patterns.why: Look up once in `Awake` and store it in a field; repeated lookups waste CPU in hot paths. If the component can be added later, use `TryGetComponent` when it appears instead.

patterns.signal: `Find`, `FindObjectOfType` or `FindWithTag` appears in `Update` or in code run per spawned object
patterns.use: Look up once, or register on spawn
patterns.why: Find walks the scene and scales with object count. Resolve once at init, or have objects register themselves with a manager or runtime set when enabled.

patterns.signal: A script reads another object's data in `Awake` and sometimes sees defaults
patterns.use: Awake for self, Start for others
patterns.why: Every `Awake` in a scene runs before any `Start`, so set up your own state in Awake and talk to others in Start. Order of the same callback across scripts is still undefined.

patterns.signal: Many scripts depend on a config or service manager being initialised before them
patterns.why: One entry point initialises services in a known order and hands them out. `[DefaultExecutionOrder]` works for a few cases but hides the order in attributes scattered across files.

patterns.signal: A short sequence over frames (blink, fade, wait then spawn) should die with its GameObject
patterns.why: Simple, tied to the object and stopped when it is destroyed or deactivated. It keeps running if only the component is disabled, cannot return values and swallows the call stack in exceptions.

patterns.signal: An `async` loop keeps running and throws `MissingReferenceException` after its object is destroyed
patterns.why: Async methods are owned by nothing, so pass the token and let cancellation end the loop. Await each Awaitable instance only once, since instances are pooled.

patterns.signal: You must wait for a load or web request and then use its result, with try/catch error handling
patterns.why: Async methods return values and propagate exceptions normally, so multi-step flows read top to bottom. Costs explicit cancellation and care about which thread you resume on.

patterns.signal: A CPU-heavy calculation (path search, parsing) causes a frame spike on the main thread
patterns.use: Background thread, then back to main thread
patterns.why: `Awaitable.BackgroundThreadAsync()` moves the work off the main thread and `MainThreadAsync()` returns to touch Unity objects. Unity APIs are main-thread only; for bulk data, the Job System scales better.

patterns.signal: Every enemy prefab carries its own copy of max health, speed and loot tables, and balance changes touch 200 files
patterns.why: Instances reference one asset, saving memory and giving designers a single place to tune. Treat it as read-only at runtime: Play Mode edits to assets persist in the Editor.

patterns.signal: Player death must notify HUD, audio and analytics, and none of them should reference the player or each other
patterns.why: A `GameEvent` asset holds listeners; the raiser and listeners only share the asset, even across scenes. Flow is harder to trace than direct calls, so name channels clearly and log raises.

patterns.signal: Systems call `FindObjectsByType<Enemy>` to get all live enemies
patterns.why: Enemies add themselves to a set asset in `OnEnable` and remove in `OnDisable`, giving an always-current list with no scene search. Clear it on play start when domain reload is off.

patterns.signal: Handlers fire on destroyed objects, or fire twice after re-enabling a component
patterns.use: Subscribe in OnEnable, unsubscribe in OnDisable
patterns.why: Pairing the two keeps listener lifetime equal to the component's active lifetime. Subscribing in Start without unsubscribing leaks handlers that keep dead objects alive.

keyPoints: Awake is for self-initialisation, Start for talking to other objects; order of the same callback across scripts is undefined unless you set it.
FixedUpdate runs zero or more times per frame on a fixed step; read input in Update, apply forces in FixedUpdate.
Coroutines stop with their GameObject but not when the component is disabled; async methods stop with nothing unless you cancel them.
Awaitable gives frame-aware, pooled async in Unity 6; pass `destroyCancellationToken` and await each instance once.
ScriptableObjects share data across instances and decouple systems as event channels, but runtime edits persist in the Editor.

quiz.q: The game runs at 30 fps with the default fixed timestep of 0.02 s. Roughly how many times does FixedUpdate run per rendered frame?
options: Exactly once per rendered frame
Once or twice, averaging about 1.7
About 0.6 times on average
Exactly twice per rendered frame
quiz.explain: A 33.3 ms frame accumulates 1.67 fixed steps on average, so some frames get one and some get two. FixedUpdate is not locked to the frame rate.

quiz.q: Every other script's Awake reads settings from `ConfigLoader`, which loads them in its own Awake. Which approach reliably runs `ConfigLoader.Awake` first?
options: Add `[DefaultExecutionOrder(-100)]` to ConfigLoader
Place ConfigLoader at the top of the Hierarchy
Load the settings in ConfigLoader.OnValidate
Make ConfigLoader's Awake method a static one
quiz.explain: Script execution order (the attribute or the Project Settings list) applies to Awake as well as later callbacks. Hierarchy position is not a documented ordering guarantee, and OnValidate is an Editor callback, not a runtime one.

quiz.q: A turret's `async Awaitable` loop keeps logging `MissingReferenceException` after the turret is destroyed. Which change fixes it?
options: Disable the turret component before calling Destroy
Replace the waits with `Task.Delay` calls instead
Pass `destroyCancellationToken` to each await call
Start the loop from Awake instead of from Start
quiz.explain: Async methods are not owned by the object, so they resume after destruction; cancelling via `destroyCancellationToken` ends them. Disabling the component would not stop an async method either.

quiz.q: A coroutine blinking a sprite keeps running after `blinker.enabled = false`. What is going on?
options: Coroutines run on a separate thread from the component
The coroutine is cached by the Animator until next frame
Disabling only takes effect after the next LateUpdate
Disabling the component does not stop its coroutines
quiz.explain: Coroutines are stopped by deactivating or destroying the GameObject, or by `StopCoroutine`, not by disabling the MonoBehaviour. Nothing about coroutines involves threads.

quiz.q: `Hud.Start` reads `player.Health` and sometimes sees 0; `Player` assigns Health in its own Start. What is the most robust fix?
options: Assign Health in Player.Awake and read it in Hud.Start
Move the HUD read into Hud.Awake so it runs earlier
Add a one-frame coroutine delay before reading Health
Put both objects under the same parent GameObject
quiz.explain: All Awake calls in a loaded scene finish before any Start, so self-initialising in Awake and reading in Start is guaranteed. Moving the read to Awake makes it worse, and a frame delay only hides the race.

quiz.q: Minimap, AI and audio code each call `FindObjectsByType<Enemy>()` every frame, and enemies spawn and die constantly. The scene search shows up in the profiler. Which approach fits best?
options: Cache the found array once, in `Start`
A ScriptableObject set filled in `OnEnable`
Poll with a coroutine every half second or so
Tag enemies and call `FindGameObjectsWithTag`
quiz.explain: Enemies add and remove themselves, so the set is always current and needs no scene search. Caching in `Start` goes stale as soon as enemies spawn or die.

topics.title: C# in Unity: Memory, Garbage Collection and Serialization
topics.summary: How Unity's managed heap and garbage collector behave, how to keep hot paths allocation-free, why destroyed objects compare equal to null, and what the serializer will and will not save.

lesson.text: A mobile shooter runs at a smooth 60 fps, except that every eight to ten seconds there is a 25 ms hitch. The profiler shows `GC.Collect` in the spike, and the GC Alloc column shows 3.2 KB allocated per frame, mostly from a damage-number system that formats strings, a LINQ query that finds the nearest enemy and a lambda passed to a sort. None of these look expensive in isolation. Together they fill the heap and force a collection mid-fight. Unity C# is ordinary C# running in an unusual runtime, and you need to know where the differences bite.
The managed heap and the GC

Unity's scripting runtime (Mono in the Editor and in Mono builds, IL2CPP for most shipped players) uses the **Boehm-Demers-Weiser** garbage collector. Two properties matter. It is **non-generational**: every collection marks the whole live heap, so cost scales with how much you keep alive, not with how much garbage you made. It is **non-compacting**: objects never move, so the heap fragments, and when no free block is large enough the heap grows. Unity does not reliably return that memory to the OS, so a one-off spike of allocations raises your memory footprint for the rest of the session.

**Incremental GC** (enabled by default in new projects for years and in Unity 6) splits the marking phase across frames, using a time slice per frame, instead of stopping the world for one long pass. It turns a 25 ms hitch into a few milliseconds spread over several frames, at the cost of write barriers that make every reference write slightly slower. It reduces spikes; it does not reduce work. If you allocate faster than the incremental collector can keep up, it falls back to a full blocking collection. Unity has announced a move toward the CoreCLR runtime, which brings a different, generational GC; check your Unity version before relying on runtime-specific behaviour.
The frame-budget arithmetic

At 60 fps you have 16.7 ms per frame for everything. A modest 1 KB per frame is 60 KB per second, 3.6 MB per minute. With a heap of tens of MB of live objects, each full mark can cost several milliseconds on a mid-range phone. The target for gameplay hot paths (Update, FixedUpdate, per-entity logic) is therefore **zero GC Alloc per frame** in steady state, measured in the Profiler's CPU module with the GC Alloc column, or with the Memory Profiler package for heap contents.

lesson.text: Common hidden allocations

items: **String building**: `"HP: " + hp` allocates a new string every call. Cache the label and only rebuild on change, or write into a `StringBuilder` / TextMeshPro `SetText` overloads that take numbers.
**Boxing**: passing a struct or enum where `object` or an interface is expected copies it to the heap, for example `string.Format("{0}", 42)` or storing structs in a `List<IDamageable>`.
**LINQ**: `enemies.Where(...).OrderBy(...).First()` allocates iterators, delegates and often buffers. Fine in tools and loading code, not in Update.
**Closures**: a lambda that captures a local or `this` allocates a closure object and a delegate each time it is created. Non-capturing lambdas are cached by the compiler.

**Array-returning APIs**: `GetComponents<T>()`, `Physics.RaycastAll`, `Mesh.vertices` and `Renderer.materials` return fresh arrays. Use the `List<T>` overloads, `Physics.RaycastNonAlloc` or `Physics.Raycast` with a preallocated buffer, and cache mesh data.
**Coroutine yields**: `yield return new WaitForSeconds(1f)` allocates each time; cache the instance if the delay is constant.
**`foreach` over an interface**: iterating a `List<T>` directly uses a struct enumerator and is allocation-free, but iterating it through `IEnumerable<T>` boxes the enumerator.

lesson.text: Structs and value semantics

`Vector3`, `Quaternion` and `Color` are structs. That is why `transform.position.x = 5` does not compile: the property returns a copy, and modifying a temporary would be lost. Copy the struct, modify, assign back. Structs avoid heap allocation and keep arrays of data contiguous, which is what makes Burst and the job system fast. But large structs passed by value cost copies; use `in` or `ref` parameters for structs bigger than a few machine words, and never mutate a struct through an interface reference, because you are mutating a boxed copy.
The fake null

Every `UnityEngine.Object` (GameObject, Component, ScriptableObject, assets) is a C# wrapper around a native object. `Destroy` frees the native side at the end of the frame, but the C# wrapper lives until nothing references it. Unity overrides `==` and the implicit bool conversion on `UnityEngine.Object` so that a destroyed object compares equal to `null`. This is the **fake null**: the reference is not null to the CLR, but `obj == null` returns true.

items: `?.`, `??`, `is null` and `ReferenceEquals` bypass Unity's operator and test the real C# reference, so `enemy?.TakeDamage()` happily calls into a destroyed object and throws `MissingReferenceException`.
Declaring a variable as `object` or an interface type also loses the override, because operator resolution is static.
`Destroy` is deferred: in the same frame right after `Destroy(go)`, `go == null` is still false.
In the Editor, unassigned serialized fields can hold a fake-null placeholder used to produce a clearer `UnassignedReferenceException`.
The overloaded `==` calls into native code to check liveness, so it is slightly slower than a plain reference comparison; in very hot loops, cache liveness instead of comparing to null repeatedly.

lesson.text: Serialization rules

Unity's serializer is what saves scenes and prefabs and what the Inspector edits. It is not .NET serialization and has its own rules. A field is serialized if it is `public` or marked `[SerializeField]`, and is not `static`, `const` or `readonly`. Properties are not serialized, but an auto-property's backing field can be with `[field: SerializeField]`. Supported types are primitives, enums, strings, Unity types such as `Vector3` and `AnimationCurve`, references to `UnityEngine.Object`s, `[Serializable]` plain classes and structs, and arrays or `List<T>` of those. `Dictionary`, multidimensional arrays and nested lists are not serialized.

lesson.text: Plain `[Serializable]` class fields are serialized **inline by value**: no null (Unity creates an instance), no polymorphism (a `Weapon` field holding a `Sword` is saved as a `Weapon`), and no shared references (two fields pointing at the same object become two copies on reload). `[SerializeReference]` changes that for a field: it serializes managed references with their concrete type, supports null and preserves sharing within the same host object. It does not work on `UnityEngine.Object` types, and renaming a class used with it breaks the stored type name unless you add `[MovedFrom]`.

Serialized values beat field initializers. If you change `public float speed = 5;` to `= 8;`, every existing prefab and scene keeps its saved 5. Renaming a field loses its data unless you add `[FormerlySerializedAs("oldName")]`.
Domain and scene reload

By default entering Play Mode reloads the scripting domain (fresh statics, re-run static constructors) and reloads the scene. On a large project that can take several seconds. **Enter Play Mode Settings** in Project Settings > Editor let you skip domain reload, scene reload or both, which can make entering Play Mode near-instant. The price: static fields, static events and singletons keep their values from the previous session. Reset them explicitly with a method marked `[RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod(RuntimeInitializeLoadType.SubsystemRegistration)]`.

Agents write idiomatic server C#: LINQ, `?.`, string interpolation, async Task everywhere. In Unity code that runs per frame, ask for allocation-free loops, `== null` (not `?.`) on UnityEngine.Object, and the List overloads of query APIs. Verify by profiling the GC Alloc column rather than reading the code. When an agent renames serialized fields or classes used by `[SerializeReference]`, require `[FormerlySerializedAs]` or `[MovedFrom]` and check a prefab still holds its values.

patterns.signal: Profiler shows GC Alloc every frame and a periodic spike, with bullets or effects instantiated and destroyed constantly
patterns.why: Reuse instances with `UnityEngine.Pool.ObjectPool<T>` or your own pool; Instantiate/Destroy cost CPU and garbage. Pools hold memory and need careful state reset on reuse.

patterns.signal: A label string is built with `+` or interpolation every frame
patterns.why: Concatenation allocates a new string per call. Rebuild when the value changes, or format into a reused `StringBuilder`; the allocation then happens rarely instead of every frame.

patterns.signal: `Physics.RaycastAll`, `GetComponents<T>()` or `mesh.vertices` is called in a hot path
patterns.why: These return fresh arrays each call. Use the `NonAlloc` variants or `List<T>` overloads with a preallocated buffer; size it for the worst case or results are silently truncated.

patterns.signal: LINQ like `.Where().OrderBy().First()` runs in `Update` or per-frame AI code
patterns.why: LINQ allocates enumerators and closures and hides O(n log n) sorts. Keep it for editor tools and load-time code; in per-frame code write the loop and track the best item yourself.

patterns.signal: A coroutine loop does `yield return new WaitForSeconds(0.1f)` on every iteration
patterns.why: Each `new` allocates. Store the `WaitForSeconds` in a field and reuse it; `null` and `WaitForEndOfFrame`-style instances can be shared too. Not needed for one-shot waits.

patterns.signal: A lambda capturing a local or `this` is passed as a callback every frame
patterns.why: Capturing lambdas allocate a closure and delegate each time they are created. Create the delegate once in a field; non-capturing lambdas are already cached by the compiler.

patterns.signal: A `Dictionary` keyed by a custom struct or enum shows GC Alloc on every lookup
patterns.why: Without it, equality falls back to `object.Equals` and boxes. Implement `IEquatable<T>` and `GetHashCode`, or pass a custom `IEqualityComparer<T>` to the dictionary.

patterns.signal: `target?.Hit()` or `cached ?? fallback` misbehaves after the target object was destroyed
patterns.use: Unity null check: `==` or implicit bool
patterns.why: Destroyed objects are fake nulls that only Unity's overloaded `==` detects; `?.`, `??` and `is null` check the C# reference. Write `if (target) target.Hit();`.

patterns.signal: A field typed as a base class or interface loses its subclass data after save or reload
patterns.why: Stores the managed reference with its concrete type, so polymorphism, null and shared references survive. Costs a heavier format and breaks if the class is renamed without `[MovedFrom]`.

patterns.signal: Renaming a serialized field resets its value on every prefab and scene
patterns.why: The serializer matches data by field name; the attribute maps the old name to the new one. Keep it until every asset has been re-saved, then remove it.

patterns.signal: You need a `Dictionary` editable in the Inspector, but the serializer drops it
patterns.use: Serialize as list, rebuild in callback
patterns.why: Store parallel lists or a list of key-value structs and rebuild the dictionary in `ISerializationCallbackReceiver.OnAfterDeserialize`. Duplicate keys must be handled explicitly.

patterns.signal: With domain reload disabled, scores and event handlers from the last Play session reappear
patterns.why: Statics survive when the domain is not reloaded. Reset them in a method marked with `RuntimeInitializeLoadType.SubsystemRegistration`, which runs before scene load on every play.

keyPoints: Unity's Boehm GC is non-generational and non-compacting; incremental mode spreads the cost but does not remove it, so target zero per-frame allocations.
Hidden allocations come from strings, boxing, LINQ, capturing lambdas, array-returning APIs and cached-but-not-cached yield instructions.
Destroyed UnityEngine.Objects compare equal to null only through Unity's `==`; `?.`, `??` and `is null` bypass it.
The serializer saves public or `[SerializeField]` fields inline by value; `[SerializeReference]` adds polymorphism, null and shared references.
Disabling domain reload speeds up iteration but leaves statics alive; reset them with `RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod`.

quiz.q: The profiler shows 0.8 KB GC Alloc per frame and a 20 ms GC spike every few seconds. Incremental GC is on. What is the most effective fix?
options: Call `GC.Collect()` manually every frame
Raise the target frame rate so frames are shorter
Remove the per-frame allocations in hot paths
Switch from IL2CPP to the Mono scripting backend
quiz.explain: Incremental GC only spreads work; sustained allocation still forces collections, so eliminating the garbage is the fix. Collecting every frame would pay a full mark each frame.

quiz.q: `target?.Hit()` throws `MissingReferenceException` after the target was destroyed last frame. Why?
options: `?.` checks the C# reference, which is not null
`Destroy` is deferred until the scene is unloaded
The native object is freed before the wrapper exists
Unity's `==` override throws on destroyed objects
quiz.explain: The null-conditional operator bypasses Unity's overloaded `==`, so the live C# wrapper passes the check and the call reaches a dead native object. Use `if (target != null)` instead.

quiz.q: A `Weapon` field holds a `Sword` (subclass) assigned in code. After reloading the scene, it behaves like a plain `Weapon`. Which fix preserves the subclass?
options: Make the `Weapon` field public instead of private
Mark the `Weapon` class with `[System.Serializable]`
Change the field's type to `object` for flexibility
Annotate the field with `[SerializeReference]`
quiz.explain: Plain serialized classes are stored inline by declared type, dropping the subclass; `[SerializeReference]` stores the concrete type. Visibility and `[Serializable]` do not change the inline-by-value behaviour.

quiz.q: With domain reload disabled, the second Play session starts with last session's score and duplicate event handlers. What is the right fix?
options: Re-enable scene reload while keeping domain reload off
Reset statics in a `SubsystemRegistration` init method
Move the score into a field initializer on the class
Mark the static score field with `[NonSerialized]`
quiz.explain: Without domain reload, statics survive between sessions and must be reset explicitly; `RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod(SubsystemRegistration)` runs early on each Play. Scene reload does not touch statics.

quiz.q: You change `public float speed = 5f;` to `= 8f;` in a MonoBehaviour. Existing enemy prefabs still move at 5. Why?
options: Prefabs cache compiled scripts until a reimport
Public fields are read-only once the prefab is saved
Serialized values in the prefab override initializers
Field initializers only run in development builds
quiz.explain: The prefab already stores `speed: 5`, and deserialization overwrites the initializer's value. Only newly added components pick up the new default.

quiz.q: A proximity sensor calls `Physics.RaycastAll` in `Update`, and the Profiler's hierarchy shows about 1 KB of GC Alloc per frame from that call. Which change removes the garbage?
options: Call `GC.Collect()` at the end of each frame
Filter the hits with LINQ into a new `List<T>`
`RaycastNonAlloc` with a reused hit buffer
Run the cast in a coroutine every frame
quiz.explain: The NonAlloc variant writes into a buffer you reuse, so no array is created per call. Forcing `GC.Collect()` just trades steady garbage for a guaranteed main-thread stall.

topics.title: Rendering in Unity: Pipelines, Batching, Shaders and Lighting
topics.summary: How Unity's render pipelines turn scenes into draw calls, how the SRP Batcher, instancing and batching cut CPU cost, and how shader variants, baked lighting and Render Graph fit together.

lesson.text: A city-builder hits 24 fps on a mid-range Android phone. The GPU timing is 11 ms, but the main thread spends 19 ms and the render thread 17 ms, and the Frame Debugger shows over 2,000 draw events with 900 SetPass calls. The art is not too heavy for the GPU; the CPU is drowning in state changes because buildings use 300 slightly different materials and an old custom shader that breaks batching. Unity rendering performance is usually about how much work the CPU does to describe the frame, and the tools below exist to shrink it.
Three pipelines

items: **Built-in Render Pipeline**: the legacy fixed pipeline. Still present, but feature development has moved to the Scriptable Render Pipelines, and new projects should not start on it.

**URP (Universal Render Pipeline)**: the default for most projects, scaling from mobile and Switch-class hardware to PC and console. Forward, Forward+ and Deferred rendering paths, Renderer Features for custom passes, Shader Graph support.
**HDRP (High Definition Render Pipeline)**: physically based, high-end PC and console target with volumetrics, ray tracing integration and a heavier baseline cost per frame.
Shaders and many assets are pipeline-specific: a Built-in shader renders magenta under URP. Switching pipelines mid-project is a migration, not a toggle.

lesson.text: Both SRPs are C# code in packages that you can read, which is how you find out what a setting actually does. A pipeline's per-frame job: cull renderers against each camera, sort them, set up passes (shadows, depth, opaques, skybox, transparents, post-processing) and issue draws through the graphics API.
Where CPU rendering cost comes from

A **draw call** asks the GPU to draw a mesh. What is expensive on the CPU is mostly the **state setup** before it: binding a shader variant (a **SetPass call**), uploading material properties and per-object data, and validating state in the driver. Rough guidance: mobile projects aim for a few hundred draw calls and far fewer SetPass calls per frame; PC and console handle thousands. The batching techniques below attack different parts of this cost.
SRP Batcher

The **SRP Batcher** does not merge meshes. It makes consecutive draws that use the same shader variant cheap. Material properties live in a persistent GPU constant buffer (`UnityPerMaterial`) that is only re-uploaded when a material changes, and per-object data (`UnityPerDraw`) is uploaded in bulk. So 300 different materials sharing one shader variant become one batch of fast draws instead of 300 full setups. For a shader to be compatible, all material properties must be declared in a single `CBUFFER_START(UnityPerMaterial)` block. URP Lit and Shader Graph shaders are compatible; hand-written legacy shaders often are not, and the Inspector of a shader says whether it is.

lesson.text: Setting per-renderer properties with a `MaterialPropertyBlock` makes that renderer incompatible with the SRP Batcher. For per-object variation, prefer distinct material instances on an SRP-compatible shader, or GPU instancing with per-instance properties when the objects share a mesh.
GPU instancing, static and dynamic batching

items: **GPU instancing**: draws many copies of the same mesh with the same material in one call, with per-instance data such as transforms and colours. Ideal for grass, rocks, crowds. In URP and HDRP the SRP Batcher takes priority, so instancing applies to renderers that are not SRP Batcher compatible or to explicit calls like `Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced`.

**Static batching**: for objects marked Batching Static, Unity combines meshes into large shared vertex and index buffers at build time and draws ranges of them with fewer state changes. It costs memory (a combined copy of every mesh instance) and the objects cannot move.

**Dynamic batching**: transforms small meshes (a few hundred vertices) on the CPU every frame into one buffer. It trades CPU vertex work for draw calls and is rarely a win on modern hardware; URP leaves it off by default.

**GPU Resident Drawer** (Unity 6, URP and HDRP): uses the BatchRendererGroup API to keep scene renderers in GPU memory and draw them with instanced indirect calls, which can cut CPU rendering cost dramatically in large static-heavy scenes. In URP it requires the Forward+ rendering path (or Deferred+ in Unity 6 releases that offer it) and keeping BatchRendererGroup shader variants in Graphics settings.

lesson.text: Materials, shader variants and Shader Graph

A shader source compiles into many **variants**, one per combination of enabled keywords per pass per platform. `#pragma multi_compile _ FOG_ON` always compiles both states; `#pragma shader_feature _ DETAIL_ON` only includes variants that some material in the build uses. Keywords multiply: ten independent binary `multi_compile` keywords produce 1,024 variants per pass. The results are long build times, large builds, high memory for loaded shaders and runtime hitches the first time a variant and its pipeline state object are created on device. Strip aggressively (Graphics settings, URP asset feature toggles, `IPreprocessShaders`) and prewarm the variants your game actually uses.

lesson.text: **Shader Graph** generates pipeline-specific HLSL from a node graph. It produces SRP-Batcher-compatible code, supports custom nodes from HLSL, and its keyword nodes create variants just like hand-written pragmas, so a graph with several Boolean keywords can explode variants as easily as code. **Materials** are assets that pick a shader and set its properties; `renderer.material` silently clones the material (a new instance that you must destroy), while `renderer.sharedMaterial` edits the asset.
Lighting: realtime, mixed and baked

Each light is **Realtime**, **Mixed** or **Baked**. Realtime lights are computed every frame and cost per light per object (or per tile in Forward+). Baked lights are precomputed into **lightmaps** by the Progressive Lightmapper and cost nothing at runtime except texture memory and sampling. Mixed lights do both, according to the scene's **Lighting Mode**: **Baked Indirect** (realtime direct light and shadows, baked bounce light), **Shadowmask** (baked shadows from static objects stored in a mask, realtime direct lighting) and **Subtractive** (everything baked, a single realtime shadow from the main light on dynamic objects; cheapest, least accurate).

Lightmaps only light static geometry. Dynamic objects get baked **global illumination** from **light probes**: points that store spherical-harmonic lighting, interpolated for each moving renderer. Classic Light Probe Groups need manual placement; **Adaptive Probe Volumes** (URP and HDRP in Unity 6) place probes automatically in a density-adaptive grid and sample per pixel, avoiding the blotchy per-object look.
Render Graph in URP

Since Unity 6, URP builds each frame with the **Render Graph** system. Custom passes declare what they read and write in `RecordRenderGraph`; the graph then culls unused passes, allocates and aliases transient textures, and on tile-based mobile GPUs merges compatible passes into native render passes so intermediate results stay in on-chip memory instead of round-tripping through main memory. Older `Execute`/`OnCameraSetup` style passes rely on a compatibility mode that is being phased out.
The Frame Debugger

Window > Analysis > Frame Debugger freezes a frame and lists every rendering event in order. Selecting an event shows the shader, keywords, material properties, render target and, crucially, why it was not batched with the previous draw. For Render Graph, the Render Graph Viewer shows passes, resource lifetimes and which passes were merged or culled. Pair them with the Profiler: the Profiler tells you whether you are CPU or GPU bound, the Frame Debugger tells you why.

Agents frequently produce Built-in pipeline shaders (`CGPROGRAM`, `UnityCG.cginc`) or pre-Render-Graph URP passes from older training data. Tell the agent the exact pipeline and Unity version, require HLSL with properties in a `UnityPerMaterial` CBUFFER, and require Render Graph `RecordRenderGraph` for custom passes. Verify in the Editor: the shader Inspector should report SRP Batcher compatible, the Frame Debugger should show the pass where you expect it, and the build's variant count should not jump.

Before optimising rendering, read the Profiler's main thread, render thread and GPU times side by side. High CPU with a lightly loaded GPU means batching and SetPass work; high GPU time means fill rate, overdraw, shader cost or resolution.

patterns.signal: Frame time is too high and you do not yet know whether the CPU, render thread or GPU is the limit
patterns.why: Compare main thread, render thread and GPU times before changing anything. Cutting draw calls does nothing for a GPU-bound frame; cutting shader cost does nothing for a CPU-bound one.

patterns.signal: Hundreds of SetPass calls; objects use many materials on a legacy or hand-written shader
patterns.why: Put material properties in `CBUFFER_START(UnityPerMaterial)` so objects sharing a shader variant skip per-draw setup. Gains come from fewer variants, not necessarily fewer materials.

patterns.signal: Per-object colours are set through `MaterialPropertyBlock` and render CPU cost goes up
patterns.use: Shared material variants instead of MPBs
patterns.why: Renderers with a property block drop out of the SRP Batcher. Use a few shared materials, or encode variation in vertex colour or a texture. MPBs remain fine for Built-in or instanced paths.

patterns.signal: Thousands of copies of one mesh and material (grass, rocks, crowds) need drawing
patterns.why: One draw call renders many instances with per-instance data, ideally via `Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced` or indirect drawing. Loses per-object culling and LOD unless you implement them.

patterns.signal: Many non-moving props share a few materials and draw calls dominate the CPU
patterns.why: Combines static meshes into big buffers drawn with fewer state changes. Costs extra memory for the combined copies and the objects can never move.

patterns.signal: A Unity 6 URP scene has many GameObject renderers and CPU draw submission is the bottleneck
patterns.why: Moves draw submission for eligible renderers to GPU-driven instanced paths, cutting CPU cost. Requires Forward+ and compatible shaders; check the manual for current constraints.

patterns.signal: Distant objects with full-detail meshes inflate vertex count and GPU time
patterns.why: Swaps to cheaper meshes as screen size shrinks, culling at the end. Costs authoring time and memory for each level; cross-fade hides popping at extra shader cost.

patterns.signal: Dense interiors where walls hide most objects, yet the frame still draws everything in the frustum
patterns.why: Baked visibility data skips hidden renderers. Costs bake time and memory, and gives little in open scenes where most things are visible anyway.

patterns.signal: Many small sprites or UI images each use their own texture and break batching
patterns.why: Packing into one texture lets them share a material and batch. Costs atlas memory for every sprite in it, so group atlases by screen or level, not the whole game.

patterns.signal: Build size and shader compile time explode; a shader has many `multi_compile` keywords
patterns.why: Variants multiply per keyword. Use `shader_feature` for material toggles, strip unused variants, and prewarm needed ones. Over-stripping causes missing or pink materials at runtime.

patterns.signal: Static scenery is lit well by lightmaps but moving characters look flat and unlit
patterns.use: Light probes or Adaptive Probe Volumes
patterns.why: Probes sample baked light in space so dynamic objects receive matching indirect light. Probes need placement or volume setup and do not capture sharp shadows.

patterns.signal: Mobile frame is GPU bound with many realtime lights and shadows on geometry that never moves
patterns.why: Lightmaps move lighting cost to build time, leaving few realtime lights. Costs lightmap memory and bake iteration time, and baked lights cannot change at runtime.

keyPoints: URP is the default pipeline; HDRP targets high-end hardware; Built-in is legacy and its shaders do not work in SRPs.
The SRP Batcher cuts per-draw setup for objects sharing a shader variant; MaterialPropertyBlocks and non-CBUFFER shaders break it.
Instancing, static batching, dynamic batching and the GPU Resident Drawer reduce CPU cost in different ways with different trade-offs.
Shader keywords multiply variants; strip unused ones to protect build size, memory and first-use hitches.
Baked lighting covers static geometry; light probes or Adaptive Probe Volumes light dynamic objects; Render Graph manages URP passes and resources.

quiz.q: Main thread 19 ms, render thread 17 ms, GPU 9 ms, 900 SetPass calls. Buildings use 300 materials on a legacy custom shader. What change helps most?
options: Lower the render resolution to 75 percent
Port the shader to be SRP Batcher compatible
Switch every light in the scene to Realtime
Enable dynamic batching on the URP asset
quiz.explain: The CPU is bound by per-material setup, which the SRP Batcher removes for draws sharing a compatible shader variant. Lowering resolution targets the GPU, which is not the bottleneck.

quiz.q: You set colours on 500 trees through `MaterialPropertyBlock`, and CPU render cost rises. The shader is SRP Batcher compatible. Why?
options: Property blocks force a shader recompile each frame
Property blocks disable frustum culling for renderers
Those renderers drop out of the SRP Batcher path
Property blocks duplicate the mesh into GPU memory
quiz.explain: Renderers with a MaterialPropertyBlock are not SRP Batcher compatible and fall back to slower draws. Use instancing with per-instance colour, or material variants, instead.

quiz.q: A shader has eight independent `multi_compile` on/off keywords in one pass. How many variants of that pass are compiled per platform?
options: 256 variants for the pass
16 variants for the pass
8 variants for the pass
64 variants for the pass
quiz.explain: Each independent binary keyword doubles the count, so 2^8 = 256. `shader_feature` would compile only combinations used by materials in the build.

quiz.q: Moving characters look flat inside a level lit with lightmaps, while walls look great. What is missing?
options: Static batching on the characters' renderers
A Shadowmask lighting mode for the main light
Higher lightmap resolution in the bake settings
Light probes or probe volumes for dynamic objects
quiz.explain: Lightmaps only apply to static geometry; dynamic renderers receive baked indirect lighting through light probes or Adaptive Probe Volumes. Lightmap resolution does not affect moving objects at all.

quiz.q: On a tile-based mobile GPU, a URP custom pass written for Render Graph makes the frame cheaper than the same pass written the old way. Most likely why?
options: Render Graph merges passes to keep data on chip
Render Graph moves blits to an async compute queue
Render Graph skips post-processing on mobile GPUs
Render Graph runs the pass at half resolution
quiz.explain: Declared reads and writes let Render Graph merge compatible passes into native render passes, avoiding costly memory round-trips on tilers. It does not change resolution or skip effects.

quiz.q: A meadow has 8,000 copies of one grass mesh sharing one material. The render thread is the bottleneck, the GPU is mostly idle, and the objects must keep varying scale. What should you reach for?
options: Static batching of all the grass meshes
Occlusion culling baked for the whole meadow
A LOD Group added to every single blade
GPU instancing with `RenderMeshInstanced`
quiz.explain: Instancing draws many copies of one mesh and material in a few calls with per-instance data. Occlusion culling gives little in an open field where most blades are visible anyway.

topics.title: Physics, Input and Animation in Unity
topics.summary: How Rigidbodies, colliders, the fixed timestep, input handling and the Animator actually fit into Unity's frame.

lesson.text: A classic first bug in a Unity project: the player character jitters when the camera follows it, bullets occasionally pass straight through thin walls, and the jump button sometimes does nothing. Three different symptoms, one root cause: the code mixes up two clocks. Unity renders on a variable-rate **frame loop** (`Update`, `LateUpdate`), but PhysX simulates on a **fixed-rate loop** (`FixedUpdate`). Physics, input and animation all live at the seam between those two loops, so understanding the seam is most of the job.
Rigidbody, colliders and who owns the transform

A **Collider** (Box, Sphere, Capsule, Mesh, Terrain) is shape data registered with the physics scene. A **Rigidbody** makes the object a simulated body: PhysX integrates its velocity, applies gravity and resolves contacts, then writes the result back to the Transform. Once a non-kinematic Rigidbody exists, the physics engine owns the position; setting `transform.position` every frame fights the solver, teleports through contacts and breaks interpolation. Move dynamic bodies with forces, velocity (`linearVelocity` in Unity 6, formerly `velocity`) or `MovePosition`/`MoveRotation`.

items: **Static collider**: collider with no Rigidbody. Meant never to move; level geometry.

**Kinematic Rigidbody** (`isKinematic = true`): moved by your code via `MovePosition`, pushes dynamic bodies but is not pushed back. Use it for anything with a collider that you animate or move from script: doors, moving platforms, trigger volumes that follow a character.
**Dynamic Rigidbody**: fully simulated. Mass, damping, constraints and collision detection mode matter.

**MeshCollider**: a dynamic Rigidbody needs a convex MeshCollider (max 255 triangles for the generated hull); concave meshes are for static or kinematic use. Primitive colliders are much cheaper than meshes for contacts and queries.

lesson.text: Layers, the collision matrix and triggers

Every GameObject has one of 32 **layers**. The **Layer Collision Matrix** (Project Settings > Physics) decides which layer pairs are even considered during the broadphase. Turning off pairs that can never meaningfully touch (enemy bullets vs enemy, pickups vs terrain, UI-world objects vs everything) is free performance and removes whole classes of bugs. Layers also feed the `LayerMask` argument of every physics query.

lesson.text: A collider with `isTrigger` set does not produce contact forces; it reports overlap through `OnTriggerEnter/Stay/Exit`. Messages only fire if at least one of the two objects has a Rigidbody (a kinematic one is fine). `OnCollisionEnter` needs at least one non-kinematic Rigidbody in the pair. A trigger volume on a static object touching another static object will never report anything; that single rule explains most 'my trigger does not fire' threads.
FixedUpdate, the accumulator and interpolation

The lifecycle lesson covered the fixed-step accumulator: each frame Unity runs `FixedUpdate` plus a physics step as many times as needed to catch up in steps of `Time.fixedDeltaTime` (default 0.02 s), capped by Maximum Allowed Timestep. The point here is the consequence: at 144 fps most frames run zero physics steps, at 30 fps most run one or two, so anything rendered or read per frame is out of phase with the simulation.

Because rendering samples the physics state at arbitrary points between steps, a followed object appears to stutter: some rendered frames show the same physics position twice. **Rigidbody interpolation** (`RigidbodyInterpolation.Interpolate`) renders the body between its previous and current physics poses, at the cost of up to one fixed step of visual latency. Enable it on the player and anything the camera follows, not on hundreds of debris objects. Extrapolate predicts forward instead and overshoots on collisions.

lesson.caption: Physics runs every 0.02 s while frames arrive every ~7 ms at 144 fps: without interpolation the body holds a pose across several frames, with Interpolate it glides one step behind.

lesson.text: Note the latch: input is read per frame, consumed per fixed step. Checking `GetKeyDown` or `WasPressedThisFrame` directly inside `FixedUpdate` misses presses whenever a frame runs zero physics steps, and double-fires when a frame runs two. That is the 'jump sometimes does nothing' bug.
Tunnelling and physics queries

Discrete collision detection checks overlap only at step boundaries. A 0.1 m bullet moving at 300 m/s travels 6 m per 0.02 s step and skips thin walls. Options: `CollisionDetectionMode.Continuous`/`ContinuousDynamic` (swept tests, more expensive), `ContinuousSpeculative` (cheaper, can cause ghost contacts), or, for real bullets, do not simulate them as bodies at all: raycast from the previous to the current position each step.

Queries (`Raycast`, `SphereCast`, `OverlapSphere`, `CapsuleCast`) run against the physics scene, not against the Transforms. If you move colliders in `Update` and query in the same frame, results reflect the last sync unless `Physics.autoSyncTransforms` is on (off by default since 2018.3 because syncing on every query is costly) or you call `Physics.SyncTransforms()`. Always pass a LayerMask and a max distance, prefer the `NonAlloc` variants to avoid GC allocations, and use `RaycastCommand` to batch hundreds of rays across worker threads.
Input: Input Manager vs the Input System package

The legacy **Input Manager** (`Input.GetAxis("Horizontal")`, `Input.GetKeyDown`) is a polling API configured in a global axis list. It is simple but hardcodes devices, has no runtime rebinding, and handles gamepads and multiple players poorly. The **Input System package** (`com.unity.inputsystem`) separates **actions** (Jump, Move) from **bindings** (Space, gamepad south button, touch), groups actions into **action maps** (Gameplay, UI, Vehicle) you enable and disable, supports control schemes, rebinding, local multiplayer via `PlayerInput`, and both polling (`action.ReadValue<Vector2>()`) and callbacks. Unity 6 ships a project-wide actions asset by default. The **Active Input Handling** player setting selects Old, New or Both; 'Both' is a migration crutch, not a destination.

items: Input System events are processed at the start of the frame by default (dynamic update). Its update mode can be switched to fixed update, but then UI and per-frame reads become coarser; latching as above is usually better.
Enable only the action map that matches the current context; otherwise Space both jumps and presses the focused UI button.
Touch and mouse pointer events for uGUI need the Input System UI Input Module on the EventSystem, not the legacy StandaloneInputModule.

lesson.text: Animation: Animator, blend trees and Timeline

**Mecanim** is the Animator component plus an **Animator Controller** asset: a state machine of states (clips or blend trees) and transitions driven by parameters (float, int, bool, trigger). **Layers** with **Avatar Masks** let an upper-body layer play 'reload' while the base layer runs. A **blend tree** mixes clips continuously by parameter: a 1D tree blends idle, walk and run by speed; a 2D Freeform Directional tree blends strafe directions by a velocity vector. Set parameters with hashed ids (`Animator.StringToHash`) and use damping on `SetFloat` to avoid popping.

lesson.text: **Root motion** lets clips move the character (the animation decides displacement), versus code-driven motion where you move the body and pick clips to match. Mixing both without intent produces foot sliding or drift. The Animator's **update mode** can evaluate in sync with physics for characters driven by Rigidbodies, and its **culling mode** (Always Animate, Cull Update Transforms, Cull Completely) decides what happens off-screen. Animators are not cheap: hundreds of skinned characters with complex controllers cost several milliseconds on mobile. Use culling, the rig import option to strip unused transforms (Optimize Game Objects), and for crowds consider baked vertex or GPU animation.

**Timeline** is for authored sequences: cutscenes, scripted camera moves, a boss intro. A PlayableDirector plays a Timeline asset with tracks (Animation, Activation, Audio, Signal, Control). Both Timeline and the Animator are built on the **Playables API**, a graph of nodes that evaluate and mix. Use the Animator for reactive gameplay state, Timeline for linear choreography, and Signals to call back into gameplay code at authored times.

Moving a non-kinematic Rigidbody through `transform.position`, polling one-shot input in `FixedUpdate`, and querying physics right after moving colliders in `Update` are the three most common sources of 'random' physics bugs. All three are clock-mixing errors.

Tell the agent which input stack the project uses (check Active Input Handling) and which Unity version; models trained on older code default to `Input.GetAxis` and `rb.velocity`. When it writes movement code, verify: forces and velocity are applied in `FixedUpdate`, one-shot inputs are latched, queries pass a LayerMask and use NonAlloc, and it did not 'fix' jitter by moving the camera into `FixedUpdate` instead of enabling interpolation. Ask it to state which layer pairs it expects to collide and check the matrix.

patterns.signal: Rigidbody forces applied in `Update` feel stronger at high frame rates and weaker at low ones
patterns.why: Physics steps on a fixed timestep, so forces applied there are frame rate independent. Read input in Update; only the application of forces moves to FixedUpdate.

patterns.signal: `WasPressedThisFrame()` checked in `FixedUpdate` misses jumps at high frame rates
patterns.use: Latch input in Update, consume in FixedUpdate
patterns.why: FixedUpdate may not run on the frame the press happened. Set a flag in Update and clear it after the physics step uses it, so no one-frame event is lost.

patterns.signal: A follow camera shows a Rigidbody stuttering, especially on high refresh displays
patterns.why: Interpolate renders the body between physics steps, so motion is smooth at any frame rate. Adds up to one fixed step of visual latency; use it on player-visible bodies, not everything.

patterns.signal: Fast bullets or balls pass through thin walls between physics steps
patterns.why: For hitscan-like bullets, raycast along the path each step. For physical objects use continuous detection modes, which cost more and should be limited to the few fast bodies.

patterns.signal: A platform moved by `transform.position` jitters riders and misses trigger events
patterns.why: A moving collider without a Rigidbody is treated as static and is expensive to move. A kinematic body moved in FixedUpdate interacts correctly and carries riders.

patterns.signal: Raycasts hit the player's own collider or triggers, and broadphase cost is high in crowded scenes
patterns.use: Layers, LayerMask and the collision matrix
patterns.why: Disable layer pairs that never interact and pass a LayerMask to queries. This removes bugs and broadphase work; keep layer usage documented since there are only 32.

patterns.signal: Gameplay code polls `Keyboard.current.spaceKey` directly and now needs gamepad support and rebinding
patterns.why: Code reads a `Jump` action; bindings for keyboard, gamepad and touch live in the asset and can be rebound. Costs some setup and an indirection when debugging a binding.

patterns.signal: Menu and gameplay both react to the same button, causing double actions when a menu is open
patterns.why: Enable the `UI` map and disable `Gameplay` when a menu opens. Context switches become explicit; forget to re-enable a map and input appears dead.

patterns.signal: Animation logic is a nest of bools and `Play("Run")` calls with fragile transitions
patterns.use: Animator state machine driven by parameters
patterns.why: Code only sets parameters like Speed and Grounded; the Animator owns states and blends. Hash names with `Animator.StringToHash` once, as string lookups each frame waste CPU.

patterns.signal: A cutscene must sync camera moves, animations, audio and events to exact times
patterns.why: Authored sequences belong in a Timeline asset with tracks, not in coroutines of waits. Use the Animator for reactive state; both run on Playables and can be combined.

patterns.signal: Feet slide because the code-driven move speed disagrees with the walk animation's stride
patterns.why: Let the animation drive displacement, optionally through `OnAnimatorMove`, so feet stay planted. Costs responsiveness and precise control; many action games scale animation speed instead.

patterns.signal: Hundreds of off-screen NPC Animators still show up as CPU cost in the profiler
patterns.why: Set culling to skip updates when renderers are not visible. Watch for gameplay that reads bone positions or animation events off-screen, which then stop updating.

keyPoints: Rendering runs per frame; PhysX runs on a fixed step (default 50 Hz). Write physics in FixedUpdate, latch per-frame input for it.
Once a dynamic Rigidbody exists, physics owns the transform; move it with velocity, forces or MovePosition, and give moving colliders a kinematic Rigidbody.
The layer collision matrix and LayerMasks cut broadphase work and bugs; trigger messages need a Rigidbody on at least one side.
Interpolation fixes follow-camera jitter; continuous detection or raycasts fix tunnelling of fast objects.
The Input System separates actions from bindings; the Animator handles reactive state, Timeline handles authored sequences, both on Playables.

quiz.q: A game runs at 120 fps. The jump code calls `jumpAction.WasPressedThisFrame()` inside `FixedUpdate`. Players report that jumps are frequently ignored. Why?
options: The Input System only reports presses during LateUpdate callbacks
FixedUpdate runs at 50 Hz, so the jump is clamped by Maximum Allowed Timestep
Most frames run no physics step, so the press frame often has no FixedUpdate
WasPressedThisFrame requires a kinematic Rigidbody on the player object
quiz.explain: At 120 fps most rendered frames execute zero fixed steps, so the one frame where the press is true often has no FixedUpdate to see it. Latch the press in Update or a callback and consume it in FixedUpdate.

quiz.q: A trigger volume is a BoxCollider with isTrigger on an empty GameObject. The player has a CapsuleCollider, is moved via its Transform and has no Rigidbody. OnTriggerEnter never fires. What is the minimal fix?
options: Add a kinematic Rigidbody to the trigger volume GameObject
Switch the trigger collider to a convex MeshCollider instead
Enable Physics.autoSyncTransforms in the physics settings
Move the OnTriggerEnter handler into FixedUpdate instead
quiz.explain: Trigger messages need a Rigidbody on at least one of the two objects; a kinematic one on the volume is enough. Converting to a MeshCollider or moving the handler changes nothing about that rule.

quiz.q: The camera follows a Rigidbody-driven car smoothly in the editor at 50 fps but the car visibly stutters on a 90 Hz device. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Set the car's collision detection mode to ContinuousDynamic
Move the camera follow code from LateUpdate into FixedUpdate
Raise the fixed timestep to 0.05 seconds to reduce physics cost
Set the car Rigidbody's interpolation mode to Interpolate
quiz.explain: At 90 Hz rendering against 50 Hz physics, some frames show the same physics pose twice; interpolation renders between poses. Moving the camera into FixedUpdate just makes the camera stutter at 50 Hz too.

quiz.q: Rifle bullets are spawned as small dynamic Rigidbodies moving at 400 m/s and sometimes pass through 10 cm walls. What is usually the best approach for hitscan-like bullets?
options: Increase the bullet's mass so contacts resolve more strongly
Raycast from previous to current position each fixed step
Lower the solver iteration count to speed up each physics step
Mark the walls as triggers so overlap is reported instead
quiz.explain: At 400 m/s a bullet moves 8 m per 0.02 s step, so discrete detection skips thin walls. A per-step raycast along the travelled segment is exact and cheaper than continuous detection on many bodies.

quiz.q: A character controller script moves a kinematic platform in Update by setting transform.position, then immediately calls Physics.Raycast to see if the player is on it. The ray reports the old platform position. What explains this?
options: Raycasts ignore kinematic bodies unless QueryTriggerInteraction is Collide
Kinematic bodies are only queried after their OnCollisionStay callback
Transform changes are not synced to physics until the next sync point
Raycasts always use the previous frame's interpolated positions instead
quiz.explain: Queries run against the physics scene, and with autoSyncTransforms off (the default) moved transforms are synced at the next simulation step. Call Physics.SyncTransforms or move the platform with MovePosition in FixedUpdate.

quiz.q: Opening the inventory with `I` leaves the Jump and Fire bindings live, so clicking an item also shoots and Space jumps the character. What is the cleanest fix?

topics.title: UI in Unity: uGUI, UI Toolkit and TextMeshPro
topics.summary: How Unity's two UI systems render and update, why UI is often the hidden frame-time hog, and how to pick between them.

lesson.text: A mobile game hits 60 fps in gameplay, then drops to 40 the moment the HUD shows a ticking timer and a scrolling kill feed. The profiler blames `Canvas.SendWillRenderCanvases` and `Canvas.BuildBatch`, and the culprit is a single Canvas containing the whole HUD, the timer text and a decorative spinning icon. UI is frequently the most expensive 'cheap' system in a Unity game, because it looks static while rebuilding geometry every frame.
uGUI: Canvas, Graphics and rebuilds

**uGUI** (the `com.unity.ugui` package) is the GameObject-based UI: a **Canvas** at the root, children with **RectTransform**s, and **Graphic** components (Image, RawImage, TextMeshProUGUI) that generate quads. A Canvas has three render modes: Screen Space - Overlay (drawn on top, no camera), Screen Space - Camera (placed in front of a camera, can use post effects and depth), and World Space (a quad in the scene, for diegetic UI and VR).

Every Graphic owns a mesh. When anything about it changes (color, sprite, text, size, enable state), it is marked **dirty**. Before rendering, the CanvasUpdateRegistry runs **layout rebuilds** (recalculate RectTransform sizes for dirty layout elements) then **graphic rebuilds** (regenerate vertex data). Then the Canvas **re-batches**: it sorts all its elements by depth, material and texture, and merges them into as few draw calls as possible. Batching is done per Canvas, and one dirty element forces the whole Canvas to rebuild its batch. Batching is partly multithreaded, but the cost still scales with the element count of the Canvas.
Splitting canvases

The main tool is to split by update frequency. A **nested Canvas** (a Canvas component on a child object) is batched independently: when it dirties, its parent does not re-batch. Typical structure: one Canvas for the static frame of the HUD, one for elements that change every frame (timer, health bar, minimap marker), one per popup or screen. Do not go to the extreme of a Canvas per element either; each Canvas costs its own batch and draw calls cannot merge across canvases.

lesson.text:
HUD (Canvas, Screen Space - Overlay)
  StaticFrame        <- borders, icons, labels: rebuilds almost never
  Dynamic (Canvas)   <- timer, ammo, health fill: dirties every frame
  KillFeed (Canvas)  <- dirties on events only
PauseMenu (Canvas, disabled Canvas component when hidden)

items: Hide a screen by disabling its **Canvas component** rather than calling `SetActive(false)` on the GameObject: disabling the Canvas stops drawing but keeps the generated geometry, while toggling the GameObject runs OnDisable/OnEnable on every child and forces full rebuilds.
Animating UI with an Animator dirties the animated elements every frame even when the curve is flat. Prefer tweens that stop, or put animated elements on their own Canvas.
Batches break when materials or textures differ; put UI sprites in a Sprite Atlas so Images share a texture, and check the Frame Debugger to see why consecutive elements did not merge.

lesson.text: Raycast targets and the EventSystem

The **GraphicRaycaster** on each Canvas tests the pointer against every Graphic with **Raycast Target** enabled, on every pointer event. Images and texts default to raycast-target on, so a dense HUD tests hundreds of decorative elements that can never be clicked. Turn it off on everything that is not interactive; remove GraphicRaycaster entirely from canvases that have no interactive content. Invisible full-screen Images left as raycast targets are also the classic 'buttons below stopped responding' bug.

lesson.text: Layout groups cost

Horizontal/Vertical/Grid Layout Groups and Content Size Fitter are convenient but expensive: a layout rebuild walks up to find the root layout and recomputes every child, calling `GetComponents` along the way. Nested layout groups (a vertical list of rows, each row a horizontal group, each cell with a fitter) can turn a single text change into a cascade across hundreds of elements. Use anchors for static layout, compute positions yourself for big scrolling lists, and use pooled, recycled list items rather than instantiating 500 rows in a ScrollRect.
