lesson.text: TextMeshPro

**TextMeshPro** renders text with **signed distance field** (SDF) font atlases: each glyph is stored as a distance field, so one atlas renders crisply at many sizes, with outlines and shadows done in the shader. Font assets are **static** (pre-baked character set) or **dynamic** (glyphs rasterized into the atlas at runtime as they appear). Fallback font assets cover additional scripts. In Unity 6, TextMeshPro is part of the uGUI package rather than a separate package. Pitfalls: a dynamic atlas for CJK can grow large or require fallback chains; Auto Size runs a sizing search on every text change and is costly on frequently updated labels; formatting a new string every frame (`$"{score}"`) allocates garbage, which `SetText` with numeric arguments avoids.
UI Toolkit

**UI Toolkit** is the retained-mode UI system inspired by web technology. Structure lives in **UXML**, styling in **USS** (a CSS subset with selectors and variables), and layout is flexbox via the Yoga engine. At runtime a **UIDocument** component with a **PanelSettings** asset hosts a tree of **VisualElements**. It powers the Unity Editor's own UI and is the recommended choice for editor tooling. It renders through a single uber-shader with dynamic atlasing, so a large panel draws in very few batches, and it has a data binding system in Unity 6.
Choosing between them

items: **UI Toolkit**: editor tools and inspectors (default choice), data-heavy runtime screens like menus, settings, inventories and shops, teams with web/CSS experience, large UIs where batching and styling consistency matter.

**uGUI**: world-space and diegetic UI, heavy use of custom shaders or particle effects inside UI, Animator-driven UI animation, mature third-party assets, and existing projects already built on it. UI Toolkit has been closing these gaps across Unity 6 releases, so check the version you target.
Mixing is legitimate: UI Toolkit menus with a uGUI world-space nameplate system is common. What hurts is two parallel styling and input stacks with no rule for which owns what.

lesson.text: To measure UI, look at `Canvas.SendWillRenderCanvases` (layout and graphic rebuilds), `Canvas.BuildBatch` and the UI rendering markers in the CPU profiler, plus the UI and UI Details profiler modules, which show batches and why they broke.

Tell the agent which UI system each screen uses; agents freely mix `UnityEngine.UI.Text`, TextMeshPro and UI Toolkit code in one feature. Verify generated uGUI code does not call `SetActive` to toggle whole screens every few frames, does not add a Layout Group to every row of a long list, and turns off raycastTarget on decorative graphics. For UI Toolkit, check it queries elements once (cache the `Q<T>` result) rather than every frame, and that USS classes are used instead of inline style writes scattered through C#.

patterns.signal: Button handlers modify game state directly and UI scripts read player fields, so screens break when gameplay changes
patterns.use: MVP: presenter between view and model
patterns.why: The view only displays and raises input events; a presenter talks to game state. Views become swappable and logic testable without UI. Costs one extra class per screen.

patterns.signal: A UI Toolkit screen has dozens of fields that must mirror a settings or inventory object
patterns.why: Bind elements to a data source with the MVVM pattern instead of hand-written sync code. Version dependent and adds binding overhead; for a few labels, direct updates are simpler.

patterns.signal: The HUD polls player health, ammo and score in `Update` and rewrites labels every frame
patterns.use: Observer: update HUD on change events
patterns.why: Model raises `HealthChanged`; the HUD updates only then, avoiding per-frame rebuilds and allocations. Unsubscribe when the HUD is disabled or destroyed.

patterns.signal: Back button behaviour is a tangle of ifs over which panels are open, and popups sometimes stack wrongly
patterns.why: Push screens on open, pop on back; the top screen gets input and focus. Model the outer flow (title, loading, in-game) as a small state machine above the stack.

patterns.signal: Profiler shows `Canvas.BuildBatch` every frame; a big static HUD shares a Canvas with a ticking timer
patterns.why: A dirty element re-batches its whole Canvas. Put frequently changing elements on a nested Canvas of their own. Each extra Canvas adds draw calls, so do not split per element.

patterns.signal: A ScrollRect with 1,000 instantiated rows takes seconds to open and scrolls slowly
patterns.why: Create only the visible rows and rebind them as they scroll; UI Toolkit `ListView` virtualises this way. Costs more complex item code, and variable row heights are harder.

patterns.signal: Changing one text causes a spike in layout rebuilds through nested Layout Groups and Content Size Fitters
patterns.use: Anchors instead of nested Layout Groups
patterns.why: Layout Groups cascade rebuilds up to the root. Use anchors for fixed layouts and keep Layout Groups for truly dynamic lists, ideally one level deep.

patterns.signal: Opening a menu with `SetActive(true)` causes a frame spike on a large panel
patterns.use: Toggle the Canvas component to show and hide
patterns.why: Disabling the Canvas stops drawing but keeps its geometry and layout, so re-showing is cheap. Scripts on it keep running, so pause their Update logic yourself.

patterns.signal: Clicks are swallowed by an invisible overlay, or GraphicRaycaster shows up in the profiler
patterns.use: Raycast Target only on interactive graphics
patterns.why: Every Graphic with Raycast Target on is tested on input and can block clicks beneath it. Turn it off on decorative images and text; use `CanvasGroup.blocksRaycasts` for whole panels.

patterns.signal: A TextMeshPro score label is set with string concatenation every frame and Auto Size is on
patterns.use: TMP `SetText` with numbers, Auto Size off
patterns.why: `SetText("Score: {0}", score)` formats without a string allocation, and fixed sizes avoid repeated layout passes. Update only when the value actually changes.

patterns.signal: You need a quick debug overlay or editor tool and do not want to build prefabs or UXML
patterns.why: IMGUI rebuilds the UI from code each call, so it is fast to write and has no asset state. It allocates and redraws every frame, so keep it out of shipping player UI, which suits retained mode.

patterns.signal: HUD elements clip under phone notches or stretch on ultrawide screens
patterns.use: Anchors, Canvas Scaler and safe area
patterns.why: Anchor to edges, scale with a reference resolution, and inset a root rect by `Screen.safeArea`. Test multiple aspect ratios early; fixed pixel positions fail on the first new device.

keyPoints: uGUI regenerates and re-batches per Canvas: one dirty element rebuilds the whole Canvas batch, so split canvases by update frequency.
Disable the Canvas component to hide screens; turn off Raycast Target on non-interactive graphics.
Nested Layout Groups and Content Size Fitters cascade rebuilds; use anchors and pooled list items for large or dynamic layouts.
TextMeshPro uses SDF atlases; watch Auto Size, dynamic atlas growth and per-frame string allocations.
UI Toolkit (UXML, USS, flexbox) is the default for editor tooling and data-heavy screens; uGUI remains strong for world-space, effects-heavy and Animator-driven UI.

quiz.q: A HUD Canvas holds 400 static elements and one timer label updated every frame. Profiling shows Canvas.BuildBatch taking 2 ms per frame. What is the most effective fix?
options: Switch the Canvas render mode from Overlay to Screen Space - Camera
Move the timer label onto its own nested Canvas under the HUD
Turn off Raycast Target on all 400 static elements in the HUD
Wrap the 400 static elements in a single Vertical Layout Group
quiz.explain: Batching is per Canvas, so the one dirty label forces all 400 elements to re-batch. A nested Canvas isolates the frequently changing element; raycast targets affect input cost, not batching.

quiz.q: Opening the pause menu causes a 25 ms spike. The menu is shown with `menuRoot.SetActive(true)` and has 300 elements. What change most directly reduces the spike?
options: Add a Content Size Fitter to the root so layout is calculated once
Replace every Image in the menu with a RawImage component instead
Move the menu to a World Space Canvas positioned in front of the camera
Keep the object active and toggle its Canvas component's enabled flag
quiz.explain: SetActive runs OnEnable on every child and forces full layout and graphic rebuilds; disabling only the Canvas component stops drawing while keeping generated geometry. The other options do not avoid the rebuild.

quiz.q: After adding a full-screen fade Image (alpha 0) to the top of the HUD Canvas, buttons beneath it stop responding. What is the cause?
options: The fade Image has Raycast Target enabled and absorbs pointer events
The transparent Image breaks batching, so buttons stop receiving input
Alpha 0 Images force the Canvas into a layout rebuild that blocks input
The EventSystem only processes the topmost Canvas in the scene hierarchy
quiz.explain: The GraphicRaycaster hits any Graphic with Raycast Target on, regardless of alpha, and the topmost one consumes the click. Disable raycastTarget on the fade or use a CanvasGroup with blocksRaycasts off.

quiz.q: A team is building a new inventory and shop screen with hundreds of styled entries, sorting and filtering, and several web developers on the team. No world-space or particle effects are needed. Which choice fits best?
options: uGUI with a Grid Layout Group per entry and Animator transitions
IMGUI with OnGUI calls, as it has the lowest per-element overhead
UI Toolkit with UXML templates, USS classes and data binding
uGUI with one Canvas per entry so each item batches independently
quiz.explain: Data-heavy screens with consistent styling are UI Toolkit's strength and match web skills. IMGUI is for editor and debug tools, and a Canvas per entry destroys batching.

quiz.q: A score label using TextMeshPro with Auto Size enabled is updated every frame with `label.text = "Score: " + score;`. It shows up as a CPU and GC hotspot. Which pair of changes addresses both costs?
options: Use a static font asset and enable Raycast Target on the label
Disable Auto Size and use SetText with a numeric format argument
Switch the font atlas to dynamic and add a Content Size Fitter
Move the label to UI Toolkit and keep the same string concatenation
quiz.explain: Auto Size runs a fitting search on every text change, and string concatenation allocates every frame; SetText with numeric arguments avoids the allocation. The other changes either add cost or keep the allocation.

quiz.q: The Back button logic is a tangle of ifs over which panels are open, and sometimes a settings popup opens behind the shop instead of on top. Which approach fits best?
options: Keep an `isOpen` bool per panel and check in order
Screen stack: push on open, pop on back
Toggle each panel's Canvas component on and off
Bind each panel to a UI Toolkit data source
quiz.explain: A stack gives one rule: the top screen gets input and Back pops it. Per-panel bools just recreate the ordering ifs you have now.

topics.title: Accessibility and localization
topics.summary: Designing Unity games that more players can perceive, control and understand, and that ship in many languages without retrofits: colour, input, subtitles, screen readers, string tables, plurals, fonts and pseudo-localization.

lesson.text: A co-op shooter launches in twelve languages. Within a week the reviews say: colour-blind players cannot tell squad markers from enemy markers, the German shop buttons read `Kaufe…`, Japanese players see empty boxes in chat, and a German player's save file fails to load because `3,5` will not parse as a float. None of these are hard problems on day one. All of them are expensive after launch, because the decisions behind them (state encoded only in colour, text baked into prefabs, fonts that only cover Latin, culture-dependent parsing) are spread through every screen of the game.
Why accessibility matters

Accessibility is about who can finish your game. Roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of colour vision deficiency, many players have reduced hearing, limited grip strength or tremor, and far more have situational limits: playing one-handed, on a bus with the sound off, or tired after work. Subtitles are a good example of an accessibility feature most players turn on. There is also outside pressure. Platform holders publish guidance such as the **Xbox Accessibility Guidelines**, store pages increasingly surface accessibility features to buyers (Apple's App Store has accessibility labels on product pages), and law reaches parts of games: in the US the CVAA covers in-game communication such as text and voice chat, and the European Accessibility Act covers things like e-commerce flows. Treat the specifics as something to check with your platform and legal contacts per release, not as a fixed checklist.
Visual: colour, contrast, text and subtitles

The core rule is **never use colour alone** to carry information. Red-green deficiencies (deuteranopia, protanopia) are the most common, so red-for-enemy and green-for-friend is exactly the pair that fails. Add a second channel: shape, icon, pattern, position or a text label. Colour-blind filter modes that recolour the screen are a useful extra, but they are a patch over a design that already lost information; a shape-coded HUD works for everyone without a setting.

items: **Contrast**: aim for at least 4.5:1 between text and its background (3:1 for large text), the WCAG thresholds. In a 3D game the background changes every frame, so put text on a backing plate or add an outline rather than trusting the scene.

**Text size and scaling**: test at the real viewing distance; a TV across the room needs much larger text than a phone held close. Offer a UI or text scale option and build layouts that survive 150-200% text, which is the same flexibility localization needs.

**Subtitles**: on by default or offered at first launch, with **speaker labels**, a **background box** with adjustable opacity, adjustable size, at most two or three lines at a time, and captions for gameplay-relevant sounds (`[footsteps behind you]`, `[alarm]`).
Do not rely on audio alone either: a sound cue that warns of an off-screen attack needs a visual equivalent such as a directional indicator.

lesson.text: Motor: remapping, hold vs toggle, timing

items: **Full input remapping** for every action on every device, including menus. Never hard-code keys in gameplay code; read actions, not buttons. With the Input System, interactive rebinding and saving overrides as JSON are built in.
**Hold vs toggle**: sprint, aim, crouch and charge should each offer a toggle option. Holding a trigger for long stretches is fatiguing or impossible for many players.
**No required rapid inputs**: button-mashing and fast quick-time events need an alternative (a single press or hold, or an auto-complete option).
**Aim assist and sensitivity**: adjustable aim assist strength, look sensitivity and dead zones per stick.
**Adjustable timing**: longer reaction windows, a game-speed slider or pause anywhere, so precision timing is a choice rather than a gate.

lesson.text: Cognitive load, motion and flashing

Difficulty is an accessibility setting: separate sliders (enemy damage, timing windows, puzzle hints) or an assist mode let players remove the specific barrier they hit without changing the whole game. Keep the current objective one button press away, make tutorials replayable, and avoid burying critical information in a single line of dialogue. For vestibular and photosensitive players, offer toggles for camera shake, head bob, motion blur and field of view, and keep flashing below about three flashes per second, especially large, saturated red flashes. A warning screen does not make a seizure-triggering effect acceptable; reduce the effect.
Screen readers and the Unity accessibility APIs

On iOS and Android, VoiceOver and TalkBack read the native view hierarchy. A Unity game draws everything into one surface, so by default the screen reader sees a single opaque view and a blind player cannot navigate your menus. Since Unity 2023.2, the `UnityEngine.Accessibility` namespace includes screen reader support for iOS and Android: you build an **accessibility hierarchy** of nodes, each with a label, a role such as button, a screen rectangle and an activation callback, and the platform screen reader lets the player swipe through and activate them. Platform coverage, how it integrates with uGUI and UI Toolkit, and access to OS settings such as font scale have changed between releases, so check the Accessibility section of the manual for the exact version you ship on.

Test with real players who have the disabilities you are designing for, early, with a build where the options already exist. Checklists such as the Game Accessibility Guidelines catch the obvious gaps; players catch the ones you did not imagine, like a remapping screen that itself cannot be navigated without the action being remapped.
Localization: design for it from day one

Retrofitting localization means finding every player-facing string in code, prefabs, scenes, textures and audio. The rules that avoid that: no player-facing text in code or baked into textures, every string referenced by a **key**, no sentences built by concatenation, and layouts that let text grow and flip direction. The **Unity Localization package** (`com.unity.localization`) implements this. You define **Locales** (en, de, ja, ar), and a **String Table Collection** holds one table per locale sharing the same keys. **Asset Table Collections** do the same for sprites, audio clips, fonts and prefabs, so a voice line or a sign texture swaps with the locale. A **Locale Selector** chain decides the starting locale (saved player choice, command line, system language), and components such as **Localize String Event** push the resolved text into a TextMeshPro label and update it when the locale changes.

Plurals are where hand-written code breaks. English has two forms (1 item, 5 items), Japanese has one, Polish and Russian have three or four depending on the number, and Arabic has six. The package's **Smart Strings** (based on the SmartFormat library) let the translator write the forms in the entry itself, and the plural formatter picks the right one using the locale's plural rules. Variables come from arguments or from **local and global variables** attached to the LocalizedString, so changing a variable refreshes the text.

lesson.caption: One key, two inputs: the selected locale chooses the table row and the count chooses the plural branch, so code never builds the sentence itself.

lesson.text: Text expansion, right-to-left and fonts

Translated text is usually longer than English: German runs about 30% longer on average, and short UI strings expand far more (a 4-letter English label can double). Design containers that grow or wrap, set a sensible minimum font size if you use Auto Size (and remember its cost from the UI lesson), and keep a per-key maximum length for places that truly cannot grow. **Right-to-left** scripts (Arabic, Hebrew) need more than reversed text: Arabic letters change shape depending on their neighbours, and the layout itself mirrors, so back arrows, list alignment, progress bars and tab order flip. Things that represent physical direction, such as a media play icon or a clock, do not flip. TextMeshPro has a right-to-left option, but it reverses character order without doing Arabic shaping, so you need a shaping solution or a text system that supports complex scripts; check what your Unity version's text stack provides before committing.

lesson.text: Fonts are a memory problem. Chinese and Japanese need thousands of glyphs, and an SDF atlas of 4096 x 4096 at 8 bits per pixel is 16 MB. In TextMeshPro each font asset has a **fallback list** (and the TMP Settings asset has a global one): when a glyph is missing from the primary Latin asset, TMP searches the fallbacks, so a CJK asset can sit behind your stylised Latin font. For known text, generate **static** atlases from the characters actually used in your string tables; use **dynamic** atlases (with multi-atlas enabled) for player-generated text such as names and chat. Load each language's font assets with its locale, through Asset Tables or Addressables, so an English player does not pay for three CJK atlases. And do not use one CJK font for all three languages: Han unification means the same code point is drawn differently in Japanese, Simplified and Traditional Chinese conventions, and native readers notice.

Numbers, dates and currencies follow the culture too: `1,234.5` in English is `1.234,5` in German and `1 234,5` in French. Format for display with the locale's culture and always serialize data with the invariant culture, or a German player's save writes `3,5` and fails to parse. Currency formatting only changes symbols and separators; real prices come already localized from the store's product metadata.
Pseudo-localization and the vendor handoff

**Pseudo-localization** finds problems before any translator is hired. A pseudo-locale transforms your source text automatically: accented characters (`Šéttîñĝš`), padding to simulate expansion, and brackets around each string (`[Šéttîñĝš ~~~~]`). The Localization package ships a Pseudo-Locale with methods like these. Play the game in it: any text that appears plain was never routed through a table (a hard-coded string), any text whose closing bracket is missing was truncated, and any box glyph is a font coverage gap. Running a screenshot pass in the pseudo-locale on CI keeps new hard-coded strings from creeping back in.

items: **Export, do not hand over the project**: the package can export and import CSV and XLIFF and sync with Google Sheets. Vendors work in translation tools, so give them files they can import and merge back without touching Unity.

**Give context with every key**: a comment saying where it appears, a screenshot, a maximum length, what each Smart String variable means, and the speaker or gender where the language needs it. `shop.buy` alone could be a verb on a button or a heading.
**Keys are stable IDs**: never reuse a key for a different meaning, and change the key (or flag the entry) when the source text changes meaning, so stale translations are not shipped silently.

**Freeze, then verify in game**: set a string freeze before translation milestones, and run linguistic QA (LQA) on device, since many errors (truncation, wrong context, broken variables) are only visible on screen.

lesson.text: `"You have " + n + " coins"` is the most common localization bug. It hard-codes English word order and English plural rules, and no translator can fix it from a spreadsheet. Make every sentence one table entry with variables.

Agents are good at the mechanical half of this work. Ask one to sweep the project for player-facing text (string literals assigned to `.text` or `SetText`, `text` attributes in UXML, strings serialized in prefabs and scenes), propose keys, add the entries to the right String Table and replace the call sites, then list what it deliberately left alone: log messages, analytics event names and save keys must stay unlocalized. Have it write an Edit Mode test that fails when a key is missing in any locale or a Smart String does not parse, and a check of your UI colour pairs against the WCAG contrast ratios. Do not ship its translations: machine output is fine for placeholder builds, but real text goes through translators and in-game LQA. Review any accessibility feature it adds for state that is still encoded in colour alone, and for toggles it wired to only one input device.

patterns.signal: Map markers or team indicators differ only by colour, and colour-blind testers cannot tell them apart
patterns.use: Redundant encoding: shape, icon or text
patterns.why: Pair each colour with a shape or label so the information survives any colour vision. Colour-blind filter modes help less, because they only fix the cases you anticipated.

patterns.signal: A mechanic needs a long trigger hold or rapid mashing, and testers with limited grip report pain
patterns.why: Offer a toggle for every hold and a single-press option for mashing, plus adjustable timing. They are opt-in settings, so the fight stays the same for everyone else.

patterns.signal: Controls are fixed per device, or remapping exists for keyboard only
patterns.why: Let players rebind every action on every device, built on Input System action rebinding. Requires conflict handling, a reset to defaults and saving bindings per profile.

patterns.signal: Dialogue subtitles are small white text, and deaf players miss who is speaking and key off-screen sounds
patterns.why: Add speaker labels, a background, size options and captions for gameplay-relevant sounds. Costs authoring sound captions and UI space.

patterns.signal: Players report nausea from camera shake, head bob or flashing effects
patterns.why: Provide settings to reduce shake, bob and blur and limit flashes per second. Wire effects through one intensity setting so new effects respect it automatically.

patterns.signal: A mobile player using VoiceOver or TalkBack reports the screen reader announces nothing in your game
patterns.why: Engine-rendered UI is invisible to OS screen readers until you publish nodes with labels and roles. The Unity APIs are version dependent, so check the manual for your version.

patterns.signal: Literal strings like `"Quit"` are scattered through scripts and prefabs, or one label stays untranslated
patterns.why: Reference every string through a key in a String Table so translators and tools see all of it. Costs a lookup and a key-naming discipline, which pays off on the first new language.

patterns.signal: Code builds sentences like `"You have " + count + " coins"` from translated fragments
patterns.use: Smart Strings with plurals and variables
patterns.why: One translatable entry with placeholders lets each language reorder words and pick plural forms. Fragments assume English word order and plural rules, which most languages break.

patterns.signal: Voice-over, flag sprites or fonts must differ per language, and all of them load for every player
patterns.why: Map each locale to its own assets and load only the active one, through Asset Tables or Addressables. CJK fonts especially are large; load them as per-locale fallbacks.

patterns.signal: Parsing `"1.5"` from a save or config fails on German or French machines
patterns.why: Use `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` for saved and network data and the player's culture only for displayed numbers and dates. Mixing them corrupts saves across regions.

patterns.signal: Arabic or Hebrew is on the roadmap and the UI layout assumes left-to-right
patterns.why: Mirror layouts, progress direction and text alignment for RTL locales and use a text renderer that shapes Arabic correctly. Retrofitting late is costly; build layouts mirror-ready now.

patterns.signal: Hard-coded text and truncated labels are only discovered after translations arrive
patterns.why: A pseudo-locale accents, brackets and expands every string, so unlocalised text and overflow show up on day one. Costs nothing but a test pass per screen.

keyPoints: Never carry information by colour alone; add shape, icon or text, and keep text contrast at WCAG levels on a backing plate.
Motor access means full remapping on every device, a toggle option for every hold, no required rapid inputs, and adjustable timing and aim assist.
Subtitles need speaker labels, a background, size options and captions for important sounds; motion and flashing need toggles and limits.
Unity games are opaque to mobile screen readers unless you expose an accessibility hierarchy; the APIs are version-dependent, so check the manual.
Reference every string by key through String Tables, write plurals and variables as Smart Strings, and swap fonts, sprites and audio via Asset Tables.
Plan for expansion, right-to-left mirroring, CJK fallback fonts loaded per locale, and culture-aware display with invariant-culture data.
Pseudo-localize early to expose hard-coded text and truncation, and give translators exported files with context for every key.

quiz.q: A strategy map marks available objectives with green dots and locked ones with red dots. Colour-blind testers cannot tell them apart. Which change fixes it for the most players?
options: Add a filter mode that recolours the whole screen on request
Swap to a blue and orange pair but keep the identical dots
Give locked objectives a padlock icon and keep the colours
Raise the saturation of both colours so each stands out more
quiz.explain: A second channel (the icon) works for every type of colour deficiency, in greyscale and with no setting to find. A filter or a new colour pair still encodes the state in colour alone, and saturation does not separate hues a player cannot distinguish.

quiz.q: A boss fight requires holding the right trigger for four seconds to charge each shot. Players with limited grip strength report pain after a few attempts. Which change helps them without changing the fight for everyone?
options: An option that makes charge a toggle: press to start, press to fire
Shorten the charge time to two seconds on every difficulty level
Add aim assist so that charged shots home in on the boss target
Allow remapping the charge action to the other trigger instead
quiz.explain: The barrier is sustained holding, and a toggle option removes it for the players who need it. Remapping moves the hold to another finger, aim assist addresses a different problem, and a global change alters the fight for all players.

quiz.q: Code builds the label as `"You have " + count + " coins"` with both fragments in the string table. The Polish translator says it cannot be translated correctly. What is the right fix?
options: Polish runs longer, so the label needs a wider RectTransform
Polish lacks those glyphs; add a Latin Extended fallback font
Translate the two fragments and choose a suffix in C# by count
Make it one Smart String entry with a plural rule over count
quiz.explain: Polish uses different noun forms for 1, 2-4 and 5+, and may need a different word order; fragments joined in code fix both to English rules. A single entry lets the translator write every form, and the plural formatter picks one using Polish rules.

quiz.q: Your game ships in English, Japanese and Simplified Chinese. A memory capture from an English player shows three 4096 x 4096 CJK font atlases resident. What is the best change?
options: Use one shared CJK font asset for both Japanese and Chinese
Load each locale's font assets only when that locale is active
Switch the CJK font assets to dynamic atlases of 8192 x 8192
Enable Auto Size on TextMeshPro labels so glyphs are shared
quiz.explain: Fonts are content like any other; loading them per locale (Asset Tables or Addressables) means English players never pay for CJK atlases. Sharing one CJK font is wrong for Han-unified glyphs and still loads it, and bigger atlases or Auto Size do not reduce memory.

quiz.q: With the pseudo-locale active, every pause menu label appears accented and bracketed except Quit, which reads as plain `Quit`. What does this tell you?
options: The Quit entry has no translation yet in the German table
The Quit font asset lacks the accented glyphs pseudo-loc uses
The Quit text is set in code or the prefab, not via a table key
Pseudo-localization skips strings shorter than five characters
quiz.explain: The pseudo-locale transforms whatever comes through the string tables, so plain text means the label never asked a table for its string. Missing glyphs show up as boxes, and pseudo-localization does not depend on real translations.

quiz.q: Playtesters report nausea and headaches during sprints, which add strong camera shake, head bob and screen flashes. Which change addresses this?
options: Toggle alternatives for every held input button
Speaker labels and sound captions in subtitles
Reduce-motion setting for shake, bob, flashes
Publish a screen reader accessibility hierarchy
quiz.explain: A reduce-motion setting, ideally one intensity value all effects read, targets the cause. Subtitles and captions help players who cannot hear, not those made ill by motion.

topics.title: Assets and Content Management
topics.summary: Import settings, texture compression, atlases, Resources, AssetBundles and Addressables, and how content turns into memory.

lesson.text: A mobile build crashes on 3 GB Android phones after the second level. The memory profiler shows 900 MB of textures, including two copies of the same character atlas, a 4096x4096 uncompressed background and a pile of shop icons nobody has opened. None of this is a code bug in the usual sense; it is content management. In Unity, most of a shipped game's memory and download size is determined by import settings and by how assets are grouped and loaded.
Import pipeline and meta files

Unity never uses your PNG, FBX or WAV at runtime. On import it converts each source file into an engine-native, platform-specific artifact cached in the `Library` folder, according to **import settings** stored in the adjacent `.meta` file. That same file holds the GUID that every reference to the asset uses (see the fundamentals and version-control lessons), so meta files must be committed and `Library` must not. Changing an import setting rewrites the meta file and triggers a reimport, which is why import settings are reviewable in diffs.
Texture import settings and compression

Textures dominate memory, so their settings matter most. Key settings: **Max Size** (downscales at import), **Compression/Format** per platform, **Generate Mipmaps** (adds about 33% memory, needed for 3D surfaces, usually off for UI), **sRGB** (on for colour, off for masks and normal-like data), and **Read/Write** (keeps a CPU-side copy, roughly doubling memory; leave off unless code reads pixels).

2048 x 2048 texture, memory per format (without mips; add ~33% with mips)
RGBA32 uncompressed   32 bpp   16.0 MB
ETC2 RGBA8 / BC7       8 bpp    4.0 MB
ASTC 4x4               8 bpp    4.0 MB
ASTC 6x6            ~3.56 bpp   ~1.8 MB
ASTC 8x8               2 bpp    1.0 MB
BC1 / ETC2 RGB (no a)  4 bpp    2.0 MB

lesson.text: GPU block compression formats stay compressed in VRAM and are sampled directly, unlike PNG, which must be fully decompressed. Platforms differ: desktop and consoles use the **BC** family (BC1 for opaque, BC7 for high-quality RGBA, BC5 for normal maps), modern mobile uses **ASTC** with a selectable block size trading quality for size, and **ETC2** is the Android baseline for older GPUs. If the chosen format is unsupported on a device, the texture is decompressed at load time to an uncompressed format, which silently multiplies memory and load time. Set per-platform overrides deliberately and enforce them with an `AssetPostprocessor` or preset rather than relying on artists remembering.
Sprite atlases

A **Sprite Atlas** packs many sprites into one texture so UI and 2D renderers can batch into fewer draw calls. The pitfall is granularity: when any sprite from an atlas is needed, the whole atlas texture is loaded. Atlas by usage (one per screen or feature, a shared atlas for common icons), not by art folder, or a single shop icon will drag a 16 MB atlas of all shop content into the main menu. Sprites that are packed into an atlas and also referenced directly from bundles can be duplicated, so check builds with the tools below.
The Resources folder

Any folder named `Resources` is included in the build in full, whether referenced or not, and is loadable by string path via `Resources.Load`. It looks convenient and Unity explicitly recommends against it for shipping content: the build contains everything in it, Unity builds a lookup index of all Resources objects that is loaded at startup (increasing launch time with size), memory can only be reclaimed with the global `Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets`, and string paths break silently on rename. Keep Resources for a handful of small bootstrap objects, if at all.
AssetBundles

An **AssetBundle** is an archive of serialized assets built for one platform, loadable from disk or the network at runtime. Bundles let you ship content after release, split downloads and control memory, but the raw API leaves the hard parts to you. If asset A in bundle 1 references texture T, and T is not explicitly assigned to any bundle, T is **implicitly copied into bundle 1**. If bundle 2 also references T, it gets its own copy too: double the download and, once both are loaded, two separate texture objects in memory. Dependencies between bundles must be loaded first, and `AssetBundle.Unload(false)` unloads the bundle but leaves loaded objects alive and disconnected (reloading creates duplicates), while `Unload(true)` destroys objects still in use, producing missing textures.

lesson.text: Addressables

The **Addressables** package (`com.unity.addressables`) is the layer on top of AssetBundles that most projects should use. You mark assets as addressable, give them an address and labels, and arrange them in **groups** whose settings control bundle packing (pack together, separately, or by label), local versus remote hosting, and compression. At build time it generates bundles plus a **catalog** mapping addresses to bundle locations, resolves dependencies, and at runtime loads bundles and their dependencies automatically.

Addressables is **reference counted**: each load increments counts on the asset and its bundles, each `Release` decrements, and a bundle unloads when its count reaches zero. Forgotten releases are memory leaks; double releases unload content still in use. A subtle point: an asset loaded from a bundle generally stays in memory until its whole bundle unloads, so a 'pack together' group of 200 enemies keeps released enemies resident while any one is still in use. Group content by what is loaded and unloaded together. Use the Addressables **Analyze** rules and build reports to find duplicated dependencies, and assign shared materials, shaders and atlases to their own group.

lesson.text: Memory unloading

items: `Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets` walks the object graph and frees assets with no references. It is expensive (a long main-thread stall on large projects) and is called automatically on non-additive scene loads; call it yourself only at natural pause points.
`Destroy` on a GameObject does not free the textures and meshes it used; only unloading unreferenced assets or releasing their bundle does.
Managed references from static fields, events and caches keep assets alive; the Memory Profiler shows the reference chain that pins an object.
Device memory budgets are much lower than device RAM: on a 3 GB Android phone the OS may kill a game well before 1.5 GB, so set an explicit budget per platform and track it in CI.

lesson.text: A 'small' asset duplicated into ten bundles is ten downloads and potentially ten copies in memory. Duplication is invisible in the Project window; you only see it in build reports, Addressables Analyze or a memory snapshot.

Agents reach for `Resources.Load` and string paths because it is the shortest working code. Tell the agent the project's loading strategy (Addressables groups, labels, who owns release). Verify every `LoadAssetAsync` or `InstantiateAsync` has a matching `Release` or `ReleaseInstance` on a clear lifecycle, that it does not call `Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets` every frame or on every screen change, and that new textures it creates or imports have per-platform compression set. Never let an agent regenerate or delete `.meta` files to 'fix' an import error.

patterns.signal: Addressables Analyze or a memory snapshot shows the same texture twice, once per group whose prefabs use it
patterns.why: Make shared textures, materials, shaders and atlases addressable in their own group so bundles reference one copy instead of each implicitly embedding it. Costs an extra bundle to load first.

patterns.signal: You release most enemies from a large Pack Together group, but memory barely drops while one is still in use
patterns.why: A bundle unloads only when its whole reference count hits zero, so group what loads and unloads together (per level, per feature). Too many tiny groups add bundle overhead and catalog size.

patterns.signal: `LoadAssetAsync` or `InstantiateAsync` calls are scattered around and memory grows with every level visited
patterns.use: Owner pairs every load with Release
patterns.why: Addressables is reference counted: one clear owner holds the handle and calls `Release` or `ReleaseInstance` on a lifecycle event. Missed releases leak; double releases unload content still in use.

patterns.signal: Code calls `Resources.Load("Prefabs/Boss")` and startup gets slower as the project grows
patterns.why: Resources ships everything in the folder, builds a startup index and only frees via the global `UnloadUnusedAssets`; string paths break on rename. Keep Resources for a few tiny bootstrap objects at most.

patterns.signal: Opening the main menu loads a 16 MB atlas because it shows one shop icon
patterns.use: Atlas by usage, not by folder
patterns.why: Any sprite pulls in its whole atlas texture, so pack per screen or feature plus one shared atlas for common icons. Finer atlases mean slightly more draw calls across screens.

patterns.signal: Texture memory on Android is several times the expected size; textures show RGBA32 or an unsupported format
patterns.why: ASTC on modern mobile, BC on desktop and consoles stay compressed in VRAM: a 2048 texture drops from 16 MB to about 1.8 MB at ASTC 6x6. Unsupported formats decompress at load and erase the gain.

patterns.signal: A UI texture drawn only by an `Image` has Read/Write and mipmaps enabled
patterns.why: Read/Write keeps a CPU copy (about double memory) and mips add about 33% that screen-space UI never samples. Keep Read/Write only when code reads pixels.

patterns.signal: Frame hitches on every screen change, and the profiler shows `Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets` each time
patterns.use: Unload only at natural pause points
patterns.why: It walks the whole object graph on the main thread, and non-additive scene loads already call it. Run it behind loading screens; rely on Addressables releases for steady-state memory.

patterns.signal: Producers want to ship new levels or events without a store update
patterns.use: Remote groups with a content catalog
patterns.why: Addressables remote groups on a CDN plus an updatable catalog let you swap content after release. Code changes still need a binary, and you take on hosting, cache and version compatibility.

keyPoints: Import settings in .meta files decide the runtime format; GUIDs in meta files hold every reference together.
Texture format dominates memory: GPU block compression (ASTC, ETC2, BC) stays compressed in VRAM; Read/Write and mipmaps cost extra.
Avoid Resources for shipping content; it bloats builds, slows startup and cannot be unloaded selectively.
Unassigned shared dependencies get duplicated into every AssetBundle that references them; assign shared assets to their own group.
Addressables is reference counted: pair every load with a release and group content by what loads and unloads together.

quiz.q: Two Addressables groups, Level1 and Level2, each contain prefabs using the same 8 MB rock texture, which is not itself addressable. Memory shows 16 MB of rock texture after both levels' bundles load. What fixes it?
options: Enable Read/Write on the rock texture so both bundles share one copy
Call Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets after each level's bundle has loaded
Switch both groups to Pack Separately so each prefab gets a bundle
Make the texture addressable in a shared group so both depend on it
quiz.explain: An unassigned dependency is copied into every bundle that references it, producing two distinct objects. Assigning it to its own group makes both bundles reference one copy; packing separately would duplicate it even more.

quiz.q: A 2048x2048 RGBA UI texture is imported as RGBA32 with mipmaps and Read/Write enabled. It is only drawn by an Image. Which settings change gives the biggest memory reduction without changing resolution?
options: Disable sRGB and enable the Alpha Is Transparency import flag
Use ASTC compression, disable mipmaps and disable Read/Write
Move the texture into a Resources folder and load it on demand
Enable Generate Mipmaps streaming and keep RGBA32 for quality
quiz.explain: RGBA32 with mips is about 21 MB on the GPU, and Read/Write keeps a CPU copy as well. ASTC cuts the GPU copy to a few MB, UI does not need mips, and disabling Read/Write drops the CPU copy.

quiz.q: A game loads 300 MB of content from Resources folders. Players complain about a long startup before the first scene even appears. Which explanation fits?
options: Resources assets are always decompressed into memory at startup
Resources textures cannot use GPU compression on mobile devices
Unity loads a lookup index of all Resources objects at launch
Resources.Load forces a synchronous shader warmup at startup
quiz.explain: The Resources system builds an index of every object in all Resources folders, and that index is loaded during startup, so its cost grows with Resources content. Assets themselves are not all loaded or decompressed at launch.

quiz.q: Using Addressables, a team loads a level's enemy prefabs individually from one Pack Together group of 200 enemies. After releasing 199 of them, memory barely changes. Why?
options: Assets generally stay resident until their entire bundle is unloaded
Addressables never frees memory until Application.Quit is called
Release only works on handles created with InstantiateAsync calls
Pack Together groups disable reference counting for their assets
quiz.explain: The bundle is still referenced by the one remaining enemy, and assets loaded from a bundle generally remain until the bundle unloads. Group content by what is loaded and unloaded together, or pack it more finely.

quiz.q: An artist imports a new texture and an agent 'fixes' a warning by deleting and regenerating its .meta file. Afterwards, three prefabs show missing textures. What happened?
options: The texture was reimported with a different compression format
The Library folder cache was invalidated for the whole project
Addressables catalog entries were rebuilt without the texture
The regenerated meta file has a new GUID, so references broke
quiz.explain: References between assets are stored as GUIDs from the meta file. A new meta file means a new GUID, so every prefab and material pointing at the old GUID now has a missing reference.

quiz.q: The profiler shows a 150 ms hitch on every screen change, and the hitch is `Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets` called from your transition code. What should you reach for?
options: Call `GC.Collect()` after each screen change instead
Move the screens' assets into Resources folders
Call the unload every frame in small slices
Unload only behind loading screens at pause points
quiz.explain: It walks the whole object graph on the main thread, so it belongs where a pause is invisible; steady-state memory should come from Addressables releases. `GC.Collect()` frees managed memory, not unused assets.

topics.title: The Tech Art Pipeline: From DCC Tools to Unity
topics.summary: How models, rigs and textures travel from Blender, Maya, Substance and Photoshop into Unity, and how budgets, conventions and automated import checks keep that pipeline honest.

lesson.text: A new hero character lands in the project. It looks fine in the Scene view, but the spawner sets its rotation to identity and it falls flat on its back, 1.8 cm tall. Its textures are 4096 pixels, the body is 85,000 triangles, the rig has 140 bones and the mask texture makes the armour glow oddly. Nobody broke a rule, because none was written down. A **tech art pipeline** is the contract between the tools artists author in (DCC tools: Blender, Maya, Substance 3D Painter, Photoshop) and the engine: units, axes, naming, import settings and budgets, enforced by code instead of by someone squinting at a review.
Units, axes and transforms at export

Unity is **Y-up, left-handed, and 1 unit = 1 metre**. Blender is Z-up and right-handed with metres by default; Maya is Y-up and right-handed with centimetres by default. FBX carries its own up axis and unit scale in the file, and Unity's model importer reads them: **Convert Units** turns the file's units into metres, **Scale Factor** multiplies on top, and **Bake Axis Conversion** pushes the axis change into the mesh data instead of the root transform. The classic Blender symptom is a model that looks right but whose root has Rotation X −90 (often −89.98) and Scale 100: the axis and unit conversion is stored as a transform rather than baked into vertices.

That hidden transform leaks into gameplay. Code that resets `rotation` or `localScale` undoes the conversion, physics and colliders inherit a scale of 100, animation clips authored against an identity root are off, and every child attachment point is in the wrong space. The rule to agree with art is simple: **the imported root arrives at Rotation 0, Scale 1, with the mesh in metres and Y-up**. Get there at the source (apply rotation and scale in the DCC, use the exporter's unit and axis options, such as Blender's Apply Scalings and Forward/Up settings) or with Bake Axis Conversion in Unity, and check it automatically rather than by eye.

items: **Pivots** are gameplay data: base centre for props that sit on the floor, the hinge for doors, between the feet for characters. A pivot in the wrong place means every placement script and snap tool needs an offset.
**Facing**: characters and vehicles face +Z in Unity, so `transform.forward` means 'ahead'. Agree which DCC axis maps to it once, in the export preset.
**Export presets** in the DCC (saved FBX settings per asset class) beat a wiki page: one click, the same units, axes, smoothing and selection rules every time.

**Naming**: a short, checked scheme such as `SM_` static meshes, `SK_` skinned meshes, `T_Crate_BC` base colour, `_N` normal, `_M` packed mask, and `_LOD0` to `_LOD2` suffixes. Names are how automation decides which rules apply.

lesson.text: Model import settings
Each FBX gets a `ModelImporter` whose settings live in its `.meta` file. The ones that matter for performance and correctness:

items: **Read/Write Enabled** keeps a CPU-side copy of the mesh next to the GPU copy, roughly doubling its memory. Turn it on only when scripts read or modify vertex data at runtime.
**Mesh Compression** quantises vertex data in the build to reduce disk size. It does not reduce runtime memory (the mesh is decompressed on load) and can cause visible artifacts at higher levels.

**Normals and Tangents**: import them when the normal map was baked against the exported normals, or let Unity calculate MikkTSpace tangents to match bakers that use MikkTSpace (Blender and Substance do). A tangent-space mismatch shows up as seams and wrong shading across UV islands. Unity expects OpenGL-style normal maps (green channel up).
**Materials**: set the importer not to create materials (or remap to project materials) so every FBX does not spawn its own duplicate materials.
**Index Format**: 16-bit indices address at most 65,535 vertices per mesh; Auto picks 32-bit above that, which costs memory and is a sign the mesh may be over budget.

lesson.text: Two numbers drive cost: vertices processed and draw calls issued. The vertex count Unity reports is usually higher than the DCC's, because a GPU vertex is a unique combination of position, normal, UV and other attributes: every UV seam, hard edge and material boundary splits vertices. Budget in Unity's numbers, read from the imported mesh, not the modeller's viewport. Every submesh with its own material is at least one draw call, multiplied again by shadow and depth passes, so a prop with five materials costs five times a prop with one, whatever its triangle count.
LODs

A **LOD Group** swaps meshes by how much of the screen height the object covers: LOD0 above, say, 50%, LOD1 above 20%, LOD2 above 6%, culled below 2%. If an FBX contains meshes named with `_LOD0`, `_LOD1` and so on, the importer builds the LOD Group automatically, so the naming convention is the authoring interface. Each level usually halves the triangles; the transition heights belong in the budget sheet next to the triangle counts, because a LOD1 that only appears at 5% screen height saves almost nothing. Recent Unity 6 releases can also generate mesh LODs at import; check the Mesh LOD documentation for your version before relying on it.
Rigs and avatars

The Rig tab sets the **Animation Type**. **Humanoid** maps the skeleton onto Unity's standard humanoid Avatar, which enables retargeting clips between differently proportioned characters and humanoid IK, at a higher CPU cost per animated character and with bones outside the humanoid map handled separately. **Generic** plays curves on the exact bones that exist: cheaper, and the right choice for creatures, vehicles, props and any skeleton that does not share humanoid clips. Pick per asset class and write it down; a crowd of 200 spiders does not need retargeting.

items: **Bone count** drives skinning cost and is a budget line per character class (hero, crowd, background), not a per-asset discussion.

**Skin weights per vertex**: the Quality settings and the importer's Skin Weights option cap the influences per vertex (commonly 4, or 2 on low tiers). Extra weights are dropped and the rest renormalised, so a face rigged with 8 influences creases differently on low-end devices. Agree the cap before rigging, not after.
**Optimize Game Objects** removes the bone Transforms from the hierarchy (the animation system still drives them); expose only the bones gameplay attaches things to, such as hands and weapon sockets.
**Strip Bones** drops bones that have no skin weights, which removes helper and control bones exported by accident.

lesson.text: Textures: authoring for the GPU

GPU compression works on blocks of texels (4x4 for BC and ETC, a chosen block size for ASTC), so dimensions should be multiples of the block size, and **power-of-two** sizes (256, 512, 1024, 2048) keep the mip chain clean all the way down; Unity can rescale non-power-of-two textures at import, but that resamples the artist's pixels. Size itself should come from **texel density**: pixels of texture per metre of surface. If the team agrees 512 px/m for props, a 2 m crate gets 1024 pixels across, and a mug at 0.1 m gets a small slice of a shared atlas, not its own 1024 texture. Mixed densities read as some objects crisp and others blurry in the same frame, and halving density quarters memory, so density is both the look and the budget.

**Channel packing** stores several greyscale maps in the R, G, B and A channels of one texture. HDRP's Lit Mask Map uses R metallic, G ambient occlusion, B detail mask and A smoothness; URP's Lit shader reads smoothness from the alpha of the metallic or base map and takes occlusion as a separate texture, and a custom shader can use any layout the team agrees. One packed texture means one file, one sample and one set of import settings instead of four. Packed masks hold data, not colour, so they must be imported with **sRGB off**, or the gamma conversion bends every value; they need a format with good per-channel quality and an alpha channel (BC7 on desktop, ASTC on mobile); and normal maps stay in their own texture type. Substance 3D Painter's export presets and Photoshop channels can produce the packed file directly, so nobody packs by hand.

lesson.text: Author once at master resolution and let import settings decide what each platform gets. The **Default** settings plus per-platform **overrides** (for example Android ASTC 6x6 at 1024, desktop BC7 at 2048) set format and **Max Size** per target; a format the device does not support gets decompressed at load, as the assets lesson showed. Keep a **single source of truth**: the `.blend`, `.spp` or `.psd` source lives in version control (Git LFS or the art repository), the exported FBX or PNG in `Assets/` is regenerated from it, and nobody hand-edits an exported file, because the next export silently overwrites the fix.
Materials and shader ownership

Shaders are code: every keyword multiplies variants and compile time (see the rendering lesson), and every distinct shader breaks SRP Batcher grouping. A workable split is that engineers and technical artists own a small library of master shaders (Shader Graph or HLSL) with deliberately exposed properties, and artists create **materials and Material Variants** from those, changing values but not structure. New shader requests go through the owners, who can often add a property instead of a shader. Materials auto-generated by the FBX importer are the usual source of near-duplicates, which is another reason to turn material creation off and remap to library materials.
Budgets as a contract

Budgets are agreed per **asset class**, not argued per asset, and written in the units the engine measures: triangles and bones read from the imported mesh, draw calls, texture size and format per platform, texel density. They come from profiling the target device (the profiling lesson), are owned jointly by the art lead and an engineer, and live in one place that both people and tools read, such as a ScriptableObject or a JSON file in the repository.

Example budget sheet (mobile, agreed with art, lives in one asset)

Asset class        Tris LOD0  Bones  Draw calls  Texture max, Android    Texel density
Hero character      25,000     75        2       2048, ASTC 6x6          1024 px/m
Crowd character      6,000     30        1       1024, ASTC 8x8           512 px/m
Hero prop            8,000      -        1       2048, ASTC 6x6           512 px/m
Background prop      1,500      -        1        512 (atlas), ASTC 8x8   256 px/m

LOD steps: about 50% triangles per level; cull below 2% screen height.
Automating the contract

**Presets** set starting values: the Preset Manager can assign a default importer preset per folder or name filter. Default presets apply when an asset is first imported, so they do nothing for assets already in the project. An **AssetPostprocessor** runs on every import on every machine; use it to fix what can be fixed silently (clamp size, set sRGB, add platform overrides) and to report what cannot (a mesh over its triangle budget) as an import error attached to the asset. If the rules read from a budget asset, make sure a change to it triggers a reimport: bump `GetVersion()` or declare the dependency through the import context (see the `AssetImportContext` docs for your version).

Import hooks only run when something imports, so the last line of defence is a **validator in CI**: a batch-mode method that walks `Assets/Art`, checks every importer and mesh against the budget sheet and naming rules, prints one line per violation and exits non-zero. Run it on every change that touches art. It catches assets imported before a rule existed, settings changed by hand in the Inspector, and anything the postprocessor only warned about, and it turns 'please check your textures' into a failing check with a file name.

lesson.text: Roll out a new rule as a warning first, publish the list of current violations, let art fix the backlog, then flip it to an error. A rule that turns 300 assets red on day one gets disabled by the end of the week.

Do not budget from the DCC's statistics. Triangle counts roughly survive export, but vertex counts grow at every seam and hard edge, and an FBX can carry hidden helper meshes, cameras and unused bones. Measure the imported asset in Unity.

Agents are good at turning a written budget sheet into an `AssetPostprocessor` and a batch-mode validator, and at sweeping existing assets to report violations. Give the agent the budget asset, the folder and naming conventions and the target platforms, and ask for a report before any change. Verify with fixture assets: a deliberately over-budget mesh and a 4096 texture in a test folder must fail or be clamped, and a compliant one must pass. Do not accept 'fixes' that raise a budget, skip a folder or disable a rule to make the check green, and do not let an agent bulk-edit `.meta` files by text when it can change importers through the API. Agents cannot judge looks: a flipped normal-map green channel or a bad LOD pop still needs a human on device.

patterns.signal: An imported Blender model looks right but its root shows Rotation X -90 and Scale 100
patterns.use: Bake axis and units at export
patterns.why: Apply transforms and set exporter axis and units, or use Bake Axis Conversion, so roots arrive at Rotation 0, Scale 1 in metres. Otherwise code that resets rotation or scale undoes the conversion.

patterns.signal: A wiki lists import rules, yet new textures keep arriving at 4096 with the wrong compression
patterns.why: Runs on every import on every machine: silently clamp size, set sRGB and platform overrides, and log import errors for what cannot be fixed. Bump `GetVersion()` when rules change to reimport.

patterns.signal: Each new asset in a folder needs the same starting importer settings
patterns.why: Default presets set importer values on first import with no code. They never touch assets already in the project, so pair them with a postprocessor or validator for enforcement.

patterns.signal: Assets imported before a rule existed, or changed by hand in the Inspector, still break the budget
patterns.why: Walk `Assets/Art`, check every importer and mesh against budgets and naming, print one line per violation and exit non-zero. Catches what import hooks never re-run on; costs CI Editor time.

patterns.signal: Every art review turns into a debate about whether this prop's triangle count is acceptable
patterns.why: Agree triangles, bones, draw calls, texture size and format per class (hero, crowd, background) from device profiling, stored in one asset both people and tools read. Needs an owner to revisit it.

patterns.signal: Metallic, occlusion and smoothness ship as separate textures, or a packed mask shades too dark and rough
patterns.why: One texture, one sample, one set of import settings. Masks are data, so import linear with a format that keeps channels independent (BC7, ASTC); normal maps stay separate.

patterns.signal: Some props look crisp and others blurry in the same frame, and texture sizes are chosen per asset
patterns.why: Pick pixels per metre per asset class: a 2 m crate at 512 px/m gets 1024 px. Consistent look and predictable memory; halving density quarters memory, small objects share atlases.

patterns.signal: Every FBX creates its own materials and artists ask for a new shader per asset
patterns.why: Engineers own a few master shaders with exposed properties; artists make materials and variants. Keeps keyword variants and SRP Batcher groups under control at the cost of a request queue.

patterns.signal: LOD Groups are set up by hand inconsistently and tools cannot tell meshes from textures
patterns.why: Prefixes like `SM_`, `SK_`, `T_` and suffixes `_N`, `_M`, `_LOD0` let the importer build LOD Groups and let tools pick rules. Only works if the scheme is short and checked automatically.

patterns.signal: A crowd of creatures or props uses a Humanoid rig though no clips are shared between skeletons
patterns.why: Generic plays curves on existing bones and is cheaper per character. Humanoid buys retargeting and humanoid IK; pay for it only where clips are shared across proportions.

patterns.signal: A fix made directly to an exported PNG or FBX disappears after the next export
patterns.use: Single source of truth in DCC files
patterns.why: Version the `.blend`, `.spp` or `.psd` (LFS or art repo) and regenerate exports from it. Nobody hand-edits exported files; costs storage for large sources.

patterns.signal: A new validation rule would turn hundreds of existing assets red on day one
patterns.why: Ship the rule as a warning with a published violation list, let art clear the backlog, then flip to an error. A rule that blocks everyone at once gets disabled within the week.

keyPoints: Unity is Y-up, left-handed and metric; imported roots should arrive at Rotation 0, Scale 1, with the conversion baked at export or import.
Budget in Unity's numbers: imported vertex and triangle counts, bones, draw calls per material, texture size and format per platform.
Channel-packed masks save files and samples, but must be imported with sRGB off and a format that keeps channels independent.
Texel density per asset class sets both visual consistency and texture memory; halving density quarters memory.
Engineers own a small shader library; artists work in materials and variants, so variants and batching stay under control.
Presets set defaults on first import, AssetPostprocessors enforce on every import, and a CI validator catches everything else.

quiz.q: A Blender prop imports looking correct, but its root shows Rotation X −90 and Scale 100. A spawner sets `localScale = Vector3.one` and the prop becomes tiny. What is the right fix?
options: Multiply the spawner's scale by 100 for every Blender asset
Set the importer's Scale Factor to 100 for the Blender files
Bake axis and unit conversion so the root imports at identity
Enable Read/Write so the spawner can rescale the mesh vertices
quiz.explain: The conversion lives on the root transform, so any code that resets it undoes the conversion. Baking it into the mesh (at export or with Bake Axis Conversion and unit settings) leaves an identity root that code can safely overwrite.

quiz.q: A packed mask (metallic in R, occlusion in G, smoothness in A) was imported with the default texture settings. Surfaces look rougher and occlusion darker than in Substance. What is the most likely cause?
options: sRGB is on, so the linear mask data is gamma-converted on sampling
Mipmaps average all four channels together at the lower mip levels
Packed masks must be imported with the Normal Map texture type
The alpha channel is stripped unless Read/Write is turned on
quiz.explain: Masks hold linear data. With sRGB on, the GPU applies a gamma decode when sampling, which pushes mid values down: smoothness drops and occlusion darkens. Mipmaps filter each channel independently, and Read/Write only adds a CPU copy.

quiz.q: An artist reports 10,000 vertices in Blender. Unity's imported mesh reports about 17,000. Assuming no hidden objects were exported, what explains the difference?
options: Unity triangulates quads, which doubles every face's vertex count
Mesh Compression stores extra vertices for each quantisation level
The importer adds a duplicate vertex set for the shadow caster pass
Vertices are split where UVs, normals or materials differ at seams
quiz.explain: A GPU vertex is a unique combination of attributes, so UV seams, hard edges and material boundaries duplicate positions. Triangulation adds indices, not vertices, which is why budgets should use Unity's imported counts.

quiz.q: A game needs 200 identical robot spiders on screen, each with custom eight-legged animations made only for that rig. Which rig setup fits best?
options: Humanoid, so the clips can be retargeted onto the spider skeleton
Generic with Optimize Game Objects, exposing only needed bones
Humanoid with the front leg bones mapped onto the avatar's arms
Legacy, because it is the only animation type that supports crowds
quiz.explain: Humanoid retargeting only helps when clips are shared across humanoid skeletons, and it costs extra CPU per character. Generic plays the authored curves directly, and Optimize Game Objects removes the bone Transforms from the hierarchy, which matters with 200 instances.

quiz.q: The team adds a default Preset setting Max Size 1024 for `Assets/Art/Props`. A week later, older prop textures are still 4096. What explains it, and what enforces the rule?
options: Presets apply only during builds; run the player build on CI to apply them
Presets need Read/Write enabled; turn it on and then reimport the folder
Presets apply on first import; add a postprocessor plus a CI validator
Presets apply only to new folders; move the textures to a fresh folder
quiz.explain: Default presets set values when an asset is first imported and never revisit existing assets. An AssetPostprocessor enforces the rule on every (re)import, and a batch-mode validator in CI catches anything that slips past.

quiz.q: You add a validator rule that flags textures above 2048 px, but 600 existing textures violate it and CI would go red for everyone on day one. How do you roll it out?
options: Ship it as a warning list first, then an error
Fail CI immediately so the backlog gets cleared quickly
Add a Preset for the folder and call it enforced
Silently downsize all 600 with a postprocessor
quiz.explain: Artists can clear a published backlog, then the rule flips to an error. A rule that blocks everyone at once tends to be disabled within the week.

topics.title: Profiling and Performance in Unity
topics.summary: Measuring on device with the Profiler, Frame Debugger and Memory Profiler, finding the real bottleneck, and when Jobs, Burst and DOTS pay off.

lesson.text: A team spends a week optimizing scripts because the editor profiler shows `PlayerLoop` at 14 ms. On the target phone, the game is GPU bound at 22 ms, and after ten minutes it throttles from 60 to 40 fps. The week was wasted because it measured the wrong thing in the wrong place. Performance work in Unity follows one rule above all: **measure on target hardware, find which unit is the bottleneck, then optimize that**.
Frame budgets

items: 60 fps = 16.67 ms per frame; 30 fps = 33.3 ms; 120 fps = 8.33 ms.
On mobile, aim for roughly 65-70% of the budget (about 11 ms at 60 fps) in sustained play so the device has thermal headroom.
Mobile platforms default to 30 fps unless you set `Application.targetFrameRate`; many 'why is my phone build capped' questions end here.
A frame has a main thread, a render thread, worker threads and the GPU running in a pipeline. The slowest of them sets the frame rate.

lesson.text: The Unity Profiler

The **Profiler window** (Window > Analysis > Profiler) records per-frame data from modules: CPU Usage, Rendering, Memory, Physics, UI, Audio, GPU and others. In the CPU module, the **Hierarchy** view aggregates time and **GC Alloc** per marker, and the **Timeline** view shows every thread side by side, which is how you see waits and dependencies. Sort Hierarchy by GC Alloc too: any steady per-frame allocation eventually triggers garbage collection spikes, even with the incremental GC.

By default the profiler only records Unity's built-in markers and the top-level calls into your scripts (`Update`, `FixedUpdate`, coroutines). **Deep Profiling** instruments every managed method call. It answers 'which function' when you have no idea, but its overhead is large (often several times slower, worse for many small calls) and skews results toward call-heavy code. Use it briefly to locate a region, then add explicit markers and profile normally.

`ProfilerMarker` costs almost nothing when the profiler is not recording and is compiled out of non-development builds, so leave markers in. They also show up in the **Profile Analyzer** package, which compares captures across many frames (median, worst frames, before vs after a change) instead of eyeballing a single spike.
Profiling on device

Editor numbers include editor overhead (`EditorLoop`, inspector repaints, the Scene view), run on a desktop CPU and GPU, and use Mono with JIT rather than IL2CPP. Build with **Development Build** and **Autoconnect Profiler** enabled, then attach over USB or the network. Development builds have small overheads of their own; avoid **Script Debugging** when measuring because it adds significant cost. For GPU work, platform tools (Xcode GPU frame capture and Instruments, Android GPU Inspector, Arm Performance Studio, RenderDoc, PIX) see what Unity's profiler cannot: per-pass GPU timings, bandwidth and shader occupancy.
CPU bound or GPU bound

Read the main thread in the Timeline view. If the main thread is busy for most of the frame with scripts, physics, animation or culling, you are CPU bound there. If the main thread finishes early and then sits in **Gfx.WaitForPresentOnGfxThread** (or the render thread waits for the GPU), the GPU is the bottleneck. If the render thread is busy submitting while the main thread waits in a sync marker, draw call submission is the problem. **WaitForTargetFPS** means you are simply idling to hit the target frame rate. A quick sanity test: lower the render resolution drastically; if frame time drops, you are GPU bound (likely fill rate or fragment shader cost); if it does not, look at the CPU.

Example capture on a phone, target 60 fps (16.7 ms)
Main thread:   PlayerLoop 6.1 ms ... Gfx.WaitForPresentOnGfxThread 15.8 ms
Render thread: 5.0 ms submitting, then waiting
Frame time:    22 ms
Verdict: GPU bound. Optimizing C# scripts will not change the frame rate.

lesson.text: Frame Debugger and Memory Profiler

The **Frame Debugger**, introduced in the rendering lesson, is the next step once the Profiler says rendering is the problem: it explains why draws did not batch, and it also works on a connected development build, not just in the editor. The **Memory Profiler** package (`com.unity.memoryprofiler`) captures full snapshots: every native and managed object, its size and the references keeping it alive. Take a snapshot after loading a level and another after returning to the menu; comparing them shows leaks like a retained level texture or a static list of destroyed enemies.
Mobile thermal throttling

Phones have no fans. A game that holds 60 fps for two minutes may heat the SoC until the OS lowers CPU and GPU clocks, and frame time rises by 30-50%. Always run soak tests of 15-30 minutes on a mid-range device. Mitigations: cap at 30 fps for less demanding content, leave budget headroom, reduce GPU work (resolution scaling, cheaper post-processing), and use the **Adaptive Performance** package where supported to react to thermal warnings by scaling quality.

lesson.text: C# Job System, Burst and DOTS

When CPU work is genuinely heavy and data-parallel (crowds, projectiles, procedural meshes, pathfinding batches), move it off the main thread. The **C# Job System** schedules structs implementing `IJob` or `IJobParallelFor` onto Unity's worker threads. Jobs operate on **NativeContainers** (`NativeArray<T>` and friends) allocated outside the managed heap; a **safety system** detects race conditions and missing dependencies in the editor. **Burst** compiles a subset of C# (no managed objects, no classes, no GC) through LLVM into highly optimized, often SIMD-vectorized native code; speedups of 10x or more over plain C# for math-heavy loops are common.
