lesson.text: **DOTS** (Data-Oriented Technology Stack) combines Jobs and Burst with **Entities**, Unity's ECS. Entities are ids; components are plain structs stored by **archetype** in 16 KB chunks, so systems iterate tightly packed memory. Authoring still happens with GameObjects in **subscenes**, which **bakers** convert into entity data. Entities Graphics renders them, and Unity Physics and Netcode for Entities build on it. DOTS shines for tens of thousands of similar simulated things; it costs a different programming model, a smaller ecosystem and more complex tooling. Most projects benefit more from Jobs plus Burst on hot spots inside an otherwise GameObject-based game.

Classic misreads: optimizing scripts in a GPU-bound game, trusting editor timings, treating a Deep Profile capture as representative, and calling `handle.Complete()` immediately after `Schedule()`, which makes the job run while the main thread waits and removes most of the parallelism.

Give the agent real profiler evidence: device, build type, frame time, the top markers from the Timeline view, and whether the main thread waits on the GPU. Without it, agents default to micro-optimizations like caching `GetComponent` that rarely move the frame. When an agent writes jobs, verify it uses Burst-compatible types, disposes every `NativeArray` with the right Allocator, does not call `Complete()` right after scheduling, and marks read-only inputs `[ReadOnly]`. Require a before and after capture (Profile Analyzer) on device for every claimed optimization.

patterns.signal: Optimization decisions are based on Play Mode timings in the Editor profiler
patterns.use: Profile a development build on device
patterns.why: Editor numbers include EditorLoop, a desktop CPU and GPU, and Mono JIT. Use Development Build plus Autoconnect Profiler on the target device, without Script Debugging, which adds its own cost.

patterns.signal: Timeline shows the main thread finishing early, then waiting in `Gfx.WaitForPresentOnGfxThread`
patterns.why: Script optimization will not move the frame. Lower render resolution as a test, then reduce fill rate, overdraw, post-processing or shader cost, using platform GPU tools for per-pass timings.

patterns.signal: `Update` of a system costs 6 ms and you cannot tell which part, and Deep Profiling inflates call-heavy code
patterns.why: Markers cost almost nothing when not recording and compile out of release builds, so leave them in. Use Deep Profiling only briefly to locate a region, never for numbers.

patterns.signal: Someone claims a speedup from comparing one spiky frame before and after a change
patterns.why: Compare medians and worst frames over many frames of two captures on device. Single frames are noise; insist on a before and after capture for every claimed optimization.

patterns.signal: Memory stays 300 MB higher after returning from a level to the main menu
patterns.why: Snapshot before the level and after returning, then diff: leaked objects appear with the reference chain pinning them, such as a static list or event. Snapshots are large and pause the game.

patterns.signal: The Profiler says rendering is the cost and draw calls are higher than expected
patterns.why: Steps through every draw and states why consecutive draws did not batch (different material, shader keywords, lightmap). Works on a connected development build, not only the Editor.

patterns.signal: The game holds 60 fps for a few minutes on a phone, then settles near 40 with the same content
patterns.why: Run 15-30 minute tests on mid-range devices and budget about 65-70% of the frame; cap at 30 fps or scale quality, via Adaptive Performance where supported.

patterns.signal: A hot loop updates thousands of positions, projectiles or mesh vertices on the main thread
patterns.why: `IJobParallelFor` over `NativeArray` runs on worker threads and Burst vectorizes it, often 10x or more. Needs blittable data, no managed objects, and explicit disposal of native containers.

patterns.signal: Code calls `handle.Complete()` on the line right after `Schedule()`
patterns.why: Immediate completion makes the main thread wait for the job, removing most parallelism. Schedule as early as possible, do other work, complete only when results are needed.

patterns.signal: Hierarchy sorted by GC Alloc shows steady kilobytes per frame and periodic GC spikes
patterns.why: Cache arrays and strings, avoid LINQ and boxing in hot paths, use non-allocating API variants. Even incremental GC eventually spikes; allocation at load time is fine.

patterns.signal: Hundreds of projectiles or effects are instantiated and destroyed every second
patterns.why: Reuse deactivated instances instead of Instantiate/Destroy, removing allocation and setup cost. Pools hold memory at peak size and need careful state reset on reuse.

patterns.signal: The design calls for tens of thousands of similar simulated units and GameObject overhead dominates
patterns.why: Archetype chunks give tightly packed iteration with jobs and Burst. Costs a different programming model and tooling; most games are better served by Jobs + Burst on hot spots.

keyPoints: Measure on the target device with a development build; editor timings and Deep Profiling distort results.
Use the Timeline view to decide CPU vs GPU bound: a main thread waiting in Gfx.WaitForPresent means the GPU is the bottleneck.
ProfilerMarkers, Profile Analyzer, Frame Debugger and Memory Profiler each answer a different question; compare snapshots to find leaks.
Mobile needs budget headroom and long soak tests because thermal throttling raises frame time after minutes.
Jobs plus Burst give large wins on data-parallel hot spots; full DOTS/Entities pays off for very large simulations.

quiz.q: A phone capture at a 60 fps target shows the main thread doing 5 ms of work, then waiting 14 ms in Gfx.WaitForPresentOnGfxThread; frame time is 20 ms. Which optimization is most likely to help?
options: Lower render resolution or cut fragment shader and overdraw cost
Convert MonoBehaviour Update loops to Burst-compiled jobs
Cache all GetComponent calls made in frequently run scripts
Reduce the physics fixed timestep from 0.02 to 0.04 seconds
quiz.explain: The main thread is idle waiting for the GPU, so the game is GPU bound and CPU-side changes will not raise the frame rate. Reducing pixel and shader cost targets the actual bottleneck.

quiz.q: With Deep Profiling enabled, a function making 50,000 tiny calls shows as 9 ms. Without Deep Profiling, its enclosing Update shows 2 ms. What is the right conclusion?
options: Deep Profiling is accurate, the normal profiler hides managed time
The 9 ms is real time spent in garbage collection during those calls
Deep Profiling overhead inflates many-small-call code; use markers
The 2 ms reading is wrong because IL2CPP is not used in the editor
quiz.explain: Deep Profiling instruments every call, so code with many small calls is inflated far more than code with few large ones. Use it to locate a region, then measure with ProfilerMarkers and normal profiling.

quiz.q: A game holds 60 fps for the first five minutes on a mid-range phone, then settles at about 42 fps with no change in scene content. What is the most likely cause?
options: Incremental GC is disabled after the first few minutes of play
Thermal throttling has reduced the device's CPU and GPU clocks
The fixed timestep accumulates error and adds physics steps
Texture streaming has evicted all mipmaps from video memory
quiz.explain: A gradual drop with constant content on a fanless device is the signature of thermal throttling. Leave budget headroom, consider a 30 fps cap, and run long soak tests.

quiz.q: A job is scheduled with `var h = job.Schedule(n, 64); h.Complete();` at the start of Update, followed by other main-thread work. The profiler shows little speedup. What is the main issue?
options: The batch size of 64 is too small for a parallel job to help
The job is missing the ReadOnly attribute on its output array
Burst cannot compile jobs that are scheduled from Update calls
Completing immediately makes the main thread wait for the job
quiz.explain: Calling Complete right after Schedule blocks the main thread until the job finishes, so no main-thread work overlaps with it. Schedule early, do other work, and complete as late as possible.

quiz.q: After returning from a level to the main menu, memory stays 300 MB higher than before the level. Which tool and workflow most directly finds what is keeping it alive?
options: Memory Profiler snapshots before and after, then compare them
Frame Debugger stepping through the menu's draw calls one by one
Deep Profiling the menu scene and sorting the Hierarchy by time
Profile Analyzer comparing median frame times of both scenes
quiz.explain: Comparing Memory Profiler snapshots shows which objects remain and the reference chains that pin them. The other tools measure time or draw calls, not retained memory.

quiz.q: The profiler says rendering is expensive and you count 1,400 draw calls, far above what you expected. The materials look identical in the scene. Which tool should you use next?
options: Deep Profiling, to count the draws per script
Frame Debugger, to see why draws did not batch
A Memory Profiler snapshot of the render targets
`ProfilerMarker` around the camera render call
quiz.explain: The Frame Debugger steps through every draw and states why it broke from the previous one, such as keywords or lightmaps. Deep Profiling measures script calls, not batch breaks.

topics.title: Editor Scripting and Tooling
topics.summary: Extend the Unity Editor with inspectors, windows, importers and batch-mode entry points so content work scales and automation has a front door.

lesson.text: A mid-size game has thousands of assets and dozens of designers touching them. Somebody imports 400 UI textures with mipmaps on and compression off, and the build grows by 300 MB. A level designer spends an afternoon dragging spawn points into a list by hand. A CI job needs to bake addressables and lightmaps without a human clicking buttons. All three problems have the same answer: Unity's Editor is itself a C# application you can extend, and on a real team the editor tooling is as much a product as the game.
Where editor code lives

Unity compiles scripts into assemblies. Code that references the `UnityEditor` namespace cannot ship in a player build, because that namespace does not exist at runtime. There are three ways to keep it out:

items: **Special `Editor` folders**: any script under a folder named `Editor` (at any depth) goes into the predefined `Assembly-CSharp-Editor` assembly, which is excluded from players. This is the legacy mechanism and still works when you do not use assembly definitions.

**Assembly definitions (`.asmdef`)**: an asmdef whose Include Platforms list contains only `Editor` produces an editor-only assembly. Once a folder has an asmdef, the special `Editor` folder rule no longer applies inside it, so the asmdef is what decides. A common layout is `Game.Runtime.asmdef` plus `Game.Editor.asmdef` that references it.

**`#if UNITY_EDITOR` blocks**: for small editor-only hooks inside runtime classes, such as an `OnValidate` that calls `AssetDatabase`. Use sparingly; every block is a place where the editor and the player diverge.

lesson.text: A common surprise: adding an asmdef to a folder means scripts in it can no longer see `Assembly-CSharp`. Runtime code that worked before may stop compiling until the referenced code also gets an asmdef, because predefined assemblies can reference asmdef assemblies but not the other way round.

Asmdefs matter beyond correctness. Without them every script change recompiles all of `Assembly-CSharp`; on a large project a domain reload after a one-line change can take 10 to 30 seconds. Splitting into assemblies means only the changed assembly and its dependents recompile, and editor tooling changes stop triggering runtime recompiles.

lesson.text: Custom inspectors and property drawers

A custom inspector replaces how one component type is drawn. You subclass `Editor`, tag it with `[CustomEditor(typeof(Spawner))]`, and override either `OnInspectorGUI` (IMGUI, immediate mode, redrawn every repaint) or `CreateInspectorGUI` (UI Toolkit, a retained visual tree built once). New tooling should generally use UI Toolkit; IMGUI remains everywhere in existing code. A property drawer is smaller in scope: it changes how one field type, or fields carrying a given `PropertyAttribute`, render in any inspector. A `[MinMaxRange]` drawer written once applies to every component that uses the attribute.

The key under the hood: inspectors edit a `SerializedObject`, not the C# object directly. `SerializedProperty` walks the serialized data that Unity will write to disk. Going through it gives you undo, multi-object editing, prefab override tracking (bold labels) and correct dirtying for free. Writing `((Spawner)target).count = 5` bypasses all of that: the change may not be saved, may not be undoable, and will not register as a prefab override.

Note the pairing in `CollectChildren`: when you do write fields directly, call `Undo.RecordObject` before the change (it also marks the object and its scene dirty), and if the target can be a prefab instance, call `PrefabUtility.RecordPrefabInstancePropertyModifications` after it. Skipping these is the classic cause of edits that look applied and vanish on reload. `EditorUtility.SetDirty` is for assets changed without undo, not a substitute for either.

lesson.text: Windows, menu items and ScriptableObject tools

`EditorWindow` gives you a dockable panel: subclass it, open it with `GetWindow<T>()`, and build UI in `CreateGUI`. `[MenuItem("Tools/Level/Validate Spawns")]` on a static method adds a menu entry; a second method with the same path and `true` as the validate argument controls whether it is greyed out. `[ContextMenu]` adds entries to a component's gear menu.

ScriptableObjects are the natural data model for tools. Instead of hard-coding import rules or level metadata in C#, make an asset type with `[CreateAssetMenu]` and let designers own the data. A texture rules asset, a list of scenes in the build, a table of enemy stats: all diff-able text assets that tools read. The rule of thumb is code defines behaviour, ScriptableObjects hold the knobs.
AssetPostprocessor: enforce rules at import

`AssetPostprocessor` subclasses get callbacks during import: `OnPreprocessTexture`, `OnPreprocessModel`, `OnPostprocessModel` and the static `OnPostprocessAllAssets`. Preprocess hooks run before the importer and can change its settings through `assetImporter`; this is where you enforce that everything under `Assets/Art/UI` is a sprite without mipmaps and with a max size of 2048. Because the rule runs at import, it also runs on every machine and in CI, so no one can forget it.

Two numbers make the point: a 2048x2048 RGBA32 texture is 16 MB uncompressed and about 21 MB with mipmaps; the same texture as ASTC 6x6 is under 2 MB. One missed setting on a hundred textures is the difference between fitting in a mobile memory budget and crashing on a 3 GB device. Bump the postprocessor's `GetVersion()` when rules change so Unity reimports affected assets.

lesson.text: Batch mode and -executeMethod

Every editor feature reachable from a static method is reachable from the command line. `-batchmode` runs the Editor without UI, `-quit` exits when done, `-executeMethod Namespace.Class.Method` calls a static method after the project loads, and `-logFile -` streams the log to stdout. Exit codes are how CI knows what happened: call `EditorApplication.Exit(1)` on failure rather than throwing and hoping.

Unity -batchmode -nographics -quit \
  -projectPath ./MyGame \
  -executeMethod Tools.Validation.RunAll \
  -logFile -

items: Only one Editor can open a project at a time; a batch job on a project already open in the GUI fails on the lock.
Startup cost is real: importing a cold `Library` folder can take tens of minutes, so CI caches `Library`.
Batch methods must not open dialogs; `EditorUtility.DisplayDialog` has no one to click it.

lesson.text: Editor scripts are the safest interface between an AI agent and a Unity project. Ask the agent to make changes through a `MenuItem` or `-executeMethod` entry point that uses `SerializedObject` or `Undo`, not by editing `.unity` or `.prefab` text. Verify that editor code sits in an editor-only asmdef or `Editor` folder (agents often drop `using UnityEditor` into runtime scripts, which compiles in the Editor and breaks the player build), and that batch methods return non-zero exit codes on failure.

Make the first tool you build a project validator: one menu item, also callable from batch mode, that checks missing scripts, broken references and import rules. It pays for itself the first week and becomes the agent's verification step.

patterns.signal: A tool writes `((Door)target).locked = true` and the change is not undoable and vanishes on reload
patterns.why: `SerializedProperty` edits give undo, multi-object editing, prefab override tracking and dirtying for free. Remember `ApplyModifiedProperties()` after changes.

patterns.signal: A button must mutate a component directly, such as rebuilding a list from child Transforms
patterns.why: Record before the change (also marks dirty), then `PrefabUtility.RecordPrefabInstancePropertyModifications` for prefab instances. `EditorUtility.SetDirty` alone loses undo and overrides.

patterns.signal: The same min/max or ID-picker field appears on many components and each draws it differently
patterns.why: Write the drawer once and every field tagged with the attribute renders it in any inspector. Scope is one field; use a custom editor for whole-component layout or buttons.

patterns.signal: Designers need buttons, validation hints or grouped fields on one component's inspector
patterns.why: `[CustomEditor]` with `CreateInspectorGUI` builds a retained tree; `PropertyField` keeps default drawing and binding. IMGUI remains in legacy code but redraws every repaint.

patterns.signal: A designer repeats a multi-step workflow across many assets or scene objects by hand
patterns.why: A dockable panel built in `CreateGUI` can hold state, lists and batch operations. Costs ongoing maintenance, so build it where the repeated time clearly exceeds that.

patterns.signal: An occasional one-shot action (validate spawns, rebuild atlas) lives in a doc as manual steps
patterns.why: A static `[MenuItem]` gives a discoverable entry, and a validate method greys it out when not applicable. The same static method can be the batch-mode entry point.

patterns.signal: The Editor runs fine but the player build fails with `UnityEditor could not be found`
patterns.why: Put editor code in an asmdef whose platforms include only Editor, referencing the runtime asmdef. Inside an asmdef folder the special `Editor` folder rule no longer applies.

patterns.signal: A one-line change to an editor window triggers a 25 second recompile of all gameplay code
patterns.why: Only the changed assembly and its dependents recompile. Costs explicit references: asmdef code cannot see `Assembly-CSharp`, so dependencies must get asmdefs too.

patterns.signal: Import rules, scene lists or enemy stats are hard-coded constants inside tool code
patterns.why: Code holds behaviour, a `[CreateAssetMenu]` asset holds the knobs designers own, and changes are diffable text. Tools must handle the asset being missing or edited mid-session.

patterns.signal: A CI job must bake, validate or build without anyone clicking in the Editor
patterns.why: Run a static method with `-batchmode -quit -logFile -` and call `EditorApplication.Exit(1)` on failure. No dialogs in batch mode, and cache `Library` to avoid long cold imports.

patterns.signal: A runtime class needs a small editor-only hook such as an `OnValidate` that calls `AssetDatabase`
patterns.why: Keeps the hook out of the player without a separate assembly. Each block is a place where Editor and player diverge, so keep them tiny and never around serialized fields.

patterns.signal: Missing scripts and broken references are only found when someone happens to open a scene
patterns.why: One validator for missing scripts, broken references and import rules, runnable from a menu and `-executeMethod`. Becomes the verification step for humans, CI and agents.

keyPoints: Editor-only code must live in an editor-only assembly (asmdef or `Editor` folder) or the player build fails on `UnityEditor` references.
Inspectors and drawers should edit through `SerializedObject`/`SerializedProperty` to get undo, multi-edit, prefab overrides and saving for free.
`AssetPostprocessor` enforces import rules on every machine and in CI, which beats documentation every time.
ScriptableObjects hold tool data as diff-able assets; code holds behaviour.
Batch mode with `-executeMethod` turns any static editor method into an automation entry point; signal failure with an exit code.

quiz.q: A tool button sets `((Door)target).locked = true;` on a prefab instance. The inspector updates, but after reopening the scene the value is back to false and Ctrl+Z did nothing. What is the best fix?
options: Modify the value via `serializedObject.FindProperty` and `ApplyModifiedProperties`
Call `AssetDatabase.Refresh()` after setting the field on the target
Move the button logic into `OnValidate` on the runtime Door component
Mark the field `[SerializeField]` in addition to it being public
quiz.explain: Going through `SerializedProperty` records undo, dirties the object and registers a prefab override so the change is saved. `AssetDatabase.Refresh` only rescans files on disk and does nothing for an unsaved in-memory scene edit.

quiz.q: The project builds fine in the Editor, but the iOS build fails with `The type or namespace name 'UnityEditor' could not be found` in `Assets/Scripts/Enemy/EnemyGizmos.cs`. The scripts folder has a `Game.Runtime.asmdef`. Which change fixes it correctly?
options: Add `UnityEditor` to the references of `Game.Runtime.asmdef`
Move the file into an `Editor` subfolder under `Assets/Scripts/Enemy`
Move the file into an asmdef whose Include Platforms is only Editor
Switch the scripting backend from IL2CPP to Mono for iOS
quiz.explain: An editor-only assembly is excluded from players, so the reference disappears from the build. Inside a folder already covered by an asmdef, the special `Editor` folder rule does not apply, so moving it into an `Editor` subfolder would still compile it into the runtime assembly.

quiz.q: Artists keep importing UI textures with mipmaps enabled despite a wiki page. What is the most robust enforcement?
options: A custom inspector for `TextureImporter` that shows a red warning label
A pre-commit hook that greps the `.meta` files for `enableMipMap: 1`
An `EditorWindow` that lists every texture and lets leads fix them
An `AssetPostprocessor` with `OnPreprocessTexture` that sets the importer
quiz.explain: A preprocess hook changes importer settings before import on every machine and in CI, so the rule cannot be forgotten. Warnings and windows rely on people noticing, and grepping `.meta` text catches problems late and is fragile.

quiz.q: A CI job runs `Unity -batchmode -quit -executeMethod Build.Validate`. The method logs errors when validation fails, but the CI step is always green. What is missing?
options: The `-nographics` flag so errors reach the log
Calling `EditorApplication.Exit(1)` when validation fails
Wrapping the method in `[MenuItem]` so it is discoverable
Running with `-logFile -` so CI parses the error lines
quiz.explain: The process exits 0 unless the method sets a non-zero exit code, and CI steps pass or fail on exit codes. Log flags only change where output goes, not the result.

quiz.q: On a 300-script project, every change to an editor window script triggers a 25 second recompile of gameplay code. What reduces it most directly?
options: Splitting runtime and editor code into separate asmdefs
Wrapping every editor window in `#if UNITY_EDITOR` blocks
Converting the editor window from IMGUI to UI Toolkit
Moving the gameplay scripts into a `Plugins` folder
quiz.explain: With separate assemblies only the changed assembly and its dependents recompile, and a runtime assembly does not depend on the editor one. `#if` blocks keep code out of players but still compile everything together in the Editor.

quiz.q: Twelve components each draw a min/max range field with hand-written inspector code, and every one looks slightly different. What should you reach for?
options: A shared static helper copied into each custom editor
An EditorWindow that lists every range field
A PropertyDrawer bound to a custom PropertyAttribute
A ScriptableObject holding all the range values
quiz.explain: Tag each field with the attribute and one drawer renders it identically in any inspector. A shared helper still needs a custom editor per component to call it.

topics.title: Builds, Platforms and Testing
topics.summary: How Unity turns C# into a shipping player, what IL2CPP and stripping do to your code, and how to prove it works with EditMode and PlayMode tests in CI.

lesson.text: The game runs perfectly in the Editor. The Android release build crashes on launch with a `MissingMethodException` from your JSON library, and the iOS build takes 40 minutes and then fails in Xcode. None of this showed up in Play Mode, because Play Mode runs on Mono with JIT, with the full .NET class library available and every editor assembly loaded. A player build is a different program, produced by a different toolchain, and most build bugs live in that gap.
The build pipeline

A player build roughly does this: compile scripts for the target platform with that platform's define symbols; collect the scenes in the build list plus everything they reference, plus everything in `Resources` folders; convert assets into platform formats (texture compression, shader variant compilation, audio encoding); serialize them into content files; process the managed assemblies (stripping, then IL2CPP conversion if selected); and finally package or hand off to a native project (Xcode for iOS, Gradle for Android). Shader variant compilation and IL2CPP are usually the slow parts.

Builds can be scripted with `BuildPipeline.BuildPlayer(BuildPlayerOptions)`, which returns a `BuildReport` with the result, total size and per-file breakdown. `IPreprocessBuildWithReport` and `IPostprocessBuildWithReport` let you hook the start and end, for example to stamp a build number or fail early on validation errors. In Unity 6, Build Profiles let you save per-platform build configurations as assets, which is easier to keep in version control than editor-global settings.
Mono vs IL2CPP

C# compiles to IL (intermediate language). With the **Mono** backend the player ships IL and a JIT compiles it at runtime. With **IL2CPP**, Unity converts the IL to C++ at build time and the platform's native compiler produces machine code: ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation.

items: IL2CPP is required on iOS, WebGL and consoles, where JIT is not allowed or not available. Android builds that need ARM64, which Google Play requires, must use IL2CPP.
IL2CPP usually runs faster and is harder to decompile, but builds take much longer (minutes, not seconds) and incremental builds help less.

AOT means no runtime code generation: `System.Reflection.Emit` does not work, and generic instantiations that only appear at runtime through reflection may have no compiled code. Unity has improved this with full generic sharing, but reflection-heavy libraries still need care.

Mono is fine and faster to iterate for desktop development builds; many teams use Mono for daily desktop builds and IL2CPP for release candidates, which means release-only bugs must be tested on IL2CPP builds regularly.

lesson.text: Managed code stripping and link.xml

Before conversion, the Unity linker removes code it cannot prove is used, starting from roots such as scenes, `MonoBehaviour` types and their called methods. The Managed Stripping Level setting goes from Disabled (Mono only) through Minimal, Low, Medium to High; IL2CPP always strips at least at Minimal. Stripping saves real size, often several megabytes, which matters on mobile and the web. The cost is that anything reached only through reflection looks unused: a JSON deserializer creating a DTO by type name, a dependency injection container, `Type.GetType("...")` calls. Those types get removed and you see `MissingMethodException` or silently null fields at runtime, only in the player.

<linker>
  <!-- keep every type in our DTO assembly -->
  <assembly fullname="Game.Network.Dto" preserve="all"/>
  <!-- keep one type and all its members -->
  <assembly fullname="Game.Runtime">
    <type fullname="Game.Save.SaveData" preserve="all"/>
  </assembly>
</linker>

A `link.xml` anywhere under `Assets` tells the linker what to keep. For your own code, `[Preserve]` on a type or member does the same inline. Prefer narrow preservation; `preserve="all"` on every assembly gives back the size you were trying to save.

lesson.text: Defines and platform-specific code

Unity sets platform define symbols such as `UNITY_EDITOR`, `UNITY_IOS`, `UNITY_ANDROID`, `UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN`, `UNITY_WEBGL` and `DEVELOPMENT_BUILD`. You add your own scripting define symbols in Player Settings per platform, and asmdefs can use Define Constraints (only compile this assembly if a symbol is set) and Version Defines (set a symbol when a package version is present). The trap: code inside `#if UNITY_IOS` is not compiled at all while the active target is Android, so it can rot unnoticed. Keep platform branches thin, ideally behind an interface with one small implementation per platform, and compile every target in CI.

Never wrap a serialized field in `#if UNITY_EDITOR`. The Editor writes data for a field the player does not have, and the serialized layout no longer matches; depending on the backend you get warnings, lost data or a crash on load. Keep editor-only data in editor-only assets instead.
Unity Test Framework
The Unity Test Framework (`com.unity.test-framework`) is NUnit plus Unity-specific runners. Tests live in their own asmdef that references the test assemblies.

items: **EditMode tests** run in the Editor without entering Play Mode. They are fast (milliseconds each) and ideal for pure logic, editor tools, asset validation and serialization round-trips. The test asmdef targets the Editor platform.

**PlayMode tests** enter Play Mode (or run in a built player) so `Awake`, `Update`, physics and coroutines run. Use `[UnityTest]` returning `IEnumerator` and `yield return null` to advance a frame. They are slower, often seconds each, because of scene loads and frame stepping.
Design for testability: keep game rules in plain C# classes that EditMode tests can hit directly, and reserve PlayMode tests for integration behaviour that genuinely needs the engine loop.

lesson.text: Running tests in CI

The Editor runs tests from the command line with `-runTests`, `-testPlatform EditMode` or `PlayMode`, and `-testResults path.xml` (NUnit XML that CI systems can display). Optional `-testFilter` and `-testCategory` narrow the run. Do not pass `-quit` together with `-runTests`: the runner exits by itself when tests finish, and `-quit` can end the process before tests run. A non-zero exit code means failures.

Unity -batchmode -projectPath . \
  -runTests -testPlatform EditMode \
  -testResults ./results/editmode.xml -logFile -

CI practicalities: a licence must be activated on the runner; cache the `Library` folder per platform to avoid full reimports; and run at least one IL2CPP build regularly, because stripping and AOT bugs never appear in EditMode or Editor PlayMode runs. PlayMode tests can also run inside a built player on device, which is the only way to catch platform-specific failures in tests.

lesson.text: Tests are the verification loop that makes AI agents usable in Unity. Ask the agent to put logic in plain C# with EditMode tests, run them via `-runTests` in batch mode, and read the result XML rather than claiming success. Watch for common agent mistakes: adding `-quit` to test runs, using `System.Reflection.Emit` or reflection-based serializers without `link.xml` entries, and putting code in `#if UNITY_IOS` blocks it never compiled. Ask for a player build (not just Play Mode) before accepting changes that touch serialization or reflection.

patterns.signal: A save or JSON system works in the Editor but IL2CPP builds throw `MissingMethodException` or load default fields
patterns.why: The linker strips types reached only by reflection. Preserve the specific assemblies or types; disabling stripping or `preserve="all"` everywhere gives back the size you wanted to save.

patterns.signal: Daily builds use Mono and a release candidate crashes in a way nobody saw before
patterns.why: Mono for fast iteration is fine, but stripping and AOT bugs only show in IL2CPP players. Build and smoke-test IL2CPP regularly; it costs minutes per build.

patterns.signal: A dependency uses `System.Reflection.Emit` or generates code at runtime
patterns.why: IL2CPP compiles ahead of time, so runtime code generation fails on iOS, WebGL and consoles. Choose source-generated or AOT-compatible serializers and DI instead.

patterns.signal: Game rules live inside a MonoBehaviour, so testing them requires a scene and frames
patterns.why: Move logic into a plain C# class the MonoBehaviour delegates to; test it in fast EditMode tests. The thin component stays untested or covered by a few PlayMode tests.

patterns.signal: You need to check a combo multiplier or damage formula across dozens of input cases
patterns.why: Pure-logic NUnit tests run in milliseconds without Play Mode, so many cases stay cheap. They cannot catch engine-loop, physics or platform behaviour.

patterns.signal: A behaviour depends on `Awake`, `Update`, physics or coroutines advancing over frames
patterns.why: `IEnumerator` tests yield frames so the engine loop runs. Slower, often seconds each, so keep them for integration paths and run them in a built player for platform issues.

patterns.signal: A CI test step finishes quickly with no results file
patterns.why: The test runner exits on its own; `-quit` can end the process before tests run. Pass `-testResults` and fail the job on the exit code and the NUnit XML.

patterns.signal: Platform code in `#if UNITY_IOS` compiles fine for Android but fails on the first iOS build
patterns.why: Keep platform branches thin behind an interface with one small implementation each, and compile every target in CI. Code in an inactive `#if` is never compiled.

patterns.signal: A serialized field is wrapped in `#if UNITY_EDITOR` and players warn about layout or lose data
patterns.why: Editor and player must agree on serialized layout. Move editor-only data into assets the player never loads instead of conditionally compiling fields.

patterns.signal: Release builds are made by hand from someone's Editor and settings differ between machines
patterns.why: `BuildPipeline.BuildPlayer` from a batch method plus versioned Build Profiles makes builds reproducible, and the `BuildReport` gives result and size. Requires CI licence setup.

patterns.signal: The player size jumps after a content change and nobody knows which assets caused it
patterns.why: The per-file breakdown shows which assets and Resources content landed in the build; diff it between builds to catch duplicates and stray references before release.

patterns.signal: Each CI run spends most of its time reimporting the whole project
patterns.why: A warm `Library` turns cold imports of tens of minutes into short incremental ones. Key the cache by platform and Unity version; a stale cache can hide import bugs, so purge occasionally.

keyPoints: Play Mode is Mono plus JIT plus editor assemblies; a player build, especially IL2CPP, is a different program and needs its own testing.
IL2CPP is AOT: required on iOS, WebGL, consoles and ARM64 Android, slower to build, and incompatible with runtime code generation.
Managed stripping removes reflection-only code; fix with narrow `link.xml` or `[Preserve]`, not by disabling stripping everywhere.
EditMode tests for logic and tools, PlayMode tests for engine-loop integration; run both headless with `-runTests` and fail CI on exit codes.
Code inside a platform `#if` is not compiled for other targets; build every platform in CI.

quiz.q: A save system works in the Editor and in Mono desktop builds, but in the IL2CPP Android build loading returns objects with all fields at default values. The serializer creates types by reflection. Most likely cause and fix?
options: Android file permissions block reads; request storage permission at startup
IL2CPP float parsing differs; switch the serializer to invariant culture
Stripping removed reflection-only members; preserve the DTOs in `link.xml`
The Gradle build compresses saves; disable compression in Player Settings
quiz.explain: Reflection-only members look unused to the linker and get stripped, which shows up only in stripped player builds. Culture issues would corrupt specific values, not reset every field to default.

quiz.q: A team wants fast iteration and ships to iOS and Android. Which backend policy is most sensible?
options: Mono everywhere, because IL2CPP is only an optimization
Mono for daily desktop builds, with regular IL2CPP device builds
IL2CPP in the Editor too, so Play Mode matches the player
Mono on iOS and IL2CPP on Android, since iOS allows JIT
quiz.explain: IL2CPP is mandatory for iOS and ARM64 Android, so it must be exercised regularly, while Mono speeds local iteration. iOS forbids JIT, and the Editor itself always runs on Mono.

quiz.q: A CI test step runs `Unity -batchmode -quit -runTests -testPlatform EditMode -testResults r.xml`. The job finishes in 40 seconds with no results file. What is the likely problem?
options: EditMode tests require `-testPlatform PlayMode` in batch mode
`-testResults` must be an absolute path inside the Library folder
The tests need `-nographics` or the runner refuses to start
`-quit` makes the Editor exit before the test runner executes
quiz.explain: The test runner exits on its own when finished; adding `-quit` can terminate the Editor before tests run, so no results are written. The other flags are not required for EditMode runs.

quiz.q: You need to test that a `ScoreCalculator` combo multiplier is correct across 50 input cases. Which approach is best?
options: EditMode `[Test]` cases calling plain C# logic directly
PlayMode `[UnityTest]` that loads the level and plays it
A manual QA checklist run before each release build
A PlayMode test that waits one frame per case with `yield`
quiz.explain: Pure logic needs no engine loop, so EditMode tests are fast, deterministic and cheap to run in CI. PlayMode tests add scene loads and frame waits that only slow it down and add flakiness.

quiz.q: An agent adds an in-app review prompt inside `#if UNITY_IOS`. Android CI is green; the first iOS build fails to compile in that block. Which practice would have caught it earliest?
options: Raising the Managed Stripping Level to High on all targets
Adding `[Preserve]` to the class that holds the iOS code
Compiling or building every target platform in CI on each change
Running the PlayMode tests in the Editor with Android selected
quiz.explain: Code inside a platform define is not compiled at all for other targets, so only compiling for iOS reveals the error. Stripping and `[Preserve]` affect what is kept after compilation, not whether the code compiles.

quiz.q: Testing a dash cooldown rule needs a scene load and about 40 frames of waiting, so each test takes seconds and CI crawls. Which approach fits best?
options: Convert the test to a `[UnityTest]` that yields frames
Run the same tests in a built player on a device
Raise `Time.timeScale` inside the scene during tests
Move the rule to a plain C# class; test in EditMode
quiz.explain: A thin MonoBehaviour delegating to a plain class lets the rule run in milliseconds with no engine loop. PlayMode still needs the scene and frames, so it stays slow.

topics.title: Unity Projects, Version Control and AI Agents
topics.summary: How a Unity project is stored on disk, why .meta files and GUIDs are sacred, how to merge scenes and prefabs, and how to let AI agents change a project without corrupting it.

lesson.text: Two engineers branch from main. One renames `PlayerController.cs` in their IDE; the other adds a component to the player prefab. After merging, every scene shows `The referenced script (Unknown) on this Behaviour is missing!` and the prefab is half broken. Nothing in the diff looked dangerous. To work safely in a Unity repo, by hand or with an AI agent, you need to know how Unity stores references, because it is not by file path.
Project layout

items: **Commit**: `Assets/` (all content and code, plus every `.meta` file), `Packages/manifest.json` and `Packages/packages-lock.json`, and `ProjectSettings/`.
**Ignore**: `Library/` (the import cache, often many gigabytes and fully regenerable), `Temp/`, `Obj/`, `Logs/`, `UserSettings/` (per-user editor state) and IDE-generated `.csproj`/`.sln` files.
Embedded packages under `Packages/<name>/` are committed; registry packages are restored from the manifest and lock file.

lesson.text: .meta files and GUIDs

Every file and folder under `Assets` has a sibling `.meta` file. It holds the asset's import settings and, most importantly, a 128-bit GUID written as 32 hex characters. Every reference in Unity's serialized data points at that GUID, never at a path. A material references its shader by GUID; a scene references a prefab by GUID; a `MonoBehaviour` references its script by the GUID of the script's `.meta`. Within a file, objects are addressed by a local `fileID`, so a full reference is the pair `{fileID, guid}`.

This explains the opening incident. Renaming the `.cs` file outside Unity without renaming its `.meta` makes Unity treat the old meta as orphaned and the renamed file as new: it deletes the old meta and generates a new GUID, and every `m_Script` pointing at the old GUID is now missing. Renaming inside the Editor, or moving the `.meta` together with the file, keeps the GUID. The same applies to deleting and recreating an asset, or committing an asset without its `.meta`: a teammate's Editor generates a different GUID and references break on their machine but not yours. Duplicated GUIDs, from copying a folder with its metas outside Unity, cause Unity to reassign one of them, again breaking references.

lesson.text: Force Text serialization and YAML

In Project Settings, Editor, set Asset Serialization Mode to Force Text and keep Version Control Mode at Visible Meta Files (the default in modern versions). Scenes, prefabs, materials, ScriptableObjects and animation controllers are then written as a Unity-flavoured YAML. Each object starts with `--- !u!<classID> &<fileID>`: class 1 is `GameObject`, 4 is `Transform`, 114 is `MonoBehaviour`. Text makes diffs reviewable and merges possible, but it is not hand-editing friendly: fileIDs must be unique and consistent across cross-references, a prefab instance stores only overrides in `m_Modifications` against the source prefab's fileIDs, and stripped placeholder objects stand in for prefab internals.
Merging scenes and prefabs

A line-based text merge of two scene edits often produces syntactically valid YAML that is semantically broken: duplicated fileIDs, a child listed in one `Transform` but pointing at a different parent, a component orphaned from its GameObject. Unity ships a semantic merge tool, **UnityYAMLMerge** (Smart Merge), in the Editor's `Data/Tools` folder. It parses both sides as objects and merges by fileID and property. Wire it into Git as a merge driver:

# .gitattributes
*.unity  merge=unityyamlmerge eol=lf
*.prefab merge=unityyamlmerge eol=lf
*.asset  merge=unityyamlmerge eol=lf

# .gitconfig (per machine, path differs by OS and Editor version)
[merge "unityyamlmerge"]
  name = Unity SmartMerge
  driver = '/path/to/Editor/Data/Tools/UnityYAMLMerge' merge -p %O %B %A %A

Smart Merge resolves most non-overlapping edits. True conflicts (both sides moved the same object) still need a human. The bigger lever is structure: split big scenes into additive sub-scenes and nest prefabs so two people rarely touch the same file. A 5,000-object scene edited by six designers will conflict daily no matter which tool you use.

lesson.text: Git LFS vs Unity Version Control

Binary assets (PSD, FBX, WAV, textures) cannot be merged and bloat Git history, since every revision of a 200 MB PSD stays in every clone. **Git LFS** stores those in a separate server and keeps pointers in Git; track them by extension in `.gitattributes` and use `git lfs lock` for files that must not be edited concurrently. **Unity Version Control** (formerly Plastic SCM) is centralized-friendly, handles large binaries natively, supports exclusive checkouts for artists and has a simplified client for non-engineers. Rough rule: code-heavy teams already on Git do fine with Git plus LFS plus locking discipline; art-heavy teams with many non-technical contributors often prefer Unity Version Control or Perforce.
What AI agents get wrong

items: **Hand-editing scene and prefab YAML**: inventing fileIDs, copying blocks with duplicate IDs, or adding a component without wiring `m_Component` on the GameObject. It may load with silent errors or not at all.
**Creating assets without `.meta` files**, or writing `.meta` files with made-up GUIDs that collide or do not match what other references expect.
**Renaming or moving files with shell commands** and leaving the `.meta` behind, which breaks every reference to the asset.
**Assuming file paths are references**: searching for a prefab by path in scene YAML finds nothing, because the scene holds a GUID.
**Declaring success without opening the project**: the agent never saw the console, so compile errors, missing scripts and import errors go unnoticed.

lesson.text: Safer approaches

Treat serialized assets as an output of the Editor, not as source files the agent writes. The agent writes C#, and C# changes the assets through Unity's APIs: `AssetDatabase.CreateAsset`, `PrefabUtility.SaveAsPrefabAsset`, `AssetDatabase.MoveAsset` (which keeps the GUID), `SerializedObject` edits and `EditorSceneManager.SaveScene`. Three ways to run that code:

items: **Editor scripts with a batch entry point**: a static method run with `-executeMethod` in batch mode. Reproducible, reviewable and works in CI, but each run pays Editor startup.

**Running C# in a live Editor** through an MCP server or the Unity CLI connected to the open Editor. The agent can query the hierarchy, read the console, create GameObjects and run snippets without restarts, which gives a tight inspect-change-verify loop.

**Tests and validators as verification**: after changes, run EditMode tests and a project validator (missing scripts, broken references, compile errors) and read the results. The agent's claim of success counts only when these pass.

lesson.text: Give the agent explicit rules in its project instructions: never hand-edit `.unity`, `.prefab` or `.asset` YAML; never create, delete or rename a `.meta` file directly; move and rename assets through `AssetDatabase` or the connected Editor; after every change, check the Editor console and run the tests. When reviewing an agent's diff, look for new assets without `.meta` files, `.meta` files with changed GUIDs, and large YAML diffs in scenes the task did not mention; any of these is a reason to reject and redo the change through the Editor.

Run `git status` after any agent session and check that every added or renamed asset has a matching `.meta` change. A short CI check that fails on an asset without a `.meta`, or a `.meta` without an asset, catches most reference breakage before it merges.

patterns.signal: After a rename, prefabs show missing scripts and the diff shows the old `.meta` deleted and a new one added
patterns.use: Rename and move inside the Editor
patterns.why: Unity references by GUID in the `.meta`; renaming in the Editor or `AssetDatabase.MoveAsset` keeps it. Shell or IDE renames without the meta generate a new GUID.

patterns.signal: References break on a teammate's machine but not yours, and an asset was committed without its `.meta`
patterns.why: Fail on any asset without a `.meta` or meta without an asset, and flag changed GUIDs. Cheap to run and catches most reference breakage before merge.

patterns.signal: A text merge of two scene edits succeeds but the scene loads with duplicate fileID errors
patterns.why: Smart Merge parses both sides as objects and merges by fileID and property. Wire it in `.gitattributes` and git config; true conflicts on the same object still need a human.

patterns.signal: Several designers edit one 5,000-object scene and conflict daily
patterns.why: Split content so people rarely touch the same file; no merge tool fixes concurrent edits of one object. Costs load orchestration and cross-scene reference management.

patterns.signal: Clones are huge because every revision of large PSDs and FBXs stays in Git history
patterns.why: LFS stores binaries on a separate server with pointers in Git; `git lfs lock` stops concurrent edits of unmergeable files. Locking only works if everyone checks locks.

patterns.signal: An art-heavy studio keeps losing work when two non-technical artists edit the same file
patterns.why: Unity Version Control or Perforce handle large binaries natively and enforce exclusive checkout with artist-friendly clients. Code-heavy Git teams may find LFS plus locks enough.

patterns.signal: Scene and prefab diffs are unreadable binary blobs in review
patterns.why: With Force Text and Visible Meta Files, assets become reviewable YAML that Smart Merge can handle. Text is still not safe to hand-edit: fileIDs and overrides must stay consistent.

patterns.signal: `git status` shows `Library/`, `Temp/` or `UserSettings/` changes, or packages differ between machines
patterns.use: Commit only the source of truth
patterns.why: Commit `Assets` with metas, `ProjectSettings`, `Packages/manifest.json` and `packages-lock.json`; ignore regenerable folders. The lock file makes package versions identical everywhere.

patterns.signal: An agent is asked to add a component to 120 prefabs and starts editing `.prefab` YAML
patterns.why: Have the agent write C# using `PrefabUtility`, `SerializedObject` and `AssetDatabase`, run in batch mode or a live Editor. Hand-written YAML risks invented fileIDs and unwired components.

patterns.signal: An agent reports a task done but never opened the project or read the console
patterns.use: Verify in a live Editor loop
patterns.why: Connect via MCP or the Unity CLI to check console errors, query the hierarchy and run EditMode tests and the validator. Success counts only when those pass.

patterns.signal: Agents keep creating `.meta` files, renaming with shell commands or reaching for `Resources.Load`
patterns.why: State in project instructions: no YAML or meta edits, move assets via the Editor, the loading strategy, and run tests after changes. Rules reduce mistakes but still need diff review.

patterns.signal: An agent diff contains large YAML changes in scenes the task never mentioned, or changed GUIDs
patterns.use: Reject and redo through the Editor
patterns.why: Unrelated scene churn and GUID changes signal hand-edited or regenerated assets. Revert and redo the change through Editor APIs rather than patching the YAML.

keyPoints: Unity references assets by GUID stored in `.meta` files, not by path; losing or regenerating a `.meta` breaks every reference.
Commit `Assets` with metas, `Packages` manifest and lock file and `ProjectSettings`; ignore `Library`, `Temp`, `Logs` and `UserSettings`.
Use Force Text serialization and UnityYAMLMerge for scenes and prefabs; reduce conflicts structurally with additive scenes and nested prefabs.
Large binaries go in Git LFS with locking, or in Unity Version Control or Perforce for art-heavy teams.
Agents should change assets through Editor APIs (batch scripts or a live Editor via MCP/CLI) and verify with console checks and tests, never by writing YAML.

quiz.q: After a merge, a prefab shows a missing script where `EnemyAI` used to be. The branch renamed `EnemyAI.cs` to `EnemyBrain.cs` with `git mv`, and the diff shows `EnemyAI.cs.meta` deleted and a new `EnemyBrain.cs.meta` added. What happened?
options: The class name no longer matches the file name, so Unity skipped it
The new meta has a new GUID, so `m_Script` points at nothing
Smart Merge dropped the component because both sides edited it
The prefab cached the old path and needs a Library reimport
quiz.explain: References use the script's GUID from its `.meta`; deleting the old meta and generating a new one orphans every reference. The fix is to keep the original meta when renaming. A class/file name mismatch causes a different warning and does not explain a deleted meta.

quiz.q: Which set of folders should be committed in a typical Unity Git repository?
options: `Assets`, `Library`, `ProjectSettings` and `Packages`
`Assets`, `Packages`, `ProjectSettings` and `UserSettings`
`Assets` without metas, `Packages` and `ProjectSettings`
`Assets` with metas, `Packages` and `ProjectSettings`
quiz.explain: Metas carry GUIDs and import settings, so they must be committed with the assets. `Library` is a regenerable cache and `UserSettings` is per-user state; both belong in `.gitignore`.

quiz.q: Two designers edited different objects in the same scene. Git's default text merge succeeded without conflicts, but the scene now loads with errors about duplicate fileIDs. What prevents this best?
options: Configure UnityYAMLMerge as the merge driver for `.unity` files
Switch Asset Serialization Mode from Force Text to Mixed
Store scenes in Git LFS so they are merged as binary files
Add `eol=crlf` for scenes in `.gitattributes` on all machines
quiz.explain: A line-based merge can produce valid YAML that is semantically broken; Smart Merge merges by object and property. Binary or mixed serialization prevents merging entirely instead of fixing it, and line endings are unrelated.

quiz.q: An agent must add a `Health` component to 120 enemy prefabs. Which approach is safest?
options: Have the agent append a MonoBehaviour block to each `.prefab` YAML file
Copy one edited prefab's YAML block into the other 119 with a script
Run an editor script that loads each prefab and adds it via `PrefabUtility`
Rename the prefabs to `.yaml`, edit them, then rename them back
quiz.explain: Editor APIs allocate valid fileIDs, wire `m_Component` lists and save correctly. Hand-written or copied YAML risks duplicate or dangling fileIDs and missing script GUIDs.

quiz.q: An art-heavy studio with 30 non-technical artists keeps losing work when two people edit the same PSD. What is the most direct fix?
options: Switch the PSDs to Force Text serialization so they merge
Use exclusive file locking via LFS locks or Unity Version Control
Add the PSD files to `.gitignore` and share them on a drive
Configure UnityYAMLMerge as the merge driver for `*.psd`
quiz.explain: Binary files cannot be merged, so the fix is to stop concurrent edits with locking. Force Text and UnityYAMLMerge only apply to Unity's own serialized assets, not PSDs.

quiz.q: An agent finishes a task to add one field to a prefab, but its diff rewrites YAML in 40 unrelated scenes and several GUIDs changed. What do you do?
options: Revert and redo it through Editor APIs
Merge it and run the validator afterwards
Move the touched scenes into Git LFS
Hand-edit the GUIDs back to the old values
quiz.explain: Unrelated scene churn and changed GUIDs signal hand-edited or regenerated assets. Patching the YAML by hand risks inconsistent fileIDs, so redo the change with `PrefabUtility` or `SerializedObject`.

exam.q: Your game drops to 40 fps on device. The Timeline view shows the main thread busy for 23 ms, most of it in `Animator.Update` across 250 skinned NPCs, most of them off-screen. What helps most?
options: Lower the render resolution so the GPU finishes sooner
Enable Rigidbody interpolation on every NPC body
Set the NPC Animators to cull work when off-screen
Move Animator parameter writes into FixedUpdate
exam.explain: The main thread is busy animating characters nobody can see; a culling mode such as Cull Update Transforms or Cull Completely removes that work. Resolution only helps a GPU-bound frame, and interpolation adds work rather than removing it.

exam.q: A designer reports that after you renamed the serialized field `hp` to `maxHealth`, every enemy prefab lost its tuned health value. What would have preserved the data?
options: Adding `[FormerlySerializedAs("hp")]` to the new field
Adding `[SerializeReference]` to the renamed field
Turning the field into a `[field: SerializeField]` property
Reimporting all prefabs right after the rename
exam.explain: The serializer matches saved data by field name, and `FormerlySerializedAs` tells it to read the old name. The other options neither map the old key nor recover lost values.

exam.q: QA reports a crash on 3 GB phones after several boss-fight-to-hub loops. Memory Profiler snapshots show boss textures still resident in the hub, reached through a static `List<Boss>` in a stats tracker. What is the fix?
options: Call `GC.Collect()` every frame while in the hub
Clear the static list when the fight ends
Enable Read/Write on the boss textures
Load the hub additively over the boss scene
exam.explain: The static list keeps the destroyed bosses' wrappers reachable, and through them their assets, so nothing can be unloaded. Removing the reference lets the next unload free them; forcing collections cannot free objects that are still referenced.

exam.q: Which of these can a Burst-compiled `IJobParallelFor` legally do inside `Execute`?
options: Allocate a new managed `List<int>` per item
Read serialized fields from a MonoBehaviour
Format a debug string for each processed item
Do float3 math on NativeArray elements
exam.explain: Burst compiles a subset of C# without managed objects, so blittable structs, Unity.Mathematics types and native containers are fine. Managed lists, MonoBehaviour references and string formatting all require managed memory.

exam.q: You enable the GPU Resident Drawer in a URP project, but CPU rendering time and the Frame Debugger output do not change at all. What should you check first?
options: That every renderer sets a MaterialPropertyBlock
That the renderer uses the Forward+ rendering path
That dynamic batching is enabled on the URP asset
That every light in the scene is set to Realtime
exam.explain: In URP the GPU Resident Drawer only takes effect with Forward+ (or Deferred+ where available) and with BatchRendererGroup variants kept. Property blocks and dynamic batching are unrelated or counterproductive.

exam.q: A designer reports that the shop takes 400 ms to open the first time and memory jumps by 64 MB, although the screen shows only 12 icons. All item icons in the game share one Sprite Atlas. What is the best fix?
options: Enable Read/Write on the atlas so it loads faster
Move all the icons into a Resources folder instead
Split atlases by the screens that use the sprites
Generate mipmaps on the atlas to reduce memory
exam.explain: Using any sprite loads its whole atlas, so one atlas of every icon drags all of them into memory. Atlasing by usage loads only what the screen needs; Read/Write and mipmaps add memory, and Resources does not solve granularity.

exam.q: Which technique cannot work in an IL2CPP player, regardless of link.xml or stripping settings?
options: Emitting new types at runtime with `Reflection.Emit`
Reading custom attributes on types via reflection
Storing a custom struct type in a `List<T>` field
Calling interface methods implemented by structs
exam.explain: IL2CPP compiles ahead of time, so there is no JIT to run code generated at runtime. Reflection over existing metadata, generic collections of structs and interface calls all work when the code is preserved.

exam.q: A tester reports that pressing Space on the pause menu's Resume button also makes the character jump as play resumes. The project uses the Input System. What is the correct fix?
options: Read the jump action in LateUpdate instead of Update
Set Active Input Handling to Both in Player Settings
Add a GraphicRaycaster to the gameplay HUD Canvas
Enable only the action map that fits the context
exam.explain: Both the UI and Gameplay maps are listening to Space at once. Enabling the UI map while paused and the Gameplay map while playing removes the double handling; timing or input-backend changes do not.

exam.q: In Prefab Mode for `Car`, which contains a nested `Wheel` prefab instance, you change the wheel's radius and save. Where is that change stored?
options: In the Wheel asset, affecting every car that uses it
In the Car asset, as an override on its nested Wheel
In each scene that places Car, as a scene override
In the scene, because Prefab Mode edits instances
exam.explain: Editing a nested instance inside a prefab records an override on that instance within the outer prefab. To change every wheel, you would apply the override to the Wheel asset or open Wheel itself in Prefab Mode.

exam.q: A UI Toolkit HUD calls `root.Q<Label>("ammo")` inside Update to set the ammo text, and the query shows up in the CPU profiler. What is the most direct fix?
options: Query the label once in OnEnable and cache it
Move the query and text update into LateUpdate
Replace the USS class with inline C# style writes
Rename the label so its query matches a USS class
exam.explain: Q walks the visual tree every call; caching the reference makes the per-frame cost a simple text assignment. Moving the call or changing styles leaves the repeated tree search in place.

exam.q: You need a method that waits for a server response, returns the parsed score to its caller, and stops cleanly if the object is destroyed. Which fits best?
options: A coroutine that writes the score to a static field
An `async void` method started from Update each frame
An `async Awaitable<int>` using destroyCancellationToken
A FixedUpdate loop that polls the request every step
exam.explain: Awaitable methods can return values, compose with other async calls and honour cancellation tokens. Coroutines cannot return values, and `async void` hides exceptions and is started repeatedly here.

exam.q: After adding a Shader Graph with five Boolean keywords set to Multi Compile, builds take 40 minutes longer and grow by 200 MB. Materials only set these toggles at edit time. What helps most?
options: Enable the SRP Batcher in the URP asset
Mark materials that use it as Batching Static
Raise texture compression to ASTC 4x4 blocks
Change those keywords to Shader Feature
exam.explain: Multi Compile builds every combination, while Shader Feature keeps only combinations used by materials in the build. Batching and texture formats do not change how many shader variants are compiled.

exam.q: Which per-frame code is allocation-free in steady state?
options: A for loop over a `List<Enemy>` comparing sqrMagnitude
A LINQ `OrderBy` over the enemy list to find the nearest
A lambda capturing `this` passed to `List.Sort` each frame
`Physics.RaycastAll` to collect every hit along a ray
exam.explain: Indexing a List and comparing floats allocates nothing. LINQ allocates iterators and delegates, capturing lambdas allocate closures, and RaycastAll returns a new array each call.

exam.q: A CI build job takes 35 minutes, of which 30 are spent importing assets on a fresh runner each time. What helps most?
options: Commit the Library folder to the Git repository
Cache the Library folder per platform between runs
Pass `-nographics` so the asset import is skipped
Switch the scripting backend from IL2CPP to Mono
exam.explain: The import cache in Library is regenerable but expensive to rebuild, so CI caches it per target platform. Committing it bloats the repository, `-nographics` does not skip imports, and the backend affects compilation, not import.

exam.q: A moving platform has a BoxCollider and is driven by a script along a path. Players riding it should be pushed correctly. Which setup is right?
options: Keep it static and set transform.position in Update
Add a dynamic Rigidbody and set transform.position
Make the collider a trigger and move it in LateUpdate
Add a kinematic Rigidbody and use MovePosition
exam.explain: Moving colliders should carry a kinematic Rigidbody moved with MovePosition in FixedUpdate, which pushes dynamic bodies and interpolates correctly. Moving a static collider or teleporting a dynamic body fights the physics engine.

exam.q: Your game drops to 40 fps when the inventory opens, and the profiler shows `Canvas.SendWillRenderCanvases` at 6 ms. The ScrollRect holds 500 instantiated rows, each with a Horizontal Layout Group and Content Size Fitter. What is the best fix?
options: Turn off Raycast Target on each row's background
Disable mipmaps on the item icon textures
Recycle a small pool of rows without layout groups
Switch the inventory Canvas to World Space
exam.explain: SendWillRenderCanvases is the layout and graphic rebuild, driven here by hundreds of nested layout components. Pooling only the visible rows and positioning them directly removes most of that work; raycast targets, mipmaps and render mode do not.

exam.q: A 2 m crate has a 2048 texture unwrapped once across its width; a 0.5 m mug beside it has a 1024 texture unwrapped the same way. The mug looks oddly sharp. Which change matches their texel density and saves memory?
options: Raise the crate to 4096 so both reach 2048 pixels per metre
Drop the mug to 512 so both sit at about 1024 pixels per metre
Drop the crate to 1024 so both sit at about 1024 pixels per metre
Keep both sizes and enable mipmaps, which equalises the density
exam.explain: The crate is 2048 / 2 m = 1024 px/m; the mug is 1024 / 0.5 m = 2048 px/m. A 512 mug gives 1024 px/m, matching the crate at a quarter of the mug's previous memory. Mipmaps change sampling at distance, not authored density.

exam.q: A face rig authored with up to 8 bone influences per vertex looks right on high-end devices but creases badly on the low quality tier. What is the likely cause?
options: Humanoid avatars ignore every bone that is not in the face mapping
Mesh Compression quantised the bone weights to fewer bits each
Optimize Game Objects removed the face bones from the hierarchy
The skin weight cap drops the smaller influences per vertex there
exam.explain: The Skin Weights setting limits influences per vertex per quality level; weights beyond the cap are dropped and the rest renormalised, which changes deformation. Agree the cap before rigging and test on the lowest tier.

exam.q: Each prop artist builds their own Shader Graph. Shader variants, build time and SRP Batcher batches all grow every sprint. Which policy addresses the cause?
options: Engineers own a few master shaders; artists make material variants
Artists keep their graphs but strip every keyword from each of them
Convert every Shader Graph to hand-written HLSL before shipping
Give each prop its own material so batching treats them equally
exam.explain: Every distinct shader adds variants and splits SRP Batcher grouping. A small owned shader library with exposed properties, used through materials and Material Variants, keeps both under control while artists still adjust looks.

exam.q: German players report that their settings reset every launch. The save code writes `volume.ToString()` and reads it back with `float.Parse(text)`. What is the correct fix?
options: Force the thread culture to en-US at startup for every player
Write and parse saved values with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture
Store floats as strings with the player's locale tag attached
Replace float.Parse with Convert.ToSingle on the current culture
exam.explain: German culture writes `0,8`, which the parse rejects or misreads; data must always use the invariant culture. Forcing en-US breaks culture-correct display for the UI, and the other options keep culture-dependent data.

exam.q: Which subtitle setup best serves deaf and hard-of-hearing players during a busy combat scene?
options: Large centred text with no background so the scene stays visible
Subtitles only in cutscenes so gameplay dialogue never distracts
Fast word-by-word text synced exactly to the voice line timing
Speaker names, a backing box, and captions for off-screen sounds
exam.explain: Speaker labels say who is talking when the speaker is off-screen, a background keeps text legible over a changing scene, and captions convey gameplay-relevant sounds. The other options drop legibility, coverage or reading time.

exam.q: You are mirroring the UI for an Arabic release. Which element should keep its left-to-right orientation?
options: A media play button's triangle pointing in the playback direction
The back arrow in the top navigation bar of the settings screen
The order of tabs in the horizontal tab bar across the screen
A horizontal progress bar showing how far a download has got
exam.explain: Icons that represent physical or media direction, like play, are not mirrored. Navigation arrows, tab order and progress fill follow the reading direction and do flip in a right-to-left layout.

exam.q: A component sits on an active GameObject in a scene that loads, plays a few frames, and is then destroyed. Put its callbacks in the order they first run.
steps: `Awake`
`OnEnable`
`Start`
`Update`
`OnDisable`
`OnDestroy`
exam.explain: Awake runs on load, OnEnable right after it, and Start once before the first Update, after every Awake and OnEnable in the scene. On destruction OnDisable runs first, then OnDestroy.

exam.q: Put the stages of a player build in the order Unity runs them.
steps: Compile scripts with the target platform's define symbols
Collect build scenes, their references and `Resources` content
Convert assets to platform formats and compile shader variants
Serialize the converted assets into content files
Strip managed assemblies, then convert them with IL2CPP
Package the player or hand off to Xcode or Gradle
exam.explain: Scripts compile first, then the content set is collected and converted (texture compression, shader variants, audio) and serialized. Managed assemblies are stripped before IL2CPP converts them, and the result is packaged or handed to the native toolchain. Shader variants and IL2CPP are usually the slow steps.

exam.q: Within one frame where physics steps once, order these from first to last.
steps: `FixedUpdate`
Physics simulation and collision callbacks
`Update`
Animator update for normally updated animators
`LateUpdate`
Rendering and `WaitForEndOfFrame` coroutines
exam.explain: FixedUpdate and the physics step (with trigger and collision callbacks) run before Update; the Animator evaluates between Update and LateUpdate, which is why follow cameras go in LateUpdate; rendering and end-of-frame coroutines come last.

exam.q: The turret's target can be destroyed by another system. Click the line that throws or misbehaves once that happens.
exam.explain: Line 8: `?.` checks the C# reference, not Unity's overloaded `==`, so after Destroy the fake-null wrapper passes the check and `TakeDamage` touches a dead object. Write `if (target) target.TakeDamage(damage);`.

exam.q: This flash effect throws `MissingReferenceException` when the object is destroyed mid-flash. Click the buggy line.
exam.explain: Line 9: the token is fetched but never passed, so the await resumes after the object is destroyed and line 8 touches a dead SpriteRenderer. Use `WaitForSecondsAsync(0.1f, token)` so destruction cancels the wait and the catch handles it.

exam.q: Players with a German system locale lose their volume setting every launch. Click the buggy line.
exam.explain: Line 10: the value is written with the invariant culture (`0.8`) but parsed with the current culture, which in German expects `0,8` and misreads it. Parse with `float.Parse(text, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`.

exam.q: What does this log, in the same frame?
options: `False`, then `False`
`True`, then `False`
`True`, then `True`
`False`, then `True`
exam.explain: `Destroy` is deferred to the end of the frame, so the native object still exists and Unity's `==` reports it as alive. `ReferenceEquals` checks the C# wrapper, which is never null here; after the frame ends, the first line would log `True`.

exam.q: Over the next few frames, what does this component log?
options: `1`, then nothing more
Nothing is ever logged
`1` and `2` only
exam.explain: `StartCoroutine` runs the body up to the first yield immediately, logging `1`. Disabling the component does not stop its coroutines; only deactivating or destroying the GameObject does, so `2` and `3` follow on the next frames.

title: Game Case Studies
tagline: Six classic games taken apart: the components, the algorithms and why the choices work.
intro: The earlier sections teach the parts: rendering, the loop, physics, AI, networking, Unity. This one puts them together. Each topic tears down one classic kind of game: a chess engine, a 2D platformer, a kart racer, a first-person shooter, an open-world RPG and a competitive multiplayer game. For each you see which subsystems it needs, the algorithms inside them, the decisions a team makes and why those decisions hold up, including what the alternatives would cost. The aim is to recognise the shape of a game before you write a line of it, and to judge whether a design, or code an agent proposes, fits that shape.

topics.title: Case study: Chess
topics.summary: How a chess game with a computer opponent is built: a pure rules core, bitboards and perft, alpha-beta search with ordering, quiescence and a transposition table, evaluation, difficulty levels and server-authoritative online play.

lesson.text: Your app has a board, a click-to-move UI and a 'Play vs computer' button. The first prototype picks a random legal move, and it holds up for ten minutes. Then one tester castles through an attacked square, another watches the bot hang its queen, and a third asks why the hard level needs 40 seconds to move at move 30. Chess is a good first teardown because it is small and exactly specified: a perfect-information game with 20 legal moves in the start position and about 35 in a typical middlegame. Every part of an engine exists to fight that branching factor, and the rules are strict enough that you can test most of it against published numbers.
Components

items: **Rules core.** Position, moves, legality, draw rules, FEN in and out. Pure data and functions, no UI types.
**Move generator.** Attack tables and bitboard tricks produce pseudo-legal moves; a legality test drops the rest.
**Search.** Negamax with alpha-beta, iterative deepening, move ordering, quiescence and a transposition table.
**Evaluation.** Turns a quiet position into one number in centipawns, from the side to move's point of view.
**Engine shell.** A UCI-style text protocol, clock handling, difficulty settings and a worker thread.
**Front ends.** The Unity UI for local play and a game server for online play. Both talk to the core, never to search internals.

lesson.text: Data flows one way. The UI turns a click into a move and asks the core to validate and apply it. The shell sends the move list and the clocks to the engine; search calls the move generator and the evaluation millions of times per second and returns one `bestmove`. The server runs the same core to validate whatever clients send.
The rules core: a position is more than a board

A position is the piece placement plus the state that decides which moves exist. FEN writes all of it in one line: placement, side to move, castling rights (`KQkq`), the en passant target square, the halfmove clock and the fullmove number. The start position is `rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1`. Castling rights are lost when the king or that rook moves, or the rook is captured, so they are state you cannot recompute from the board. The en passant square lives for one ply, right after a double pawn push. The halfmove clock counts plies since the last capture or pawn move and drives the **50-move rule**: at 100 plies a player may claim a draw, and FIDE makes it automatic at 150. A **threefold repetition** needs the same position three times with the same side to move, rights and en passant possibilities. Keep a history of Zobrist hashes and look back only as far as the halfmove clock, because a capture or pawn move can never be undone.
Board representation: three ways to hold 64 squares

An **8x8 array** (or a flat 64-entry array) is the obvious choice and is fine for a UI or a one-ply bot. Its weak spot is the edge: every ray walk needs bounds checks. A **0x88** board uses a 16-wide, 128-entry array, so a square is on the board exactly when `(sq & 0x88) == 0`, and the difference between two squares identifies their direction and distance in one table lookup. It makes edge tests free and was a staple of older engines. **Bitboards** keep one bit per square in a 64-bit integer: twelve masks (six piece types times two colours) plus cached occupancy. Set operations become single instructions. All white pawn pushes are `(pawns << 8) & ~occupied`, and 'is this square attacked' becomes an AND against a precomputed mask. Strong engines are bitboard-based because 64-bit CPUs make these operations as cheap as an array read while replacing whole loops.
