lesson.text: Leapers need no occupancy, so their attacks are a table built once at startup: 64 entries of 8 bytes for the knight and the same for the king. The builder tries the eight offsets and drops any that leave the board, so edge squares simply have fewer bits and wrap-around bugs cannot appear at runtime. Sliders depend on blockers, and **magic bitboards** solve that. Mask the occupancy down to the squares that can block the ray (at most 12 bits for a rook, 9 for a bishop), multiply by a per-square magic constant found by offline search, shift right, and use the result as an index into a precomputed attack table. The multiply maps every blocker pattern to a distinct index, or to a harmless collision with the same attack set. With the common compact layout the tables hold about 100,000 rook entries and 5,000 bishop entries, under 1 MB in total.
Move generation and perft

Generate **pseudo-legal** moves first: every move that follows piece movement rules, ignoring whether it leaves your own king in check. Then make the move and test whether your king is attacked, and discard it if so. That keeps the generator simple, because pins, discovered checks and the odd en passant capture that exposes the king along a rank all fall out of one test. The cost is making a few illegal moves, a small share of the work. Castling needs explicit checks: rights present, squares between empty, and the king not in check, not crossing and not landing on an attacked square. For make and unmake you can keep an undo stack, or use **copy-make**: a bitboard position is about 120 bytes, so copying it per node is cheap and removes a whole class of unmake bugs. In C# make it a struct, or copy into a preallocated slot per ply, so the search does not allocate a new object at every node.

Test the generator with **perft**: count the leaf nodes of the full move tree to a fixed depth and compare with published values. From the start position, perft(1) = 20, perft(2) = 400, perft(3) = 8,902, perft(4) = 197,281, perft(5) = 4,865,609 and perft(6) = 119,060,324. The start position is gentle (no castling or promotions in the first plies), so also run the well-known 'Kiwipete' position `r3k2r/p1ppqpb1/bn2pnp1/3PN3/1p2P3/2N2Q1p/PPPBBPPP/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1`, which gives 48, 2,039, 97,862 and 4,085,603 for depths 1 to 4. When a count is off, **perft divide** prints the count under each root move. Compare it with a reference engine and recurse into the one move that differs until you reach the single wrong position.

Perft validates move generation only. It never touches repetition, the 50-move rule, clocks, evaluation or search, so those need their own tests: a position that must be drawn by repetition, one at halfmove clock 99 and 100, known mate-in-N puzzles. A passing perft can also hide a hashing bug: put castling rights and the en passant file into the Zobrist key, or the table will merge positions that differ only there.
Search: negamax and alpha-beta

Minimax assumes both sides pick the best move for themselves. **Negamax** folds the two cases into one function using `max(a, b) = -min(-a, -b)`: every score is from the side to move's view and a recursive call returns `-Search(child)`. At a branching factor of about 35, plain minimax visits `35^d` leaves, which is 1.8 billion at depth 6. **Alpha-beta** carries a window: `alpha` is the best score the side to move can already guarantee, `beta` is the best the opponent will allow. When a move scores at least `beta`, the opponent would never let the game reach this line, so the remaining moves are skipped (a **beta cutoff**). The returned value equals the minimax value; only the work changes. With perfect ordering the tree shrinks to about `b^(d/2)` leaves (exactly `b^ceil(d/2) + b^floor(d/2) - 1`), so depth 8 costs about 2 x 35^4 = 3 million leaves instead of 2.25 trillion. With poor ordering you save much less, which is why ordering matters more than anything else in the search.

lesson.text: Move ordering
Cutoffs come early only if the best move is tried first, so the engine sorts moves by a cheap guess before searching them. The usual order:

items: **Hash move.** The best move stored in the transposition table from an earlier or shallower search of this position. Try it first.

**Captures by MVV-LVA.** Most valuable victim, least valuable attacker: score `10 * victim - attacker`, so pawn takes queen comes before queen takes pawn. Many engines use static exchange evaluation (SEE) to push losing captures to the back.
**Killer moves.** Two quiet moves per ply that recently caused a cutoff in a sibling node. The same refutation often works next door.
**History heuristic.** A table indexed by side, from and to that grows when a quiet move causes a cutoff, so moves that have worked anywhere float upward.
**The rest.** Remaining quiet moves, sorted by history score.

lesson.text: In a well-ordered engine the first move tried causes the cutoff in the large majority of cutoff nodes, commonly cited at well over 90 percent. Count it. A drop in that number is the cheapest way to notice an ordering bug.
Quiescence search and the horizon effect

A fixed-depth search stops in the middle of exchanges. Suppose the last ply is `Qxd5`, winning a pawn that a pawn on e6 defends. A static evaluation sees +100 centipawns and never sees `exd5` winning the queen. Pushing such losses just past the search depth is the **horizon effect**. **Quiescence search** fixes it: at depth 0, do not evaluate, call a search that first takes the static evaluation as a 'stand pat' lower bound (the side to move can usually decline to capture), then tries only captures and promotions, recursing until nothing more is worth taking. Order captures by MVV-LVA and skip those that SEE says lose material, or the capture tree explodes; even so it is often half of all nodes or more. When the side to move is in check, standing pat is not allowed, so search every evasion.
Transposition table and Zobrist hashing

Different move orders reach the same position (1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3 and 1.Nc3 Nf6 2.Nf3), and iterative deepening revisits the same positions on every iteration. A **transposition table** (TT) caches results by position. The key is a **Zobrist hash**: fill a table with random 64-bit numbers, one for each (piece, square) pair (12 x 64), one for the side to move, 16 for the castling-rights combinations and 8 for the en passant files. A position's hash is the XOR of the numbers for everything present. XOR is its own inverse, so a move updates the hash incrementally: XOR the piece out of `from`, in at `to`, out of any captured square, then toggle the side, castling and en passant keys. That is a handful of operations instead of rescanning 64 squares.

Each TT entry holds the hash (or its upper bits) to detect index collisions, the depth searched, the score, a **bound type** (exact, lower bound from a beta cutoff, or upper bound from a fail-low) and the best move: about 16 bytes in a simple engine. The index is `hash & (size - 1)` with a power-of-two size, so a 64 MB table holds 4,194,304 entries. A probe can return a score outright when the stored depth is enough and the bound proves a cutoff; either way the stored move is tried first. Two cautions. A 64-bit key still collides rarely, so check that a hash move is legal before playing it. And mate scores need care: a score like `Mate - ply` counts plies from the root, so store it as a distance from the node and convert it back on probe, or a mate found at ply 8 is reported at the wrong distance when reached at ply 12.
Iterative deepening and time management

You cannot know how deep you can get in 800 ms, because tree size varies by 100x between positions. **Iterative deepening** searches depth 1, then 2, 3 and so on until time runs out. It sounds wasteful, but the costs form a geometric series: if each ply costs about 3 times the last, all earlier iterations together add only about half of the final one. In return you always have a playable best move, the transposition table is full of good moves for ordering the next depth, and the previous best move is searched first at the root. **Time management** gives each move a budget; a common starting rule is the remaining time divided by about 30, plus most of the increment. Keep a soft limit (do not start another iteration once about a third of the budget is used, since the next one costs about twice everything so far) and a hard limit (poll the clock every 2,048 nodes and abort at once). An aborted iteration is discarded, unless its first root move had already finished, since partial results are unreliable.

lesson.caption: Each finished depth hands its best move and table entries to the next. Depth 7 starts too late and is cut off, so depth 6's move is played; a soft limit would not have started it.

lesson.text: Wall-clock limits make bugs unrepeatable, because the same position searches to a different depth on every run. Test and debug with a fixed node limit (`go nodes 500000`), which is deterministic on one thread, and keep time limits for play. Lazy multithreaded search is nondeterministic by design, so compare results with one thread.
Evaluation

At a quiet leaf the engine needs one number. The classic **hand-written evaluation** starts with material in centipawns (pawn 100, knight 320, bishop 330, rook 500, queen 900). It adds **piece-square tables**, a 64-entry bonus per piece type (a knight is worth more on e4 than on a1), and then small terms for pawn structure, mobility, king safety and the bishop pair. The king shows why one table is not enough: it wants shelter in the middlegame and the centre in the endgame. A **tapered evaluation** computes a middlegame and an endgame score plus a game phase from the remaining material (knight and bishop 1, rook 2, queen 4, so 24 at the start), then blends them. The result is returned from the side to move's view, which negamax requires. Top engines now use **NNUE** (efficiently updatable neural network), which Stockfish adopted in version 12 in 2020. Its first layer is updated incrementally as pieces move instead of recomputed, so a network evaluation costs a few vector operations per move. A tuned hand-written evaluation is enough to beat nearly every casual player; NNUE is the upgrade for when you chase strength.
Engine and GUI: the UCI split

Put the engine behind a text protocol. **UCI** (Universal Chess Interface) is the de facto standard: the GUI sends lines such as `position startpos moves e2e4 e7e5` and `go wtime 60000 btime 60000 winc 1000 binc 1000`, the engine streams `info` lines and ends with `bestmove`, and `stop` interrupts. Search runs on its own thread so the main loop can still read `stop`; in Unity that is a background thread or task, and the main thread only polls for the result. The split buys three things: you can test the engine headless from a script, you can plug in Stockfish to benchmark yours, and the UI can never reach into search state. Even if you never speak UCI over a pipe, keep the same shape in-process: a position plus limits in, a best move out. WebGL has no regular threads, so slice the search across frames with a node budget per frame, or run it on a server.

GUI    -> uci
Engine -> id name MyEngine 0.1
Engine -> uciok
GUI    -> position startpos moves e2e4 e7e5
GUI    -> go wtime 60000 btime 60000 winc 1000 binc 1000
Engine -> info depth 12 score cp 31 nodes 1830211 nps 2400000 pv g1f3 b8c6
Engine -> bestmove g1f3
Difficulty levels

A weak engine and a broken engine are different things. A bot that plays random legal moves hangs its queen and misses mate in one, and players read that as a bug. Three dials make a convincing weaker player. **Limit the search** by depth or, better, by nodes, since a node limit gives the same strength on any device and is deterministic. **Add evaluation noise** at the root: score every root move, then pick randomly among the moves within a margin of the best (say 20 to 150 centipawns, scaled by level). **Add guard rails**: keep quiescence at every level, always take a mate in one, and refuse any move that loses more than a set amount even when noise favours it. Stockfish exposes similar settings as `Skill Level` and `UCI_Elo`. Calibrate levels by playing them against a fixed reference and measuring the win rates, not by trusting the numbers on the slider.
Online play

In online chess the client is a display and an input device. The server holds the authoritative position, validates every move with the same rules core the client uses (shared as a library) and rejects illegal ones. The message is tiny: game id, from, to, promotion piece and the expected ply number, which also makes retries idempotent. **Clocks are server-authoritative**: the server records when the turn began and when the move arrived, subtracts the difference, adds the increment, and arms a timer that ends the game when time runs out. The client runs a local countdown for display only and corrects it from the remaining times in each server message. Some servers credit a bounded amount of measured latency so that a slow connection is not punished. Draw rules run on the server from the hash history, and the move list from the start FEN lets you replay any game for review, reconnection and disputes.
Decisions and why they work

items: **Keep the core pure.** No UnityEngine types and no scene-bound statics. It then runs in EditMode tests, on a server and on a worker thread; logic buried in MonoBehaviours can do none of that.

**Bitboards over an array.** Attacks, pawn pushes and occupancy become shifts and ANDs. The cost is harder debugging (print boards, not hex) and a magic-number setup. An array stays acceptable for a UI-only or one-ply bot.
**Pseudo-legal moves plus a check test.** One simple test covers pins, discovered checks and en passant. A fully legal generator is a little faster but much easier to get wrong.

**Perft before search.** A rare movegen bug (castling, promotion, en passant) is invisible in casual play and silently corrupts every search result built on it. Published counts make it cheap to catch.
**Ordering and quiescence before evaluation terms.** Depth is the biggest multiplier, and ordering decides how deep you get in the same time. A bonus for rooks on open files can wait.

**A TT with a replacement policy.** At 2 million nodes per second a 64 MB table fills in seconds. Always-replace throws away deep work and never-replace fills with stale data, so keep deep entries and age out old ones.

**Iterative deepening with a hard clock check.** It costs about half again in nodes at a factor of 3 per ply, but a move is always ready, which a fixed-depth search cannot promise when the position suddenly gets sharp.
**Difficulty from limits and noise, not random moves.** The weak bot still sees one-move tactics, so it loses like a human beginner and not like a broken program.
**Server owns validation and time.** Any rule a client enforces is a rule a modified client can skip. The server's full check costs microseconds per move.

lesson.text: Delegate the boilerplate: attack-table initialisation, the UCI parser, piece-square tables, FEN parsing and the perft harness. Verify everything with oracles you control. Pin the published perft counts (start position and Kiwipete) in a test the agent may not edit, and if a count fails, make it work from `perft divide` output instead of changing the expected number. Require every search or evaluation change to come with a self-play result of several hundred games against the previous build, because speed-ups that lose strength look fine in unit tests. Check by hand that the search loop allocates nothing (agents like `List<Move>` per node), that mate scores are adjusted by ply in the TT, and that repetition uses the halfmove clock. Evaluation weights and difficulty feel are your call.

patterns.signal: The engine plays a capture that wins a pawn and loses a piece on the very next ply
patterns.why: A static evaluation after a capture ignores the recapture. Searching captures until the position is quiet removes the horizon effect at a modest node cost.

patterns.signal: Search reaches the same depth as before but needs far more nodes than expected
patterns.why: Alpha-beta cost depends on trying the best move early. Hash move, MVV-LVA captures, killers and history can shrink the tree by a large factor with no strength loss.

patterns.signal: A movegen change breaks rare moves such as castling, en passant or promotion
patterns.why: Perft is a deterministic oracle. Compare several positions with known counts, then use divide to find the first wrong root move and recurse into it.

patterns.signal: The same positions are searched again after transpositions and on every deeper iteration
patterns.why: Incremental XOR hashing costs a few operations per move. Stored scores skip re-search, and stored best moves improve ordering at the next depth.

patterns.signal: The bot must answer within a clock, but search time varies a lot between positions
patterns.use: Iterative deepening with soft and hard limits
patterns.why: Every finished depth is a playable move, so you can stop at any time. Poll the clock every few thousand nodes and do not start an iteration you cannot finish.

patterns.signal: The easy bot feels random: it hangs pieces and misses mate in one
patterns.use: Weaken with a depth cap and bounded noise
patterns.why: Cap depth or nodes, then pick among moves within a small margin of the best. Keep quiescence and one-move tactics on, so mistakes look human, not broken.

patterns.signal: A client reports its own clock or claims a move is legal
patterns.use: Server validates moves and owns the clocks
patterns.why: The client is untrusted. Run the same rules core on the server, reject illegal moves, and compute elapsed time from server receipt timestamps.

patterns.signal: A draw by repetition fires late, or the UI and engine disagree about draws
patterns.use: Keep a hash history and a halfmove clock
patterns.why: Compare Zobrist keys only back to the last pawn move or capture. Inside search, treat one repeat as a draw; the game rules need three.

keyPoints: Keep the rules core pure and testable: FEN state, hash history and the halfmove clock cover castling, en passant and both draw rules.
Bitboards turn attacks and pawn pushes into shifts and table lookups, and perft against published counts proves the move generator.
Alpha-beta returns the minimax value but visits about b^(d/2) leaves with good ordering: hash move, MVV-LVA, killers, history.
Quiescence search removes the horizon effect, and a Zobrist-keyed transposition table avoids re-searching transposed positions.
Iterative deepening gives a playable move at any time and feeds ordering; the clock is polled every few thousand nodes.
Difficulty comes from node limits, root noise and guard rails, and online the server validates every move and owns the clocks.

quiz.q: Perft(5) from a test position returns 4,865,612 but the reference says 4,865,609. What is the most efficient next step?
options: Run perft(7) from the same position and see whether the gap widens further
Play a self-play match and check whether the engine blunders in similar spots
Run perft divide, compare per-move counts, and recurse into the odd one
Increase the transposition table size to rule out hash collisions in the count
quiz.explain: Divide localises the error: the one root move whose subtree count differs holds the bug, and repeating the diff one ply deeper narrows it to a single position. A deeper perft only makes the gap bigger, self-play can miss rare moves for thousands of games, and plain perft does not use a transposition table.

quiz.q: After you improve move ordering, the engine reaches depth 8 in the time it needed for depth 6, and the score at each fixed depth is unchanged. Why?
options: Alpha-beta gives the same value in any order; good ordering just cuts earlier
Better ordering raises the evaluation accuracy, so the search needs fewer plies
Ordering changes which moves are pruned unsoundly, trading accuracy for speed
Ordering lets the engine skip quiescence at the horizon, which saves nodes
quiz.explain: Alpha-beta returns the exact minimax value whatever the move order; order only decides how many branches are cut. Evaluation is untouched, alpha-beta pruning is sound (unlike heuristic forward pruning), and quiescence is not skipped.

quiz.q: At depth 4 your engine plays Qxd5, winning a pawn that a pawn defends, and loses the queen next move. What is missing, and what is the fix?
options: A larger evaluation weight for the queen so it avoids trades
A transposition table that remembers the earlier recapture
Iterative deepening so the capture is searched at more depths
A quiescence search that resolves captures until the position is quiet
quiz.explain: The leaf is evaluated in the middle of an exchange, so the recapture lies past the horizon. Quiescence extends only captures until the position is quiet. A heavier queen value does not reveal the recapture, a TT stores what was searched, and iterative deepening still ends every iteration at a noisy leaf.

quiz.q: Why is XOR the operation used to build and update Zobrist hashes?
options: XOR of random keys can never collide, so table keys are always unique
It is its own inverse, so a move only XORs the features that changed
It keeps the hash sorted by square so that nearby positions share table slots
It makes hashes symmetric, so a position and its mirror get the same key
quiz.explain: XORing a key twice cancels it, so removing a piece and adding it elsewhere is the same cheap operation and costs a few XORs instead of a 64-square rescan. Collisions are rare but possible (so entries store a check), and hashing does not sort or mirror positions.

quiz.q: A client sends its remaining time with every move, and a modified client always reports 30 s. What is the right design?
options: Sign each message with a key stored in the client binary so reports cannot be edited
Average the client report with the last server value to limit how far it can drift
Compare the client clock with NTP at login, then trust its reports for the game
Ignore client times; the server measures each turn from its own timestamps
quiz.explain: Only the server can be trusted with time. It stamps when a turn started and when the move arrived, so a client can only lose by lying. A key in the binary can be extracted, averaging still lets the client steer the result, and a login-time check says nothing about later reports.

quiz.q: Your easiest bot picks uniformly random legal moves. Testers say it feels broken: it hangs its queen and ignores mate in one. Which move from the patterns fits?
options: Add a transposition table so it stops repeating mistakes
Give it a longer clock so that it plays more like a human
Weaken with a depth cap and bounded noise, keep quiescence
Add more random moves so the blunders look natural
quiz.explain: A real search at a capped depth, with the choice made among near-best moves, loses by small positional errors like a beginner while still seeing one-move tactics. A TT does not change strength much, more time makes it stronger, and extra randomness is what makes it look broken.

topics.title: Case study: 2D platformer
topics.summary: How a tight 2D platformer is built: a fixed-step kinematic controller, per-axis tile collision, jump physics derived from designer values, forgiveness windows and a smoothed camera.

lesson.text: A player sprints toward a ledge, steps off it, and presses jump 90 ms later. On screen the character is already falling. The game jumps anyway, and the player never notices that it cheated. A tight 2D platformer is built from dozens of small decisions like this one, each tuned in milliseconds and pixels. This case study takes the genre apart: the loop that keeps it deterministic, the collision code that keeps a character on a tile grid, the numbers behind a jump, the forgiveness that makes it fair, and the camera that follows. The examples use 16 px tiles and a 60 Hz simulation, and the code is Unity-flavoured C#, but nothing here depends on an engine.
Components

items: **Input** samples the device every frame and turns it into intent: move axis, jump pressed, jump held, dash pressed.
**Simulation** runs at a fixed 60 Hz: the player state machine, velocity, gravity and the forgiveness timers.
**Collision** moves a box through the tilemap one axis at a time and reports contacts: floor, wall, ceiling.
**World** holds the room's tilemap, its entities (enemies, moving platforms, hazards) and the active checkpoint.
**Camera** reads the player after each tick and follows with a dead zone and smoothing.
**Presentation** draws the previous and current tick blended by alpha, and plays animation and effects.

lesson.text: Data flows one way: input, then simulation (which calls collision), then camera, then render. Rendering never writes back into the simulation. That one rule is what makes replays, automated tests and exact tuning possible.
Fixed timestep and render interpolation

Jump height must not depend on frame rate. With a variable `dt`, the integrator `y += v * dt` accumulates different error at 30, 60 and 144 fps, and a jump tuned to clear a 4-tile gap at 60 fps can fall short at 30. The fix is the fixed timestep from the game loop section: simulate in constant 1/60 s ticks (16.7 ms) and let the renderer run at any rate. An accumulator collects real time and the loop spends it in whole ticks. Clamp the accumulator to about 0.1 s so one long hitch cannot trigger a spiral of catch-up ticks.

The renderer then draws the state between the last two ticks. This costs up to one tick (16.7 ms) of display latency, and it removes the stutter you get when 60 Hz motion is shown on a 144 Hz display, where some frames would otherwise repeat the same position. Inside the tick, integrate with semi-implicit Euler: update velocity first, then move by the new velocity.
Why a kinematic controller, not a rigidbody

A dynamic rigidbody moves because forces and impulses act on it. It has mass, friction, bounce and rotation, and a solver decides where it ends up. A platformer character is the opposite case. The designer wants to say 'run speed 90 px/s, reached in 6 ticks, apex 56 px', and get exactly that every time. Mario-style feel needs things a physics engine avoids: instant mid-air direction changes, different gravity going up and down, a wall jump that sets both velocities at once, and no sliding or being shoved by a crate. With a dynamic body you fight the solver for each of these, and the result depends on the physics step (Unity's default is 0.02 s) and the solver's iteration count.

In a **kinematic controller** your code owns velocity and position, and collision only stops the box at solid tiles. The price is writing that collision yourself: roughly 200 to 400 lines for tile AABB tests, one-way platforms and moving platforms. That is a small price for code that is deterministic, cheap and easy to unit test. In Unity you can still keep a kinematic `Rigidbody2D` for triggers, or skip the physics engine and test directly against the tile array.
Tilemap collision with AABB

The tile grid is already a spatial partition. The world is a 2D array of tile ids, 16 x 16 px each. A box with edges `left, right, top, bottom` can only touch columns `floor(left / 16)` to `floor((right - 1) / 16)` and the matching rows. A 14 x 24 px character spans at most 2 columns and 3 rows, so a collision query reads at most 6 array cells. There is no tree and no hash: the lookup is one multiply and one index per cell.

lesson.text: Move on X first and fix it, then move on Y and fix it. Each pass is one-dimensional: if the box overlaps a solid tile, snap its edge to the tile's edge and zero the velocity on that axis. There are no contact normals and no penetration-depth maths. The passes also answer the questions gameplay asks. A hit while moving down means the character is grounded. A hit while moving up is a head bump. A hit on X is a wall, which is what wall-slide needs. Resolving both axes at once cannot tell which face of a corner was struck, and the usual result is a character that sticks to walls.

**Tunneling** happens when one tick moves the box farther than the geometry is thick, so the final position is already past the wall and no overlap is found. At 60 Hz a 240 px/s fall is 4 px per tick, and a 16 px tile cannot be skipped. A 480 px/s dash is 8 px per tick, still safe. A knockback at 2400 px/s is 40 px per tick and can skip a whole tile. The cheap fix is the loop above: step one pixel (or at most half a tile) at a time and test after every step. A swept test against tiles expanded by the box size gives the same answer in fewer queries, at the cost of more code. Unity's `BoxCast` sweeps for you at the price of a physics query.

items: **One-way platforms.** Solid only when the box is moving down (or still) and its bottom edge was at or above the platform's top on the previous tick. Jumping up through it, or pressing down to drop, skips the test.

**Slopes.** Treat a slope tile as a height function. While grounded, sample the surface under the box's centre and place the feet on it. Going downhill, snap down by a few pixels so the character does not hop off every step. Integer height tables for 45 degree slopes are the robust option; arbitrary angles multiply the edge cases.
**Moving platforms.** Move the platform first, then move each rider by the same delta through the normal `MoveX` and `MoveY`, so a rider is stopped by walls instead of being carried into them.

lesson.text: Deriving the jump from designer values

Designers think in heights and times, not in gravity. 'The jump peaks at 3.5 tiles after 0.35 s.' Derive the engine values from that. Under constant gravity the rising speed falls linearly from `v0` to 0 at the apex, so `v0 = g * t`. The distance covered is the average speed times the time, `h = (v0 / 2) * t`. Solve the pair: **g = 2h / t²** and **v0 = 2h / t**. With h = 56 px and t = 0.35 s, g is about 914 px/s² and v0 is 320 px/s. Change the designer's numbers and the physics follows; nobody hunts for a magic `-9.81`.

The 60 Hz integrator lands a few pixels under the analytic apex (about 53 px here), because each tick uses the new velocity for a whole step. Treat the equations as the starting point and tune the final value by playing. What matters is that the tuning knobs are the height and time the level designer already reasons about.
Variable height, fall speed and apex hang

A tap should hop and a hold should leap. When the button is released while the character is still rising, cut the upward velocity (multiply by 0.5). Height scales with v², so releasing on the first tick leaves `(v0 / 2)² / 2g = h / 4`: a 14 px hop against a 56 px jump. The alternatives are extra gravity while the button is up, which is smoother but makes the peak less predictable, and a minimum hold time, which adds input latency.

Two more tweaks shape the arc. A **fall gravity multiplier** of 1.5 to 2 makes the way down faster than the way up: at 1.6x the fall from the apex takes 0.28 s against 0.35 s rising, which reads as snappy instead of floaty. **Apex hang** halves gravity while the button is held and `|vy|` is below about 40 px/s, which adds roughly 70 ms of airtime at the top (with the 1.6x fall gravity) for precise landings. Cap the fall speed (for example 360 px/s) so the character stays readable and the tunneling bound above holds.

float g  = 2f * h / (t * t);              // h = 56 px, t = 0.35 s -> 914
float v0 = 2f * h / t;                    // 320 px/s

if (intent.jumpReleased && vel.y > 0) vel.y *= 0.5f;   // variable height

float scale = vel.y < 0 ? 1.6f : 1f;                   // heavier fall
if (intent.jumpHeld && Mathf.Abs(vel.y) < 40f) scale *= 0.5f;  // apex hang
vel.y = Mathf.Max(vel.y - g * scale * dt, -maxFall);   // maxFall = 360

lesson.text: Forgiveness: coyote time, buffering, corner correction

Humans press jump a few frames early or late, and the game should treat both as correct. **Coyote time**: after the character walks off a ledge, jump stays legal for about 0.1 s (6 ticks). **Jump buffering**: a press up to about 0.1 s before landing is remembered and fires at touchdown. Both are countdown timers, and a jump fires when both are positive. Typical windows sit between 0.05 and 0.15 s: shorter is not felt, longer starts to look like jumping in mid-air.

**Corner correction** fixes the most irritating failure: jumping straight at a platform and clipping its corner by a pixel. If the head hits a ceiling tile but only the outer 3 or 4 px of the box overlap it, nudge the character sideways by that amount and continue the move instead of stopping. Applied to the feet, the same trick lets a jump land on a ledge's lip. None of these three change what the game looks like. They change which inputs count, and they cost a few lines each.
The player state machine

items: **Idle and run.** Horizontal speed accelerates toward the stick direction (for example 90 px/s reached in 6 ticks) and slows faster on the ground than in the air. Many teams treat idle and run as one state with an animation switch.
**Jump and fall.** Jump is rising with the release cut; fall is descending with the heavier gravity. Both use reduced air acceleration and read the coyote and buffer timers.
**Wall-slide.** Entered when airborne, falling and pushing into a wall. Fall speed is clamped (about 40 px/s) and a wall jump sets velocity on both axes at once.
**Dash.** A fixed velocity for 0.15 s (for example 320 px/s, so 48 px or 3 tiles), gravity off, input ignored, then back to fall. One charge, restored on the ground.

lesson.text: Each state is a small class or function with `Enter`, `Update` and `Exit`. Transitions are checked after the tick's movement from facts collision reported (`onGround`, `wallDir`), never from animation frames. One state at a time means a combination such as dashing while wall-sliding cannot exist by accident.
The camera
The camera is a second small simulation, and each rule answers a specific complaint from playtesters.

items: **Dead zone.** A window around the camera centre (here 80 px wide). Focus movement inside it is ignored, so small steps do not shake the screen.
**Look-ahead.** The focus is the player plus about 30 px in the facing direction, so the screen shows more of where the player is heading.
**Vertical snap.** Follow vertically only when grounded, and snap to the current platform's height. Following every jump makes the screen heave at each hop.
**Smoothing.** Move toward the target with exponential decay, `1 - exp(-k * dt)`, with k about 6 to 8. It does not depend on frame rate and cannot overshoot.

lesson.text: Update the camera after the tick, using the same interpolated position the sprite uses, or the camera and sprite jitter against each other. Pixel-art games also round the final camera position to whole pixels of the render target.
Levels, enemies and input

A level is a set of rooms. A room is a tilemap (for example 40 x 22 tiles, which is 640 x 352 px at 16 px per tile and 880 bytes at one byte per tile) plus a list of entities with positions and properties. Tile ids index a tileset: empty, solid, one-way, slope, spike. A **checkpoint** stores a room id and a spawn point. Death reloads the room from authored data instead of patching live state, and respawn should take well under a second, because players will die many times.

Enemies reuse the player's collision code and run small state machines. A patroller walks at constant speed, turns when the tile ahead of its front foot is empty or the tile in front is solid, pauses in **Idle** for about 0.5 s, then walks again. A chaser adds a **Notice** state when the player enters a radius. Reuse means one collision system to debug, and enemies obey one-way and moving platforms for free. Damage tests are overlaps against hitboxes a few pixels smaller than the sprite, which feels fair.

Input goes through a rebinding layer and produces one `Intent` per tick: move axis, jump pressed, held and released, dash pressed. Analog sticks get a dead zone of about 0.2. Presses are latched in the frame loop and cleared when a tick consumes them, so a tap that starts and ends between two ticks is not lost.
Decisions and why they work

items: **Fixed 60 Hz tick with interpolation.** The same jump on every device, and replays and tests are exact. Variable `dt` makes jump heights and gap clearances depend on hardware. The cost is up to one tick of display latency.
**Kinematic controller with your own collision.** Direct control of every velocity. A dynamic rigidbody fights you over mass, friction, bounce and solver steps.

**Per-axis, pixel-stepped tile collision.** Contacts are unambiguous, nothing tunnels at platformer speeds, and it is easy to debug. Swept collision against arbitrary shapes handles any geometry but costs far more code and edge cases.
**Jump derived from height and time.** Designers edit numbers they can see on the level grid. Hand-tuned gravity and impulse values break whenever a gap in the level changes.
**Forgiveness windows.** Coyote time, buffering and corner nudges cost a few lines each and turn near misses into hits. Strict windows read as an unfair game.
**A state machine instead of flags.** Exactly one state at a time. A pile of booleans such as `isJumping` and `isDashing` multiplies impossible combinations.
**Camera as its own smoothed system.** Parenting the camera to the player copies every small step and every hop onto the screen.
**Rooms rebuilt from data on death.** Resets are deterministic. Patching entity state back by hand leaks bugs between attempts.

lesson.text: Do not drive gameplay from `Time.deltaTime`, and do not read button events inside `FixedUpdate`. Both are works-on-my-machine bugs: jump heights differ between a 60 Hz and a 144 Hz monitor, and presses vanish or repeat when a frame runs zero or two ticks. Latch input in `Update`, consume it in the tick, and test at several frame rates by forcing `Application.targetFrameRate`.

Agents are good at the mechanical parts: the tile array, the per-axis collision pass, state-machine boilerplate, unit tests and a room editor. Give them the numbers (tile size, tick rate, h and t) and ask for pure functions with no engine types, so tests run headless. Verify what they cannot feel. Ask for tests such as 'a held jump with h = 56 peaks within 4 px of it, a tap peaks near 14', 'a 40 px move never ends inside a wall' and 'a press 5 ticks before landing fires, 8 ticks does not'. Then play it yourself. Passing tests do not prove the feel is right, and an agent that 'simplifies' the fixed step into `deltaTime` has broken the game.
Reading the symptoms

patterns.signal: Testers say a jump pressed just before landing does nothing and the game eats inputs
patterns.why: Remember the press for about 0.1 s and fire the jump on the tick the character lands. Humans mistime by a few frames, and the buffer converts that error into the jump they meant.

patterns.signal: Players say they pressed jump at the ledge but fell; the press came a few frames after leaving it
patterns.why: Start a timer when the ground is lost without a jump, and allow a jump while it is positive. Clear it on takeoff so one press cannot jump twice.

patterns.signal: A jump straight up clips a ceiling or platform corner by 1 to 3 px and the player bonks
patterns.why: If only the outer few pixels of the box overlap the corner, shift the box sideways and continue the move. It removes a frustrating failure without changing level geometry.

patterns.signal: Jump height or gap clearance differs between a 60 Hz and a 144 Hz machine
patterns.use: Run gameplay on a fixed timestep
patterns.why: Variable dt changes integration error and tick-order effects. Simulate in constant 1/60 s ticks and keep rendering separate.

patterns.signal: Motion hitches on a 144 Hz display while the 60 Hz simulation is correct
patterns.use: Interpolate between previous and current tick
patterns.why: At 144 fps some frames get no new tick and repeat a position. Drawing Lerp(prev, curr, alpha) fills them in, for up to one tick of extra latency.

patterns.signal: A dash or knockback passes through a thin wall at high speed
patterns.use: Step the move in sub-steps of half a tile
patterns.why: Testing only the final position skips geometry thinner than the per-tick displacement. Stepping 1 px, or at most half a tile, and testing after each step cannot skip it.

patterns.signal: A designer asks for 'a jump 4 tiles high that peaks in 0.4 s'
patterns.use: Derive g and v0 from height and time
patterns.why: From h = v0 t / 2 and v0 = g t you get g = 2h / t² and v0 = 2h / t. Designers keep editing readable numbers and the physics follows.

patterns.signal: The screen shakes with every small step and heaves with every hop
patterns.use: Add a dead zone and grounded-only vertical follow
patterns.why: Ignore focus movement inside a window around the camera and follow vertically only when grounded. The camera then moves for real changes in position, not for noise.

keyPoints: Simulate at a fixed 60 Hz and render interpolated between the last two ticks, so jump height never depends on frame rate or display.
A kinematic controller owns velocity and position; collision only stops it. That gives exact, deterministic feel that a dynamic rigidbody fights.
Resolve tile collision one axis at a time and step in sub-steps of at most half a tile: contacts are unambiguous and fast moves cannot tunnel.
Derive jump physics from designer values: g = 2h / t² and v0 = 2h / t. Add a velocity cut on release, heavier fall gravity and a short apex hang.
Coyote time and jump buffering (about 0.1 s each) plus corner correction turn near misses into hits. Consume both timers when the jump fires.
The camera is a smoothed system: dead zone, look-ahead, grounded-only vertical snap and exponential decay with `1 - exp(-k * dt)`.

quiz.q: A designer asks for a jump that peaks 48 px high after 0.3 s. Which gravity and launch speed does that give?
options: g = 533 px/s², v0 = 160 px/s
g = 1067 px/s², v0 = 160 px/s
g = 1067 px/s², v0 = 320 px/s
g = 160 px/s², v0 = 533 px/s
quiz.explain: From h = (v0 / 2) t and v0 = g t you get g = 2h / t² = 96 / 0.09 = 1067 and v0 = 2h / t = 96 / 0.3 = 320. The first option forgets the factor of 2 in both formulas. The second mixes a correct g with that half-size v0, which would peak at only 12 px. The fourth swaps the two values.

quiz.q: Why does the controller move and resolve the X axis completely before it moves on Y?
options: Each pass is one-dimensional, so the face that was hit is unambiguous
It lets the box skip tiles that it would overlap at high speed
It removes the need for a grounded flag because gravity handles the floor
Tile maps cannot store collision data for diagonal movement at all
quiz.explain: A single-axis pass needs only a snap to the tile edge and a zero velocity, and the axis tells you what was hit: down is floor, up is ceiling, sideways is wall. It does not prevent tunneling (that needs sub-steps), it does not replace the grounded flag (a downward hit sets it), and tile maps can represent any move; the issue is ambiguity at corners, not storage.

quiz.q: The jump code multiplies upward velocity by 0.5 when the button is released. If the player releases on the first tick, how high is the hop compared with a full jump?
options: About half as high, because the speed is halved
About one eighth as high, because gravity also doubles
No hop at all, because the cut cancels the launch
About a quarter, because height goes with v squared
quiz.explain: Rise height is v² / 2g. Halving v leaves one quarter of the height, so a 56 px jump becomes about 14 px. Half height would hold only if height were linear in speed. Gravity is unchanged by the cut, so there is no eighth. The character still moves up at half speed, so it does hop.

quiz.q: A camera smooths with `cam = Lerp(cam, target, 0.1f)` each frame and trails by different amounts at 30 and 144 fps. What is the fix?
options: Multiply by Time.deltaTime and clamp the result between 0 and 1
Blend by `1 - Mathf.Exp(-k * dt)` using each frame's dt
Move the camera into FixedUpdate and keep the 0.1 constant
Cap the frame rate at 60 and keep the constant
quiz.explain: The exponential form removes the same fraction of the remaining distance per second at any frame rate, and it cannot overshoot. Multiplying by deltaTime is only a first-order approximation and misbehaves on long frames. A camera in FixedUpdate jitters against an interpolated sprite. Capping the frame rate hides the bug on one device and leaves it on others.

quiz.q: The simulation ticks at 60 Hz and the display runs at 144 Hz. Jump height is right but motion visibly hitches. What is the standard fix?
options: Raise the tick rate to 144 Hz so every frame gets its own tick
Multiply movement by Time.deltaTime inside the simulation
Draw Lerp(prev, curr, alpha) using the leftover accumulator time
Turn vsync off so frames are not repeated
quiz.explain: Interpolating between the last two ticks gives every frame a distinct position for about one tick of extra latency, at any refresh rate. Raising the tick rate costs more simulation, changes every timer that counts ticks (coyote, buffer), shifts the tuned feel and still fails at 240 Hz. Variable dt in the simulation is exactly what breaks jump height. Turning vsync off adds tearing and does not change repeated positions.

quiz.q: Testers on a patch build say jumps pressed just before landing are ignored. Coyote time already exists. What is the right move?
options: Raise the coyote window from 0.1 s to 0.3 s so presses count longer
Remember the press for about 0.1 s and fire the jump at landing
Increase jump height so players land later and have more time
Poll the jump button twice per frame to catch fast presses
quiz.explain: The failure is an early press, which is what jump buffering fixes: store the press and fire when grounded. Coyote time covers late presses after leaving a ledge, so widening it does nothing here and 0.3 s would feel like jumping from air. Higher jumps do not change the timing error, and polling more often cannot recover a press that happened before the character landed.

topics.title: Case study: Kart racer
topics.summary: How an arcade kart racer is built, from raycast suspension and spline-based race progress to AI, items, split-screen and online prediction, and why each choice keeps the game fun and fair.

lesson.text: Eight karts leave the grid on a 1.8 km track. Lap one is clean. On lap two a player cuts across a grass strip, falls off the edge, and respawns 300 m further along the track than where they left it. A second player finishes in 3rd on their screen and 5th on the server's. A third reports that the last-place kart "cheats" by catching up on every straight. None of these are rendering bugs. A kart racer is a small set of systems (suspension, track data, AI, items, camera, netcode) that each make a deliberate trade between realism and fun, and each fails in a specific way. This teardown walks through them in the order data flows.
Components

Every fixed tick (50 or 60 Hz) input becomes forces on a rigid body. The body's position is projected onto a track spline to get progress, progress sorts the karts into positions, and positions feed back into AI speed and item odds. Cameras and the network read the result; they never drive it.

items: **Vehicle physics.** One rigid body, four raycasts, forces for suspension, grip, drive and drift. Runs in `FixedUpdate`.
**Track data.** A closed spline centerline, per-point width and banking, ordered checkpoints, a kill plane below the track.
**Race state.** Progress per kart, lap count, finish order, wrong-way flag, respawn requests.
**AI drivers.** Produce the same input struct a human does: steer, throttle, drift, item. They get no special physics.
**Items.** Position-weighted rolls, plus projectiles that follow the spline.
**Camera and view.** One spring-arm camera per local player, split-screen viewports.
**Network layer.** Input upload, authoritative server state, prediction for the local kart, interpolation for the rest.

lesson.text: Arcade physics, not simulation

A simulation kart models tyre slip curves, weight transfer and a drivetrain. It is accurate and hard to drive: small steering errors at the limit cause spins. An arcade kart is a single rigid body with a low centre of mass and four **raycast wheels**. Each wheel casts a ray down from a mount point, and if it hits the ground the code applies a spring force, a lateral grip force and (on driven wheels) a drive force at the contact point. There are no wheel colliders to tune, the handling is a handful of numbers a designer can read, and the cost is four raycasts per kart per tick.

lesson.text: The **spring-damper** is the core. Let `compression = restLength - hitDistance`, clamped at 0. Then `F = k * compression - c * compressionSpeed`, applied along the ground normal. The first term holds the kart up; the second removes energy so it does not bounce. Sizing it is simple: for a 120 kg kart on four wheels, each wheel carries about 295 N. To sit at 0.08 m of compression, `k = 295 / 0.08`, about 3,700 N/m. Critical damping is `2 * sqrt(k * m)` with m = 30 kg per wheel, about 670 N·s/m; a damping ratio of 0.5 to 0.7 (c of roughly 330 to 470 N·s/m) settles in about one bounce. Too stiff and the kart skips over small bumps; too soft and it bottoms out on landings.

**Lateral grip** is what makes it feel like a kart rather than a hovercraft. At each wheel, take the velocity at that point, project it on the wheel's sideways axis, and apply an impulse that cancels a fraction `grip` of it. `grip = 1` is a rail, `grip = 0` is ice. Steering uses a **speed curve**: a maximum steer angle of about 30 degrees at standstill falling to about 8 degrees at top speed (28 m/s, roughly 100 km/h), so the kart is nimble when slow and stable when fast.

Keeping the kart upright is mostly tuning. Lower the **centre of mass** (`rb.centerOfMass`, about 0.3 m below the mesh centre) so lateral forces create little roll. Add an **anti-roll** force that pushes the more compressed side up. Add **downforce** that grows with speed so jumps and crests do not unload the tyres. While airborne, apply a **self-righting torque** that aligns the kart's up vector with the last ground normal, and if it is upside down for about 2 seconds, treat it as a respawn.
Drift and mini-turbo

Drift is a state, not a different physics model. Holding the drift button while steering switches the kart into a state where the rear grip drops (for example from 1.0 to 0.6), the steering is biased into the turn, and a **charge timer** starts. The tiers are time thresholds. Example values: 0.7 s gives a small boost, 1.5 s a medium one, 2.5 s a large one. On release the kart gets a **mini-turbo**: a speed multiplier (for example 1.3x) for 0.6, 1.0 or 1.5 s. The loop is risk and reward: a long drift costs steering precision and lap time on the corner, and pays back on the straight.
Track representation and race progress

The track is a closed **spline centerline**, sampled once at build time into points about every 2 m (about 900 points for 1.8 km) with an arc-length table, plus a width, a banking angle and a tangent at each point. Everything about the race hangs on one function: given a kart position, find the **nearest point on the centerline** and read its distance along the track, `s`. Then `progress = lap * L + s`, where `L` is the lap length. That single float orders the karts, drives the wrong-way check and feeds the AI.

lesson.text: A global nearest-point search over 900 points for 12 karts is about 11,000 distance checks per tick, which is cheap. The problem is correctness: where a road passes over or next to itself, the globally nearest point can be on the other road, and progress jumps by hundreds of metres. Search a **window** instead: start at the kart's last index and check about 30 samples either side (60 m each way), then wrap the index at the end of the lap.

Progress alone is not enough to count a lap, because it can be gamed. Place **ordered checkpoints** (gate planes across the road, here six) and require that each kart crosses them in sequence. A lap counts only when the finish gate is crossed with all gates seen in order, so cutting a corner through the infield skips a gate and does not score. **Wrong-way detection** compares velocity with the spline tangent: if `dot(velocity, tangent)` is negative for more than about 1 second, show the warning. **Respawn** on a fall (kill plane below the track) or a stuck timer places the kart at the **last checkpoint it passed**, facing the tangent, with a short invulnerability. Respawning at the nearest spline point looks better but lets a player fall off, land beside a later section and skip track.

**Position ranking** is a sort of 8 to 12 floats by progress every tick. Use a stable sort so ties do not flicker, lock the order when a kart finishes, and consider a small hysteresis on the HUD (a kart must lead by about 1 m before the number changes) so positions do not flash when two karts run side by side.
AI drivers

AI karts are not scripted paths. They run the same physics as the player and produce the same input struct. Each point on the spline stores a **racing line** as a lateral offset from the centerline (inside on corners, wide on entry). The AI uses **pure pursuit**: pick a target point on the line a **lookahead** distance ahead, `lookahead = 6 m + 0.4 * speed`, steer toward it, and control speed from the curvature ahead (`vMax = sqrt(aLat / curvature)` with a lateral limit around 12 m/s squared, below which the kart brakes before the corner). The lookahead grows with speed because a short one oscillates at high speed and a long one cuts corners.

Identical AI looks robotic, so each driver gets variation: a `skill` scale on top speed (for example 0.92 to 1.0), a constant line offset of up to 1.5 m, a slow noise term on that offset, a reaction delay on braking, and a small chance of a mistake (a wide turn) that is higher on harder corners. All of it is data on a per-driver asset, so designers tune difficulty without touching code.
Rubber banding and items

**Rubber banding** scales AI speed by the gap to the human player. Example: when an AI kart is 100 m behind, its top speed is scaled by up to 1.10; when 100 m ahead, by 0.95, with linear interpolation between and hard caps. It keeps races close for the whole pack, which is what makes a mid-race item hit matter. It is also **controversial**: players who build a lead feel punished, and visible cheating (an AI kart that passes a boosting player on a straight) breaks the sense that skill matters. The mitigations are to keep the caps small, scale smoothly instead of switching on, apply it to AI only, and never let it bend the rules of the physics a human sees.

lesson.text: **Items** are the second catch-up system, and it is honest because humans get it too. When a kart drives through an item box, roll a weighted random choice from a table indexed by its race position. The weights are data: the leader gets defensive or weak items, the last kart gets boosts and homing attacks. Roll on the server in multiplayer, and make the roll a pure function of `(position, rng)` so it can be tested. A **homing item** does not path-find. It follows the spline: its own `s` increases at about 1.4 times the leader's top speed, it steers toward the target when within a short range, and it falls back to the spline if the target is lost. Following the spline means it cannot get stuck on walls.
Camera and split-screen

The **spring-arm camera** targets a point behind and above the kart (for example 5 m back, 2.2 m up), moves toward it with the frame-rate independent smoothing from earlier lessons, and lags its rotation more than its position so turns feel heavy. It raycasts from the kart to the desired position and pulls in if a wall is hit. **FOV rises with speed**, from about 60 degrees at rest to about 80 on a boost, with speed lines at the edges; the wider view is the cheapest way to sell speed. Rotation should follow the kart's velocity direction during a drift, not its facing, or the player sees the scene swing sideways.

**Split-screen** is a CPU problem more than a pixel problem. Four viewports each cover a quarter of the screen, so total pixels shaded stays about the same. But the scene is culled and drawn four times, so draw calls, culling and shadow passes cost roughly four times as much. At 60 fps there is 16.6 ms per frame, so each view gets about 4 ms of CPU. The standard moves are a lower LOD bias per view, no or cheaper shadows on the secondary views, fewer particles and a shared static batch, because resolution is not the bottleneck.
Online play

Online karts at 60 Hz physics cannot wait for the server before turning. **Client prediction** runs the player's own kart locally the moment input is read and tags each input with a tick number. The server simulates authoritatively and sends snapshots at about 20 Hz. When a snapshot for tick 600 arrives and the client is at tick 605, the client sets its kart to the server state for tick 600, **replays the stored inputs 601 to 605**, and blends away any visible difference over a few frames. Other players' karts are not predicted. The client **interpolates** them between two buffered snapshots about 100 ms in the past (two snapshot intervals at 20 Hz), which is smooth and tolerates one lost packet. Extrapolating forward on a turn is a guess that visibly pops when wrong.

Collisions between karts are the hard part: the local kart's prediction does not include other karts' true positions (they are 100 ms in the past on your screen). The practical answer is **lenient collisions**. Kart-to-kart contact is a soft push resolved on the server with small impulses, the local view does not predict it, and item hits use generous radii and are decided server side. The result is that the player sees a hit that matches what they saw, rather than a physically exact one that was wrong on their screen.
Decisions and why they work

items: **Raycast wheels, not wheel colliders.** Four raycasts and two numbers per wheel (k, c) give predictable handling designers can reason about. Full tyre models are more realistic and much harder to make forgiving.

**Grip as a tunable fraction, not friction.** Cancelling a fraction of sideways speed lets you make drift, ice and boost pads by changing one number. A friction-coefficient model gives the same results only after hours of tuning.
**One progress float per kart.** Position order, wrong-way, AI targets and respawns all read the same value. Computing them separately lets them disagree.
**Windowed nearest-point search.** It costs about 60 checks per kart and cannot jump to a different road. Global search is simpler and fails exactly on overpasses.
**Respawn at the last checkpoint.** It is slightly less tidy than the nearest point, and it cannot skip track. Exploits found in playtest cost more than the tidiness.
**AI uses the player's input struct.** It exercises the same physics, so tracks that work for humans work for AI. A separate AI movement model needs its own debugging and breaks on new items.
**Small, smooth rubber band plus item odds.** Two soft catch-up systems keep races close without one big visible cheat. A hard speed-up for trailing karts reads as cheating.
**Predict the local kart, interpolate the rest.** The player gets zero-latency control and a world that never visibly rewinds. Waiting for the server feels like driving through mud.

lesson.text: Agents write the data-driven parts of a kart racer well: the spline sampler, the arc-length table, the item weight table, the lap and checkpoint state machine. Give them the invariants as tests. For example: a kart driven by recorded inputs finishes three laps with progress strictly non-decreasing; skipping any gate never increments the lap; respawn never reduces progress below the last gate; two runs from the same seed give the same finish order. Have the agent write an editor gizmo that draws the spline, windows, gates and AI target. Verify yourself the things only a human can judge: how the suspension and drift feel, whether the rubber band is visible, and netcode behaviour under 100 ms of latency and 3 percent packet loss. Do not accept a physics change without playing a lap.

The classic pitfalls: counting time or boost in frames instead of seconds, so the mini-turbo differs between 30 and 60 fps; using the global nearest spline point, which jumps on overpasses and near shortcuts; making rubber banding so strong that a human who drives a perfect lap still sees AI karts glued to their bumper; and letting the client decide item hits, which any modified client can abuse.

patterns.signal: Kart bounces for seconds after landing from a jump, or bottoms out on every big drop
patterns.use: Add damping along the ray, then tune k
patterns.why: F = k*compression - c*velocity. k carries the weight and c removes energy. A damping ratio of about 0.5 to 0.7 settles in one bounce; raising k alone only makes the oscillation faster.

patterns.signal: Kart slides like on ice at speed, or the steering is twitchy and spins out on the straight
patterns.use: Cancel sideways speed and use a steer curve
patterns.why: Grip is the fraction of lateral velocity removed per tick, so it is one number. Cut steering from about 30 degrees to about 8 as speed rises so high-speed input stays controllable.

patterns.signal: A kart's race progress jumps by hundreds of metres where the road crosses or runs beside itself
patterns.use: Search a window near the last index
patterns.why: A global nearest-point search can pick the other road. Checking about 30 samples either side of the last index is cheaper and cannot jump, as long as the index wraps at the seam.

patterns.signal: Players skip track by cutting through the infield or by falling off at a good spot
patterns.use: Require ordered gates, respawn at the last
patterns.why: A lap counts only if every gate was crossed in order, and respawn restores the last gate. Progress then cannot be gained by leaving the road, whatever the geometry allows.

patterns.signal: AI drivers all take the same line and brake at the same spots, so the field looks like a train
patterns.use: Add per-driver line offset and skill
patterns.why: A skill scale on top speed, a constant line offset and slow noise on it make each driver differ in data, with no new code. Identical AI also stack up behind one another and never overtake.

patterns.signal: Trailing players quit because the leader is never caught, and the leader holds items that stay strong
patterns.use: Weight item rolls by race position
patterns.why: A table of weights per position gives the last kart boosts and homing items and the leader weak ones. It keeps the pack close with a system every player can see and use, unlike hidden AI speed.

patterns.signal: Remote karts jitter at a 20 Hz snapshot rate, and fast turns snap when a packet is late
patterns.use: Interpolate remote karts 100 ms in the past
patterns.why: Blending between two buffered snapshots is smooth and survives one lost packet. Extrapolating guesses where the kart will be, and a turn makes the guess visibly wrong.

patterns.signal: Four-player split-screen drops below 60 fps while every single view alone runs fine
patterns.use: Cut per-view CPU cost, not resolution
patterns.why: Each view repeats culling, draw calls and shadow passes, so CPU cost is about 4x while total pixels stay the same. Lower LOD, shadows and particles on the extra views instead of lowering resolution.

keyPoints: Arcade handling uses one rigid body with four raycast wheels: spring-damper F = k * compression - c * velocity, and lateral grip as a fraction of sideways speed cancelled.
Stability comes from tuning: a low centre of mass, anti-roll, speed-based downforce, a steering angle that shrinks with speed and a self-righting torque.

Race progress is lap * L + s, where s is the distance along the spline of the nearest point, found in a window around the last index; ordered checkpoints stop shortcuts, and respawn uses the last gate.
AI drivers use pure pursuit on a stored racing line, with lookahead that grows with speed and per-driver skill, offset and mistake data; they use the same inputs as the player.
Catch-up should be small and visible: capped smooth rubber banding on AI plus item odds weighted by position, rather than a large hidden speed boost.
Online, the local kart is predicted and reconciled by replaying inputs, remote karts are interpolated about 100 ms in the past, and collisions and item hits are lenient and resolved on the server.

quiz.q: After landing from a jump, a kart's suspension keeps oscillating for several seconds before settling. The spring force is `k * compression`. What is the right fix?
options: Increase k so the springs push back harder after the landing
Add a damping term, c times compression speed, along the ray
Lower the rest length so the springs have less travel to use
Raise the fixed tick rate so the spring is evaluated sooner
quiz.explain: A pure spring has no way to lose energy, so it rings. The c * velocity term removes it, and a damping ratio of 0.5 to 0.7 settles in about one bounce. A larger k makes the ringing faster, a shorter travel makes bottoming out more likely, and a higher tick rate only samples the same oscillation more often.

quiz.q: On a track with an overpass, one kart's race progress suddenly jumps ahead by about 400 m while it drives on the lower road. What is the cause and fix?
options: The lap counter ran twice, so reset the lap when crossing the finish
Floating point error at large distances, so use doubles for progress
A global nearest-point search chose the upper road, so search a window
The checkpoint was missed, so add more gates along the track
quiz.explain: The upper road is physically close to the kart, so a global nearest-point search can pick it and return an s hundreds of metres away. Searching about 30 samples either side of the last index cannot jump. Float precision is not an issue at 1.8 km, and extra gates do not change which spline point is nearest.

quiz.q: Playtesters say AI karts zoom back to the pack and cheat. The rubber band scales AI speed by up to 40 percent. What is the best change?
options: Cap the scale near +10% and -5% and ramp it smoothly with the gap
Remove all catch-up so every AI kart has one fixed speed
Raise the cap to 60% so the gap closes faster and ends sooner
Apply the same scaling to the human so the rules are fair
quiz.explain: A small, smooth, capped scale keeps races close and is hard to notice. Removing it leaves pack spread that no item can fix, a bigger cap is more visible cheating, and scaling the human changes the physics the player is tuning their driving to.

quiz.q: Remote karts in an online race stutter even though snapshots arrive every 50 ms. The client draws each remote kart at the newest snapshot position. What is the fix?
options: Predict remote karts with their last input so they never wait
Raise the server tick rate to 120 Hz and send every tick
Extrapolate remote karts forward by the round-trip time
Interpolate between snapshots, rendering about 100 ms behind
quiz.explain: Drawing the newest snapshot moves the kart in 50 ms jumps. Interpolating between two buffered snapshots is smooth and survives a lost packet. We do not have the remote player's input in time to predict, and extrapolation guesses wrong whenever the kart turns.

quiz.q: A four-player split-screen mode drops to 40 fps. GPU time is 6 ms, CPU render thread time is 25 ms. Which change helps most?
options: Lower the resolution of each of the four viewports
Cut per-view CPU work: LOD, shadow casters, particles
Add MSAA so the smaller viewports look sharper
Enable a larger shadow cascade count for the leading view
quiz.explain: The frame is CPU bound: each view repeats culling and draw submission, so cost is about four times a single view. Lowering resolution reduces GPU pixels, which are not the limit. More MSAA or more cascades add work without cutting the CPU cost.

quiz.q: Last-place players in your kart racer say they never get a chance, because the item box gives them the same items as the leader. Which move from the patterns applies?
options: Add damping along the ray, then tune k
Search a window near the last index
Interpolate remote karts 100 ms in the past
Weight item rolls by race position
quiz.explain: A position-indexed weight table gives trailing karts stronger items and the leader weaker ones, a visible comeback mechanic. The other moves address suspension, progress projection and netcode, none of which change who gets which item.

topics.title: Case study: FPS shooter
topics.summary: How a first-person shooter fits movement, aim, weapons, hit detection, AI, netcode and level visibility into one 16 ms frame, and why each choice was made.

lesson.text: A player peeks a corner on an 80 ms connection, puts the crosshair on a head and clicks. On his screen the target flinches and a hit marker flashes. On the server the target stepped behind the wall 90 ms earlier, so the answer depends entirely on how the team built hit detection. Meanwhile a campaign level has 12 enemies, a 16.6 ms frame budget, and a designer who wants every firefight to feel fair. A first-person shooter is a stack of small systems that all have to agree on one thing: what the player saw, when he saw it, and what he was allowed to do about it.
Components

Think of one server tick (15.6 ms at 64 Hz) as a pipeline. Input commands come in, movement runs, weapons fire, hit detection resolves, damage applies, and snapshots go out. The client runs a copy of the first stages ahead of time so the player never waits for the network.

items: **Input and camera.** Raw mouse deltas and key state become a command per tick: move axes, view angles, buttons, a timestamp.
**Character controller.** A kinematic capsule moved by shared code, identical on client and server so prediction works.
**Weapons.** Data assets (rate, damage, spread, recoil) read by one fire routine; hitscan or projectile.
**Hit detection.** Rays or sweeps against per-bone hitboxes, after the server rewinds them to the shooter's view time.
**Feedback.** Hit markers, sounds, decals and tracers, mostly cosmetic and driven from events, not polled.
**AI.** Perception, navigation, a decision layer and a token system. Runs on the server only; clients see the result as replicated entities.
**Level and audio.** Visibility data, sightlines and occlusion that serve rendering, AI and sound at once.

lesson.text: Player movement

Shooter movement is not physics simulation. It is a hand-tuned velocity model on a kinematic capsule. The classic Quake family model has two steps per tick. First apply **friction**: reduce speed by `max(speed, stopSpeed) * friction * dt`. Then **accelerate** toward the wish direction (the direction the keys ask for). Quake 3 uses about 320 units/s run speed, friction 6, ground acceleration 10 and air acceleration 1, with the stop speed at 100 units/s so low speeds decay quickly instead of creeping.

The clamp is on the speed **along the wish direction**, not on total speed. That one choice creates **air control**. In the air there is no friction, and turning the mouse while holding a strafe key rotates the wish direction, so each tick there is fresh room to add speed. Players gain speed beyond the run limit (strafe jumping, bunny hopping). Source engine games clamp the wish speed to 30 units/s in the air but allow a large air acceleration, which keeps the effect while limiting its size. Modern console shooters usually cap horizontal speed and give limited, slower air steering. Keeping the quirk gives a skill ceiling and a movement subculture. Removing it makes the game easier to learn and the maps easier to balance.

Around that sits the **character controller**. It is a capsule (about 0.4 m radius, 1.8 m tall for a standing player) swept through the world, not a rigid body. Each tick the controller sweeps the capsule along the velocity, and on contact projects the remaining motion onto the hit plane and sweeps again, up to about four times. Unity's `CharacterController` does this for you, with defaults of a 45 degree slope limit and a 0.3 m step offset. Three details decide how the movement feels:

items: **Step-up.** Raise the capsule by the step height, sweep forward, then sweep down to the floor. If the landing surface is walkable and within the step limit, keep the result. Stairs then feel like flat ground.
**Crouch.** Shrink the capsule (about 1.8 m to 1.0 m) and lower the eye. To stand, first test the tall capsule for overlap, or the player pops into the ceiling.
**Ground check.** Treat a slope as ground only below the slope limit. Above it the player slides, which stops wall climbing without invisible walls.

lesson.text: Camera, input and the view model

Aim is the one place where the game must not be clever. Read **raw mouse deltas** (the Input System's `Mouse.delta` or the OS raw-input API), never the cursor position, so OS pointer acceleration and screen edges cannot change the result. Convert counts to angle linearly: `yaw += counts * sensitivity * 0.022` degrees, the constant used by Quake and Source. At 800 DPI and sensitivity 1.0 that is 360 degrees per about 20 inches, which is why players can carry a sensitivity value between games. No smoothing and no acceleration: both add latency or make the same hand motion produce different angles. Apply look every rendered frame (at 240 fps the view updates every 4.2 ms instead of every 15.6 ms tick) and put the angles into the next command. **Field of view** is a gameplay setting. Players expect a horizontal FOV of around 90 degrees, adjustable up to 100 to 120. Unity's `Camera.fieldOfView` is vertical, so convert: `vfov = 2 * atan(tan(hfov / 2) / aspect)`. A 90 degree horizontal FOV at 16:9 is about 58.7 degrees vertical. Define the slider at 16:9 and keep that vertical FOV on wider screens (Hor+), so an ultrawide shows more at the sides instead of cropping the top and bottom.

The weapon in the player's hands is a **view model**. If it lives in the world camera, it clips into walls when you stand close, and raising the world FOV to 110 stretches it. The fix is a second camera that renders only the view-model layer with its own FOV (about 60 to 70 degrees), its own near and far planes, and a cleared depth buffer, so the gun is always drawn on top. In URP this is an overlay camera in the base camera's stack. The costs are one more camera and some draw calls, and the gun will not receive world shadows correctly without extra work. The alternatives, pushing the gun back when a wall is near or squashing its depth in a vertex shader, each cost animation work or shader complexity.
Weapons as data

A weapon is a row of numbers read by one fire routine. Designers tune a `ScriptableObject`; engineers do not touch code to rebalance. The important fields are fire interval, damage, a **range falloff** curve, **spread** (a cone that grows with continuous fire and movement and recovers over time), a **recoil pattern**, and whether the weapon is hitscan or projectile. Store the rate as RPM and convert once: 600 RPM is one shot per 0.1 s.

Fire timing deserves care on a tick-based server. At 64 Hz a tick is 15.625 ms, so 600 RPM is 6.4 ticks per shot. If the code rounds the cooldown to whole ticks it fires at 6 ticks (640 RPM) or 7 ticks (549 RPM), and the weapon is quietly rebalanced. Keep a fractional `nextFireTime` and add the interval to it on each shot instead of resetting it to now. The same value on the client and server also keeps predicted shots from being rejected. **Recoil** comes in two flavours. A fixed **pattern** (shot 1 kicks up, shot 7 drifts right, and so on) can be learned, so skill comes from compensating a known curve. Random **spread** cannot be learned, so skill comes from burst control and positioning. Most competitive shooters mix them: a deterministic pattern for the view kick, and a small random cone on top. The random cone must be seeded from the shot index and the command tick so the client and server agree on where the bullet went.

**Hitscan or projectile** is decided by travel time. A rifle bullet at 900 m/s covers about 14 m per 15.6 ms tick, so over typical combat ranges simulating flight adds cost and bugs for no gameplay gain: one raycast resolves the shot instantly. A rocket at 20 to 40 m/s is a different weapon: players dodge it, lead targets and bounce it off walls. Projectiles must be spawned by the server, predicted on the client, and swept (a capsule or ray cast per tick from last to new position) so a fast projectile does not tunnel through thin walls.

Hits are tested against **hitboxes, not the render mesh**. A character mesh has 20,000 to 60,000 triangles skinned on the GPU, so its true vertex positions are usually not even available on the CPU. Hitboxes are 10 to 20 simple capsules and spheres attached to skeleton bones (head, chest, pelvis, upper and lower arms and legs). A ray against a capsule is a few multiplications, and the shape is stable and tuned: head slightly generous, hands often not tested at all. Each hitbox carries its own damage multiplier, so a head shot is `base * 2.0 * falloff` and a leg shot `base * 0.75 * falloff`. One ray tests world geometry and hitboxes together, so the nearest surface wins, and penetrable materials may pass the bullet through at reduced damage.
